So far it seems to be a good game. Has the basic elements of crafting that make a sandbox-esque game enjoyable. I like that people are able to work together to build things, and there are cool little things like the immersive, roleplay style chat system where when you're incapacitated/turned into a ghost from dying, you get garbled text output.
Things I don't like, that I expect are relatively easy to change or improve--
The hit boxes for combat are awful. If I end up fighting an enemy that moves even a little bit, suddenly i'm no longer focused and my attacks don't connect at all, which is not something I think has any place in an open-world 3d fighting setup. Swinging a weapon should check the hit boxes in general, not whether you're focused on them. I get killed by weak enemies due to this.
The character animations could use some improvement, as of now they remind me of n64 duke nukem style animations.
Entering crafting menus and any kind of storage units are, like the aforementioned hit boxes, really 'stiff', they aren't very easy to access. The right click and drag is neat, as it allows you to cancel your menu with mouseup, but I think in order for it to be smooth and enjoyable its better to adjust the camera so that in third person you treat things like it. At the moment it treats it as if my character needs to look at it, so theres this awkward way I have to offset it to get proper focus onto a target.
Since this is a new game I'm hoping the devs stay on it and continue to improve it. Me and my relatively large group of friends will all likely be long-time players if they continue to add content and polish the game. If I have any suggestion besides the things above, its to make sure to add 'content'. By that, I mean plenty of neat new items and such to check out. Plenty of neat variations in the world, like biomes. I also like to decorate quite a bit, so please don't skip out on the items that don't have a practical use besides looking nice or creating a setting =)
Good job on getting it this far, I look forward to seeing it improve.

Tree of Life is another attempt on making a multiplayer sandbox survival game, and unlike some other recent releases, this is quite successful on a glimpse, at least from most of the reviews.
GRAPHICS:
The art style is cartoonish, which may not suit everyone.  I am okay with this so far since I am not focusing too much on the graphics, but there are definitely lots of room for improvement, e.g. the low polygon modeling of structures, awkward animations etc.
GAMEPLAY:
As with all you would expect from a survival game, you punch trees, you make tools, and you build houses. The gameplay is solid, yet the complexity of the system makes it hard to grasp from the start. The skill point system reminds me of Ultima Online, which seems to be a popular trend in all the new multiplayer sandbox games (I am looking at you, Life is Feudal). You grind items to level up your skills, which unlocks more items you can grind to level up more skills.
The items you can craft are not shown until you reaches certain skill level, which is sometimes confusing when you are not leveling all skills and you don't know how to craft certain materials from the certain skill while leveling a different skill. This is where the multiplayer part come in - you can have different people leveling different skills and helping each other out.
The UI is clean and functional, though sometimes irresponsive. The control is classic WASD with F to pickup items on the ground. However, the game does not have a keybind remapping option nor does it shows which key does what, so you may need to try all the keys on your keyboard to see what they do.
COMMUNITY:
I am playing on the Asia server. The community seems indifferent, most people do not respond. Trolls and thieves are common in game, but that is part of the gameplay. It is hard to survive on your own, so grab some buddies to accompany you on your journey and remember - lock everything you can. It is up to you to protect yourself.

Since it is still early access, it is difficult to judge a game. I see potentials in this game, but whether or not it can grow into a mature multiplayer sandbox survival game depends on the developer's dedication. Nevertheless I am willing to support the game and hopefully it will turn out to be great at release.

Do you like space sims? If not, just go somewhere else, why are you even reading this... If you're on the fence, it's probably still not for you, it's not an easy game to like. If you love em, go ahead and give this a try. When it's on sale.
There's a fair bit to the game - some nice looking worlds, a fair number of ships and some parts to strap to them. Some missions to do. For the most part it's all there, just not enough of 'it' for my tastes. Lets take ships for a start:
There's a couple of dozen hulls, but the hull you pick just gives you more (or less) ability to strap a better engine to it, or better shields. There's not much in the way of trade-off, one engine isn't super fast and another super agile. Some shields aren't better at one sort of weapon or worse at another, it's all just a ladder to climb.
That means money. Missions are fine but you wont see much profit out of them: fuel is pricy, repairs can be too, and new missles aren't found in the bargin bin. That means you'll probably go mining a lot. It's good money but it's a massive time-sink - no danger involved, just... time. You're going to get sick of the music pretty fast when you're listening to it this much. The fastest way to make money is trading goods between system, but it's still no more exciting.
Reputation is another thing you'll be spending a lot of time working on and it's no different than a grind in any other game, it gets old a little too fast. Missions become overly repetitive under the strain of getting someone to like you and the fun evaporates.
None of what it has is bad, but the sandbox world leaves you soon feeling too directionless and the available content isn't enough to really populate the void of space. While it's fun to start, I think the majority of people would tire of it quickly - not that it should scare anyone off giving it a try, just wait for a sale to pick it up.

This game gets a "must buy" rating from me for anyone who is interested in this genre of spaceflight simulation/comba/trading game. The realistic newtonian physics model and controls are so much better than the status quo "airplane physics in space" in practically every other similar game, and you really can seamlessly fly down onto a planet's surface! And you really can fly anywhere between solar systems without jump gates, though it would take 100s of jumps without a "special" hard to find type of jump drive. All of this is done very well.
The main drawback of the game is that lots of areas feel kind of lacking in depth. For example, you can craft things and customize your ship but there isn't that much variety. You can land on planets and stations looking for missions or things to buy, but there are no characters with scripted conversations to talk to. Capital ships aren't very detailed or specialized, and are more like scaled-up very slow versions of fighters with lots of hit points. Basically there are lots of things you can do that you can't do in other games, but not that much intracacy in any particular part of the game.
Stll, I think most people who are interested in this sort of game will want to spend at least 10s if not 100s of hours playing it. So it's worth buying at full price, especially with multiplayer support (which honestly I haven't tried yet.)

Pro's and Con's:
+ Unique gameplay: Simultaneous turnbased strategy!
+ Completely free to play (NOT pay to win! more below).
+ Zero RNG
+ fast paced: 20 second turn timer, matches of about 15 minutes
+ good teamplay is rewarded
+ Active development, devs care about the community
+ fairly good balancing
- small playerbase
- can be confusing or overwhelming at the start
- hard to convince other people of the game, because:
- more fun to play than it looks
- only really 1 major game mode
- still has some performance or technical issues for some people
As you probably already guessed, I really like and recommend the game.
If you like strategy or teambased multiplayer games, this is a must-try in my opinion.
Gameplay looks roughly like this:
You play a 4v4, where every player controlls one hero unit. Every player on both teams decides his attacks and actions for the turn and afterwards the turn plays out. The clue is, that you can screw with other people or play mindgames, if you can predict what they will do. For example there are abilities to dodge enemy attacks and return fire on their position, to lay traps for them to step on or shielding abilities to protect your allies.
Note that this game has no RNG / dicerolling at all. You aim your abilities at people and if they are in the targeting zone, they will be hit. You can take cover behind walls, which reduces incoming damage from that direction by 50% or use "dash abilities" to move out of the way, but it is never random.
About the business model: The game is completely free to play, meaning you can unlock EVERYTHING in the game just by playing. The game uses the "League of Legends model", where you can play only characters out of a given set, which rotates each weak or buy characters you like with in game currency. Alternativly you can also "buy the game" for 20$ and unlock everything instantly.
Beyond that the game gives you free lootboxes for playing, containing cosmetic items to customize your characters, emotes, etc., similar to Overwatches lootboxes.
Overall I would recommend the game for its unique and solid gameplay, diverse characters and playstyles and for its teambased tactics focus.

After just completing the main story and all of the major activities around the world, I can say that AC: Rogue is a welcome part of the AC storyline/universe.  If you liked Black Flag (as I'm sure you've read in nearly every other review) you'll like this addition just as much, if not, more as it is similar to BF in nearly every aspect.  Rogue was created in a hurry before the release of AC: Unity, which did not include "older" generations of consoles - entitiled fanbois weren't happy, so they scrapped together Rogue for release on older platforms to help appease the masses, hence it's near identical structure of BF.  That doesn't take away from Rogue's fun.
Rogue tells the story of an Assassin turned Templar, Shay Cormac, while tying in the stories of AC 3, Black Flag, and Unity creating a good bridge between the games.  The events that make Shay turn to the 'dark side' are sketchy and ill-conceived at best.  They don't make sense with EVERYTHING else in the whole series that defines what an Assassin is, but if you just run with it, it doesn't detract from the story (if you swap any mentions of 'Assassins' and 'Templars', the story is a typical AC story).
The 'brand new' combat system is glitchy, leading to several "WTF" moments while fighting and executing baddies, but those glitches are rare.  Rogue excels at one of the things that made me fall in love with Black Flag - Naval combat!  It's equal parts AC game as it is "18th-century naval combat simulator" (as explained by another review) and it improves on Black Flag's pirating in nearly every way.
The story is short (you can complete it within hours) but nearly 40 hours later, I'm almost completed with doing ALL the other things available in the world.  Check out my playtime - you'll see Rogue is definately the shortest of all the AC games, but it's one of the most fun.
I can't wait for AC: Origins, and after playing all the other AC's (including the handheld titles), I'm really glad I found Rogue on sale for so cheap a few weeks ago - it's a welcome addition to my AC catalog.
tl;dr - get it, it's fun.  It's basically a REALLY big expansion pack for AC: Black Flag.

I've had to think long and hard about this one. Ultimately, it's not recommended from me. Here's why:
The game is built on a decent mechanic, the combat was fantastic when it first released, and it was fluid, made sense, and was intense. After it was out for a while, people began to find exploits that would make it difficult for others to block, or even attempt to block their hits. Which, I understand the arguement that it's part of the game, and it can be used. I agree. But at the same time, the developers have not even addressed this AS part of the game, they neglect to even acknowledge that it's a thing!
That on top of the already elitist community, you have a recipe for disaster and it has shown over the years. This game has died out and left no one but the true die hard fans that have practiced these exploits time and time again, to be playing this game. While this was free not too long ago, I would not recommend spending money on this game. Not only is the playerbase extremely low and highly 'skilled' at this point, it's a game that has essentially cashed out. Stay away!

Great game for both single-player and co-op.  The graphics are stunning, the music is surprisingly great, and the gameplay is nothing short of phenomenal, with choices galore.  Playing with friends is also amazing, as everyone has an incredible amount of freedom (perhaps a little TOO much from our playthrough) to talk to and fight whoever they want.  The story isn't the greatest, but certainly better than D:OS especially with the fleshed-out companion backgrounds and questlines.
My only gripe would be that the game can seem pretty difficult to complete on normal if you don't complete all the side quests, as the power gap between levels can feel quite large, especially towards the end.  This means that on one or two playthroughs, there isn't too much to come back for besides adventuring with the other companions you ignored and a few quest choices.  But considering the quality of this game, it's probably worth it.

Just recently beat this game with good and bad ending and all I can say for this game is that it's a great addition to the classic style of Sonic infact this game might be the best game for the classic games. The game brings you back to old zones you wish you went back to while still keeping that new style to it. The bosses in this game are one of the incredible points of this game, each boss has their own quirk and it's actually a challenge, not what I would expect tbh. There are secrets and extras in this game that you have to grind and unlock for, and that alone pulls you in for many replays for the stages. You have your normal trio: Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles all three still play the same as the classics and each character have their own style of exploration; which brings me to the zones in this game, they are infact the best addition to the game, You can explore more and more with each character you play as, the music in each zones are great. The downside of this game is that there are no online multiplayer, only local which I kind of get but for a game that has local in steam and not online is a bit iffy in my opinion. A lot of people are refunding this game because of DRM (Digital Rights Management) companies such as Denuvo because they block out modders and possible piracy companies to put out the game for free, they're also accused of Malware which is a big stretch, I have yet to run into a virus with this game. I don't really mind it that much as long as it doesn't affect my gameplay (which it hasn't btw) In conclusion I give this game a solid 9/10 It's the best Sonic game to reignite the classic style, if not one of the best tbh. I recommend this game for people who like to play the classics but also want a modern kind of feel. It's really great.

Denuvo sucks and has had a negative impact on other games that used it, such as performance issues and bugs. Some have even said that it ruined there PC but I would take it with a grain of salt as I havnt heard of many eople with that problem and people's PC tend to get ruined by the weirdest thing sometimes.
Sonic Mania however? I don't have any problems at all, sure it had the online only bug that fans belive was caused by Denuvo itself but SEGA stated that it wasn't caused by that and they actually patched it and they patched it pretty quick too. Yes its very annoying that they delayed it for 2 weeks only for it to come with that DRM and that bug but still, the game is an absolute blast!
Level design is fantastic! Both new and old levels bring insane joy and man, I get some serious nostalgia playing through the game but it also feels very new and fresh. When I heard that this will also feature remake of old levels, I felt that maybe it would suck out the enjoyment a bit becuae I only wanted new levels and not reshashes of what I already experienced. Mania however manages to bring new life to the old levels through better graphics and an updated soundtrack but the levels have also been edited, Sonic is known for going fast and it would get annoying when you crash into an obstacle like an oddly placed Spike on he path, it would seriously ruin the momentum in the old games. Mania fixes this though, the levels have been edited and updated with new path ways and a lot of problems from the old games have been fixed without changing the original level design too much.
Then you have the amazing controls and some new abilities to further enhance your experience, its so much easier to go fast through the levels but the challenge remains intact. A lot of remakes tend to make things easier and more "accessible" for new players (remove Crash Bandicoot from your minds for a minute!) by adding a bunch of bullcrap so they can never learn to improve their gaming skills. Mania doesn't suffer from this, thankfully. The added modern features like auto saving just make it more enjoyable now. Being able to know you can stop and come back to the same level you left at, takes away a lot of the unnecessary tension we had from older titles.
New levels though, I can't believe how good they are, Levels like Studiopolis, really show what the devs are truly capable of and how much they understand on what made Sonic great in the first place! These new levels fit right in with the old and the amount of thought, love and pssion they put into them (and even old levels) really shows I hope there's a Sonic Mania 2 with just new levels because these are so good!
The look of the game is just beautiful. Everything is just pure retro, I HATE the look of a lot of remakes as they always tend to move away from the original visuals, ruining the animation of the characters and giving it this too clean look, there's always something wrong with em and rarely do they hit the mark. Oddworld New n Tasty has this bright look with fancy lights that don't contain a single shred of the dark atmosphere the original gave off, Sonic The Hedgehog 4 has this 2.5d look (yeah i know its a seuql but still) and Crash Bandocoot running animation still look better in the original trilogy. Mania said "F*** that! We taking in time god damnit!"  and they just gave us Sonic from the old days without ruining the original look and style. The animations are smooth and retro too. Its perfect!
Music in this game is just...10/10 m8, I love the music, I love how they remade the classic music for classic without taking away the original sound, you can tell the music was remade from scratch as you hear all those instruments, you think "Yeah, this was not ripped from the old games, it was actually remade" I mean it sounds like the old games....but just better, enhanced somwhow. I can't put it into detail but it just sounds amazing. The music for the new levels sound awesome, just awesome. I'm sorry i can't go into more detail, i just have a hard time explainin music for some reason, I will say that the soundtrack alone is worth buying.

Immersive hacking game, intended to simulate "movie hacking" rather than the real thing.
There is a plot - but the real joy comes from exploring the sandbox and seeing what you can get away with.
The missions you accept to earn cash act to prompt you to try various more and more elaborate things - starting with simple data theft and moving on to hacker tracing, changing government records, moving money around and framing people for crimes.
Each run is short and drops money into the pot for hardware and software upgrades - which creates and enjoyable "just one more mission..." frame of mind.
If you are caught hacking you lose everything (permadeath - or at least very long jail time) and have to start over.
Problems
- A few issues with the interface mostly around text scaling at high resolution, X style mouse focus and lack of cut and paste.
- It gets a bit repetitive after a while as there isn't that much variety in the mission objectives (especially if you get caught and have to start over from nothing)
Well worth the time and money, especially as its on sale and in bundles fairly often.
Thanks to Rock Paper Shotgun's "Have you played..." feature for getting me to try this odd looking title that had been in my library for ages.

Ok. Let's do a quick rundown.
Pros:
-Cutesy and quirky little game. Fun to be in, fun to play and not horribly clumsy.
-Crafting is interesting and resources are(mostly) largely available.
-The community, so far, is indeed a lot friendlier than in other forced multiplayer survivalist games
Cons:
-So far, there is no wiki or guides on how to do anything beyond "Equip food on hand, right click, drag to the side to eat". For example. I spent at least 30 min wandering around, punching trees, looking for [firewood] until I realized that the logs that trees drop could be punched into firewood.
At no point is this even hinted at.
-Lack of a particular resource means that anything you build can be accessed and used by just about anyone. This led to 3 rider players running into my home and looting all my crafting tables.
-Lack of a particular different resource forced my progress to a grinding halt.
-My biggest issue is, as with all survivalist multiplayer games, that anyone can attack you for any reason.
To conclude. Yes it's fun. No I won't keep playing it.
I can only recommend these kind of games to someone who has a group of friends interested in guild battles and endless gathering.
It gets a recommendation, yes, but do consider this is not my kind of game.
Now. If this game decides to have a no-pvp or no-grief server, I'll definitely give it another shot.

As someone who's a junior in a Computer Science degree and has already completed an actual assembly course, this game is honestly harder than any code I've attempted to write for a grade, and it's fantastic. As you're given very few commands, and a limited input space for them to be executed, TIS-100 challenges you to perfect your code, *just to complete the level as-is*, not to mention improving it further and further to compete with others online.
I will say the game can be *incredibly* difficult at times. If you're not one for sticking on a puzzle for a long time, trying and trying, this game will definitely not be for you. If you like coding, and can manage some mid-level math, I can confidently say you'll love this game.

Yes the game is hard, and it has "perma death" so if you're caught then thats it. Game over. Unless you have security, but thats another story for another day. However once you've been caught and had to re start a couple of times you get the hang of things and then the fun really begins.
The adrenaline rush you get when you're trying to disable a proxy with only 40 seconds on the trace left before you are caught and you succeed and manage to clear all trace of your being there and disconnect with 4 seconds left is second to none.
Another great thing is when you launch the game there are no logos or anything to suggest that this is actually even a game. It feels like YOU are logging into YOUR gateway to start hacking real targets and thats what makes this game a real gem.

This game took me a while to get comfortable with but after getting there I can confidently say there is no other space combat game out there that has been as exciting and realistic for me to play. Once you get the systems down and learn navigation (There are a multitude of youtube instructional video's I highly recommend you watch as you begin playing) you are given free range of a vast universe with a multitude of locations and enemies. One of the most interesting concepts for me initially was being able to fly down to the surface of planets from space. The planets vary in type and in atmosphere some even have hostile weather systems or visibility conditions that make atmospheric flight very difficult which I found really cool. The main draw for me also being the realistic physics involved in flight. You cannot just drop through an atmosphere without burning up so you have to approach at the correct speeds and angles and flight controls shift from atmospheric to space seamlessly. Also in space you can fly using true newtonian flight or switch on the fly to an adaptive system that mimics atmospheric flight by compensating for the intended forward direction. Being able to continue on a trajectory at enormous speeds and rotate on any axis without impacting your trajectory has always been the draw of space combat for me but is rarely implemented in space games. Flipping over at speed and accelerating in the opposite direction or setting a trajectory and flipping on your side to strafe a capital ship at incredible speeds is amazing and it's made manageable by being able to switch back to a directional flight mode when you just want to point and fly. The gauges need to be researched a little bit (also on the video's) if you are unfamiliar but provide spectacular feedback that not only brings realism but adds depth and enables more control with a clear idea of the forces at work from and on your ship.
I play a ton of games but there is something special about this one that keeps me coming back. There is a great community of people willing to help out and some incredible mods available. I have some for my HUD that uses the HUD from the ship on the movie Oblivion that's really well done and mods that make the nebulae and space in general look absolutely phenomenal. There isn't a ton of story or progression, there are a lot of different ships, weapons, components, etc. and you are given the ability to edit your own ship designs by choosing components and altering their size and placement on your ship allowing every ship to be completely different even if using identical components. I have spent hours creating and saving ship designs alone with the different components and different levels of components. There are also ship mods made by the community that use models from popular franchises like Star Wars and Star Trek. You can trade although trading is limited since cargo is extremely limited even at the highest levels but quantity is not what I assume was the goal. There are many alert style missions where a commodity is needed at a particular station or planet that appears with a timer and you need to acquire and deliver it to get the reward which is usually substantial. There are many different levels of missions with varying goals of taking out single ships to entire fleets or mining asteroids for particular minerals and even cleaning giant solar arrays with tractor beams where you remove the dirt from the panels with your ship.
The solar systems are VAST and can contain many planets and stations that require jump drives to navigate and gates connect the systems although the gates are placed in different areas in each system but do not act as doors at the barriers between rooms, you can fly past the gates and on into space if you so choose.  Many gates are actually located in the center of the systems so it's not a N,S,E,W square setup. It's vary natural and organic. The stations offer vendors, supplies, components, fuel, commodities, repairs, missions and a few other things. You fly in to the stations and dock with them to interact and you are protected within until you undock and exit the force field. There are also varying levels of difficulty in the different systems with some containing very few hostile ships, some with many and although I haven't made it out there yet some are active war zones and incredibly hostile. There are also different factions that inhabit the systems with who you can build up your standings by running missions for or against their enemies. The faction standings are system specific and do not carry over throughout the universe which i found adds a lot more gameplay in that your standings affect your ability to use different stations and the prices of things like fuel and other commodities. You may also purchase licences that allow you to hunt the enemies of that faction for rewards.
This game is the closest I have ever felt to actually having a ship in space with the freedom to fly anywhere and do anything. The realism is incredible and comes through in scope of environment, optional objectives and the feel of opening up a universe for you to inhabit as you so choose. I've actually just flown around as I imagine I would to relax and enjoy the majesty and solitude of space and no other game has inspired that kind of feeling for me. That says a lot.
Disclaimer: I live in and run a home for homeless and disabled Veterans where we have multiple computers and Steam accounts so hours played does not always reflect my actual experience with the game being reviewed other than showing the minimum amount of time I have personally played as this is my personal account.

Extremely fun space simulator that is absolutely worth the price of admission.
This is a rare title in which gameplay makes up for dull and recycled in-game missions. Having access to both an inertial dampening flight system and pure newtonian physics mode adds an entirely new dimension to space travel and combat. Dogfighting becomes more like a well calculated jousting match and mastering your sliding techniques allows you to overcome enemies with much larger firepower. This is a game that rewards patience and experience.
While some of the art looks fantastic (planets from a distance), low resolution textures on space stations, backgrounds and ships hinders the experience slightly. Mods are available to help slightly rectify this problem.
Great news is this games support for Surround/Eyefinity AND gamepad/joystick setups is phenomenal.
Most other titles require the use of a third party application/driver that merges multiple joysticks together, however Evochron allows you to map each separately. This is fantastic for people with separated HOTAS systems (ie T.16000M Joystick + Saitek Throttle)
Warning to New Pilots: When the game begins it will seem very daunting. After the tutorial section, play with the various tools at your disposal and you will catch on very quickly. Reach out to the amazing community if you are in need of help, or tune into a Let's Play series that can help jumpstart you into the universe.

Back in the day I used to have this demo disc for my Playstation, I think I got it with a Playstation Magazine or something. On one of the discs was a game titld "Overboard", which was a funny little platform game about a (pirate?) ship. I really liked the game and I wanted to buy the game but I was very young and simply did not have the money.
You've probably guessed it "Hands On Deck" is heavily inspired by "Overboard", in fact it almost looks like the exact game but sadly it's simply not as great (yet), which would be OK if the game was still in Early Access, which it's not apparently.
Hands On Deck's graphics do look a bit smoother than the classic game but aside from that 'Overboard' had a lot more details.
Overboard was a pretty fast game but 'Hands On Deck' seems to take a much slower approach making it less fun to play. Also, one of the most fun parts about the original game was the fact you could lose your 'pirates' in the water after you had been hit and you could pick them up again before they would drown. Hands On Deck seems to have removed that feature so all you got left is a barebone version of the classic 'Overboard', which is a shame because it could have been much more.

This game is the Freshman effort of a brand new developer.  A young guy decided to make a game about what it would feel like to sail a small galleon ship through waters that a galleon should never be sailed through.
The first thing you'll notice when you load up the game is the programmer art.  It's obvious that the young man made the models by hand, and for some reason that does provide a bit of charm to the game.  It has the look and feel of a child's representation of pirate life.  While they're certainly nothing fantastic and there are a few graphics glitches here and there, the game's art serves its purpose and I'd even say it has a generally pleasing aesthetic.
The controls aren't really that bad, either.  There's some difficult to describe sluggishness to the controls - like you're moving a big boat, duh - and maneuvering your ship to fire the stronger side cannons at your opponents is a big part of good combat.
However, as you can tell from my playtime, I was immediately bored.  Immediately.  The objectives of the first level were already quite plain, and I had no interest in trying to go further.  I just couldn't imagine trying to play the game for a long period of time, in its current state.  I didn't find anything really "wrong" with the game, as far as its mechanics, other than the entire thing could be tightened up significantly so that there weren't so many long periods of just sailing.
It's not a really great game, but at the same time, it's a weird change of pace from what we're all used to in gaming, and I think that deserves some attention.  Maybe at like $2.99.

Mechanically, the game isn't a unique multiplayer shooter, but it's a good one. Capture-and-hold and one-flag CTF modes are mixed in with the team deathmatch, and the shooting feels nice and solid. The requisite character-progression system is robust enough to give you a huge number of options in building out your character, from five body types that dictate your speed and health, to a ton of weapons that range from typical rifles to freeze guns and boomerangs. The perks system feeds into the comic book motif by framing your peripheral abilities as fun facts (like you'd see on a trading card) and a psych profile. And a selection of gadgets--most of which come in the form of modes of transportation--make the gameplay feel more mobile and dynamic than your typical Call of Duty clone, since you can soar around on glider wings or shoot a grapple gun to get you up to higher ledges. Using the gadgets to get around the map quickly is key to winning, especially in the objective game types.

Although this game may have a steep learning curve compared to many others, the challenge of completing various "simple" tasks in a stripped-down assembly language is incredibly enthralling. What most programming languages can accomplish in a single line of code (e.g. multiplication, division) may require two-to-three dozen instructions in this game. On its face, this concept sounds quite dull, but after working through the first few puzzles, you will find that it is pure magic. Each task stretches the brain immensely, and indeed, some of the later tasks may take several hours of thinking, programming, and debugging to solve. This perseverance ultimately rewards you with a sense of accomplishment and a newfound insight into the lowest-level workings of a computer.
To break much of the tedium of programming for hours on end, the game supplies an intriguing backstory into the nature of the TIS-100 computer system, communicated through several journaled entries by the previous owner of the fictional machine. My only gripe is that this story, despite all of its potential, simply does not provide enough depth to be satisfying. Whereas well-developed stories weave into the game seamlessly, motivating the player to continue playing in order to reveal more of the plot, this one seems more like a sideshow or distraction. Fortunately, the problems themselves are enticing enough to make TIS-100 a time-worthy game.
Although programmers may have an easier time adjusting to the practice of writing pseudo-assembly code, those without coding experience need not be intimidated by the game. Zachtronics did an excellent job keeping the language itself as simple as possible, while still crafting complex problems with multiple possible solutions. I would genuinely recommend this game to anyone who enjoys puzzles that require deep thinking, programmers with an interest in low-level code, and individuals who revel in finding more efficient solutions to problems they have already solved.

Loot rascals is a lightweight rogue-like. A true roguelike, complete with turn-based gameplay, random level generation, permadeath and tactical decisions. Only ASCII graphics are missing but who needs them really?
Its unique feature is card-based improvement. Many slain enemies will drop a card that has either an offensive or a defensive value. You place those cards in 2 by 5 grid to improve your stats. Some cards just have a value, but others have special feature : bonus/malus depending on where you put them on the grid, bonus/malus conferred to surrounding cards, etc. Other cards give you special abilities if you attach them to regular cards : the usual fire/ice/electric "spells",  healing or teleportation. Those abilities need to recharge (with time) each time you use them.
Maximising your stats from your cards is a fiddly but enjoyable process. You sometimes also need to adapt to the particular situations (because sometimes you need more defence than attack)
Another unique mechanism is the day/night cycle. The cycle lasts 10 turns (5 day turns + 5 night turns). A monster type either attacks first at day and second at night or first at night and second at day. This is how combat is resolved: a monster has no defence and a single value that is both its attack and its hit points. When you attack a monster, you substract your attack from that unique value. When a monster attacks, you divide that unique value by your defence and this gives the amount of hit points you lose (remainders are treated probabilistically: a monster hitting you with 8 while your defense if 16 will give a 50% chance of losing one hit point). It's therefore important to hit a monster first, so as to ideally kill him before he can retaliate, or at the very least diminishing its attack value. The current status of a monster (its unique value and whether he'll attack first or second) is always clearly visible.
This mechanism gives the opportunity for constant tactical decisions and you're always chasing some monsters while avoiding others, only to see everything reversed every five turns.
Of course, there are slight complications : some monsters' unique values change according to the time of day, or even every turn. Some monsters attack from afar, etc. I could also mention the light online features, other special cards or the handful of side-quests, but this is enough to get the idea of what the game feels like.
Overall, Loot Rascals is very fun. A full run takes about an hour, and there's enough elements that you need to track to keep things interesting, but not so many that you're lost. The visuals and monster sound effects are quirky but delightful and the music isn't half-bad either.
If you're in the mood for a light, beatable but true roguelike, this is one of the best choices available. Don't give it a pass simply because of how bad EA and co. have made anything related to "loot" sound horrible

I found this game fun to play, however after playing more than 3 hours I found it very annoying how hard the ai is in this game, so I recommend only playing this with a mate who owns the game. The developer 'Orange Juice' used vibrant colours in the game and a refreshing art style that I have not seen by any other dev although the music is great it became very annoying after the third loop. Overall this game was fun to play, had extremely difficult ai, based upon luck, great visuals, tons of campaigns and content and great but catchy soundtrack. Not quite worth 6.99us asking price through for the content in this game however is definitely worth it if you have friends to play with.

I'm writing this review five days after launch and I fully intend on adding another edit later to update how I feel.
Tree of Life is a fairly unique sandbox game, it's gone through a few iterations over the years and I feel the developers have learned certain lessons from past problems.  The current gameplay revolves around group play, solo play is not recommended unless they add in a PvE only option.
If you enjoy a sandbox pvp experience, you'll enjoy this game for a good many hours.  Does the game still have issues, hell yes, but will they stop you from enjoying this game for 100+ hours?  Probably not.
Look at the negative reviews, most of them are from people with 100-600 hours in the game and somehow they can't recommend the game...it's odd because they've clearly gotten their monies worth but can't admit they enjoyed the game but the issues just got to them.
As of right now what you need to do is enjoy this game while it lasts.  Buy it now, enjoy yourself for the next month or two and in a year or so from now you'll remember this experience fondly.
This is my edit from 2016
Edit.  I just wanted to add that this game once again seen a huge spike in players, in March of 2016 the game spiked once again to 3000+ players, those players started disappearing again April and the game went back down to it's normal 300 or less players by June.  The developers once again had the bull by the horns and then ran that bull directly into a brick wall of their own making.
This is my old review from 2015, it still stands.
This game had a lot of potential, it's in a nice niche genre, looks nice, lag isn't too bad and the way the game is designed (to a certain extent) is fun and exciting...but the main thing holding this game back are the developers.
Their lack of communication and obliviousness to really bad ideas really kills this game.  Just as an example of their poor judgement they decided to recently upgrade the map size to 4x as large.  Initially I, among others, were really hyped for this until we actually logged in and seen what they did.
They've essentially locked off about 70% of the map from construction and then covered those areas with a blanket of fog that doesn't give you any view distance at all making traversing those areas agonizing.  The worse part about this is all of the end game materials are in those areas...  It's one of the worst ways I've ever seen a developer 'gate' off an area, you'd think they'd maybe add more hostile npc's to the area or even make the view distance on the fog bearable but you're basically running blind and it's incredibly easy to fall off a cliff.
Also, they've changed the crafting system so your skill level is far less useful then you'd expect.  I actually ended up crafting worse gear then someone with half my tailoring (sewing) levels and we both used the same quality mats.
It really seems they've been making the game much more RNG dependant and now they're adding in a cash shop with (in my opinion) overpriced items because it's painfully obvious they are running out of money.
In my personal opinion this game is a train wreck and I, as well as many others, can't stop watching the train crash and burn, so please don't look at our playtime as confirmation of how playable the game is, take it as a confirmation that the game was once a bright and shining star that has faded overtime and is now only a glimmer of what it could have been.

Tree of Life, the type of sandbox game I enjoy most. Quirky, laid back music, practicing Wing Chun on trees, punching veins, punching Chickens, punching Kobolds, getting punched by Zombies. Makes punching better than Minecraft!
Okay, let's get serious.
For an early access game, I did not expect much. Being a huge fan of sandbox games, Tree of Life holds a lot of promise and the game is already delivering. So far, I have not encountered any bugs and/or glitches in the game, which surprises me. If music is a big deal for you, then this game is just right. Truth be told, if I can get my hands on Tree of Life's soundtrack, I'd buy it. 10/10. It's that good.
As far as the community in the game goes, I'm fortunate enough to have friends who actually play the game, but I've met some pretty cool people so far and have had little conflict with others. If roleplaying is your thing, there are some villages that encourage roleplay. If you just want to play the game as is, there's always that too. There's already a lot to do in the game, so I'm excited to see what else the devs have in store for us!
The only thing I don't like is that there's a delay when you're trying to switch to a bandage after swinging a melee weapon. Granted, this isn't much of a big deal and can easily adjust to, but I don't know if it's intentional to make the game semi-realistic or if there's just a delay. Either way, it's just something I was curious about.
Overall:
If you enjoy sandbox games, cartoony graphics, amazing music, and using a chicken as a punching bag, Tree of Life is definitely for you.

Sonic Mania is to the Sonic franchise what Mega Man 9 did for the Blue Bomber, a brand new game that looks and feels like the older titles so it gives a new experience with that old-school feel. However Sonic Mania takes the idea a step further, instead of sticking to the look and feel of the old games it improves its presentation tenfold and updates the game's feel to a degree that it feels more like a continuation of the old series instead of a mere throwback.
Gameplay-wise it plays almost exactly like the old Sonic games did by combining elements of all of the games in the classic series. The premise is the same old in which you go from level to level with special stages to tackle and a true final boss unlocked after obtaining all Chaos Emeralds along with each characters’ super form. New to Sonic’s moveset is the Drop Dash, a move that if you hold the jump button while in mid-air you’ll immediately do a spindash when you land so you can keep momentum. Blue Spheres also make a return as this game’s Bonus Stages; by completing them you can unlock extra modes and settings for the main game.
There are 12 zones in total, eight of them are old zones remixed in a way so that they look familiar with an upgraded look yet completely new in terms of level design and gimmicks that they might as well be entirely new levels as far as feel goes. Four of them are completely original zones and these are simply the best of the bunch, sporting some unconventional level tropes and absolutely wonderful graphics and music that fit the rest of the levels nicely.
The graphics are GORGEOUS. The entire game boasts a broad color palette with superb pixel art and animation that would make any developer in the late 90s jealous. This also extends to the game’s sound design which is pretty much flawless, with old song remixes and new songs that sound straight out of a Saturn or PSX game with a redbook audio soundtrack.
Not all is sunshine and flowers for Mania however. The Blue Spheres bonus game has no impact on your current game session and they tend to break the pace of the game more often than not and offer no incentive to play them after all medals have been collected. The new 3D special stages are fantastic but the controls take some time getting used to and are also very easy to fail, leading to some early frustration and rendering them quite unforgiving the first time around. The boss battles in Mania also rely a lot on gimmicks, switching the gameplay focus and waiting around for a vulnerable spot which slows the pace of the game and downright probably shouldn’t belong in a Sonic game in some specific cases.
All in all, despite some small pitfalls Sonic Mania is still a wonderful game that’s not only a nostalgia blast but also an entirely new experience that newcomers and veterans alike can easily enjoy.

To those worried about Denuvo,
This is the only platform I could get the game on, so of course I quickly heard about Denuvo and the problems it seems to cause. I have a simple laptop that I use as a personal computer and a school computer. I am an overall casual gamer, so I wondered if Denuvo would create any problems for me as opposed to those that are more 'professional' and would be rightly alerted to problems with Denuvo that they see and I miss. Here is my consensus so far:

Denuvo does not seem to affect gameplay for me. A frozen frame or two when loading new zones, but nothing more.

That being said, Sonic Mania is a great game so far, personally. Zones both old and new are enjoyable, with new mechanics to spice things up when they get stale, if ever. The intro animation and few 'cutscenes' made me grin. Denuvo and the numerous problems others claim it caused aside, the game is perfectly enjoyable and easy to lose the time with. Of course, Sonic Mania without Denuvo would be a definite plus, but hundreds of other reviews have already voiced the same opinion. Congrats to all who worked on this project, and thanks for fun you gave me.

text: Adorable little turn-based roguelike, with an interesting inventory management system of powering up.
My take on Loot Rascals:

This game is way too expensive for what it is. Automated battles and random card pickups.
I generally enjoy roguelikes, but this one seems to have a bit more randomness to it. I like the ability to improve on each run. The way that you do that here is you die, and a monster takes one of your cards. Then, you must wait for another player to run into the same monster, beat it, and decide to send a card back to you, which you may get at the beginning of a run. This happens rather infrequently.
Also, sometimes you get bored of this game, but it starts a new game automatically, but there's no save feature. If you were sent a card, and you decide to quit, you lose the card.
There are better games out there for less money than this quasi multiplayer rougelike.

Visuals and audio are great. Mechanics are sloppy.
I haven't even played that much and I can tell that the other reviews are right in saying something is seriously wrong the game's way of creating a procedural world. It's not like
which has kind of a set progression that allows you to make up for a bad start with skill and knowledge. You always start with 3 attack and 3 defense, but sometimes the monster blocking your way out the base has 12 attack and sometimes it has 1. Then you realize that stronger enemy doesn't equal stronger loot, and you're like, what is even the point? And why randomize everything? Each floor has a sidequest where you retrieve a unique item for the Chef in exchange for important improvements. Sometimes this unique item is a really niche buff which you need to build a setup around. Sometimes it's an extra 3 health, which you're gonna have a hard time choosing between when the other option is an improvement to your limited inventory space.
There's acceptable margins of randomness which make a game exciting, and then there's randomness that makes you feel as if you have nothing to do with whether or not you're succeeding. Randomness which makes you feel cheated.
Other gripes:
1. Hexagonal turn-based world when you have WASD real-time controls is irritating as I found myself overshooting on movement or moving into the wrong tile a lot of the time and losing HP as a result. Surely this game is supposed to be tactical in some way?
2. The whole Dark Souls type "be invaded by other player's ghosts or whatever" does not really add much to this game. I can't even say I see the point of the send a card to yourself thing. Again, this is because I feel like these things do not affect how well you're doing at the game as much as whether or not you lucked out on the spawn.
3. Why is the distance to see the monsters' stats/whether or not they're unique so small?
I don't care about a save feature. Might keep playing but still gets a thumbs down until I see some improvement.

There is just no way to truly explain in words amazingness of this turned base combat system.
--It is a 4 v 4 game.
--Each player only uses one character with 5 moves.  1 move is a special ultimate.
--Each turn, all players have 20 seconds to map out their moves.  You can see what your allies are doing (if you understand how their character plays).  You can coordinate your attack with your allies to perform combos.  For example.  One person can lay down a trap and another person can execute a knockback that throws the enemy into the trap for massive damage.
--Each turn has a "prep" "dash" "action" phase.  Each move your character has will activate in one of those phases.  So all dashes happen before most attacks.  Basically they are dodges.  All preps before dashes.  so healers can heal during prep before their allies take damage.  It's a near perfect system with tons of fairness.
--If you play with friends a lot you can voice chat and strategize combos on the spot.
--the character have a "Champions Online" look and are extremely unique compared to other online PvP and Moba games.
--There is an ingame story and events and special gamemodes coincide with the events.
--THERE IS NO PAY TO WIN.
--Barely any grind.
--Characters are customizable, but the grind to get no abilities is not bad and the starting abilities are all very good.
--EXTREMELY WELL BALANCED CHARACTERS.  OP characters practically non existant.  Everyone can get outplayed.
This is just one of those games you must try to truly understand how much of a gem it is.

An excellent deterministic game (no luck involved) at its core with different units that have strengths and weaknesses. I find it works in principle very similar to chess, another deterministic game without luck involved. Although this game has the advantage from a pure principle perspective in that there is no first move advantage; both players execute their moves simultaneously.
Randomized maps can give one person an unlucky starting situation though, however I find that adds to the fun and keeps the game fresh. It also proves skill; its easy to memorize maps and with enough play through with different people, get an intuitive feel for what is common and what is not, and play accordingly. But with new maps generated and starting positions semi-random, it can really determine between two players who actually has adaptive skill, and who perhaps does not.
I would recommend this game especially on discount for anyone who enjoys strategy/tactical games.

Probably the best space sim I will ever play.  Evochron Mercenary is an amazing achievement because it excels at its primary purpose: putting you in the cockpit of a wide-open universe.  And I do mean wide open.  While there are a jump-gates, jump-drives and other, more-exotic means of travel, the universe is a continuous whole.  You could drift from one side to the other given enough time. . . though I am not sure if there are sides or just an infinite extension of the void.  There are also hundreds of systems -- yes, HUNDREDS -- in the game many of which have yet to be discovered.  Also you can land on planets (or burn up in their atmospheres).
In addition to providing such a vast expanse to explore, Evochron's other principle virtue is its flight system: the game operates on Newtonian mechanics.  This is more than a clever gimmick because it radically changes the nature of combat: weapons systems can be rotated to face any direction regardless of the ship's vector; without drag and friction, momentum also cannot be carried into another vector.  As a result, the game demands a unique brand of piloting, and your first encounters with racing and combat will see you spinning out of control.  This necessarily adds to the joy when you get it right.  The game does ease the burden through the well-implemented use of assisted flight mode (IDS), which the player can toggle on and off.  When on, the computer automatically fires thrusters to orient the ship onto its current heading.  The Newtonian physics nonetheless remain in this mode and (especially at high speeds) your ship will continue moving under its own momentum until your thrusters are capable of compensating. For example, if you were to spin your ship around 180 degrees you would nonetheless fly "backwards" until your engines were capable of canceling out that momentum (if the IDS were off, you would just keep traveling on that heading regardless of orientation).  Incidentally, if you were just thinking of Babylon 5, you might as well stop reading and add this to your cart.
While I stand by that glowing endorsement, Evochron is not for everyone.  Those who are looking for the massive empire building found in something like X may very well find this game underwhelming (I personally despise X for its unforgivably bad AI, obtuse interface, and ho-hum combat).  Trading and building elements are in Evochron but not to anything approaching the degree that they are in X.  The game was also made by one man -- which is mind-bendingly awesome -- and this does show in some of the production values.  Simply put, you won't find as much variety in textures and geometric detail in ship design as you will in most games.  Having said that, the game oozes atmosphere; it just nails the big picture thing.  In this respect, I think it is comparable to Skyrim: up close not terribly spectacular, but the vistas are breathtaking.  As a sandbox game, you must also find your own motivation.  That the game was built by one man also reflects that it is largely a labor of love; complementing its roughness and quirks are design choices that would never survive a profit-motivated studio, e.g. Newtonian physics that scare off casual gamers and a hands-on navigation system that has more in common with a sextant or Ti86 than with gMaps.
Evochron also has a pretty steep learning curve, though my experience is that this curve mostly reflects actual complexity in piloting the ship and learning where to buy/sell in order to make money rather than a stupidly convoluted interface (Yes, that was a cheap shot.  And no, I will not apologize to X3 nor to Windows 8).  Nonetheless, there are some aspects of the game -- especially when starting out -- that will have you bringing up the steam overlay to google: "How do I _____ in Evochron."  With the exception of the navigation system, the interface is however pretty smooth and intuitive.
In sum, this is the game for you if you want to get in touch with your inner Malcolm Reynolds or Han Solo.  For that matter, it is also the game to for you if you want to get in touch with your inner Starbuck or Freddie Prince Jr. from that really bad 90s movie.  And you need not take my word for it: the developer provides a free demo on his official website.

This is easily the best game I've played this year, maybe ever.
The story is... something else. The game drags you into a world where your actions matter, and everything from dialogue choices to the turn to turn actions you take can shape the world around you. This is a game where your actions can and will have permanent consequences. But best of all, the story isn't completely linear, meaning multiple playthroughs can go completely differently and tell different parts of an overarching story.
The combat is, quite honestly, pretty daunting at first. Things (enemies, elements, enviornmental objects, etc.) interact with each other in so many ways that it can seem impossible to figure out. But it's not. And figuring it out is incredibly rewarding. The feeling of turning a long, grueling, fight to the death fight into a lopsided slaughter through good use of mechanics, environments, and positioning is amazing.
The attention to detail is astounding. Small things like blind/sleeping enemies having no sightlines, or the seemingly aesthetic but actually intentional placement of environmental hazards and objects add a degree of polish occasionally lacking from even AAA games. Big things, like how fluidly the elemental system actually works make the game more satisfying. After all, who can deny the satisfaction of dousing an entire group of enemies in oil, then incinerating them?
Overall, this is a game well worth your time if you like games that not only let you break most of their rules, but expect and it and adapt. A game where 5 playthroughs can each have entirely different story and character progression. A game where, once you've bought it, you're getting a full, polished game. No strings attached, no additional money necessary.

I got this game after I played Skyrim, and even though I haven't really played it that much, it is a very good game. For every other Skyrim player who has been curious about this game, here are some differences I have found between the games so far:
-The Controls: while moving around and dialogue options are the same as Skyrim, some of the controls are switched around. E to jump, SPACE to interact; F to sheath/unsheath weapons, R to switch from first and third person view. Also, you can't sprint, but you can switch between walking and running using the SHIFT and CAPS LOCK keys.
-Lockpicking: Not only does it have a different name (security), but the format is also different and can be hard to get used to. Once you understand how it works, it's a lot easier than Skyrim's guess and check system, as long as you have sound because your success kinda depends on that. There's also an auto-solve feature, where there is a chance that you will still fail.
-Speech: Increasing this skill means talking to NPCs and playing a mini-game that is complicated at first, but not too bad once you get the hang of it, or bribing them.
-Race Perks: For the most part, they are the same as Skyrim, just not as many, for example Khajiit don't have the claw perk, but they are still good thieves.
-Standing Stones: They don't exist in Oblivion. However, you do get to choose a birth sign in the beginning, which is almost the same, but you can't change it later on.
-Leveling Up: In Skyrim, your character gets xp from every skill that levels up. In Oblivion, only leveling up in a specific set of skills will give your character xp. You also have to sleep in a bed to do this, and your enemies get stronger as you level up, so working on other skills is highly reccommended.
-Equipment: It wears down the more you use it, and can break if you're not careful. You can also fix it by using a hammer, as long as you have one in your inventory, at any time. Keep in mind that the hammer only has so many uses before it breaks, so you may have to get a new one.
-Interactions with NPCs: Expect to get a lot more comments about your character's race within this game. Make friends with them with conversations, and they will tell more information on topics. You can even have conversations with the guards.
-Pickpocketing: It still counts if you look inside an NPCs inventory but don't take anything.
Of course, there are more differences that I haven't noticed yet, as I am still exploring the world, but there are plenty of places on the Internet if you want to see a good comparison of the games. I was personally intimidated by the differences
I found online, but I can tell you that I do not regret my decision to buy this awesome game.

This game is an excellent return to roots for our favorite discolored anthropomorphic hedgehog. It succeeds at bringing back the classic feel of the Genesis and Sega CD Sonic in a way that Sonic 4 definitely didn't do, and even in a way that Sonic Generations failed to do.
The same mechanics as before are back: fast paced momentum based platforming with tight controls. Contrary to what seems to be popular opinion, I'd argue that the level design is even better than in Sonic 1, 2, 3&K, and CD, as it has fewer cheap unforeseeable hazards and generally is based more around Sonic's speed (funny someone should think of doing the thing that focuses on the main selling point of the franchise). On top of that, while it uses old zones from the four games previously mentioned, it does more than just rehash old ideas within them. It instead puts them in a new light completely, and adds mechanics from other zones from other games into it that seem at first glance like they shouldn't fit together. But boy, does it work!
Like Sonic CD in particular, the levels are very speedrunning-friendly, due to the focus on skill rather than trial and error, but the acts are much, much longer than in the older games. Like, Carnival Night Zone Act 2 and Sandopolis 2 from S3K long. Despite that, none of the levels overstay their welcome, and I still had the same giddy, giggly face at the end of each zone as I did in the beginning.
Other things worthy of note:
Boss Fights: Almost all of them were creative and memorable, and just generally a good time.
Bonus Stages: I'm a big fan of Sonic 3's Blue Sphere stages, and Sonic Mania brings back old stages and adds new, very creative, and very challenging ones. I. LOVE. These bonus stages.
Special Stages: These stages to get the Chaos Emeralds have quite a difficulty curve, but it makes them oh, so satisfying to overcome. They use a variety of old and repurposed aesthetics and mechanics to make the best special stages to date in my book.
New Zones: They are imaginitive and original while fitting in seamlessly with the old levels. I love them as much as everything else in this game.
Music and Sound Design: As soon as I find a purchaseable soundtrack for this game, I'm buying it because the music and sound design for this game were flawless! It may not all have the same feel as music from the old titles, but I like it that way. It feels more like a natural evolution of it just as Sonic 2 and 3 expanded on the "Sonic music feel" from Sonic 1 and 2, respectively.
These things being said, this game isn't perfect, but my only complaints about this game are very minor nitpicks, so who cares?
If you even remotely appreciated the classic Genesis era of Sonic, BUY THIS GAME! You'll love it!
As a final note, a lot of users seem to be complaining about Denuvo and how it is supposedly breaking their game, and giving this game bad ratings because of that. I don't know anything about what it is, but I know that I had absolutely no issues with this game's performance. Either way, it's a $20 game, so very low-risk with a much greater reward.

Loot Rascals is a turnbased roguelike where you move on a hexagonal grid mettling your attack and defense stats against enemies. The enemies have day/night affinities which decide who goes first when attacking - you or the enemy. The one attacking first
has the advantage in the battle! Attacking an enemy lowers their attack, which reduces their chance of dealing damage to you.
Cards dictate your attack and defense values. These drop randomly from enemies with different values and with different bonuses and penalties. Good placement while equipping them is essential to get the most out of your cards. Some enemies drop ability-frames which give you one out of six different skills to use on the grid such as burn, teleportation or a dummy which taunts enemies in to attacking it instead. Utility cards exist to alter gameplay such as going from a turnbased game to a timed game or confusing enemies, but those are a lot rarer.
The enemies are most of the time quite predictable, so if you know their moves you will not have difficulty beating them! Well, unless their power level would kill you.
---
The art has to be the best part of this game - it's colorful, original and hilarious (I'd love to see more of this!). The voice acting and music are just as great. It's such a shame that a game this good looking doesn't have more of a story or flesh out the characters more! The story has an beginning and end, but not much in between. The gameplay is great and surprisingly addictive, though!
The main criticism this game has received is the lack of a save feature in the middle of a run, which I personally think is a bit of a detrimental way of rating the game as a whole (missing feature vs. gameplay). A complete run in this game, from beginning to end (without dying), takes about 60 minutes. So if you don't have this much time to spend in one sitting, I suggest picking another game (or begging for a save feature in the forums).
Another criticism I've read is that you lose everything after dying - but that is how most roguelike games work. Once you die, you start over, even in Loot Rascals. So don't get too attached to your cards! You'll find better ones, I'm sure!
And the third criticism... the procedural generation. Some have had difficult enemies spawn right outside the base when starting out - which has occurred to me a few times. But most of the time the attack values haven't been absolutely off the charts. I personally think that the procedural generation makes for varied gameplay, but sometimes the enemies/cards/terrains aren't spawning in equal amounts, which does make the game a bit unbalanced run for run.
All in all I recommend this game wholeheartedly if you're willing to look past the save feature - it took me about 9-10 hours of
playtime before I beat the game the first time (seed: 110166016). So the game is not impossibly difficult! Success relies on luck and strategy, but the weight is definitely on the latter and making the best out of your cards.
It's as hard as the rumors say, but it's worth a try just to see how WEIRD the rascals are!

Something to understand before playing this game: its not a game for the masses. It's not an extreamly popular genre, it has confusing controls, and one might even say that it has qwerky mechanics. But its a game unlike anything you've ever played before. Asyncronous Turn-Based Strategy. A brilliant idea, but where it excedes in Frozen Synapse is in the execution. This game could be reviewed by an unenlightened gamer as an "annoying, confusing, turn-based strategy game", but what it actually does is it makes you think. And then it makes you think again. And again.
In the words of Sun Tzu:
“To know your Enemy, you must become your Enemy.”
You must think like your enemy. You must find every possible senerio and make a counter for each, or take a risk, and prepare for the most likely one. All the while knowing that your enemy is thinking just like you. It require a mental skillset that not only do most gamers not want to have to use, but do not have at all. However, if you think you have what it takes, and you think that you are able to not just think for yourself, but think for your enemy, and plan ten steps ahead, then this just may be the game you've been waiting for.

Uncle Randy unexpectedly passed away recently and you have inherited an old computer he was working on — a machine that was manufactured in 1980 known as the TIS-100.  Unfortunately much of the operating system’s code is corrupted — despite your late uncle’s best efforts to repair it — rendering the computer's origin and purpose a mystery.  Now that your curiosity has been piqued, will you be able to finish his work and figure out the reason for its existence?
If the synopsis doesn't intimidate you then
.  It is an assembly language programming interface and
must come up with the code required to solve the conundrums it presents.  These problems often seem deceptively simple to resolve, and initially they are, but thanks to the limited number of instructions available on such an archaic system — not to mention the limited space to enter code — they quickly become very challenging.  As far as puzzle games go, TIS-100 makes Sudoku look about as threatening as noughts and crosses... but that is not a criticism; the complexity is what makes it so good.
You just have to understand before buying that it gets very hard very quickly, and any satisfaction comes out of learning new concepts and solving the problems yourself.  This sometimes involves spending considerable time making notes and devising solutions on paper because the mental gymnastics required of you occasionally get too much.  Yes, it can be frustrating, but it’s a fantastic feeling when the solution finally hits you.  I even had a couple of
moments while taking a bath and ended up rushing — stark-naked and dripping-wet — to my
trusty TIS-100 for that much sought-after rush.
Obviously this game will appeal to programmers more than most, but such credentials aren't essential.  You’re just as likely to enjoy it if you got good grades in maths and are partial to number puzzles.  On the other hand, I’ve come across users who don't fit this profile and love the game, but for this type of person I think the initial purchase will always be a gamble.
Consequently, I give TIS-100 a glowing recommendation but with the caveat that it won’t be everyone’s cup of tea.

Almost all games can lean on graphical fidelity to a degree to enhance their appeal. TIS-100 is an exception to this rule. Yes it has a rudamentary graphical interface which is styled in the command line aesthetic, but it's not trying to be visually appealing like undertale or terraria. It's functional, and that's all that it's really there for. TIS-100 is therefore unusual because the pure and distilled form of a game; that is: something that has rules and a winning condition.
The rules are simple, and well laid out in the manual which accompanies the game. They are simple commands that can be used to manipulate data in a certain way. I have no background in programming or coding and I could quite easily understand them.
The goals are also simple, you have to take input(s) and turn them into output(s) using the commands laid out in the rules.
The solutions however, are anything but simple. You have to think through problems to use simple logic to come up with ingenious solutions to the problems. However, after the first few puzzles, you will likely be left scratching your head for a bit. But this is the best part of the game! You keep at it untill you find the solution and a glorious stream of numbers are spat out from your code indicating that you have successfully achieved the goal. The feeling of reward when this happens is larger than i've felt in a game for a long time. The lack of hand holding in this game does make it difficult, but it only amplifies the rewards at the end of a puzzle because you'll have solved it all on your own. The puzzles themselves are varied, and the developer has clearly spent a long time devising them. There is also much replayability, as you can see how many commands and steps it took others to solve the puzzles, so you can try to optimise your own code to be like the best of them.
Ultimately, it's a game of pure logic. If that sort of thing floats your boat then I whole heartedly reccomend it. If you're more of a non stop action kind of gamer, or someone who just loves a good story, then you probably won't like it. Horses for courses, or courses for horses; which ever way round the saying goes.

Still new to the game, but having played a day's worth, enjoy it allot.  Can be VERY frustrating though, at first.  Be aware that you can be PK'd, and its best to try and work with others, but can play solo.  Nights are dangerous.
Couple of tips!
1) Work on getting food first.  I kept starving, and even though you do not die, you get slowed via a debuff until you put food in your stomach.  Apples CAN be cooked in a fire, and fill you up better when done so.  Make a fishing pole right away, and get some fish, cook them, and eat.
2) Punch trees!  Yes, go all fisticuffs on the trees, and then when you kill a tree, do the same to the dropped logs.  You'll need the firewood, but be careful, they don't stack well in your inventory, and can fill it up quickly.
--> You'll want to get food, twigs, and logs first off.
3) Major game mechanic is to hold down the right-click button and DRAG (not click) the mouse pointer to a nearby icon to do that action (start a fire, cast your fishing pole, etc.).  So for example, to use a Bonfire, you have to make it, put it down on the ground by right-click and drag to the drop icon, get your torch equipted, stand in front of the dropped bonfire, right-click and drag to the fire icon, and that'll light the bonfile.  Then you right-click and drag to the gear icon for the bonfire, and a dialog opens up where you can put food substance on the left side slot, and firewood (or old club) on the right side, and your fish/apples/whatever will start cooking.  Fishing is similar, equip fishing pole, right-click and drag to the cast pole icon to the left, and release right mouse button.
4) Watch the evil ground spots, they can spawn, well, evil stuff!
5) Vines when destroyed drops one of the mats you need to make a fishing pole.
6) Some mobs will drop rare items.  For example, a walking tree stump monster dropped a voodoo mask that gave +defense.
Hope this helps! (My first Steam review evar!)
