At first, I thought of reviewing both Spartan Assault and Spartan Strike as one game, then noting their differences. The Twin-Stick shooter gameplay is similar to make you think that SS is the same as SA (which came first).
However, after playing all of SA and 80% of SS, there is a subtle difference in how each game plays that may or may not to be to your liking: The mission structure in SA is less "Halo" than SS, which I think is to the game's benefit.
The PC port for Halo: Spartan Assault (and Spartan Strike) is a mobile/tablet port for an isometric twin-stick shooter (made by the same guys who made Gatling Gears, Vanguard Entertainment).
Almost all buttons can be remapped, save for the fire, the grenade and the pause button. Controller support is optional, and the keyboard and mouse controls are almost all perfect. The only lacking thing for controls are the vehicles. There are also simplistic options, nothing that is going to tax your computer.
Importing the mechanics of the Halo franchise works, to my surprise, quite well for the genre change with some tweaks to how they all work. Along with some alterations to work within the new genre. For example, no reloading for weapons and the alterations to certain guns like the Spartan Laser's sustained fire.
Some carry-overs from the Halo franchise: The two limit arsenal, the armor abilities, the Skull difficulty modifiers, the later addition of loadouts (which uses XP you earn in completing missions to unlock one-time weapon unlocks and other changes for your loadout), and the very limited arsenal and vehicles. (Yes, you can board them.)
You'll fight only the Covenant in this game (Elites, Grunts, Jackals and Brutes, which I'm confused to why they're here, but I guess I should've paid more attention to the date). Their AI acts exactly like how they would in the Halo games. Elites are more mobile, Grunts go on sucide runs, Brutes charge at you. You get the idea.
(And the human AIs for your teammates are useful for once. Go figure.)
Oddly enough, as this game takes place as a pseudo prequel to Halo 4, you don't actually have a ton of diversity for weaponry. Nor all the Halo stable vehicles. There is no Halo 4 weaponry, and not even all the weapons before that game show up (no BR, no light-machine-gun, no energy swords, no carbines, etc.)
As you would expect from a mobile game, your objective is to complete simple missions and to get the best raiting. In this game's case, beat the 5 to 10 min missions in the quickest time with the most flare. This is through the medal system from the Halo franchise, which fits in to providing an enjoyable experience.
Even to someone like me who hates the three gold star systems of mobile game, I found its implementation respectful to the Halo franchise (similar to the score mode for campaign). You can get plenty of hours trying to perfect your runs, and there are 30 missions--around two and a half to four hours of content--which don't often repeat the same objective next to each other.
I also never felt undermanned nor pressured for using the special weapons you can unlock for a mission--the rocket-launcher, the sniper rifle and the Spartan laser. And even "buying" the temporary loadouts does not guarantee you'll get the best score for this game. (Trust me, I tried to break the game with the awesome rocket-launcher and found myself only getting silvers.)
If you want to buy this game for the story, you can pass this series of games right off. SA and SS are only simulations of events that you have no bearing on, and even when the game does get serious you won't care. (Plus, the Spartan IV program is a bunch of whinny wimps.)
If you do not like the mobile route, then you might not also like the series. Although I do think there is something here if you're a Halo enthusiast who found Halo Wars an interesting attempt of branching out the franchise. It doesn't do anything superb or innovative, but the game is competent and feels mostly balanced.
The vehicle controls are somewhat stiff in comparison to SS. They move based on your WASD movements, not your actual direction you move--like how Halo does it as well as SS. I never found it bothersome but you may find it more annoying.
Some people complained about the gunplay about some weapons, but I used all the weapons and they felt useful, never a wasted item in this game. I did notice some "weird" unresponsiveness to shooting my guns at times. (There were somtimes a delay on shooting the gun that I never could make sense of. SS had far more instances of this problem than SA.)
If you are interested in these games, I would definitely recommend the bundle whether on a discount or full price. You'll get your money's worth together rather than paying for them individually.
I would definitely say Spartan Assault is the better of the two games because the game plays similar enough to the Halo FPS series while making something new. Spartan Strike suffers from the same problems Halo missions can suffer from; abitrary restraints on the player.
This problem is fine for a linear FPS with checkpoints, but for a mobile game with short missions, you'll find the abitrary mission objective changes the bane of your time. Not the brevity of the missions nor the simplicity of the genre.

I got this game after I played Skyrim, and even though I haven't really played it that much, it is a very good game. For every other Skyrim player who has been curious about this game, here are some differences I have found between the games so far:
-The Controls: while moving around and dialogue options are the same as Skyrim, some of the controls are switched around. E to jump, SPACE to interact; F to sheath/unsheath weapons, R to switch from first and third person view. Also, you can't sprint, but you can switch between walking and running using the SHIFT and CAPS LOCK keys.
-Lockpicking: Not only does it have a different name (security), but the format is also different and can be hard to get used to. Once you understand how it works, it's a lot easier than Skyrim's guess and check system, as long as you have sound because your success kinda depends on that. There's also an auto-solve feature, where there is a chance that you will still fail.
-Speech: Increasing this skill means talking to NPCs and playing a mini-game that is complicated at first, but not too bad once you get the hang of it, or bribing them.
-Race Perks: For the most part, they are the same as Skyrim, just not as many, for example Khajiit don't have the claw perk, but they are still good thieves.
-Standing Stones: They don't exist in Oblivion. However, you do get to choose a birth sign in the beginning, which is almost the same, but you can't change it later on.
-Leveling Up: In Skyrim, your character gets xp from every skill that levels up. In Oblivion, only leveling up in a specific set of skills will give your character xp. You also have to sleep in a bed to do this, and your enemies get stronger as you level up, so working on other skills is highly reccommended.
-Equipment: It wears down the more you use it, and can break if you're not careful. You can also fix it by using a hammer, as long as you have one in your inventory, at any time. Keep in mind that the hammer only has so many uses before it breaks, so you may have to get a new one.
-Interactions with NPCs: Expect to get a lot more comments about your character's race within this game. Make friends with them with conversations, and they will tell more information on topics. You can even have conversations with the guards.
-Pickpocketing: It still counts if you look inside an NPCs inventory but don't take anything.
Of course, there are more differences that I haven't noticed yet, as I am still exploring the world, but there are plenty of places on the Internet if you want to see a good comparison of the games. I was personally intimidated by the differences
I found online, but I can tell you that I do not regret my decision to buy this awesome game.

Just before you buy this game just remember it is NOT Rise of Nations : Rise of Legends. Legends was done a lot better in my opinion but came at a later date.
None the less though expect a European Wars Cossacks style of play. The only difference here is you cannot build wherever you'd like. The campaign plays as so : you are given the choice of scenarios or are allowed to choose your own map to conquer (I chose the world map to conquer). You have different races to choose from with each their own tactical ability. What separates this game and what I like about it is that the more research you do, the more you are allowed to build (no duh right), but you are allowed to build cities a certain distance away from one another and establish trade routes. Serfs are needed to harvest food (5 farms per city), or can be told to gather wood (need to build a wood cutting camp), and iron and oil can respectively be collected. Buildings such as lumberyards are available to make your lumber gather skills better (likewise for food and iron).
The fighting is an RPG style of play and the formations the units line up in are awesome. Preparing your units for battle and lining them up accordingly and to which angle is made beautifully. They followed the idea of Knights and Merchants when it came to telling units in which direction to point - except this one does a better job of it.
After a fight (or before a fight) you have an overview of your world map and from here can use strategic cards to your advantage or tell units where to move. You may also upgrade your current country's wealth.
Back in the day this game would have received a higher rating from me, but as we are living in the present day and have quite the variety of games I will have to give it a 7.0/10. It has a fun factor, but it's re playability is sporadic. Multiplayer with friends is fun though.
RATING : 7.0/10

The Good: Classic RTS that won 2003 PC Game of the Year remastered, still great controls, music is still amazing (always felt a sense of wonder when listening to it), fantastic RTS formula of gather and fight, killing bombers with arrows (I know what your thinking: "how'd Civ Rev get in here!? wtf!?"), cheats still work (type in "cheat nuke" without the quotes...or maybe it's just "nuke"...but anyways don't have cursor over your base!), graphics are aged but still impressive considering when game was done, comes with the expansion Thrones & Patriots which added some improvements to original game along with more people ('Murica & Associates), advancing through ages can be interesting (see "killing bombers with archers" above), great campaigns, nations are varied with both traits and units that can extend through ages (lookin at you Mayans & Aztecs), just a dam good game
The Bad: graphics are aged a bit (gotta crticize somethin), camera can be weird at times, not realizing cheats still worked and annihilating your Classical Age town, AI is more intelligent than you think (not a bad thing as much as unexpected), some research is a bit tedious
The Ugly: I WANT TO SEE RISE OF LEGENDS REMASTERED!! COME ON GUYS!!
Overall, great remastery of classic RTS and something I completely forget about and put my orginal disc in everytime. Enjoy the game folks

“I will never beat Loot Rascals, but it is interesting…”
-Me, after a few good initial runs, before promptly getting annihilated in a huge series of very short runs.
Let’s start on the bright side:
The oddly drawn characters coupled with the strange voice actoring, high quality animation and the quirky opening cutscene got me legitimately hyped for what the real game, outside the tutorial, would be like.
The card system was daunting from all the screenshots but things start out with such simple equipment, it’s dead easy and intuitive to learn. When I did manage to get into longer runs, I felt more intimate with my inventory. It’s not just a stack on mindless buffs/nerfs, it’s a clear puzzle to progressively optimize.
Sounds effects, enemy appearances/voices and the background music all create a wonderfully brutal yet playful tone that I was infatuated with for the first quarter-hour or so of my time with the game.
The limerence of a game’s aesthetics does wear down with time to expose flaws with time and Loot Rascals is one tough game, and it feels more like that mostly because of chance.
A few things that relate to this that I was not a fan of:
Whenever you can’t one-shot, there is a chance to take (minimum) 1 damage.
Health is only regained by using 25-50 turns which makes the world more dangerous.
The whole, if “Your Defense > enemy attack, Enemy Number/Your Defense = the probability of getting hit”concept means risky encounters, even insignificant ones, have a chance to serious hinder your run.
I’ve walked out of spawn into a hallway (my only option) with an strong-ish enemy who I can’t one-shot. My run has a 50% chance of me starting with 4 health rather than 5.
I’ve tried running away in bad situations but everything follows at either a 1-1 or 1-2 pace [Your Turns-Enemy Turns] so it’s impossible to retreat without just making things tougher, especially if there’s a huge group of baddies in where you’re retreating to.
It’s pretty common to just bump into a crazy swarm of enemies or one crazy over-leveled guy that just promptly ends my run.
I suppose if you’re just looking for something to sink time into and play with no expectation of progress, give it a look. Although Loot Rascals is held back by its rogue-like mechanics, it still has some really, really good ideas and I can’t wait to see what Hollow Ponds has in store next. :)

Some cards are just ridiculously better than others, like the blenders just make some level trivial. Then in another game youll only find terrible low level cards.
If damage was reduced a bit, the procedural generation touched up to be more lenient on paths, and more reliable card drops the game would be a lot of fun.
Though the artwork is extremely weird and borderline funny, the gameplay is somewhat addictive. Starting from scratch after a death isn't my cup of tea, but it's someone's tea.

The most fun I've had with a Sonic game since S3&K.
Capturing the nostalgic vibes like no official Sonic game before it, Mania has set the bar at an all-time high for any future Sonic titles. The best part? This game was made, not by Sonic Team, but by the community, and quite literally. Christian Whitehead, the genius behind the Retro Engine that Mania and many of the Genesis ports for iOS (and the CD port for both iOS and Steam) run on, started out as a ROM hacker. "Stealth", AKA Headcannon, was also a ROM hacker, and knew the ins-and-outs of the Genesis games; these two would make quite the pairing for developing this title, not to mention the Pagoda West team, which were famous for their work on the Sonic 2 HD Remake before it being taken down.
The aesthetic design is extraordinary. With colors as vibrant as ever thanks to the advancement of technology, the environments are extravagant and very pleasing to the eye. This is also true of the Genesis levels which were remade into Mania; the high-definition pixel art and the ability for endless color give this game a style like no other 16-bit-esque titles. (Some even claim that this game would be more along the lines of 32-bit thanks to the colors and polys.) Another eye-catchingly amazing feature of this game are the animations. Sonic himself, along with his friends, have more frames of animation than their Genesis counterparts, along with their environment; rings spin at a more detailed rate, enemies look more alive, and even Dr. Robotnik himself is beautifully animated in the cutscene at the end of Green Hill Zone. And the music! Tee Lopes did a fantastic job with the music.
. Overall, it's very pleasing to both look at and hear.
Gameplay-wise, the game performs exactly like the Genesis games -- with a ton of added polish. Sonic is fast, and the developers wanted you to have fun with the game, so they based everything -- and I mean EVERYTHING -- around Sonic's blazing-fast speeds. The Drop Dash ability gives a whole new method of earning momentum, making the game a speedy blast. The levels, including those old Genesis remakes, have new gimmicks in them that breathe life into what they once were, making them more fun than even their Genesis counterparts. The Special Stages are also fun, taking inspiration from older Sonic titles while also keeping itself unique. I myself can't remember the last time I found grinding for Chaos Emeralds fun and entertaining until playing this title.
The amount of attention to detail added in by the developers just shows the player how much they actually cared about the game they were designing. That's something more developers, including those at Sonic Team and SEGA in general, need to take notes on.
I can recommend this game again and again a thousand times over.

This is a grand strategy game similar to classics like Civilization. It's set during the Middle Ages to the High Middle Ages. You take control of (or create your own) dynasty/family and try to survive.
How does it play? Slowly... very slowly.
The game is essentially just a huge map with a few single soldiers dotted about representing armies. You have a few menu's with options such as changing laws (which you have to wait for 10 years to change) and there is your council who can do a few things on the map such as fabricate claims, train troops, plot etc.
Conquest is not easy especially if you're catholic, as its full of realistic mechanics such as the pope in his pointy hat telling you ya can't invade good christians willy nilly. But these mechanics and the random events that pop up are what make the game shine, it makes it a much more realistic and satisfying experience and some are just plain funny but they do need to be made more flexible to make the game more playable. In order to conquer someone you need to justify it, so for example you could have your son marry a local lords daughter and when they have children they will have a claim to the lords land, that's the 3rd generation! So you spend a lot of time waiting around for events to pop up and people to do the things you assign them to, building up armies, waiting to get pregnant, waiting for the children to grow up, waiting for someone to kill the other heir ect.
It's like a song of ice and fire or game of thrones the game (and not that telltale♥♥♥♥♥♥ this has real freedom to create the imbred zealot dwarf family of your dreams, pushing kids out of windows and capturing concubines, smothering babies and that classic poisoned wine, each playthrough tells a unique story (if the events randomly pop up) but its in a realistic medieval setting (no targaryens but theres a good mod out there), history buffs should enjoy this game, especially if you're into that particular part of history. But like I warned you everything takes a VERY long time to do and most of the time you are sitting twiddling your thumbs which some will find boring.

I would have recommended this game, but poorly designed proceedural generation and consistent crashes ruin it.
The game seems cute and charming from the intro. And once you jump into a game or two you start to see a really good roguelike experience coming together. It's fun and challenging, and the variance does encourage you to keep playing.
But after a few hours you start to see the poor design taking form. I understand alot of roguelike/roguelite games enjoy using proceedural generation to create the illusion of variance and replayability, and sometimes it works really well, alot of games like this are designed intelligently, but Loot Rascals falls short of being playable roughly 50% of the time.
See, you spawn into every level by a homebase, which is apart of a safe zone. Enemies can't enter this area, and depending on the map that is generated your safe zone will have 1 or more exits you can freely use. The problem is the game doesn't balance what enemies decide to spawn right outside that zone. It could be a weak enemy, or one of the level's elite boss enemies, identifiable by their unique name, size and colour set.
Enemies are important in that they are your main source of equipment, you need to kill enemies by moving into the same tile as them, then an automatic fight will occur, and depending on the enemy type and whether it is day or night will determine who attacks first, then combat resolves automatically until someone dies, every enemy that dies has the chance to drop a piece of equipment that will either have an offensive or defensive improvement. If the enemies that spawn outside your safe zone are too powerful, like a boss enemy, you will have zero chance of winning that fight with your starting equipment. Each level is timed, meaning you have a limited amount of turns to escape the level, so if you're boxed into your starting zone by enemies that are too powerful, you can't spend an infinite amount of time trying to find a way past them, most of the time it's impossible and you're forced to take a fight you can't win. Standard enemies might not even drop any loot on death, the drop chance seems to be completely random and not set up to help you effectively at the start. You can get lucky and have loot drop from everything you kill, or you can kill 10 enemies and gain no extra equipment. Boss enemies will always drop loot, and it is usually better quality, but you need to loot weaker creatures to have any chance of beating the stronger enemies as the combat is only based on stats and not player skill, there are no criticals, and no chances to miss, so there is very low variance in how you can influence a fight other than timing when to start a fight, or looting enough spells/abilities to weaken stronger enemies before fights. The difficulty ramps alot between levels, so if you didn't get the loot you needed you'll be too weak for the enemies at the start of the next stage, ending your run far too early even if you're playing smart, planning ahead, and taking the risks you need to maximise your equipment.
The level design has little thought put into it. There are times where I've been bottlenecked by enemies I have no chance of killing, and on one run I was even unable to exit my safe zone at the start of the second area due to a block of ice obstructing the only way out. The level before gave me no chance of looting the ability to cast fire, which would melt the ice and let me pass. Abilities like this are 100% drops from specific enemies, but you need to hope the right enemies spawn, and that they don't spawn as boss enemies, or you can't collect those abilities. I have only been obstructed by the level design like this once in about 4 hours of playing, but the fact that the design even allows this to happen is sloppy, any noteworthy roguelikes I've played have coded in algorithms that prevent this from happening. And in a game where you're relying on randomness to provide replayability, you better make sure it doesn't make playthroughs impossible to navigate.
I want to praise this game, it starts out very fun with alot of promise for a casual roguelike that actually has a decent amount of challenge and strategy to it. But the poor procedural design and lack of even minor balancing from the very start makes this game completely unplayable 50% of the time. Add to this the possibility of the game randomly crashing half way through a really promising run - which has happened to me 5 times in 9 hours of gameplay - with no save/recover feature in place, it makes for an incredibly infuriating experience.
There are better roguelikes out there with more care put into their design, I would strongly suggest avoiding this one until it is patched and balanced.

Don't mind the hours spent in the game. After refunding it, I ended up buying it on GOG to give it another try.
I first want to preface this review by saying I went in totally blind. I have no nostalgia attached to it, and I come from a background of loving point-and-clicks. I also seek out any game of the cyberpunk genre I can get my hands on.
That said, I wanted to like this game, but it felt impossible to. I saw it and I thought it was some kind of miracle I hadn't played it already. Even its subtitle "The Cyberpunk Vampire Game" seemed perfect (as well as amazingly corny) to me. The screenshots made it look fantastic in that old time-y gritty moody kind of way. I felt like whatever its cons were, I wouldn't let it keep me from enjoying a game that looked like I would love. But despite playing for long enough to get a handle on it, it still didn't work for me.
Right off the bat the introduction has dialogue remeniscent of a real terrible early 80s B-movie, and the entire game follows a real similar note. I love B-movies, but I like the ones that have some kind of substance to them. To those who do not discriminate amongst the B-grade film and enjoy them all, you may enjoy the game's dialogue and story. I came in expecting cheesy shlock but the interactions in the game are just completely unentertaining and soulless. There's too much of it, and it all felt incredibly empty.
At first glance Bloodnet looks like an adventure game, but it's very much an RPG as well as point-and-click. Even moreso, I'd say. You construct a character in detail from the very beginning. After making one, you're thrown in with absolutely no explaination of how anything in it works. I fumbled around with the controls and tried to figure them out, but they were so convoluted and made so little sense I ended up just getting frustrated, on more than one occasion. It's very, very easy to get frustrated at this game.
The game's combat get a special mention for making absolutely no sense. After taking more than a few hours of mastering it I still have no idea how it works. Imagine arranging a bunch of sprites on a wallpaper and mashing a few keys on the keyboard; it would be about the same experience, and the only difference is doing the latter would save you from all the needlessly complicated aspects of the literal sprite-war. Speaking of, one of the more amusing things I noticed while playing was that moving your character around on the screen makes very little difference whatsoever ultimately, because you can just drag all the items in the room around the screen anyway.
The music, while I initially thought helped add to the mood and atmosphere, eventually got grating to a point I had to turn it off. It's a mish-mash of totally random notes thrown into a midi blender and forcefully churned out. I turned general sound off too because not only was voice acting painfully sub-par, but it's neccessary in order to see subtitles/text. I was just playing it in total silence at that point, which wasn't too pleasant.
I love games that throw you in with no explaination and don't hold your hand as they play, but Bloodnet goes too far with this. Even with a walkthrough, it's unbelievably difficult to get any sense of progression.
Visually, however, this is where the game succeeds. It does an absolutely fantastic job setting a mood, almost unlike any other game I've ever played before. This is what had wowed me when I first found out about the title, and the screenshots essentially secured my purchase. It reminds me of Synnergist, which is a relatively unknown cyberpunk point-and-click adventure that was released in 1996, 3 years after Bloodnet. It really puts it into perspective -- it's amazing how well even now Bloodnet works on its visuals alone. It's what sparked my interest and it's probably what's going to spark others' too. Atmospherically it's a spectacle to look at and simply experience, and if only the rest of the game followed, it could have been something a lot more.
There's a lot of potential. But I feel like the designers were too ambitious and tried too much at once. It ends up overall being a mess. It's a neat-to-look-at mess, but an unplayable one. Like others have said before me, the easiest way to sum it up is to say it has not aged well in the slightest.
Recommended only to those who have the nostalgia factor I don't, or an insane amount of patience. Looking through the flaws and figuring out all the nonsense would be tough, but there are things to like about it for those who are willing to stomach its more unpleasant aspects.

This is a true Microprose masterpiece from the good old days! As a teenager I`ve been playing it for weeks, trying to figure  out all the puzzles and quests, find every recruitable NPC with unique items\ inventory graphics, installing every possible cutting-edge cyberware, jury-rigging protective suits (about 12 of them) and weapons from junk and spare components. Background artwork is simply beautiful, music is haunting and atmospheric. Combat is complex and intense - in some situations it is highly recomended to use extra gear like doppelganger, virus-loaded data spiders against drones at TransTechnicals, holy water and wooden stakes against vampires (aim for torso, nothing else will work). You can kill almost anyone you want to at will, but please be carefull not to harm guards at Hellfire Club - it breaks the plot, making game unbeatable (learned it the hard way back then). Narrative is also intriguing, with many interesting characters and subplots.
If you are a fan of cyberpunk genre and Gibson`s Neuromancer, this game is a must have! The main drawback imo is somewhat obscure UI and general difficulty level, especially for modern player. Takes some time to get into it, and a little bit of thinking - no one is going to hold your hand and explain what to do next.
P.S About subtitles problem - you can activate them by turning off the sound in game options. It`s a pity we can`t have them with voice acting simultaneously.

I am an old school Megadrive/Genesis Sonic fan. In fact, Sonic was barely the first game I played in my youth. I did the 4 first games, as well as Spinball and Sonic 3D Flickes Island (yes), several times between the age of 4 to the age of 16-17 I'd say. Then for family reasons, the Megadrive/Genesis disappeared and I didn't play to those games for a few years, but it never left my thoughts, and I had several reminders thanks to the numerous Sonic or SEGA games collections (on GameCube, DS, 3DS and PC). Sonic is really a part of me, at least a part of my gaming history and I was very excited to try Sonic Mania. So excited that I prepared the release by playing one more time each old school games during the wait.
Today I finished Sonic Mania 2 times with the 7 chaos emeralds each, played a few more levels with Knuckles, got the gold medal into every special stage and of course unlocked every achievements. My verdict is simple : Sonic Mania is a success ! I had so much fun playing the game. I was amazed by how generous and fun it was. The new environments are very good, as well as the new soundtrack. The game is filled with good ideas, and it's funny to see how it is a patchwork of old and new stuff. Sounds have been reused from different games (even Spinball!) but they now have a different meaning. Old enemies are appearing in new environments at the side of new ones. The old songs has been remixed.
The game plays with your nostalgia but modernizes it and manages to propose something new. You partly are running into old level design and the second after you are into a new crafted section and you move from one to another. It creates some kind of alchemy where you are falling down in your childhood but the child that is within you gets to discover new things because the game offers plenty of new paths and hazards.
The game is beautiful, timeless with lots of eyecandy effects, the gameplay is just perfect and I greatly appreciated the fact that it stayed Sonic but that it took the initiative to be more fluid than the originals. It's just a pleasure to control and play, a pleasure to watch as well as a pleasure to listen to. I'm sure that even if you are not a Sonic fan as I am, even if you never played a single (2D) Sonic game and if you enjoy platformers, you'll find your happiness here, because it really is a good game.
Now I'll play some more in Time Attack mode, and then I'll let the game rest on the side, but I'll probably come back to it into the future, now and then into the years, as I did with the previous games. I wouldn't call Mania Sonic 4, because there are too many reused environments, but I would call it the best tribute to the serie, hands down. Mania suits it very well.

So many people on here are posting negative reviews simply because of the DRM, these reviews have nothing to do with the quality of the game itself. The actual game, the actual content, is simply amazing! While I quite enjoy some of the more recent Sonic titles (Generations, Colours, Heroes, and even Unleashed) there really is nothing like the jyo of a 2D Sonic title. While the DS has filled this hole somewhat, even Rush and Rush Adventure pale in comparison to Sonic Mania.
Mania is very much a love letter to the Mega Drive-era Sonic titles. There is SO much fan service here and such love put into every little detail. The gameplay is spot on with the speed and physics feeling just like they did one Sega's classic system. My only real criticism of Main is the Special Stages. Why they are cool to play, Sonic feel a little floaty in his controling. Also, the draw distance in these levels is rather short - I assume to greater emualte the feeling of a 16-bit game  - but this does cause issue as sometimes you might not have enough time to reeact to corners or, most importantly, ring placement. While I do appreciate the devs wanting to capture that 16-bit era feel and it works wonderfully for the majority of the game I feel the Special Stages would have benifited from a little more modernising.
Still, if you're an Sonic and or even just a fan of clasic 16-bit gaming you simply could not do better than Sonic Mania. It's pros FAR outweigh is few and farbetween cons. This is a must-have game!

I only kinda enjoy MOBA games. I messed around with DOTA when it was an early mod, thought it was a neat idea but hindered by the game engine. I liked some of the changes Demigod brought to the style of play, but it was held back by its own laundry list of technical problems. The other clones have pretty much universally been lesser than either of those two games, or so wrapped up in their own money-making schemes they're flat out messes to all but the most hardcore players. DOTA 2 threw the baby out with the bathwater and ditched the engine that was holding the gametype back, but refused to change a few stubborn niggling elements (namely last-hitting and a needlessly long game time due to a drawn out early game).
Awesomenauts completely turns the idea on its ear, and the result is a faster, more action-packed, and frankly a more fun game. The depth is there, the breadth is getting there. Each map is different enough that you have to change up your tactics, no two characters are alike and two of the same characters can play entirely differently depending on which upgrades you select. Add a vibrant and fresh cartoon art style that is consistent all the way through from the sound to the color palette to the character back stories, and you have a solid winner. I am very glad I took the chance on this game!

Fun rogue-like. It's turn based but animated very well so that it doesn't look it at first glance. Great character and enemy designs. It's very hard. Took me 23 hours to get a win. Your stats are determined by placing cards in a grid, and the cards affect each other so you have to arrange them right. You can also gain powers that recharge when you explore and powers that run on tokens you get from permanately discarding cards. Combat is mostly deterministic and based on a day/night cycle that shifts every 5 turns or so. Enemies will be on defense or offense based on the time of day, and many enemies have unique properties you have to keep in mind too. Really fun, really hard, and really interesting.

Loot Rascals is a game that will lead you to believe that everything is okay, just to shatter it in another move. The game focuses around a unique playstyle that I like to describe as a mix between a Roguelike similar to the Binding of Isaac mixed with a card collector like Hearthstone. If you enjoy both of these games, I feel like this is a must-try for you.
Pros:
- Interesting Art Style
Loot Rascals art is some of the oddest art I've seen in a game, but the art and music can begin to have a homey feel after playing for a while. The soundtrack, in my opinion, is great.
- Some replayability as every run is randomly generated
- Challenging and will make you think.
Unlike roguelikes that involve skill, this game is more played like XCOM or Invisible Inc in a turn based manner, it's just those turns happen very quickly.
- Can be played fast or played very slow depending on your playstyle.
This is really up to you but you may get burned relatively easily by going fast.
Cons:
- Price
At this point, there isn't enough content in the game in my own honest opinion for the game to be worth $15 USD. You can get some replayability out of it, like I said, but once you beat the game there isn't any incentive to do more runs.
- Challenging
Like seriously, this game is really freakin' hard. If you want a challenge, go for it, but this isn't "Oh I didn't beat Mom in Isaac on my first try." This is "Oh I can't finish Basement 1." It's a challenging game and it takes a while to get used to.
- Art Style
I realize I have challenging and art style as both pros and cons but it really does depend on the person. The art in this game can be satisfying for one person but look childish or just weird for another. I personally, find it a bit weird but I don't let graphics ever get in the way of my gameplay so I don't mind it. You might though.
Overall if you're a huge fan of roguelikes and enjoy card based games, I definitely would give Loot Rascals a try as you can get your money's worth for it. Otherwise, I'd wait for it to go on sale.

Warframe is one of my favorite games, as you can surely tell by the 6k hours I have on it. The devteam is also excellent, and they frequently interact with the playbase, and it is clear that they do listen to criticism.
The game does indeed have it's faults, particularly it's outdated tutorial and poor new-player experience. However, even as a new player, you will encounter countless people in the community willing to help you. In any MMO, the community i one of the most important parts, and Warframe's cordial and welcoming community is certainly the best of any I've ever been a part of.
Warframe is not for everyone. But, if you do like MMO-lite style games with a fair bit of grind, I most definitely recommend it.

(Before you start reading: I won't talk or mention Denuvo in this Review since it didn't affect me, although i do not support it as well. Also i might have made some wrong typos in there, you have been warned!)
The Sonic franchise went through many differend Games and spinoffs and is Today known for their Memes and "Cringy" Fanbase while most Recent Games in the past few Years have been Ok to Mediocre. Other Games and Genres didn't do it for me mostly and some made me upset or didn't gave me a feel of Statisfaction, except Classic Sonic Games and some few others. Sonic always has been my "Friend" since i have been growing up with him on my PS2 playing Sonic Mega Collection Plus and Sonic Gems Collection and always wanted a Pixel 2D Classic Sonic Game, like apperently many others until we got Sonic Mania. Sonic Mania, which was developed by hardcore Sonic Fans for Hardcore Sonic Fans "By the Mania, for the Mania" as they say. It captures what the Classics made so good and goes even beyond that with Solid Gameplay, 60FPS, Widescreen Support, Awesome Sprites and Animation, Physics, Music(Love you Tee Lopes!) and More while being faithful to the Originals. Whenever i play Sonic Mania i feel full of Joy and it just makes me Happy so much that i can't express myself with Words.
After the Events of Sonic3&Knuckles, Tails notices a strange Energie reading from far away and asks Sonic to join him. Together on the Tornado the two of them are back on their way to Angle Island, where the Energie reading is detected. However Dr.Eggmann noticed it as well and his new Elite Unit known as the Hard boiled Heavies arrieved there first to retrieve the Energie, which revealed to be a Ruby called the Phantom Ruby. The Phantom Ruby Sends Sonic, Tails and the nearby Knuckles back to Sonic 1's Green Hill Zone. From there Sonic and his Friends have to Stop Eggman, The Hard Boiled Heavies and get the Phantom Ruby!
Play either as Sonic(&Tails), Tails or Knuckles.
Very faithful to the Original 16-bit Genesis Titles with save states and a no save run as well as Competiton and Co-op.
You move to your left or right, Jump or Spindash your way through differend Zones with 2 Acts each,with Bosses each Act and Level Transitions like in S3&K. (Some Zones will just Fade black in and out!)
Elementalshields are back and can reflect certain projectiles of Enemies and respond to the Leveldesign, you can burn Bridges in Green Hill Zone with the Fireshield as example.
Sonic can use the Elementalshields to get a Special ability(Electroshield: You can Jump Twice, Fireshield: You can do a Dash in midair, Bubbleshield: You can bounce to the Ground to bounce back up higher, you can breath underwater(Allcharacters))
Sonic also got a new Move called Dropdash (Only works with no Elementalshield equiped), which allows him to keep rolling straight forward fast after a Jump like a Spindash. (Excellent for Speedruns!)
Tails and Knuckles are like the Originals without any Changes, Tails can Fly and Knuckles can climb Walls or Glide through the Air.
Knuckles also has in some Cases differend Pathways and Bosses to fight against.
Giant Rings from Sonic3&Knuckles are making a return that are hidden across the Level. Upon entering one of these Rings, the player will be playing a Special Stage which is a mix of old Special Stages: The Player has to Catch an UFO holding a Chaos Emeralds. By Collecting Blue Spheres the Player become Faster and Collecting Rings to extend the Timer. Should the Player Catch the UFO, the Player will be given a Chaos Emeralds. Getting all 7 Will unlock a Super Form and get you the Good Ending of the Game. You can miss some Chaos Emeralds in your first Playthrough and go back to all Zones to get the last few.
Should the Player pass a Checkpoint with 25 or more rings, he can enter the Sonic3&Knuckles Special Stage. The Player has to Collect Blue Spheres while avoiding Red ones. Upon completion, the Player will recive a Medal (Gold if Perfect and Silver if not). Collecting Medals will unlock Extra that can be used in the Main Menu or in a No Save run.
With 12 Total Zones (4 New and 8 Reimaged) and 3 playable Characters, Secrets to Unlock, Widescreen support, 60FPS and More, Sonic Mania is a must have for Newcommers to the Franchise or Hardcore Sonic Fans that used to play the Classics with tons of references to Sonic and Sega.

Imagine if you took everything great about the classic games, made them even better, and made a game out of them. In short that's what this game is. Now for the full review.
Oh boy there's a lot to say so let's start with the gameplay and move on from there. The game plays great, the control is smooth and each character has their past abilities at their disposal. You get the sense of speed as well as platforming you got from the classic games as well.
Time for level design. For the most part I love the level design in this game (except Titanic Monarch). Now yes it's true there's more returning levels then new ones but every act 2 in a stage is a completely new take on that zone (Hydrocity Zone flips that though [act 1 is new and act 2 is the original]) with new gimmicks and set pieces.
Special and Bonus Stages are present as well, and both are so well done. The Special Stages are a combo of the Special Stages from Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic CD, Sonic 3 and Knuckles, Knuckles Chaotix, and Sonic R. Your goal is to chase down a UFO while collecting blue spheres to fill your mach meter to gain speed and rings to give you more time. The Bonus Stages are the Blue Sphere stages from Sonic 3 and Knuckles, there's 32 in total and 16 are returning from S3&K while the other 16 are new. Your goal in these is to collect every ring then every blue sphere, but the longer you take the faster you go. The reward from the Bonus Stages is a medal, silver if you only got all spheres and gold if you got all rings and spheres. The medals are used to unlock a bunch of secrets and such.
The soundtrack is amazing! I love every single track in this soundtrack! And there's a new Super theme which is also fantastic.
Story is lacking but this is a trip back to the 90's so it's fitting, you can learn everything about the game in the included manual too.
The sprite work oh yes the sprite work, there's so much attention to detail and it's so good. You can feel the love put into every single frame and I just can't get enough of it.
This game is also full of replayability giving you a reason to go back to it again and again.
Overall I can recommend this game to veterans of the franchise but newer fans can still have a blast in this trip to the past.

You know, it took me quite a while to figure it all out; the learning curve actually curves back upon itself and forms a cliff dusted with all of your shattered hopes and dreams, and burning chunks of starships. But after a few hours of puttering around the universe, a universe which feels vast enough to become truly lost in, shearing minerals from asteroids, cleaning solar arrays, dashing through holographic rings for chump-change, and laser-jousting at eyeball-blistering speeds with sweet lady inertia as my copilot...I think I like it. There's a lot to see, ridiculous amounts of things to do, and you'll spend enough time tweaking your ship design, or creating the perfect kinetic particle weapon from the ground up, that if you're anything like me, you'll wonder just where the hell the day went.
It's got an unforgiving interface, more controls than you'll remember after taking a break, and you might even get the feeling that it's laughing at you when you accidentally come out of warp inside a planet's atmosphere and shear your wings off...but for all that, the gently swelling, epic score punctuated by radio static and laser blasts against that gaseous nebula, backlit by the bright white glare of a dwarf star, will lead you back in. Head first. Into an asteroid.

Oblivion is a wonderful game for many of the previously stated reasons. It combines decent combat with interesting quest lines and likable npc's. This, however, is not why I would suggest it. Any number of other RPG's have better combat, better fleshed out quests, or more realistic npc's. No, what sets this game apart is it's open world. With many other "open world" RPG's you are still pressed to follow the main quest line and, once it's done, you're done and left with little else to do. This adds to how immersive the game is and, above all else, stresses the "Role-playing" aspect of "Role-Playing Game".  So what the combat isn't as impressive as that of Dragon Age? You don't have to min-max in Oblivion: you just play and enjoy the beautiful vistas of Cyrodill. I would also like to add that there are literally thousands of mods that improve upon every problem present with the game and even improve on the good aspects. (P.S. There's no Workshop support, so you have to use a mod manager and stuff. I personally suggest OBMM (Oblivion Mod Manager) and the use of the Nexus mods webpage.)

Starts off slow but gets more challenging as you get further. Large Large Large Large focus on farming. Farming to get resources to makes guns/warframes/gear, farming for parts/blueprints for weapons/warframes/gear, farming for endo to strengthen your mods (a lot), farming standing to buy special augments/weapons from factions, farming focus in order to strengthen you focus schools, farming relics in order to get prime parts, farming missions in order to get relics, farming mastery rank by leveling guns/warframes/melee weapons.
So as you can imagine, you will be doing a lot of the same content over and over again which is where the variety and core gameplay loop come in. There are tons of melee weapons, warframes, guns, mods, and augments allowing for many different playstyles.
Do you cheese it with Loki, do you just have fun and murder everything as Nidus, or do you fly around as the slaughtering pixie Titania?
I can only say you should definitely give it a try. If you enjoy the gameplay then stick around for a while.
However, as mentioned, there is a lot of farming involved meaning this game will suck in your time like a black hole.

Naval warfare is non-existent, apparently it's in the game but I've never encountered it.  I could go on and on with the list of bad game design decisions, if I did you'd be reading this until a month of Sundays.

I have owned this game since Introversion first released it way back in 2001. Since then, I've played  countless hours,  and enjoyed every minute of it (except for the times I got tracked down and the game ended.)
The graphics and interface may be minimal, especially compared to your standard FPS, but for a hacking game, they are perfect. What few sound effects that are in the game are used extremely well - the insistent "beep...beep...beep" of the Trace Tracker as you race to complete a hack and erase your tracks gets the adrenaline going just as much as fighting off a mob of enemies in the latest Call of Duty clone.
The game is played out entirely through your computer terminal, or "gateway". Through this gateway, you accept missions, hack systems, purchase software and hardware upgrades, and try to stay a step ahead of the authorities. All communication with your employers is carried out through in-game email and text - there is very little voice recorded for this game. The missions themselves range from simple hacks where you only need to delete a single file, to complex attacks that have you navigating a local area network (LAN), blocking (or disabling) security systems in an attempt to destroy a mainframe.
All in all, I heartily recommend this game.

I can still remember my first impression, and it was... disappointing. "Man, that's not what I expected, what did I pay for?" - something like that. Then, I got into it, and things turned to the better.
That is hard to deny that the game has drawbacks. There's an uber great idea behind it, but it was not absolutely properly realized. On the other hand, revealing its full potential would have required years of development and dozens of developers.
I don't really like its graphics, for instance. It looks outdated, and the game is unable to switch between screen resolutions - so, I have to change it manually before running the app. After starting a new game, you feel a bit lost - not knowing what exactly to do, how to travel to long distances, why is the map so small, why are contracts the same again and again... Earning money becomes too easy when you find out that a bunch of cheap metal alloys can easily be turned into some expensive spacecraft equipment... The list can be continued.
Still, the game has its appeal. After some exploration you will find out how to make fun of it. Its combat system is rather fine, for example; developers also paid a lot of attention to controlling options, making it possible to control every small aspect of managing and dispatching your ship - like manual tuning of energy balance between shields and weapons to boost either of them. (I remember one reviewer saying that it's one of the few games where you can actually feel like being inside of a real spacecraft; that's quite true.)
There's some endless space you can wander, and some beautiful planets that make you want to save a screenshot. If you want to, you can land on literally any spot on any planet (except gas giants, of course), and as soon as you've earned some million dollars to buy a terrain walker, you can even leave your ship and take a walk on the surface.
It may be calm and relaxing as well as swift and exciting. And, it is generally good, though it could be even better.

It can be tedious, a bit of a grind but honestly satisfying and I've never ever played a space sim that actually made you feel like you were exploring the universe. This is the closest you'll get to space without being a qualified astronaut working for NASA.

Loot Rascals plays dirty. It’s one of those rogue-like randomly-generated dungeon crawler affairs that seems to be in vogue right now, but it’s also cunningly addictive. It’s simple on paper: slog your way through five stages with increasing difficulty and destroy the time-warping inter-dimensional gum monster that lives in the planet’s core. Then rescue a giant robot head and go home. You know, that old chestnut. But the planet you crashed on has filled itself with weird, bloodthirsty monsters. They don’t want you to progress. They want you to die.
Their murderous desires will be fulfilled the vast majority of the time. There’s a whimsical air surrounding Loot Rascals, with its nonsensical plot, goofy, exaggerated cartoon art style and vibrant pastel colour scheme, but that makes it no less viciously homicidal. A small army of alien psychopaths bar your way, existing for the sole purpose of caving in your infant-headed astronaut protagonist’s face.
Luckily, you’re given plenty of tools to fight back. Rather than the genre norm of gaining equipment drops through victory, you instead build up a collection of cards to equip. Sometimes, these cards offer straight-forward bonuses like defence or attack boosts, but the better ones come with little extra quirks. Like being reversible so that you can swap out which field it boosts on the fly, or offering bonus perimeters. A card might be bolstered if it’s placed on an odd numbered inventory slot, or lose some of its own value if it’s positioned on the bottom row. It might even grant penalties if it’s the only type of card you have in your deck. Gaining and equipping cards is a constant (ahem) shuffle, as you try to arrange things so that the one that offers +2 to the card on the right perhaps annuls the negative bonus from the one which takes -1 from the card below.

It's visually light - hearted.   It's quick to pick up and each game is plays out fast.  The cartoony art style and upbeat presentation add to the appeal.  The monster designs are fun; you enjoy killing the monsters but you can also get a laugh out of the close up when they get to loot your corpse.  Replayablity?  It definately has that 'one more game' impulse, especially since they are usually quick.
The game play is simple, but requires thinking.  Its rare that I lose because of random factors, its usually because I've made positioning mistakes.  It's easier to get wiped out in the first five minutes (and then try again) than later when you are 20 minutes into a run.
I've seem mentions of the lack of a save feature... I agree I'd prefer the option, but I havent found I miss it.  Most runs are short and the ability to capture the Seed number of the run you are on lets you try the same setup again later, which is a feature I'm enjoying.
If you don't get the special ability cards, the run can be a pain.  The cost for healing skyrockets quickly, so if you dont find a healing ability, the monsters will likely be looting you.
The ability to find another player's gear and return it to them is awesome.  It is an interesting karma system since they might help you later or send a hologram after you for revenge (similar to spoiling your run in Splunkey by robbing a shopkeep).
Feature I'd like added: More heads for the pilot, or a custom character creater,

After a friend's recommendation, I decided to give
a try, and I am really glad I did.
And yes, you read that right - this is a
in the sense that it is true turn-based gameplay. Brilliantly done, I may add. You actually move in real-time, but whenever you cross into another hex, a turn passes. There are very short day/night cycles that determine if you get first hit on an enemy. You will instantly kill the enemy if your power is greater than his 'strength' or HP. All the math is transparent, and there are only like three numbers to keep track of which makes it quite elegant. This is where the puzzle portion comes in, and fits it nicely in the puzzle-roguelike genre along other titles such as
,
, and even
, among others.
I have a hard time putting it down.
The other notable part is that there is a built in card game of sorts. The loot you collect from fallen foes is cards. The cards give you buffs depending on how you lay them out. It's all simple to learn, yet slowly reveals its depth as you figure it all out. The only other part that you may want to know is that there are no meta-game upgrades. There is a pseudo-multiplayer component, but so far I haven't found it potent enough to really matter one way or the other.
+Awesome artwork and music and just such a zany universe
+Surprisingly addictive, and it is so easy to just fall into another run
+Keyboard and mouse support is great, and so is controller support
+Daily runs and leaderboards certainly keep things fresh
+Both the turn-based combat system and collectable card game are *really* well done
-Yeah, it's brutal, but hey thats what we came for
-I do wish you could play with keyboard only, but no biggie

Tree of Life is a game in the survival genre, however on top of that it's a MMO since I believe you can have 1000 players in 1 server.
The moment you get into Tree of Life you have to choose a server, there is Europe, US and Korea to choose from. After you pick your region it's time for you to create a character, in the character customization you pick a skin color, hair color and you pick a boat.
The boat you pick is based on where you are going to spawn in the world. For example the bottom left boat (looking like a viking boat) that's the one I picked and I spawned in the bottom left. From there on out I met up with my friends on the beach and we went to trees and started chopping some trees, got some twigs and some logs. Then I pressed "E" and looked at the crafting of the game.
After that I knew the game was awesome, since you have to craft some kind of workbench and from there you can craft other structures that let you craft more and more. In order to craft the things you need a certain skill though.
Your skill points go up by using a skill more and more. For example if you want to level Tinkering you have to keep making things from Tinkering.
Now another thing is you get stats for doing these things, for example for Tinkering I got a lot of "Con" which is Max HP increase. Now for using my axe a lot I got a lot of strength.
Now about the "Karma system" if you steal something you become red. This is for I believe 30 minutes. Now if you would murder someone you become red for 60 minutes.
The consequences of being red is that if you die you lose everything you have on you and some Experience points as well, however I didn't notice that yet.
All in all I'd say the game is a blast where I only found 1 bug and that is some invisible mob that attacked me when I was on a mount. It only happened once though.
This game has a really bright future and I look forward to some good updates.

(Before you start reading: I won't talk or mention Denuvo in this Review since it didn't affect me, although i do not support it as well. Also i might have made some wrong typos in there, you have been warned!)
The Sonic franchise went through many differend Games and spinoffs and is Today known for their Memes and "Cringy" Fanbase while most Recent Games in the past few Years have been Ok to Mediocre. Other Games and Genres didn't do it for me mostly and some made me upset or didn't gave me a feel of Statisfaction, except Classic Sonic Games and some few others. Sonic always has been my "Friend" since i have been growing up with him on my PS2 playing Sonic Mega Collection Plus and Sonic Gems Collection and always wanted a Pixel 2D Classic Sonic Game, like apperently many others until we got Sonic Mania. Sonic Mania, which was developed by hardcore Sonic Fans for Hardcore Sonic Fans "By the Mania, for the Mania" as they say. It captures what the Classics made so good and goes even beyond that with Solid Gameplay, 60FPS, Widescreen Support, Awesome Sprites and Animation, Physics, Music(Love you Tee Lopes!) and More while being faithful to the Originals. Whenever i play Sonic Mania i feel full of Joy and it just makes me Happy so much that i can't express myself with Words.
After the Events of Sonic3&Knuckles, Tails notices a strange Energie reading from far away and asks Sonic to join him. Together on the Tornado the two of them are back on their way to Angle Island, where the Energie reading is detected. However Dr.Eggmann noticed it as well and his new Elite Unit known as the Hard boiled Heavies arrieved there first to retrieve the Energie, which revealed to be a Ruby called the Phantom Ruby. The Phantom Ruby Sends Sonic, Tails and the nearby Knuckles back to Sonic 1's Green Hill Zone. From there Sonic and his Friends have to Stop Eggman, The Hard Boiled Heavies and get the Phantom Ruby!
Play either as Sonic(&Tails), Tails or Knuckles.
Very faithful to the Original 16-bit Genesis Titles with save states and a no save run as well as Competiton and Co-op.
You move to your left or right, Jump or Spindash your way through differend Zones with 2 Acts each,with Bosses each Act and Level Transitions like in S3&K. (Some Zones will just Fade black in and out!)
Elementalshields are back and can reflect certain projectiles of Enemies and respond to the Leveldesign, you can burn Bridges in Green Hill Zone with the Fireshield as example.
Sonic can use the Elementalshields to get a Special ability(Electroshield: You can Jump Twice, Fireshield: You can do a Dash in midair, Bubbleshield: You can bounce to the Ground to bounce back up higher, you can breath underwater(Allcharacters))
Sonic also got a new Move called Dropdash (Only works with no Elementalshield equiped), which allows him to keep rolling straight forward fast after a Jump like a Spindash. (Excellent for Speedruns!)
Tails and Knuckles are like the Originals without any Changes, Tails can Fly and Knuckles can climb Walls or Glide through the Air.
Knuckles also has in some Cases differend Pathways and Bosses to fight against.
Giant Rings from Sonic3&Knuckles are making a return that are hidden across the Level. Upon entering one of these Rings, the player will be playing a Special Stage which is a mix of old Special Stages: The Player has to Catch an UFO holding a Chaos Emeralds. By Collecting Blue Spheres the Player become Faster and Collecting Rings to extend the Timer. Should the Player Catch the UFO, the Player will be given a Chaos Emeralds. Getting all 7 Will unlock a Super Form and get you the Good Ending of the Game. You can miss some Chaos Emeralds in your first Playthrough and go back to all Zones to get the last few.
Should the Player pass a Checkpoint with 25 or more rings, he can enter the Sonic3&Knuckles Special Stage. The Player has to Collect Blue Spheres while avoiding Red ones. Upon completion, the Player will recive a Medal (Gold if Perfect and Silver if not). Collecting Medals will unlock Extra that can be used in the Main Menu or in a No Save run.
With 12 Total Zones (4 New and 8 Reimaged) and 3 playable Characters, Secrets to Unlock, Widescreen support, 60FPS and More, Sonic Mania is a must have for Newcommers to the Franchise or Hardcore Sonic Fans that used to play the Classics with tons of references to Sonic and Sega.

Imagine if you took everything great about the classic games, made them even better, and made a game out of them. In short that's what this game is. Now for the full review.
Oh boy there's a lot to say so let's start with the gameplay and move on from there. The game plays great, the control is smooth and each character has their past abilities at their disposal. You get the sense of speed as well as platforming you got from the classic games as well.
Time for level design. For the most part I love the level design in this game (except Titanic Monarch). Now yes it's true there's more returning levels then new ones but every act 2 in a stage is a completely new take on that zone (Hydrocity Zone flips that though [act 1 is new and act 2 is the original]) with new gimmicks and set pieces.
Special and Bonus Stages are present as well, and both are so well done. The Special Stages are a combo of the Special Stages from Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic CD, Sonic 3 and Knuckles, Knuckles Chaotix, and Sonic R. Your goal is to chase down a UFO while collecting blue spheres to fill your mach meter to gain speed and rings to give you more time. The Bonus Stages are the Blue Sphere stages from Sonic 3 and Knuckles, there's 32 in total and 16 are returning from S3&K while the other 16 are new. Your goal in these is to collect every ring then every blue sphere, but the longer you take the faster you go. The reward from the Bonus Stages is a medal, silver if you only got all spheres and gold if you got all rings and spheres. The medals are used to unlock a bunch of secrets and such.
The soundtrack is amazing! I love every single track in this soundtrack! And there's a new Super theme which is also fantastic.
Story is lacking but this is a trip back to the 90's so it's fitting, you can learn everything about the game in the included manual too.
The sprite work oh yes the sprite work, there's so much attention to detail and it's so good. You can feel the love put into every single frame and I just can't get enough of it.
This game is also full of replayability giving you a reason to go back to it again and again.
Overall I can recommend this game to veterans of the franchise but newer fans can still have a blast in this trip to the past.

New stages are just what you'd expect from a modern 2D classic Sonic title as they're just as memorable and impactful as the classic stages were when they debuted.
Music, graphics and presentation are all absolutely top notch and never fail to impress. Any problems I could think of would be, at worst, nit-picks as this is a very solid, extremely enjoyable and hugely replayable game. I've yet to play as Tails alone, but Sonic and Knuckles (separately) both have slight differences in their stories and level areas and are definitely worth playing through at least once.
This is, in my opinion, on par with Sonic 3&K and I'll definitely be playing this for years. I'm only hoping for more now, with more returning characters with slightly different abilities, more new levels and please let Tee Lopes work on the the soundtrack again. I feel Rogue was a bit overlooked given it was released around the same time as Unity. Like Black Flag, Rogue carries on with the pirate theme this time taking the setting to the New York area and North Atlantic. As I enjoyed all the pirate related stuff from BF I really enjoyed more of it which Rogue has plenty of. It also improves a bit on BF with new weapons such as the really useful dart gun and less annoying missions like the eavesdropping ones from BF.
The story is also pretty good with the main character Shay, who starts off as an Assassin, turning his back on the Order and joining the Templars. Its actually quite refreshing to get the Templars perspective and the game is better for that.
Only downsides is some of the voice acting. Shay is supposed to have an Irish accent but what we get is an "Oirish" accent on par with Tom Cruises effort in Far and Away. It's brutal. Another character seems to go between Scottish and Russian. It's hard to take the story seriously at times when you have this unintended comedy.
But that aside Rogue is a great entry to the series and it didnt get as much attention as it deserved.If you enjoyed Black Flag then Rogue is well worth a try.

Well, I tried to like this. I really did. But deep down, the game has a major flaw that ruins it.
It's Halo. I've played Halo Wars, I know that Halo DOESN'T need to be an FPS, but yet IT WORKED WELL THERE, WHAT HAPPEND HERE!?
In an hour, I got bored sick of the game. And the funny thing is, even while playing with Skulls, I beated two of the five stories on the game (I also bought the sequel, which I won't even touch). In an hour. So that's like, two hours and a half of game.
The game also has a few other problems beside that, though those are really small details:
-No reloading. This makes some weapons stupidly broken. Why getting the Assaunt Rifle when I can just go Full SMG? There's plenty of ammo in some maps anyway. And in others you can just drop the weapon and pick another.
-Stages are way too short. Some of them can be beat in some miserable 2-3 minutes, and that's unexcusable when the game has 25 of them.
-The story is... Well, lack-luster. After having gems like Halo 1 and 2 on PC, AFTER SO MANY YEARS OF WAITING, this is what PC gets? A generic story about two generic Spartans who are saving planets you probably don't know because reasons, which noone of that you'll get to care at any moment.
Don't get me wrong, I do like Arcade games like these... But this? I don't really think that it's good enough, even for Halo fans (and I'm including myself there: I have played them all so far, and this is worse than ODST and it's lack-luster unfinished story mode on release). Personally, I would buy the sh#t out of Halo 1-2 if they suddenly appear in Steam, but these companies keep ignoring PC because Halo is one of the games that's making the Xbox sell these days (most of their "exclusive games" are getting into PC, and they're making the console redudant as hell).
Oh, and I couldn't find any Red vs Blue easter egg. A Halo game without Red vs Blue references (not counting Halo Wars and the original Halo Combat Evolved) is like a Disgaea game without extreme grinding. It feels soulless.
