What can i say, Larian Studios did it again. They went to kickstarter and came back with a classic turn based RPG with modern elements that raises the bar for any other game in its genre. A good main story, great side quests/stories for the companions in a beautiful world. On top of that all the dialogue is voiced from the start (no need to wait for the enhanced edition this time around) with some great voice acting.
You can craft, cook, steal and fill your entire inventory with loot you pick up along your adventure over the four large locations in the game.
Combat is off course turn based and allows the combination of elements to create some spectacular effects just like in its predecessor. Taking the high ground, freezing water or setting oil on fire, your strategic options make combat refreshing and rewarding. However, the game can get very difficult even for experienced players. I started on tactician and had more than a few moments that i wished i didn't. i soldiered on and finished the game 194 hours later but i believe i would have had even more fun if i started on a lower difficulty setting. Instead of adding more enemies, tactician keeps the same number but boosts the enemies overal health and armour stats. This means that fights can become near impossible if your party is even the slightest bit underlevelled. A single level increase boosts you stats considerably and this also counts for equipment. The search for every drop off XP, better equipment and the lowest level encounters takes the pace out of the game on high difficulty. You could say i picked my own poison but instead of forcing me in a certain playstyle and quest order, i would have liked some more freedom. The handling of the difficulty scaling is my only negative remark on the game.
As expected with a game off this magnitude there are bugs to be found. I had some broken quests, but am confident that these will get patched out in the future. The Dev's are passionate and listening.
The games performance is great and i didn't experience any crashes or stuttering with an i7 6700k, 16GB RAM and GTX980.
I recommend this game to any one that likes a classic RPG or is willing to try the genre. This is a game of the year contender in my book and the best RPG i've played in 2017.

How do you begin a review for one of the best games ever made? I pondered this for awhile before realizing that without ever playing it, a review simply doesn't do justice. The simple truth is that your experience will be completely different than mine, and therein lies the beauty of CKII. I've been with it since the beginning, playing each DLC and absorbing each change. Unlike some other reviews, I personally believe that Conclave was one of the best things that could have happened to the series - but I digress - this is a review about CKII, not CKII: Conclave.
CKII is one of the purest story building simulators I have ever experienced. The magtitude of RNG means that no two playthroughs will be the same. The depth means that you can figure out the basic controls within a couple hours but more advanced game mechanics won't be realized until 100 or 200 hours in. And that's okay, it doesn't mean that your experience will be any worse, it means there's really that much going on.
On the fence? Don't be - but if price is a concern then wait for the next DLC release. Each time a new DLC comes out the price of CKII and previously released DLC drops substantially on Steam.

THIS REVIEW WAS PUBLISHED AS OF 9/2/2017.  RECOMMENDATION IS SUBJECT TO CHANGE IN THE FUTURE:
Sonic Mania, is a lot of fun.  In fact, I haven't had this much fun with a Sonic game since Generations.  From cleverly remixed stages to new original stages that feel like an evolution of Classic Sonic level design, I can't recommend this version of the game for one reason....
Denuvo DRM.
I completely understand the need to protect this game from software pirates, BUT did it REALLY have to be Denuvo?  Games using Denovo reportedly had performance issues, and while Sonic Mania isn't a Triple A title and will suffer performance issues akin to the more modern games that use Denovu, it still irks me that this is what I waited two weeks for.  DRM with a negative reputation in the guise of "bug fixes."
I won't deny there were bugs to be fixed, but it's SO CONVENIENT for Sega to leave out "btw, we're implementing Denuvo DRM.  SEE YA!"
Not to mention Denuvo's predecessor, SecuROM, reportedly ruined some computers, and while not all computers will be ruined in the same way that not all smokers will die from lung cancer, that's STILL a major red flag for the PC gamers.
Some PC gamers work full time jobs at places they don't like, all to eventually afford the parts they need for their hard earned high end gaming PC.  They shouldn't have to worry about Denuvo potentially ruining their SDD if that's not a myth.  I'm not sure if it is or isn't.  I'm getting conflicting reports.
But Denuvo is so anti-consumer, and this site goes into better detail than I could with my limited first person perspective since I don't buy many of these high end games for high end PC's.
You CAN play offline, thankfully.  But Denuvo is still in Sonic Mania and as long as it's on there, I cannot recommend the PC version to anyone.  Get the console version instead.  And since Denuvo is part of the Sonic Mania PC package, I think it's completely justified to negatively review this game.
But should Sega pull a Doom 2016 and remove Denuvo after a few months, then by all means don't hesitate to buy this game.

If I can be honest, words cannot POSSIBLY describe how much I adore this game. It's not just a love letter; it's a love NOVEL to the Sonic community as a whole. Both old and new fans alike will definitely find at least SOMETHING they enjoy about this absolute marvel of a video game.
However, there are a few things that worry me about this. There are a few references that newer fans may not know about, such as a few of the bosses (that I won't spoil for people going into this blind). That, and there are only 4 brand-new Zones in the game compared to the 8 remastered ones. But the classic Zones are remixed enough to the point where they feel entirely new again.
Other than those minor gripes, Sonic Mania is a wonderful experience that not only Sonic fans should utter adore, but I feel like platformer enthusiasts may find something to enjoy here as well.

The levels are a mix of new versions of those from the first three games and enitrely new ones, and are designed for speed and/or open ended exploration at the players' discretion, just like the originals but with even more alternative paths, loops and long springboard sequences with just the right amount of player intervention. The boss battles are great, sometimes composed of multiple phases
I hope that this isn't a one-off fan service thing and that this turns out to be the success that it deserves to be so that Sega will employ the same team to make more Sonic games.

If you like free-form spaceflight games, in the vein of Privateer or Freelancer, this is THE game to play! Warning: Steep learning curve, and addictive game play ahead! Best of all? You can play with your friends online! Newtonian spaceflight done right!
Addendum: This game REALLY shines when you use a decent HOTAS or 6DOF flight stick! While everyone these days is talking about Elite: Dangerous and Star Citizen, this game feels like it still has a lot of features those games just aren't yet delivering, like seemless planetary landings from space and the ability to walk around and fight on the surface in a "Terrain Walker". Essentially, this game is a combination of the likes of Privateer and Elite with a dash of MechWarrior-lite. If you own a decent stick, and you're considering (or already play) Elite or Star Citizen, you need to play this.
Online play is an interesting mix of freeform adventure and clan engagements, with the ability to build Trade Stations for either yourself or your clan. These stations will actually affect the local economy, and are part of a larger strategy for asserting financial dominance in an area. Come play with us!

I am a midway fan of the Elder scrolls Series. What I mean by this is I enjoy the games, immerse myself in the lore, and have played the majority of the games. I have the first two games on an emulator, Morrowind on an Xbox in my basement, and Skyrim, Elder Scrolls Online, and the subject of this review, Oblivion, on PC. I have poured hundreds, perhaps thousands of hours into Skyrim, and I just can't say that Oblivion is better. Sure, I understand that some people prefer the medieval setting of Oblivion to the barren mountains and nordic tundra of Skyrim, and some have serious nostalgia for it, but I just like Skyrim that much better. Perhaps it is because Skyrim was the first Elder Scrolls game I played, way back in 2011.
That being said, Oblivion is a freaking MASTERPIECE.
The world design is unique and amazing for a game of that age, the characters are engrossing, the voice acting is surprisingly good, the Shivering Isles DLC is AMAZING, and there's just so much to love here. A few design choices are indeed questionable, namely the stamina system. Running takes no stamina but attacking and jumping does? Allowing a prisoner to escape throught the tunnels of a prison? Despite these choices, I often found myself marveling at the world and getting extremely into the story.
Speaking of the story, it's esily one of the best of an Elder Scrolls game. Skyrim's was mediocre and frankly, a bit forgettable, while I still can visualise every moment of the Oblivion storyline. The classic tale of one hero rising up to save Cyrrodil form the jaws of Oblivion? Sign me up!
All in all, the Elder Scrolls: Oblivion is an amazing game. It may not be as good as some other Elder Scrolls games in my eyes, but it is easily one of the best RPGs of all time. Final score: 8.5/10.

I love the idea of a Halo top-down shooter game, but unfortunately, a few fatal flaws prevented me from enjoying this game to the fullest.
First of all, I feel like there are more possibilities for the controls and game mechanics than the developers took advantage of (I should note here that I used an XBox 360 gamepad while playing).  What I mean is, with respect to the FPS Halo games, there are a number of features that seem to be lacking here (for instance, jumping and reloading).
Secondly, I was disappointed by the overall game design.  The game is divided into relatively short levels that consist of simple, rather arcade-y tasks (many levels feel like a tower defense game, except that you only control one soldier).  The FPS Halo games contain massive, story-driven sequences, with lots of things going on that are incidental to your mission objectives, and an overall epic feel; by contrast, the levels in this game feel like bite-sized arcade levels (defeat all the enemies to win!).  I don't think this is a bad thing for all games, but it certainly doesn't suit the Halo universe as well as it might another franchise (or an original IP).
Finally, I was VERY disappointed to learn, after purchasing the game and playing for a while in single player, that the Steam version of the game has NO COOPERATIVE MULTIPLAYER, whether online or offline.  I didn't realize this before purchasing it, because I was familiar with the game from XBox 360, which does have multiplayer, and I guess I just assumed...well, you know what happens when you assume.  I don't understand why the developers would omit a feature that is so integral to a top-down shooter experience--especially an arcade top-down shooter, which seems to be the feel they were going for.  Despite my first two complaints, I still probably would have recommended this game had it included a multiplayer option; but since it doesn't, and other versions of the game do, I feel absolutely gypped.  Part of the reason I bought the game was to enjoy it with friends.
Anyway, I would not recommend this game, nor would I recommend supporting the removal of multiplayer capability from the PC version of games (as if PC gamers don't have friends).  I would return it, but it's already too late (bought it during the summer sale anyway, so it was cheap).  If you have a hankering for a good top-down shooter experience, go play the Lara Croft games (spin-offs of the tomb raider series).  They are excellent.  This is not.

My journey in Tree of Life has been amazing so far. As you step off your shipwrecked boat, you're immersed in such a cute and wonderful environment. It's so simplistic it is beautiful.
As you wander around, you'll come across a few other shipwreck survivors and form a small pact together to figure out how to survive your first night. You spend some time gathering wood and stone and making yourself and your friend a fire. You'll end up making a nice fishing rod and cooking some fish to eat whilst sitting back and gathering your bearings.  As the sun sets you sit back and are glad you have food in your stomach.
However, this is where all the cute nonsense ends, as night falls you'll soon see that the light diminishes quickly and it gets so dark it's hard to see a few feet in front of you. You finally make your first torch and light it! It helps you see a little bit further into the darkness, so you wander round trying to find some shelter. After a few moments you hear foot steps and swooshing coming from beyond your line of sight. It's only zombies and skeletons after your blood.
If you manage to run away and survive the night, you'll be met with another gorgeous sunrise. The creatures of the night start burning away and taking damage from the bright sun. You're safe, for now. You gather some supplies and food and head off inland looking for a settlement. You find one. Unfortunately they don't like outsiders and they chase you away. So you spend the next few days and nights as a wanderer, trying to survive and trying find somewhere to call home. You find somewhere else, eventually, they let you in. They're pretty well set up and the have a guild hall with a few members. You follow their rules and help out and they eventually trust you enough to join the guild and not run off with the supplies. So you spend the next couple of days helping build defences and locks and weaponry to stop the lurkers in the night from doing too much damage. As you're helping build walls, another village has set up a raiding party and sneak through one of the unfinished sides and proceed to kill and steal your stock. You run and hide with some other people, you come back to a base with nothing left but ruins of buildings. After some time you rebuild everything, have managed to secure your village with gates, walls and locks and even some defence towers. So you plan a revenge attack. You're armed and ready to go... Your group sneaks up on the neighbouring village and attacks them in the dead of night leaving them the same way they left you, with nothing.
This is not the cute easy game it looks to be. It's a very complex team-work game. There are many crafts and professions to choose from and different weapon abilities you can master, but you cannot master them all (all be it, you can master quite a few). It's best to have a few of you band together and focus on one or two different skills at a time in order to achieve maximum potential of this game. Building a village doesn't happen easily. The guild I'm in seem to have managed to luckily at least one member online most of the time and they have been productive. I would reccomend this game to anyone who likes survival, crafting, hunting, building and teamwork games. It's basically everything good from other games all rolled into one very polished (for an early access) very complex and extremely satisfying game, and I'm only 10 hours of gameplay in so far.
Pros;
+Graphics that know exactly what they want to be, and run on even low end computers
+ Complexity of crafting
+Sheer volume of things to craft
+Open world PvP where looting can happen (1 item lost upon death for non-murderers, all loot for murderers)
+Amount of skills to learn and master
+More polished than some AAA releases
+Is playable as a lone wolf but more geared towards socialising and working with others
Cons;
- The learning curve, it's extremely simple to pick up and go, but each craft comes with its own learning curve, some are simple, others will have you like 'Well if I need x ingredient to make y, how the hell do I make x to begin with'.
- Some typos and bad translation, although the developers are Korean and they have got most of it down well but there are some things like 'male and female bulls'. But I'm sure they'll get this fixed.
Overall rating 9.9/10

So...Tree of Life...The game is fun, addictive in it's simplicity and thoroughly enjoyable working with a group of folks to build up a town and make neat things/live a life. However, the game is overflowing with what you would expect in an open sandbox game, griefers, thieves. Whatever you want to call them, they will stomp all over anything you are working on, with the game giving little to no opportunities as it is to protect yourself. Enjoy watching that livestock you painstakingly gathered get slaughtered by someone who was bored. Enjoy watching all your days materials get stolen overnight by a group of folks who trashed all your storage while you were asleep. That's pretty much what you can expect from the game as is. It's truly unfortunate because there is a lot to love underneath all that grime. I'll never understand why people do this kind of thing in these games, because all it does is drive off everyone else who could help breathe some life into the world, but it is what it is.
Pros:
+Gameplay is solid
+Enjoyable RPG elements to professions
+Lot of fun to see teamwork pay off
+Combat works relatively well
Cons:
-Need at least 10 people to make a functional town. Small groups will suffer from griefers and material grind.
-Current system punishes indiscriminately, meaning you can't kill a thief without becoming a criminal yourself.
-Locks, Towers and other measures to defend your town do not work yet (mostly just don't work WELL enough).
-Overflowing with griefers.
Final Verdict: The game itself is great fun with friends, ruined by a particular subset of players. Stay away unless that is what you are into. As it is the game is a firm thumbs down until the devs improve systems to allow players who want to focus on town building an ability to survive.
Update with patch notes: So they just released a patch today that adds thief criminal status and makes it easier to get defenses up around the town. It does not fix everything that I listed in my review, however, it does show that they are taking steps in the right direction to address common issues players may face. I will say this, even with all the negative stuff I put in about the game, I still am playing it. So take that for what you will, you will deal with the negative element in the game, but the gameplay is worthwhile if you're okay with that. Changing my review to a thumbs up with the devs doing exactly what needed to be done to fix the game, good on you.

This game is amazing 10/10 sanic speed, actually 9/10.
It follows in the footsteps of 3&K and manages to be better than that game with updated physics, graphics and gameplay.
Graphics: What if the game after 3&K was on the Sega Saturn and still kept the 2D style? This game embodies this question and looks beautiful. Each character and zone look very vivid, sprite scaling, and basic 3D are featured in the game look great. Worried about the 3D ruining the sprite based appearance of the game? Don't as only the special stages and only one effect in the last zone uses it.
Gameplay:
Just like a classic Sonic game, where learning how to play the game is simply by just running and jumping alongside using character specific ability. The nuance and depth to the gameplay is mastering the physics engine to launch yourself up into areas where you can find goodies such as the elemental shields and special stages. You can choose between Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles, and they both provide a unique perspective on the gameplay.
Sonic is the first character, and naturally the fastest. A new ability called the drop dash has been added which increases game flow. Sonic can also make use of the elemental shields. Although Sonic seems like the weakest character in the game, lacking Tails' flying and Knuckles' gliding, he is the most nuanced with the drop dash and shield allowing plaers that want to speed through the zones the ability to do so with practice.
The level design in the game is excellent, with every single act throwing something new and interesting at you and each zone even if reusued and remixed from another still feels unique and individual. This game features 12 Zones, 8 old, 4 new, with 2 acts each. The goal of each act is to reach the end and fight the boss. Level design can have different paths such as Green Hill and Studiopolis, or be more linear such as Chemical Plant or Titanic Monarch, however each level has secrets to find. A small critism of these levels are objects that crush the player being highly sensitivity and seemly glitchy but this only is a moderate issue in the final act.
Tails is the second character, and has the ability to fly. What he lacks in using the elemental shields' second abilities he makes up in his flight. He's a great choice for newcomers to the franchse to get used to the gameplay and control. If you want to obtain the Chaos Emeralds easily he's the best. Due to the flight ability he is the best to fight bosses as well.
Knuckles is the third character, featuring a lower speed cap and jump height. He makes this up in his unique gliding ability allowing him to latch onto walls and walls he can break in levels to access new routes. He also gets a act that Sonic & Tails do not have access to in Mirage Saloon, and can easily shake up a playthrough.
The bosses in the game are fun, but a little on the easy side. The player with the ring system can easily get hit by the boss and abuse invincibility frames to sneak hits in. Each boss is varied and different with one boss per act. Some cool bosses include Studiopolis Act 2, Press Garden Act 2, and Mirage Saloon Act 2.
The game features 2 hidden giant rings per act, which our heroes can jump into to enter a special stage. These special stages involve Sonic, Tails, or Knuckles constantly running foward on a 3D plane, needing to collect blue spheres to speed up to catch the UFO, and rings to extend the time limit. Although the strange difficult curve of these stages, and somewhat arkward controls they are fun to play. By collecting 7 Chaos Emeralds as Sonic you can access the True Ending, and play as super Sonic, and Tails and Knuckles receive their super form.
By collecting 25 rings and jumping into the stars at a checkpoint, the player can access 1 of 40 stages of Blue Sphere, a bonus game on a faux 3D plane about turning all the blue spheres into red spheres, and collecting every ring if the player wishes to collect a Gold Medal, if not a Sliver Medal. Collecting medals allows the player to access extras such as Puyo Puyo, level select, sound test, extra abilities for Sonic, and & Knuckles mode. Unfortunately these extras pertaining to Debug Mode, Sonic's abilities, and & Knuckles mode are limited to a No Save Profile.

I am a midway fan of the Elder scrolls Series. What I mean by this is I enjoy the games, immerse myself in the lore, and have played the majority of the games. I have the first two games on an emulator, Morrowind on an Xbox in my basement, and Skyrim, Elder Scrolls Online, and the subject of this review, Oblivion, on PC. I have poured hundreds, perhaps thousands of hours into Skyrim, and I just can't say that Oblivion is better. Sure, I understand that some people prefer the medieval setting of Oblivion to the barren mountains and nordic tundra of Skyrim, and some have serious nostalgia for it, but I just like Skyrim that much better. Perhaps it is because Skyrim was the first Elder Scrolls game I played, way back in 2011.
That being said, Oblivion is a freaking MASTERPIECE.
The world design is unique and amazing for a game of that age, the characters are engrossing, the voice acting is surprisingly good, the Shivering Isles DLC is AMAZING, and there's just so much to love here. A few design choices are indeed questionable, namely the stamina system. Running takes no stamina but attacking and jumping does? Allowing a prisoner to escape throught the tunnels of a prison? Despite these choices, I often found myself marveling at the world and getting extremely into the story.
Speaking of the story, it's esily one of the best of an Elder Scrolls game. Skyrim's was mediocre and frankly, a bit forgettable, while I still can visualise every moment of the Oblivion storyline. The classic tale of one hero rising up to save Cyrrodil form the jaws of Oblivion? Sign me up!
All in all, the Elder Scrolls: Oblivion is an amazing game. It may not be as good as some other Elder Scrolls games in my eyes, but it is easily one of the best RPGs of all time. Final score: 8.5/10.

+ The puzzles are interesting and there are huge solution spaces.
+ Solutions are graded on CPU cycle efficiency, code size, and core usage. Overall community statistics are provided for each puzzle.
+ The grades above provide plenty of replayability: there's always a way to shave off a few more cycles!
+ The parallel CPU architecture provides a unique twist on typical assembly programming.
+ It's very satisfying and rewarding to solve the complicated puzzles.
+ Since when were engineers given black-and-white software requirements?
- Steep learning curve, particularly if you have no programming experience.
- For the nerds: the program memory implementation is rather annoying, even whitespace, labels, and comments (ha!) use up valuable memory. I would enjoy the game much more if you were limited by the number of instructions instead. Have fun with your wall of unformatted code in some puzzles!
I'd highly recommend this game if you have a passion for programming. You likely won't have any issues  conceptualizing the overall puzzle solutions. Your challenge will be optimizing those solutions or figuring out how to implement them on the limited/unique CPU architecture.
I never thought I'd work with something that makes 1980s era microcontrollers look powerful. You're in for a treat when you realize you only have one addressible working register available per CPU core! I died a little on the inside when I found myself repurposing cores as primitive RAM/register modules...
This game will have a steep learning curve if you aren't familiar with basic programming concepts. With that said, the game has a simplified model and anyone with a logical mind could pick this up. The puzzles almost always have simple (albeit naive from a programming standpoint) solutions available. I'd recommend the game as long as you're willing to learn, the struggle will be rewarding.
Very hard.  Very satisfying.  If you like a good  challenge, you'll love it.

+ The control system is solidly designed and is intuitive in practice
+ Environmental design is escellent in a way that is characteristic of the franchise; the flow of the levels, the amount of detail, and the impressive variation all add up to a standard (good) Halo experience
+ Sound design, particularly weapon/vehicle sounds, is superb; very much sounds like a Halo game
+ Plot is nothing revolutionary, especially by the standards of the franchise, but it works very well for the length of style of the game; the cinematics that advance the story, also, are employed admirably
+ Stats and level modifiers add an extra incentive to do well, and the drive to push oneself for a better 'grade' is certainly a present factor
+ Vehicle combat is one of the game's aspects that stands out the most; intensely fun to play, and the vehicle missions are tactfully placed in a way that breaks up the pace and keeps one interested
+ Missions and their objectives offer an impressive amount of variety; this keeps the game from feeling stale
+ Soundtrack, true to Halo fashion, is spectacular
+ Works well with both a mouse & keyboard, and a controller
- Death forces level-restarts, as there are no (in-mission) auto saves or checkpoints; some may appreciate the challenge, but it often proves intensely frustrating
- Lackluster models and textures
- No multiplayer; limited replay value, overall
- Game is really very short; averages ~4 hours to finish a playthrough

Uplink is a hacking simulation game where you register for a hacking company, accept contracts to earn through hacking. Upgrade your computer to process things faster or have more memory etc. Acutal simple hacking methods are in the game.
Pros:
realistic
keeps you on your toes
active decision making
prioritising of programs
hacking basics included in game(tells you what and click to use not how)
well thought out system of tracing and logs
cons:
tutorial does not cover all basis that makes the game much easiser
lack in resolustion
whenever you get caught you need to start from scratch
starting from scratch there is an intro you cannot skip
not so noob friendly menu (takes about 10mins of playing around)
Overall it is a great game to play for its size, it is confusing at the start but gets easier as time progresses and it is a realistic simulation. (although the anti tracing computer blowing up bit isnt... as when it blows up to cover your tracks u could be using it... in real life perspective)

In Uplink you're a hacker, and you're part of an organization (guess what it's called) whose customers want illegal stuff done, which is where you come in - you fiddle with bank accounts, CVs, etc. You get paid for the jobs, and you can then use the money to buy software or hardware to improve your rig (you have an in-game PC that you use for illegal activities). In most jobs you have a certain time to finish whatever you're doing, or you'll get traced, and your save file is lost if you get caught. You also have to cover up your tracks or you'll get caught eventually (a day or two after the job).
Pros: Lots of pressure during the jobs, this game can really get your heart beating; It's fun to upgrade your rig; Good difficulty; Complex jobs; MAJOR PRO: There is freedom in this game, you can hack any company in the phonebook, you can hack into a bank and make yourself rich, you can give yourself a masters degree in Astrophysics, you can shut down hackers, ruin random peoples lives, make them rich, etc.
Cons: Can get boring, because although there are a few different types of jobs, they get repetitive since jobs in the same category are pretty much identical.
Neutral/Subjective: Pretty hardcore game, your save is lost for good if you mess up (you can back it up by going to the save folder, but if you don't, you're back to the beginning of the game); Requires patience.
Conclusion: If you're patient, cool with text based games, and like hacking (not Watch_Dogs "hacking", proper hacking - although of course this game doesn't teach you how to hack, there are firewalls, proxies, etc., you're doing more than just mashing one button to "hack"), then this game was made for you, buy it. If the theme doesn't appeal to you much, maybe get it on sale, it might surprise you.
For some reason I am not capable of giving games an X/10 review, so yeah... Either way, it's good, definitely recommend it unless you are incapable of playing anything but action games.

Even though this game doesn't actually teach you how to hack into anything, it does an exellent job of giving you that 'real feel'. Very simply interface and mulitple ways to hack and very nice. Jobs can become tedious and repetative though.

For an (experienced) assembly programmer the puzzles are not that hard to solve. Where the real game kicks in is, if you want to unleash the power of assembly and squeeze every last cycle out of it to get the most optimized solution. This is where it really shines. I wrote the first few solutions for a start but then I couldn't sleep because I was all the time thinking about alternative approaches to make it better. I had to get up in the middle of the night just to see if my idea is performing better than the last one.
So yes, definitely a recommendation! For people trying to get an idea what assembly programming is about, it might even be a good start to snoop in, without the difficulties of real assembly programming.
You have to read the documentation to get an idea what comands are available and what you can do, and usually I hate it, when I have to read the manual just to play the game. However, the PDF was fun to read, and if you focus on the commands you can just look them up as you go.
As a programer, the game is too easy and no fun for me. Why should I pay money to write programs with limited functions?

Just bought this game about an hour ago and I'm hooked. If you like Spacechem (which I loved) then this is a nobrainer. It's very similar, but instead of everything being visual you learn a very simplified fake programming language. It's not daunting, and you don't have to know anything about coding. A detailed manual is included that will get you started, and after that it's just a bunch of logic puzzles basically. An interesting story seems to be unfolding via "notes" left in the system debugger by the previous owner. Right from the start you get the impression that there is something really intriguing about the history of the TIS-100 and you'll want to keep solving puzzles to find the next note and see how it all unfolds.
If you like lo-fi indie gaming, logic puzzles, and cold war mysteries this game is a must buy, and I'm saying this within the first hour of playing it. I have a feeling I'm going to be spending A LOT of time with the TIS-100 over the next few days (or weeks, I have no idea how many puzzles there are). 10/10.
EDIT: Now that I'm thinking about it there is one minor annoyance: no soundtrack. The sound effects are good, but sparce. A nice ambient soundtrack of some kind would be a welcome addition, but whatever, it's not exactly like there is a lack of music options that can be alt-tabbed to...

I played this game because I did not own a pc that could run Skyrim very well, and now I'm only playing Oblivion because I never beat it. This game was groundbreaking for its time and while some stuff was done much better than in Skyrim, there was a lot more that was simply awful.
Some Good Stuff:
-The dialogue in this game is absolutely amazing. While there are very few voice actors, each npc seems to have their own unique dialogue, and that dialogue is rarely boring. Skyrim's dialogue got boring and seemed recycled at times.
-Spellmaking in this game  is awsome. Being able to make my own spells that can have a bunch of different effects is so cool and I seriously wish that they kept this for Skyrim.
-Cyrodiil is a wonderful and varied area to explore. You've got snowy mountains to the north, marshes and rivers to the south, and coasts to the west, and if that's not enough, you can go to Oblivion where everything is on fire. It stayed fresh as opposed to Skyrim's all snow and mountains.
-The quests were interesting and always fun to do, not much more to say about it because I don't want to potentially spoil anything, but you won't spend a lot of time playing the main quest at first.
-While not intentional, the uncanny potato faces and character creation is hilarious. I made a new guy recently after taking a long break and I decided to not care if my guy looked normal or not, so I made a Nord with a concave face, huge puffy lips, a tiny nose that almost touches his lips, and tiny eyes that are far apart, I created a monster and he is wonderful.
The Bad Stuff:
-The combat in this game is way too floaty. I never feel like I'm hitting what I'm swinging my sword at.
-Having to chose a class with major skills being your only way of leveling up is very restricting. While choosing those major skills can vary due to custom classes, players are still stuck to leveling up by only increasing those major skills, which can hurt you in the long run because you may need some of those other skills later on (my new uses swords, heavy armor, and shields but I've lately started increasing alteration to use those lockpicking spells). Being limited to only 7 major skills for leveling up does more harm than good, as it also restricts your level cap, and I don't think players should be so heavily restricted in rpgs, especially when it comes to character building.
-Increasing those major skills is broken in so many ways. Being a mage simply felt much more rewarding in Skyrim because your magic skills increasing almost as quickly as everything else. Mages are dealt a bad hand in Oblivion because all useful magic skills except alteration increase so slowly players might as well dump gold on training their other skills. I wanted to grind my sneak the other night, I go into a tavern, face a corner, and push auto-run while crouched and then left to take a dump and get something to eat. I started with 14 sneak, by the end of it, I was at 80.
-Lockpicking in this game is possibly the thing I hate the most about this game. It makes almost no sense and new players are punished for not being able to react faster than humanly possible and end up losing all of their lockpicks. I ended up just going into console commands to open chests and doors that weren't very easy before remembering about the lockpicking spells.
-Spells on the C button as a default. What? When I make a mage, I don't like using magical staves, just spells, so not being able to click to use spells really bugged me, but I may be alone on that one. However, duel-wielding spells in Skyrim opened up some possibilities. Have fire in one hand and ice in another to take out enemies that are stamina-reliant and fire/spark for magic users, and then there was the perk to make the spells even stronger by 2 of the same spell.
-The Dark Brotherhood. Once you finish their questline, there is nothing left to do with them. No more contracts to kill people, nothing. After finishing the DB questline in Skyrim, you can get radiant quests to kill unnamed npc's. While doing just that gets boring, it is really great that you can go back and kill a man/woman if you need some gold or just need to increase your sneak or marksmanship. You don't get that in Oblivion, it just ends.
This game was fun while I played it before moving on to Skyrim, but after going back, I can't get over the glaring problems Oblivion has. If you can get it for cheap or simply want some nostalgia, get this game. If you haven't played it and don't the cons listed, then this game most likely isn't for you because once you notice these problems, they never go away. Hopefully it won't take too long for the dev team to remake this game on Skyrim's engine, that'd be the Oblivion worth buying.

Atlas Reactor pretty much does everything right, given what it is. The game is a 4v4 Turn Based PvP in which player actions are put in on a time limit and then resolved simultaneously. If you already liked turn-based games or if you have a group to play with, there's a lot of fun to be had here.
The game's Free-to-Play model is manageable, but fortunately the game does include a $30 buyout to get the "Standard" edition of the game (all heroes, all new heroes, etc.).
The biggest negative is definitely the visuals. You can tell that the game was developed cheaply in order to sell skins and make money from people who dump cash into microtransactions (League of Legends players, for example). The game uses a cartoony art-style but it looks extremely dated. The graphics options in the game are bare bones as well, so older machines may have serious issues running the game because it is poorly optimized. The physics on ragdolls are also broken in this game, but to the point where it's delightfully comedic, so that gets a pass.
Overall I have had a positive experience with the game after 100 hours of free-to-play and even after the $30 buyout I'm still coming back to it and playing it with friends. It's free to try, so you might as well try it for yourself.

Atlas Reactor features mechanics from both MOBA games and turn based games like X-COM. The result is a fast paced strategy game where each Freelancer (aka LoL Champion/Dota Hero) has his uniques abilities.
Despite a pretty limited number of Freelancers, the lineups and strategies are more than enough since before every match you also get to modify your own abilities in order to improve the strength of your team.
If you have a Freelancer able to lock down the enemies in a place, you may want to improve the damage of your traps do instead of upgrading your base attack.
How the game actually works is widely known: you get 3 phases for each turn, and each skill you use comes at play during one of these etc etc...
Anyway, this game deserves more gameplay variables: there are no such things as items (for obvious reasons though) or more modifications to your Freelancer abilities. People will eventually end up using 2 sets of mods for their skills and that will be it. This kind of things bring games like this to ruin, so we'll see how Trion Games will improve Atlas Reactor's gameplay.
Notes for the F2P version: You get to play both ranked and normal matches with no limitations. Instead of choosing from the entire pool of Freelancers, you get 6 of them in rotation. You can buy other Freelancers with the in-game currency (i got 3 of them in a week) or with real money (which is not advisable since they usually cost around 8 euros and you can get all of them by buying the complete game for 30).
At the moment of this review, the game is NOT Pay 2 Win, all you can buy are cosmetics.

With immense avarice, i'm going to enhance my thoughts on Assassin's Creed Rogue. Surely, Rogue is one of my favorites in Assassin's Creed series. I would choose Rogue for it's intensive Storyline and Combat style. Besides i loved the main protagonist called Shay Cormac. Anyways, let me share my thoughts on few aspects.
The story of Assassin's Creed Rogue leads the tittle itself. Because Rogue has an intensive story. Rogue reveals the story of a former assassin called Shay Cormac. You're going to explore a furious journey as Shay who gets betrayed by his creed. The story isn't about his vengeance but about his strategy and way to save the world. That's how you find yourself in an immersive journey. Actually i loved this story more than few nicer stories. That's because of perfect sequences of the storyline. Like they presented the story in a right way.
As always, Gameplay is the most fundamental feature of Assassin's Creed titles and so as for Rogue. I would say Rogue has kind of simple gameplay. Even parkour is spontaneous as well as combat. I guess Rogue has accurate combat mechanism. So it's kinda more amusing for me to kill every guards spontaneously. But still there are some opponents which would take some time to execute. As far as i have seen, Rogue has same gameplay mechanism as Black Flag. It's like they just changed the location and characters but same combat mechanism. Well there isn't any Level up feature for you to skill up. But you can be more deadlier and efficient if you learn the combat basic and get more solid weapons. You'll be able to purchase many types of weapons, outfit and upgrade your own ship. Also i loved the Naval fight. More opportunities to upgrade the ship at it's extent and defeat legendary ships. This would take some high time for you.
Visuals, actually same as Assassin's Creed Black Flag. If i'm not wrong then i would say, Rogue doesn't have upgraded visuals than Black Flag. Just same visuals and same facial works. So there is nothing special about it. But still this ain't disappointing for me.
Honestly, Assassin's Creed Rogue has some solid and iconic soundtracks just like their old titles. Elitsa Alexandrova created an intensive OST for Rogue. Like David and Goliath, Main Theme and few more lovable background score.
Obviously, i'm getting smooth and flawless performance on Intel Core i5 4590, R9 390 STRIX and 8GB Ram with maxed presets. Besides, i haven't found any bugs, errors, crashes nor stuttering. So there is nothing to reprove.
So peeps, Without any concerns you should try this out once in a while. You might not love it at first but later on this might become your favorite title in Assassin's Creed series. Also this worths it's price definitely.

100% Orange Juice: The madness of a tabletop game now on your PC!
The game plays just as any classic tabletop game: you roll the dice , move the amount of squares you rolled and then wait for your turn. But 100% Orange Juice puts it's twist on the tabletop genre adding many more fun things such as changing one of the core mechanics of most tabletop games. Usually tabletop games require you to get to the end goal in order to win , but in 100% Orange Juice there is no end goal. The map is just a massive circle. This had me really confused at first , but then I realized what the end goal really was.
Points. Each level requires you to get a certain amount of points in order to win. You can get points by stepping on blocks that give you coins , fighting mobs such as chickens or monsters and by fighting other players. You may gave noticed a pattern by now , but fighting is another core mechanic of the game. Your attacking , dodging and evading skills all depend on the character you choose.
The fighting works just like in any turn based RPG: You attack , dodge or evade the opponent's attack then you attack again. Simple as that , yet , if you don't know all the character's stats , you may have a bad time figuring which option to choose.
The game features many unique and colorful characters , many of them being from the developer's other games which means that this is a massive crossover game. You don't need to play the developer's other games in order to get the basic idea about each character's personality , because that's why you have the story mode.
I was really hesitant to metion the story mode until now just because it is so confusing and ovet the top , but I'll try my best to explain it as briefly as possible. So one day this guy named Kai drops his wallet on the street and as he reaches for it , a little girl named Marie Poppo comes and steals it. As Kai chases the little girl , he discovers more people who had something stolen from them by the same girl. After chasing the girl some more , you find out that she was working for some kind of evil overlord girl named Tomomo who was behind this all along. You beat her , get your stuff back and keep your new friends. Well that's the basic premise of the plot.
The story mode features 5 characters with 5 chapters each but unfortunatley all the character's stories are just retelling of the story I mentioned above but from a different point of view. I recommend finishing all the stories though because some dialogue is changed and so is the ending depending on the character. If you're not interested in the full story , you can get the most out of it just by playing Kai's campagin but you wouldn't get all the cards.
Cards are another one of the game's mechanics , each card granting you unique abilities and helping you in battle. There are plenty of trap , battle and boost cards and collecting them all is a real challenge. But if that's not what you came for , you can always jump straight to the multiplayer.
The multiplayer is really fun. You can play with up to 4 friends on various stages from the story mode. You can also play with random people if that's your thing but I digress. The multiplayer can bring countless hours of enjoyment out of the game.
100% Orange Juice is a criminally fun game to play either alone or with friends once you get a hang of all the mechanics. Even if you're not into the chibi aesthethic of the game , you can at least give it a chance just for the charm and humor of the characters. Now that I drank all my OJ I can rate this game a solid 8/10

I played this game because I did not own a pc that could run Skyrim very well, and now I'm only playing Oblivion because I never beat it. This game was groundbreaking for its time and while some stuff was done much better than in Skyrim, there was a lot more that was simply awful.
Some Good Stuff:
-The dialogue in this game is absolutely amazing. While there are very few voice actors, each npc seems to have their own unique dialogue, and that dialogue is rarely boring. Skyrim's dialogue got boring and seemed recycled at times.
-Spellmaking in this game  is awsome. Being able to make my own spells that can have a bunch of different effects is so cool and I seriously wish that they kept this for Skyrim.
-Cyrodiil is a wonderful and varied area to explore. You've got snowy mountains to the north, marshes and rivers to the south, and coasts to the west, and if that's not enough, you can go to Oblivion where everything is on fire. It stayed fresh as opposed to Skyrim's all snow and mountains.
-The quests were interesting and always fun to do, not much more to say about it because I don't want to potentially spoil anything, but you won't spend a lot of time playing the main quest at first.
-While not intentional, the uncanny potato faces and character creation is hilarious. I made a new guy recently after taking a long break and I decided to not care if my guy looked normal or not, so I made a Nord with a concave face, huge puffy lips, a tiny nose that almost touches his lips, and tiny eyes that are far apart, I created a monster and he is wonderful.
The Bad Stuff:
-The combat in this game is way too floaty. I never feel like I'm hitting what I'm swinging my sword at.
-Having to chose a class with major skills being your only way of leveling up is very restricting. While choosing those major skills can vary due to custom classes, players are still stuck to leveling up by only increasing those major skills, which can hurt you in the long run because you may need some of those other skills later on (my new uses swords, heavy armor, and shields but I've lately started increasing alteration to use those lockpicking spells). Being limited to only 7 major skills for leveling up does more harm than good, as it also restricts your level cap, and I don't think players should be so heavily restricted in rpgs, especially when it comes to character building.
-Increasing those major skills is broken in so many ways. Being a mage simply felt much more rewarding in Skyrim because your magic skills increasing almost as quickly as everything else. Mages are dealt a bad hand in Oblivion because all useful magic skills except alteration increase so slowly players might as well dump gold on training their other skills. I wanted to grind my sneak the other night, I go into a tavern, face a corner, and push auto-run while crouched and then left to take a dump and get something to eat. I started with 14 sneak, by the end of it, I was at 80.
-Lockpicking in this game is possibly the thing I hate the most about this game. It makes almost no sense and new players are punished for not being able to react faster than humanly possible and end up losing all of their lockpicks. I ended up just going into console commands to open chests and doors that weren't very easy before remembering about the lockpicking spells.
-Spells on the C button as a default. What? When I make a mage, I don't like using magical staves, just spells, so not being able to click to use spells really bugged me, but I may be alone on that one. However, duel-wielding spells in Skyrim opened up some possibilities. Have fire in one hand and ice in another to take out enemies that are stamina-reliant and fire/spark for magic users, and then there was the perk to make the spells even stronger by 2 of the same spell.
-The Dark Brotherhood. Once you finish their questline, there is nothing left to do with them. No more contracts to kill people, nothing. After finishing the DB questline in Skyrim, you can get radiant quests to kill unnamed npc's. While doing just that gets boring, it is really great that you can go back and kill a man/woman if you need some gold or just need to increase your sneak or marksmanship. You don't get that in Oblivion, it just ends.
This game was fun while I played it before moving on to Skyrim, but after going back, I can't get over the glaring problems Oblivion has. If you can get it for cheap or simply want some nostalgia, get this game. If you haven't played it and don't the cons listed, then this game most likely isn't for you because once you notice these problems, they never go away. Hopefully it won't take too long for the dev team to remake this game on Skyrim's engine, that'd be the Oblivion worth buying.

I enjoy doing a bit of coding in my spare time and I enjoy puzzle games so this game seemed like something I would enjoy. Unfortunately, there are a few major flaws that detract from the overall experience and turned "fun" into "frustration."
First and foremost would be the lack of any tutorial. The game relies on you taking time to read the manual and if you try jumping right in, you will be lost. Unfortunately, the manual relies heavily on the reader having some experience with programming and is often needlessly opaque in its language. Essentially, it's a chore to read. The first couple of levels get progressively harder, which is a great way to get acquainted with what the game wants you to do. Unfortunately, as I said before, not everything is well explained in the manual so you may find yourself "missing" key commands you need to get through a puzzle.
Second problem (at least in my opinion) was the format of the game itself. You have fifteen puzzles to solve, and you unlock more as you complete the prior ones. Although this concept itself doesn't bother me, the way the game is set up doesn't give me much replay value. It relies heavily on you going through later and optomizing your code, something that I am ambivalent to. I do not hate optomizing code, but it's not something I enjoy, and certainly not what I want all of the replay value of the game to consist of.
The story is interesting, and I do like the way it is integrated into the gameplay. I also like that you have blocks that you can't use and have to work around, unfortunately these two things could not salvage the experience for me. It all boils down to a boring manual, little replay value (for myself), and little opportunity to create your own stuff with the code (as what you are given is very limited in scope).
This is by no means a bad game, but unfortunately, it just wasn't the game for me and as such, I cannot recommend it.

Speaking of Runescape the stat system is very similar too as in you perform a action and you will increase your skill level which also contributes to your stat points making you stronger the more you farm a skill. Has to be one of my favourite games of all time. There's not much to Uplink, just a text based 2001 era operating system screen, but you soon forget the simplicity when you play it. Uplink stands alone as one of the first, on of the best, and one of the few hacking sims that are worth playing. Amazing.  Uplink is old (and retro, even for its time), but it's actually a pretty good look at what hacking is like.  It's a game of strategy, deception, lies, suspicion all hiding behind a very simple UI.  Even better, it plays like a rogue-like.  You won't play once, you'll play again and again, and screw up, to have your system seized and need to start all over again.  If you just "play the missions,"  You'll miss an evolving world around you full of possibilities that you can explore.
Absolutely worth your money.

This game is old, showing its age, and may not be supported on future operating systems well. As an example, the IRC program inside doesn't run well with current IRC security protocols (it /does/ connect to real servers.)
But that doesn't mean this isn't a hell of a good game and still pretty much one of a kind.
This game takes inspiration from Hollywood hacking and turns it into an excellent simulation of such. A sandbox roguelike of sorts, you need wits, some planning, and a little luck to become rich, powerful, and save the internet from some bad guys that feel it's time to unplug everything.
I believe Introversion could make a new Uplink with the skills they've gained from games they've created since 2001, and release something truly golden. The market for hacking simulations is pretty much dominated by this decade old game, so something more 21st century would most definitely be a hit.
Until then, enjoy Uplink, and good luck on the net.
Edit: Since I finally realized my review had become one of the most popular, I did a long-needed once over for grammar. Sadly, I'm still waiting for my Uplink 2020 :(

At the time of writing, I haven't actually finished Mania Mode, but I'd say I've played enough to formulate an opinion on it.
To start off with, yes, it's very fun. It's actually the first game in a while that I've gotten absorbed in, and it's amazing that it can do that. However, I think in trying to remain faithful to the older games, it brought along with it some of its issues as well.
When playing as Sonic, the courses feel very ill suited to him. Normally this would be a nitpick, but he IS the main character of the game. Sonic wants to go fast and the courses often require you to slow down and do careful platforming, and as a result, you get this uncomfortable stop-and-go feeling as him. Playing Tails, I noticed I was doing much better, because his slower speed was forcing me to actually stop and think about the platforming.
Despite this complaint, the other aspects of the game, such as the beautiful level design, catchy music, and subtly improved yet still faithful graphics, are more than enough to offset any bad aspects. The amount of content you get for your money especially is very good. A standard indie game would probably charge you 20$ for the equivalent of JUST Sonic's campaign with no Chaos Emeralds.
Overall, this game is definitely worth your money if you're a fan of Sonic, and even if you're not, it could be worth checking out if you like platformers in general.

I'm slightly disappointed that many reviews stab the game for having Denuvo in it, without looking at the game itself. While Denuvo is a really stupid idea, I think we should also look at the game itself, and Sonic Mania is a great game.
This game is obviously catered towards long-time Sonic fans, especially those who are fans of the Genesis games. While I personally enjoyed the game a lot and chuckled at the many references to past games, I think some of the references may be very ankward to those who aren't familar with the series. For instance, in a certain level, the boss of said level has a completely different gamestyle from the game itself. It's almost like playing a different genre entirely for that one certain boss.
Another thing I didn't like was the inclusion of the Blue Sphere bonus stages (not special stages). Most of the time, these stages go on for far too long, and kind of takes you out of the experience of the game. In normal gameplay, you can run and jump with momentum, use slopes to your advantage, build up speed and so on. But in the bonus stages, which are a reference to Sonic 3's bonus stages, you walk around in a 3D environment while being aligned to a grid, as the game gradually speeds up. Again, the gamestyle is too different from the main game, and I now actively avoid these bonus stages whenever I come across one just so I can continue on with the main game.
But, if you can look past these small issues, Sonic Mania is a great game. It features a variety of zones, mostly from past games, that are visually pleasng, has fun gimmicks, and are simply a joy to play through. The developers enjoy taking past zones, and making unexpected twists that'll be sure to make you laugh out loud. I'd wished that the game had more original zones, but since this is Sega's first 2D genesis-styled game in a long time, I'll let that slide.
One of the main things that attracts me to this game is how satisfying it is to build up speed and keep that speed on your own. If you have a good memory of the levels, you might be able to beat some stages in less than a minute or two. This is, in my opinoin, what sets this gagme apart from previous titles like Sonic 4. You have to gain that speed yourself, and the game doesn't give that speed to you for free. When replaying the game, you can discover many different routes that take you to the same destination, and some of those routes may be faster. I throughly enjoyed exploring these levels and finding hidden items and special stage rings.
If you aren't a fan of the recent Sonic games, I personally think this game might be able to change your mind about the Sonic series, despite the minor issues I have with the game. This game mainly sticks to one gamestyle, and doesn't rapidly change the gamestyle like in recent Sonic games. To newcorners, I'd say this game is like Mario, but with momentum, physics and more speed. It's a blast to speed through levels and set new records in the leaderboard, or explore every nook and cranny in each level.
Overall, this game reminded me why I enjoyed the Sonic series in the first place: it's simple, unadulterated fun. If you enjoyed the first levels, then you'll likely enjoy the final levels. If you want to know how this game plays before buying the game, you can play past Genesis games as a reference, as the gameplay is basicly the same as those games.
Edit: I can't believe I went though the entire review without even mentioning the soundtrack. It is amazing.The melodies are really catchy, and are really good. One thing I really like is the fact that the music is remixed on the second half of a level. I also enjoyed the musical throwbacks to past Sonic games.

Sonic Mania embarks back to the old days of the Sega Genesis and Saturn, giving a new 2D experience with old levels remixed and new levels that are so well designed you wish they were more of them (Not surprise to see that choice was made by Sonic Team producer Iizuka). Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles control just as well as they did in S3&K and make the playthroughs different from one another.
The graphics are so beautiful in HD running at 60fps and the soundtrack done by the talented Tee Lopes makes the experience even more enjoyable. This version of the game also fixes bugs that plagued the console ports (PS I also own this game on Switch).
All in all if you're really upset with DRM then theres nothing I can say that will convince you to purchase this game, but If you don't mind like me, then you get a Sonic Game that we've needed for 20 years. I still think S3&K is better considering it still has original levels, but Sonic Mania is a must buy for any Sonic Fan!

So, what is 100% Orange Juice?
Imagine an adorable version of the games Risk, Monopoly and Labyrinth all mixed into one.
Players get to choose an objective for each round of play; collect stars or defeat enemies. Once that objective is reached, they must return to their spawn tile (marked by a flag) where they will recieve a point.
Players can attack other players when they cross paths on the board. There, they will have to option to attack, defende and evade. The games uses values shown on dice, very similar to risk. When a player is defeated by another player, the person who lost will lose half of their starts to the other person.
Game options can also add excitement to the board. There are options such as RTP, which will randomly teleport players to a random spot on the map every few turns.
Over all, this game is very enjoyable, and would recommend it to anyone who loves anime and board games.
Note: There's nothing to do with orange juice, though. False advertisement. If you're here for the juice, TURN AWAY NOW.

This is a fantastic grand strategy game with a great development team that rolls out useful patches as often as they do interesting DLC's. The learning curve is intimidating towards new players, but it is a game worth learning. Each game is a different story as it is basically a simulation of medieval Europe that you get to be involved in. Crush revolts, plot against your siblings and kill the muslims. You can attempt to dominate the world by uniting it under one empire or marry your dynasty to other kingdoms and have your family control the civilized world.
Strategy plays a role in how you acquire claims (you actually need a reason to declare war), how you manage your vassals, your gold, your council, your armies and your enemies. All of these factors can change depending on your culture, religion and type of government. Each character has a number of traits, some inheritable and other acquirable that determine stats that enable them from being good at convincing other characters to see their point of view to being able to get away with sneaky sneaky murder time.
The only big con is the price tag for the game. DLC's are required to play certain religions or types of governments. I was gifted the base game when it was about 25% off and waited until a major sale occured. I received ~$100 worth of DLC's for 30 bucks and enjoyed the game that way. If you're thinking about buying the game, I recommend adding it to your wishlist and watching for notifications of when it goes on sale. However, this is not a con to dwell too much on. Paradox Studios is a wonderful organization and I don't regret supporting them!

Having played before when you had to pay for the game I didn't really stick around long as I only got into the free weekend, which at the time I didn't really feel it could be my new time consumer because of the few concerns I had.
I've put in some solid hours in the past couple days and I think I've pretty much come to a conclusion on what I like about it so far which I'll briefly go through below:
- Queue times - not an issue, probably one of if not the fastest I've experienced in online games, nor is latency as its turn based. Unless you're really dropping out so hard that you're unable to even take your turn.
- Game play feels rewarding - Plenty to unlock through game time alone, and the Freelancers if you haven't bought in full access to them, I find the amount of currency you get just playing is at a good rate, not bad at all.
- Balance - I feel is pretty solid, seen some good (insert Freelancer here), bad (insert Freelancer here), but I've yet to come out of a match where I feel it was pretty one sided because of any one factor.
- Community - A lot of shenanigans going on in general chat but I've yet to come across a salty individual(s) in my matches which I can really get on board with. Yeah, it's probably unavoidable that'll happen at some stage but not having one in the amount of matches I've had seems like pretty good odds.
Maps both look and feel nice, some characters have pretty cheesy one-liners but that's probably just a matter of opinion, but most importantly, to me - the game play feels satisfying, outwitting, thinking ahead, playing around your team/opponents, it feelsgoodman, even losing to an extent doesn't feel to gutting.
I definitely see myself sinking more time into this quite happily, keen to see what's to come in future updates, but I also feel like it's still a bit too early to tell if things won't turn south rather quickly.

Reviewing Oblivion is very difficult without comparing it to its predecessor Morrowind, and its successor Skyrim; so I will be referring to them throughout this review (though less so for Morrowind as I have played very little of it so far). I also played Skyrim first, so I will be writing from that perspective.
As is expected, Oblivion is in most aspects a half way point between Morrowind and Skyrim. Beyond the obvious graphical comparisons, Oblivion's combat, questing, and character building is a mix between Skyrim's and Morrowind's. The first thing you will notice is that the character leveling is significantly different to Skyrim's. In Oblivion you choose a class to play as, much like you would in most fantasy RPGs, whereas in Skyrim you simply level up your skills as you use them. Whether this is good or bad is entirely dependent on your preference, but personally I find that Oblivion's way of doing things is much more rigid than Skyrim's, In Skyrim, if you play several hours into the game as a warrior who wields a greatsword, and decide you want to be a mage from then on instead, you can. In Oblivion this is much more difficult, as the class you pick decides which skills level faster than others. If you are completely sure about what kind of character you wish to play as then this is not really an issue, but for most first-time players this won't be the case.
The sense of exploration is a key part of any Bethesda RPG, and is what Skyrim does best. In Oblivion however, the sense of exploration is hindered by the unfortunate repetition of uninteresting dungeons. In Skyrim you could stumble upon a quest in a random dungeon, and even the simplest cave will likely have some backstory to it. In Oblivion you will often notice that you've seen a very similar dungeon before, and that you rarely pickup quests outside of the major towns. A similar issue, and in my opinion the worst thing about Oblivion; ironically so, is dealing with the many Oblivion Gates throughout Cyrodiil. I found myself groaning everytime I saw an Oblivion Gate, because I knew that dealing with it would be tedious. Like other dungeons, the gates' interiors are repeated often, and also happen to be full of some of the most annoying enemy types in the game (I never wish to see another Clannfear ever again). These issues unfortunately hamper the longevity of a playthrough, and the replayablity of the game.
The land of Cyrodiil is like any other fantasy woodland-style land, and far less interesting than the beautiful and varied landscapes of Skyrim, and the fascinating realm of Morrowind. Most of the towns are very, very similar, except perhaps Bravil and Bruma, and of course the Imperial City. With Cyrodiil positioned in the centre of Tamriel, you would expect the borderlands to look more interesting. Maybe a more arid and rocky border with Hammerfell? A thick tropically forested border with Elsweyr? Unfortunately the northern land bordering Skyrim is the only area with much of a difference.
The quests can be very enjoyable when you get into them though. Tha main questline, the Dark Brotherhood questline, and the Knights of the Nine questlines in particular are a lot of fun. Its just unfortunate that the interesting quests are few and far between. The Shivering Isles expansion to Oblivion is fantastic, and probably better than the game itself. The world is fascinating and much more interesting to explore; unlike Cyrodiil, and the host of new enemies, items, and characters are welcome additions. Sheogorath is the best thing about the whole expansion; extremely well voice acted, and is possibly still the best character in the entire Elder Scrolls series. On a related note, the voice acting is good, but the same voices are reused for characters far too often and it does break immersion somewhat.
For some people the combat in Oblivion will feel much more tactical than in Skyrim. Thrashing at an enemy until they drop is much harder to do. For me though, it felt like even the lesser enemies could take quite the beating until they finally drop dead, and this was more of a frustration than a challenge.
Overall, Oblivion is certainly an enjoyable game. However, having played Skyrim it is not possible to play through Oblivion without constantly comparing the games, and unfortunately Oblivion loses in these comparisons more often than not. If you enjoyed Skyrim you should enjoy Oblivion, even more so if you disliked the more streamlined nature of Skyrim. It may seem like I have focused on negatives in this review, but this is still a great game nonetheless.

If you enjoyed Spacechem or Infinifactory, this is much the same, except instead of moving elements and machines, you move numbers around. Chances are you'll know if this game is your style just by looking at it. This game has given me an appreciation both for low-level and high-level coding. Nice story as well, to the same tune as Spacechem.

If you're a programmer and you like puzzles, then you'll really enjoy this game. Most of the puzzles will be quite simple to do if you're an experienced one, but it's also fun to optimize the solutions (there are also some interesting challenges to get achievements.)
If you're not a programmer, you could still probably get into it, but, you'd have to be somewhat patient and willing to learn a bit. Be warned that all you get is a 14-page technical document, which is good and contains a lot of relevant information. But you will have to read through it and understand it, and if that's not your sort of thing then you might want to look elsewhere. (Take note of the F1-key tip for a quick reference.)
Also, I really like the whole idea of the parallell architecture which makes you think a bit differently.

Simplified version of assembly made fun. It's not that challenging for those who are already familiar with real assembly languages but you can still challenge yourself by optimising your solutions. However, if you aren't slightly interested in programming this is definetely not for you.

Another free-to-play game that makes me appreciate having been born in such era. It is a fairly well-made 2D side-scroller with decent combat system, touching story, neat designs, and good music.
The combat system, while it feels a bit stiff, provides 3 different styles you can choose to your liking, features smooth combo chains that can be combined with special skills, and provides guard/dodge mechanics that enriches the battle experience.
The story, although the game is overall short, is surprisingly quite emotional with enough character development to make you like them.
The designs are pretty neat and cute to the point where people wouldn't likely think that this game is free-to-play just from the visuals. The main characters, bosses, and mobs are all uniquely designed and well-animated.
The music are unexpectedly dramatic, have a good variety, and are beautifully set up for different scenes to really amplify the players' immersion to the story.
Therefore, RED is definitely quite a well-designed game overall that will likely impress you how solid and decent of an experience free-to-play content can offer.

Allright im going to try my best to keep this spoiler free, but that might be a little hard becuase it's a really short game.
First of i would like to say the game is far from perfect, but that doesnt mean its anthing but good. I rather enjoyed the  several 20-30 minute play throughs i did, and i believe there is alot of potential in this game, if it continues to get updates and more content.
Throughout the game you will encounter different flaws such as the translations not being fully acurate, and maybe even a little cheesy and quite weird at some points. The combos can be a bit clunky at times. While there is a little variety, theres just not quite enough to make it a more fluent experience. However that could also just be me being crap at this sort of game. I also think they could have put a bit more effort in the characters names, and by this im not realy talking about the main character Red, i mean others that are in the story, more notably green and brown. Also there is no voice acting, but that isnt so important in this type of game i would assume.
Ok so that's basicly all the flaws i found with the game, except for the menu and lack of settings, but thats kind of expected in this type of game. Now lets get into some stuff i think are going well with the game.
You play as Red. A unique character that i think is a very strong point in this game. She shares her body with two other personalities, vermilion, and Camellia. They both have their own unique combat style and looks, and personalities.
While the story is a very simple go from point A to point B, it actualy still has a pretty deep story jammed into the 20-30 minutes. You will find out the backstory of your own character and even several others. You will also come across several different monsters that all look magnificent, and bosses with their own attack patterns.
The game looks amazing with stunning environments filled filled different plants, and various things to find by pressing the space bar( This is how you unlock the 2nd ending, you have to find a specific item).
The sounds in the game are well put in, including the music. I didn't feel that it was so repetitive that i would want to turn of the sound. Like many other games out there.
While there is no steam acheivments, and the developer has stated there are no plans to add them, there is acheivments in the actual game. The achievment option will appear in the main menu along with the challange mode after finishing the game for the first time. The challange mode is basicly just vsing the bosses over, while they are scaled in difficulty, and speaking of difficulty, there are several options to choose from. Easy,Normal,Hard,Extreame. I only managed to play on normal, and i found it pretty easy. But as soon as i turned it up to hard, i couldnt even beat the first boss, so there is deffinetly difference in what you pick.
So overall i think the game has potential and i would like to see more of it. The secret ending wasnt so good for me, becuase of how it handles the main characters. But that doesnt spoil it for it for me, it was stil entertaining.
