This is easily one of the best and most entertaining games I've ever played, and a must-play title for anyone who considers himself an RTS fan.
For strategy fans, the easiest way to describe this game is as a near-perfect combination of Age of Empires and Civilization, leaning more in the direction of AoE. This is a real-time strategy game with deep but easy-to-manage economic systems and tech trees. Mechanics like territory, attrition damage, bonus-granting Wonders, and combat that rewards combined arms make this game a macromanager's dream come true, and yet Rise of Nations still rewards skilled micromanagement.
The game is a delight to play in single-player against AI opponents and the Conquer the World campaigns add elements of persistent gameplay and another layer of strategic complexity. As with most strategy games, however, Rise of Nations truly shines in its multiplayer. A variety of customization options allow you to tailor your gameplay experience. If you only want to play from the medieval period to the early industrial age, you can do that. If you think nukes spoil the late game, you can ban them outright. The ability to customize your game and to form or break alliances on the fly help make this an unforgettable multiplayer experience.
For those who have played Rise of Nations in the past and are wondering if the Steam version is worth it, I still absolutely recommend the Extended Edition. The biggest attraction is Steam-integrated multiplayer. With Gamespy now defunct, this is for all intents and purposes the only way to play this game online. I have had some hiccups trying to play online with some of my friends and the interface leaves a bit to be desired, but on the whole the system is a relatively pain-free way to get the multiplayer experience from this game. The ability to download the fully-patched version of the game anywhere through Steam is also not to be underestimated. The graphical updates were also a pleasant surprise to me. I had largely written them off when I considered buying the game on Steam, but the first time I fired up a game I noticed smoother animations, more consistent frame rates, and an overall much-improved graphical experience.
To sum up, this is one of the greats of the RTS genre that has lost none of its appeal in the decade since its release. Thise game holds up against any other RTS game before or since, and is undoubtedly worth the $20 price of admission.

I played this game when I was very young, so I undoubtly am biased to the game due to nostalgia. The gameplay itself is still very challenging and complex, especially managing the resources and multi-tasking armies, like most other RTS games.
Rise of Nations won many awards and presents execellent gameplay strategy and tactics due to it's realistic resource/market system. The five main campaigns in this game is also superb. You could play as Napoleon, conquering europe by playing very fun and interesting scenarios, such as when you gain a few armies to invade a whole heavily guarded Egypt (10/10 historical). The graphics aren't that bad either, considering that I'm very picky on graphics. There are over 40~ countries to play as in Rise of Nations, each of them with their own set of unique powers and units.
Overall, this game still remains a great RTS, with challenging and rewarding gameplay. There's no better feeling than managing to take over two countries via a huge campaign of sieging while the AI on your team does nothing but take the brunt of the enemy's force.

This is a very simple review of D:OS 2. I loved the first D:OS as well as Divinity 2. So I came into this came with high expectations. After purchasing this came on early access I watched as all the complaints or issues I had with the early stages of the game were remedied based on player feedback. Larian went out of their way to make this game as good as it could be based on their vison while also modifying mechanics based on their core player base. 10/10 just for Larian's involvement with their players. As for the game itself, if you've ever played pen and paper D&D and wished their was a CRPG with as much freedom THIS IS THE GAME FOR YOU. Want to steal something but are worried you might get caught? Distract them with another character and go for it! Tired of getting beaten by the same enemy over and over? Why not try turning them into a chicken at the start of combat? The depth of possiblities in this game is suberb. Every interaction in the game can be approached from a myriad of ways each with their own pros and cons. Need a friend let out of captivity? barter with his captors then. If your persuasion is low then why not try killing the captors? Not sure you're strong enough? Well, that captor has needs too, why not help him find is missing goods. There is no hand holding and the difficulty is up there with the best of them. You really need to use your brain with this one. Combat is tactical and fun but won't back down from you and will render you dead at the first chance it gets. If you are looking for an complex story driven CRPG that allows YOU to decide how to approach every aspect of the game in your own unique way this is the game you have been waiting for.
The only caveat being it's complexity as a whole. If you are looking for an easy straight forward game you may be taken aback by how much detail and choice there is in this game. It's not really suited for the casual gamer though if you aren't concerned with the rich story and character development you can always just run through killing stuff. Though to my mind, this approach loses a lot of what makes the game so impactful. Magic is also a clearly OP game mechanic though there is friendly fire damage so if you don't aim that AOE spell just right you stand as much risk of decimating your own party as you do destroying the enemies on screen. this evens things out a bit as you have to be very thoughtful about what you are doing.
Divinity: Original Sin was the best co-op game my wife and I had found to play together to date. Divinity: Original Sin 2 takes what D:OS started and expands upon it in all the best ways without ever lessing the originals formula. Usually with sequels you see new mechanics replacing what didn't work so well. That is not the case here as D:OS did so much right that with D:OS 2 Larian really only added to what they already had to make a game that not only rivaled what they had done before but took the extra steps to make it far and away the better game.

Sonic Mania incorporates everything you could ever want from a 2D Sonic game and more, from creative level design and catchy music to spot-on physics and rewarding platforming. I would have liked maybe one or two more new Zones, but the new twists for the classic Zones more than made up for this in my mind. The game features colorful, crisp 2D graphics that nail the Genesis look at a glance, yet take subtle advantage of the increased graphical fidelity afforded by modern hardware - namely, smooth animations, 3D models and additional sprite layers, etc, on top of a framerate that doesn't budge from 60 for better or worse - and the filter options are a nice touch for those who like to emulate the look of a CRT TV. As far as controls go, you'll feel right at home playing Mania if you've ever played a 2D Sonic game at all, and the new Drop Dash maneuver helps greatly with keeping momentum constant. Sonic Mania also boasts quite a bit of replay value, with 3 playable characters, plenty of unlockables, and multiple endings, and the Time Attack and Competition modes are nice distractions from the main game. Overall, Sonic Mania is a worthwhile package, and a portent of great things to come for the franchise going forward.

I just finished my first complete 1066-1453 play-through of this game. I have greatly enjoyed it, and have 58 hours of play. Of this, probably 50 was the full play-through. The rest were tutorial, testing things out, and false starts (where I got 50 years in, completely hosed myself, and resigned to start over).  There are a number of very great aspects to this game. It has very deep, rich, complex, and detailed gameplay. There is never a shortage of things to think about. I have had a blast playing it and am getting ready to start my next play-through from one of the earlier start dates. Below I will summarize the pros and cons of the game:
Pros:
+ Humor -You can become a homosexual lunatic cannible kinslayer if you want.
+ Roleplaying - you can actually RP your characters in your dynasty if you wish
+ Music - I really like the music in this game.
+Atmosphere - definitely feels like the middle ages.
+ Intrigue - lots of great options, from spying to murder to marrying off troublesome vassals
+ Complexity/Strategy - this really is a grand strategy game where every move counts - think ahead!
+ Replayability - So many ways to play, elective vs. inherited, republic vs. tribal vs. feudal
+ Length - even a short game, 1066-1453, played on fast speed, would take you 20+ hours.
Cons:
- Interface - it's mostly OK but there are lots of annoyances, like the lack of a 'go back' feature in many panels.
- DLC cost - There's a LOT of DLC for this game, and it will cost you to get all the best features.
- Ruler Designer locks out acheivements - I personally really hate this rule. Some love it. YMMV.
- Limited portraits - partially healed by (see above) DLC, but almost every kid looks the same, etc.
- Lack of warnings - Feudalism is very different from modern life and some rules you would not expect. Warning boxes would help a lot here.
Overall, the pros greatly outweigh the cons. I very much like this game and would definitely recommend it to people who think they might like it. I highly advise going to YouTube, searching for Arumba, and watching his tutorial or other Let's Play vidieos to get a feel for this game before playing. Those videos sold me on it but you should see for yourself.
Overall score-wise I would give this game about 8.5/10, maybe higher.

This is one of the most entertaining programming related games I've played in a while.
Don't buy this if you're looking for an actual game. It's more like a simulation for an archaic programming language. It's a challenge and forces you to think in low-level constructions. This game will improve your understanding of how multi-node systems could work, but don't try to gain any direct benefit from that knowledge.
It's an eye opener.
It's a great challenge.
It could even be considered a teaching aid.
But it's not really a game. Keep that in mind when you buy this.
It's amusing nonetheless and definitely worth it's money.
This game is a really good start for anybody that wants to get into assembly. It shows how to structure the simple parts of code.

Devilishly captivating. Some puzzles are hard, some very hard. But there are so many ways to solve them. Time well spent!
Even knowing several assembly languages this is not a simple game. The parallelism makes you think differently. The three different goals make you devise different solutions for the same problem, just to get ahead of others. Makes your brain buzz.

UPDATE: Since I originally reviewed this game, I've since played it for nearly 200 hours and beat every single puzzle in the game. I got addicted hard to this game, and even though I was terrible I just kept at it until I persevered. If you're the kind of person who gets obsessed, you'll definitely get your money's worth here.
Original Review:
I hated playing this game at first. Not because it was bad, but because I was really bad at it. I had absolutely zero prior programming experience. I couldn't even solve the first few puzzles on my own. But something about it just made me keep playing. Once you get the hang of the instructions it becomes really addicting.
I still probably won't be able to beat the game, but I've enjoyed the hours I've gotten out of it, and the few satisfying moments when I finally cracked a hard puzzle.
If you enjoy a difficult challenge then I recommend it, whether you know how to code or not.
P.S. I just thought I'd also mention that you can get jump commands from other nodes by using JRO <direction>. They didn't explain that very well in the manual and I spent half the game using a more convoluted amalgamation of JMP, JLZ, and JGZ instructions. Also F1 brings up a shorter version of the manual on the screen so you don't have to keep tabbing out to look at it

One of the most enjoyable puzzle games I've played in a very, very long time.
Ignore the fact there are no fancy visuals, or cute sound effects, no fancy physics or construction. This game will tax your logic and reasoning to it's limit. For a while at least (more on this later)
I'll not spoil the excellent little plot line that runs throughout the game, lets just say there is one.
I have some knowledge of programming and scripting, but I've never used assembly before even though I've experienced it's usage. It is arguably the most beautiful language known to man. Even in it's more modern forms like x86_64. Especially if you've ever touched hex-code...*shudders*
You DONT need ANY programming experience whatsoever to enjoy this.
There are a handful of instructions that you can input to a node and you'll have memorised those by the end of the third puzzle. You will however need to play with them a bit to fully understand how the nodes cycle and what will cause a halt. I must say, despite being rather authentic, the manual doesn't really serve the same function a real manual for a machine of this type. There just isn't enough information about data flow and cyclic processes. This doesn't matter though, a few trial and error attempts at the first tricksy little puzzleses and you'll break through that wall.
This game will get into your head. Because the language is  so natural and simple, you'll start devising programs and sequences while you're at your real job, doing real work, with real code. Just to finish that puzzle that stumped you the evening before.
I must reiterate that this is something anyone can play. You might be scratching your head by the 6th puzzle, but just keep your wits about you and you'll be able to do it. The payoff is a fantastic feeling of satisfaction we often don't get anymore. If you're unsure about how computers actually work and process information, this is a very good starting point to understand it, too!
Two thumbs up to the devs, stirling job.

In this game, you play as a mysterious hacker only known as "Crash Override." The main goal of this game is to pull off gnarly hacks and sell out other hackers for money. This game doesn't have much in the way of graphics, in fact it's really just a black screen with some words and a map. But this hacking simulator is not about the visuals, or even the journey, it's about hacking into a criminal database and putting as many people in prison as humanly possible.

I played. I lost. So I played again, using all of the skills I had gained the first time. Then I lost. Rinse and repeat.
Uplink is tough as nails, yet that just makes it more fun. You have to be so careful, so precise, because forgetting to erase a single access log entry can get you caught. The amount of stress involved in each hack, the sheer panic as I hope I crack the password before I get traced feels incredible. The 'atmosphere' (or whatever passes for it in a game made up of menus) is perfect because the game never even admits to being a game. From the moment you log into the game, it feels like you're actually a movie hacker sitting down with your tools, like a young Angelina Jolie preparing to hack the Gibson.
One problem some people might have with the game is that it's very clumsy and difficult to use the interface, and many of the tasks are repetitive. I personally liked that aspect, because there's something great about having to go through the routine every time, knowing that one mistake could be your last. Complacency is your greatest enemy. Besides, the game is about tension, and having to fight against your own tools to optimise heightens that. It also leads to interesting decisions. Should you open your hacking programs one by one, losing precious time in menus? Or should you keep all of your programs running before the hack, but deal with the increased CPU load? By far, the most annoying thing is routing your connection through as many servers as possible before each hack, but at least you can save and load your relays to save time. Still, for me, the difficulty of using the interface adds more realism, as if I'm actually hacking. Things can't all be fun and games when you play a game that's not a game.
One thing I really would love to see, though, is hotkeys. It makes sense that a game based around a computer terminal would have hotkeys for everything. Other than that, this is a splendid game that I have never won, or even come close to winning. I just keep playing because it's that good. Oh, and did I mention there's also a spectacular (if short) soundtrack?

For the better part of two years, I watched this title on the steam market, maybe like you are doing now. Being a pretty enthusiastic videogame consumer, this title seemed to sink into the background for me even when it appeared on the front page after an update. The thing that tripped me up was my conception of what actually constitutes a a "MOBA" game.
Lateley people seem to think of MOBA games as stemming from some starcraft or warcraft mod with a tedious learning curve, an awful playerbase, and very slow-paced strategic combat.
THIS IS NOT THE CASE HERE.
Awesomenauts is a Multiplayer Online Battle Arena which pits two teams of three agains one another. Each player may choose a character from an evolving list of "Nauts" catering to their own unique playstyle. Throughout the match, players are able to purchase upgrades for their characters moveset. Upgrade by killing enemy "creeps" (enemy AI units which give gold, aka 'Solar') and kill the ever-loving crap out of the enemy team.
As opposed to a conventional MOBA like DoTa 2, there is no long farming phases, the shop system is easily understood, the mechanics are fast and tight direct controls, as opposed to clicking for movement, and the upgrade combinations provide the reletively easy-to-learn movesets with a huge bag of varied playstyles for each character.
The action in any given match is literally nonstop from the moment you rocket down in your jetpod. Immediately the teams rush at one another trying to get an early kill for a leg up early on, and everyone brawls making risky chase attempts and desparate retaliations. With every trip to the shop the scales get tipped, and it becomes very easy for a team to go from underdog to victor if teamwork is utilized.
As for the features of the game, there are several that set this game apart from an others I've played
Local Co-op is always a big thing for me. In my opinion, gaming is about  experiencing cool events and challenges as a social event involving more than one person. The fact that I can play this game on the couch -conveniently, even- with my roommate who has never even touched the typical MOBA game is really cool!
The Art Style and character concepts are so totally unique, I can't say I've come across anything quite like it. This makes for a fresh new continuity with lots to discover and master!
All I can advise for those on the edge about purchasing Awesomenauts is to throw out your conception of an Isometric, slow, boring, grind-fest MOBA and imagine a gale-speed battle of force, reflexes and wits. Awesomenauts is truly the ultimate test of platforming, fighting, and skill.

The Sonic Cycle doesn't apply here.  This is the real deal, folks.
Sonic Mania might just be the best attempt at revisiting the Genesis-era titles that initially made this my favorite video game franchise of all time.  I've played a lot of rotten entries in the series in the last 20+ years, and there have been very few gems amongst a bunch of stinkers.  This one, though, really feels like it could have come right after Sonic & Knuckles.  If you played the original 2D side scrollers in the 90's and have been wanting more ever since then, give this a go.
I'll go ahead and address the elephant in the room and point out the presence of Denuvo.  Personally speaking, I did not encounter any issues with this game due to its inclusion, and I'm very glad that it did not affect my experience negatively.  Having said that, do be aware of its existence here and take advantage of your refund options if buying through Steam in case you do run into problems.  I would have rather not seen it implemented at all, and hopefully it is removed from this game sooner than later.
The music, visuals, and gameplay are all very good.  It's what I would want and expect out of a Sega Genesis game released in 2017.
It's a fairly short game - I beat the final boss after about five hours of gameplay, but I still have some chaos emeralds to collect, and there's the option of replaying the game with either Tails or Knuckles.  The replay value for this game is very high.
I do wish that there was a better balance between new zones and old zones.  More than half the game consists of zones that were seen in prior titles; the first act of each of these has felt familiar to me, but the second act seems to be a new level entirely.  Still, though, I've seen the style and heard the music of the Green Hill and Chemical Plant zones so many times, and it can get a bit tiresome.  Having said that, these remastered versions in Sonic Mania are still very nice to look at and listen to, and I can't help but get lost in the nostalgia at times.
In conclusion, this is one of the few present-day Sonic the Hedgehog games that is worth giving a look, largely because it has very little to do with present-day Sonic the Hedgehog.  It's a great nostalgia trip and provides for some familiar yet refreshing gameplay.  A lot of effort and passion was put into the development of this title, and it really shows.  I hope we see more titles like this in the future, but who knows.  Do be wary of the DRM inclusion and exercise caution, but otherwise, it's great to see this franchise relive its glory days, even if only briefly.

This game is actually really good and fun. The DRM doesn't affect anything at all, as far as I've been able to see. I didn't even know it *had* DRM until I came here to write this review. It's just a satisfying Sonic game, which, wow it's been a while since you could say that, huh? There are a couple glitches that do mar the experience, specifically with the boss of Oil Ocean Zone Act 2. I don't know why Sega has such a boner for Oil Ocean, but the Mania team actually managed to make it fairly fun to play, all up until that boss. There are several death plane bugs when you fight it, which make it really obnoxious to fight as Sonic. But that is literally the only bad boss I've encountered. There's a couple that are just duds, but none that are egregiously bad.
I dig the new Chaos Emerald minigame. I really like how some of the bosses play (the Act 1 bosses especially, they're mostly really good!). The story is kinda lackluster, but if you're coming to a classic Sonic game for the deep story you're definitely doing it wrong anyway. The control is tight, much moreso than the original classic Sonic games IMO. The original levels are *fantastic*, and I really want to see the Mania team create a Sonic game that's all their own. Don't mind the people who are trashing the game because of the DRM. It literally doesn't matter.

This game is a must-play. Simple as that. It combines all the greatness of the classic Sonic games, and adds new freshness to keep it lively and fun to play. This is definitely one of the best platformers Steam has seen. The replayability value is incredibly high, with a time-attack mode, competitive mode (just hook up some controllers and have at it), debug mode, no save mode, extras, stage select, the list goes on and on. This is definitely worth so much for the 20 dollars that you're putting down for this gem of a platformer. I strongly suggest going in as blind as you can, as I was amazed by what I found in this game. Definitely not spoiling the storyline, or even the levels is something awesome. This is an experience that you will want to keep coming back to. Oh, and did I mention one of the most amazing soundtracks I've ever heard. Well, you guys have ears, and can enjoy the soundtrack without me saying how great it is. This is a game that you just have to play. What are you waiting for?

I've tried Borderlands. I've tried Destiny. I've run screaming from many MMOs. Since December 2015 I've put 3,500 hours into this game that just seems to keep giving -- and I still play it for at minimum an hour or two a day, sometimes many more than that. It has its hooks in me like no other game before it has been able to achieve. Few other games, especially shooters, have given me the ability to traverse a level like Warframe and the customization of loadouts to obliterate anything in my path like Warframe. None of them have combined it so seamlessly as Digital Extremes has with their wonderful game that desperately needs to stop being compared to Destiny. They are two completely different monsters.
The game isn't perfect, mind you. I feel like its cardinal sin is that it gets constant updates, but DE has a bad habit of firing and forgetting, so to speak, where just released content is left in the state it is--for better or worse--and they move onto the next new, shiny idea. It's got plenty of glitches (many of which I amuse myself by abusing), and it absolutely has its moments of frustration--and yes, it's an RNG-based grindfest--but is it ever satisfying to get that ONE thing that you need. The best part is that you never feel like you need to grind for these things; they just sort of passively collect in your inventory overtime. Actually, no, I take that back. The best part is that short of certain cosmetics (tennogen) everything can be acquired in-game through trading with other players, and many of those players are wonderful to interact with.
I say this as someone who's never needed to, but has put $1,000 into the game anyway: Warframe isn't just "free to play done right", Warframe is the standard that all other free-to-play games should be compared to.

This is an amazing game:
You have a couple of processors which can exchange data through connections between them.
These processors constitute a network.
Your task is to program the processors such that their network processes input data into some wanted output data.
E.g. you input a stream of numbers and it should output a stream of numbers with twice the value of the original values each.
The fun comes from the limitations:
- Each processor has only two registers and it can only keep 15 lines of instructions.
- The assembly language has only a few instructions and few address modes.
- You have up to 12 nodes
- There are CPU nodes and stack memory nodes so far (I in the middle of the game right now)
- You can communicate with up to four neighbour nodes
Under these conditions you have to program the network to solve a given task.
Each solutions is put through automated tests which decide if your solution is valid or not.
You get some stats on network speed, node usage and instruction count, so you get an idea how efficient your solution is compared to others.
This is a beautiful simulation of assembly programming, digital signal processing and distributed computation.
Plus there there is some sci-fi background story about the device you play with.
All in 1980s micro computer look and feel.

I decided just to analyze in detail all that The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion has in its stocks in comparison with The Elder Scrolls III: Morrowind.
World
Local Culture. Oblivion is completely uninteresting world. It is full of regular churches, houses, and castles. Even the temples are of European style, despite the completely different religion involving nine gods instead of one christian god. OK, the main population of Cirodiil province are people (imperials), not elves or argonians; OK, developers can't really imagine a more original culture, but they could copy some exotic ciltures of the real world! Where is the Roman style of Imperial legion, after all? In Morrowind we had completely different architecture and clothing style.
Landscape. Designers were making money in a hurry, so they decided to make several types of terrain and quickly assemble the world by copy and paste. As a result, interest for the caves disappears very quickly. This happens in about an hour, an hour later any hope to see something new disappears too. Everywhere we have the same details, the same NPCs, and so on.
Enemies
Fauna. In Morrowind we had guars and kagutis, and in Oblivion we have all sorts of bears and wild boars. Isn't it... boring?
Daedra. Well, antronachs are certainly good, but I can't help the spider daedra wearing a stupid headdress, and Xivilai is but a copy of the Minotaur, and of course the main brute is a trained crocodile Daedrota erectus who farts fireballs through its mouth.
Undead. Was it necessary to introduce to the world the banal Lich, while Morrowiind had a very original Bone Lord?
Other creatures. Goblins and Ogres fully fit into the world, but the minotaurs in my opinion are totally irrelevant (in fact they are just casual).
Things
Weapons. It is obvious that since Morrowind in Tamriel some terrible events have happened with catastrophic consequences: the technology of the crossbow has been lost, the people have forgotten how to make spears, fighting sticks, and throwing knives (probably the same event has changed the Imperial style). All weaponry is stereotypical. The developers obviously should have taken the weaponry of Morrowind.
Armor. Armor is as stereotypical, as weapons. Moreover, the gloves are agglutinated with the gauntlets, and the pauldrons are fastened to the cuirass. Also there are no uncomplete kits and unique species.
Clothing. What prevents me from flinging on the robe above the armor? What is interesting in wearing armor on a naked body?
Artifacts. There are very few useful artifacts, especially armor.
Magic
The developers removed a lot of spells (levitation, walking on water, lock, etc.).
Story
The main quest is rather primitive. All sides of conflict are clearly divided from the very start: Mehrunes Dagon is bad and Akatosh is good, the Blades are friends and the Mythic Dawn are enemies. Recall Morrowind. You start playing without any idea what is really going on. You think Dagoth is bad and Vivek is good. And as you dive into the details of the history of Nerevar, everything flips. And we understand that we have done a very bad thing killing lord Vorin.
Levelling-up
There's no need to level up at all. You can kill the cultist of the Mythic Dawn just as scamps being on the first level.
Skills
So, now the short blade is in the same class as the claymore? You gotta be kiddin'!
Alltogether these things destroy interest for the world. Just go into any cave and collect the gear appropriate for your level. Oblivion is just a medium-quality RPG despite it's superior graphics.

"Overwhelmingly Positive" the reviews on Steam right now. To be fair my friends and I (I bought a 4-pack) only played the game for about 4 hours last night. Simplistically I could say that this game is not ready, it seems as though the developers want the players to figure literally everything out about their game as there is no rhyme or reason to a lot of the decisions made about the current state of the game.
The first thing you'll do is spawn somewhere on the island (which we believe was decided by the ship you choose in the beginning, so if you want to play with your friends faster, coordinate), when you spawn you won't have any idea where to go or what's going on. That's not necessarily a bad thing, you figure out the game on your own, at your own leisure. You skill up by doing different things, aka to get better with swords you would keep using swords to hit things, which is a neat system admittedly, but you immediately notice that this game is going to turn into a grind fest, and not only that but you have a limited number of skill points, so eventually you're going to have to choose a few key skills that you want to stick with. I think that's because they want you to group up and essentially build a town with other players, which is admittedly a cool concept, but I wouldn't expect to be able to do that right away.
Enemies are incredibly strong right away and there's no health regen unless you're well fed or have a bandage (WHICH IS REALLY HARD EARLY ON), expect a lot of really cheesy deaths. Luckily the death system is pretty forgiving. You don't really drop anything (unless you're a criminal) and you turn into a ghost for a few minutes and spawn where your ghost is, you can keep moving around and position yourself in a safer place. It doesn't really matter though because unless you're rolling around with 3-4 people, the beginning enemies are going to slaughter you. There's also this really terrible chance mechanic in the game where if you're hitting a tree to gather wood that there's a chance a Tree Ent will spawn when you're about to finish chopping it down. So not only does it waste your time sitting there chopping, you're then punished for doing a necessary action, that is probably the FIRST action any new player is going to do. The Tree Ent is way stronger than you right when you start, so unless you're totally ready for it, it's probably going to kill you, which means you're out of the game for three minutes.
Combat is really glitchy and wonky, it's trying to go for a 3rd person action/combat mmo feel, except early on is not indicative of what will actually be apart of the game. For now it seems like you have melee weapons, and melee weapons consists of sitting in front of the enemy and rapidly clicking to do damage. If you try any funny business, like running around and trying to actually 'get into' the game by moving around and fighting (PVP style), you're punished because the game doesn't apparently have a true "free" targeting system. Instead you're better off standing completely still because the game has to highlight the creature and THEN you can click to do damage. If you run around and try to get into it the game punishes you because you won't be able to target the creature or player easily, BUT the creature can totally target you during all of this, so unless you're running away it's not worth it because the creature will perpetually attack you while that's happening. So you're left sitting perfectly still so you can optimally attack a creature. Not very fun. The best strategy that some friends and I adopted was to gang up on an enemy. Have someone with high life tank the first couple hits, stand perfectly still and then have the other people run up and start wailing on it. It's the most efficient way of doing things early on, unless you want to be a ghost for the majority of your time playing.
The crafting itself is pretty standard affair. You can craft a few things in your hands but otherwise you will need specialized workbenches to do the majority of your crafting. Not necessarily a bad thing, but also not really anything new. The hardest part will come with finding out how to get your skills to level up to some necessary levels to keep continuing down your chosen path. A lot of the time you need to level up your skills in order to unlock things you can craft... okay not really a bad thing... at first... when everything is attainable to new players. What this essentially means though is that you will gather a bunch of supplies, realize that you want to make this better thing that actually helps you 'progress', but you can't because your 'tinkering' or 'carpentry' skills aren't a high enough level. So you actually waste all the supplies you've spent gathering building things you already have! Which means you have to go back out during the day, gather a bunch more supplies and keep making the things you already have so that you can level up your skills to get to the 'new and better' things.
This is all amplified to a worse degree when you realize that you are completely incapable of combat at the beginning of the game. All of the monsters are incredibly strong early on, there doesn't seem to be any real distinguishable zones either. Which means that it seems like there's a lot of the same stuff everywhere, and it's also a really huge world. All of this is amplified AGAIN when you realize there's a day and night cycle, and at nighttime the enemies come out (all of which are stronger then you), forcing you to literally sit around a campfire for about 15 minutes or longer? I'm not sure how long the day/night cycles are, but Nighttime lasts WAAAAY too long (at least for anyone starting out) forcing you to essentially stop everything you're doing until daytime when most of the enemies will die to the sunlight. You could start a fire, which seems to scare off a lot of the night time enemies (we're not sure though?). But firewood doesn't last NEARLY long enough, one firewood lasts about 20 seconds or so, so a fire will literally suck your supply of wood out of you in a single night, WHAT... WHY?!
You can tell this game is not made for anyones convenience right now, I believe the only reason that I had fun playing the game was because I was playing with my friends, that's more than half of the game right there. The beginning of the game is so slow. It does at least pick up a little bit once you get into building a few things and you start farming (like actually start a farm) a little bit, but It's a hard game to recommend to anyone right now. Do not trust the other reviews, they are being far too kind. This game would be hard to recommend even months from now when (HOPEFULLY) they fix a lot of these issues and flesh out the early game and progression a lot more. It seems like this game could be totally awesome... like two years from now. For now just add it to the pile of unfinished early access survival games. Wait. Just wait. WAIT to see if the developers actually make changes, do not give them your money, do not give them your money for the CHANCE that this game will be good.

SEGA made a mistake. Don't you love anti-consumer practices?
In early August, Sonic Mania's release was delayed from the 15th of that month to the 29th. The official Sonic twitter had stated that it was to ensure that the game would be more "detailed" and "polished." This tweet came from SEGA, however, and not the development team for Mania. People started blaming the dev team, and that was pretty bad.
To compensate, though, SEGA gifted people who pre-ordered Sonic Mania a gift copy of Sonic 1
The bulk of the preorders for Sonic Mania were purchased before the delay was announced, and not many people found reason to decline the gift.
Fast forward to release date, it was discovered that Sonic Mania had secretly implemented Denuvo "DRM" to prevent offline play and cracking (the game was cracked in four days, by the way). Denuvo has been heavily rumoured to cause SSD failure and decrease PC performance as well as, well, keep people from playing single-player games without good internet connections.
The Sonic Mania development team has been very clear that they didn't know about Denuvo, and are angry that their game was delayed for so long only to threat hard-drives. Furthermore, the game's Steam store page didn't display any information about Denuvo before it's release.
Are you aware of a steam policy regarding gift purchases?
If you're gifted a game due to a purchase on the Steam store, you cannot refund the game you'd purchased. Many people WANTED to refund the game after hearing about the intrusive software that is Denuvo being so under-handedly stuffed onto consumer's PCs, but they couldn't because SEGA thought ahead. This is anti-consumer practice at it's worst, and it's ridiculous.
I love this game, and I want infinite sequels. I just hate SEGA. They found a way to mess up what is otherwise perfection.
EDIT 9/23/17
Denuvo no longer prevents offline play, and many rumours such as Denuvo's intrusive practices and SSD corruption have been dispelled. SEGA was still underhanded, however, so, note that. Since the game is good, and Denuvo, as far as I know, doesn't actually kill computers, thumbs up TO THE MANIA DEV TEAM. SEGA gets no credit.

It's really a shame this game got caught up in a PR nightmare. Because it marrs an otherwise flawless masterpiece.  If the DRM fiasco is that much of a dealbreaker for you, pick it up on console. Any console. You're seriously missing out if you don't play Mania.

Not a bad game to pick up on sale if you enjoyed Black Flag and want something that is more of the same with a few tweaks, the story was alright but didn't feel as special as some other AC games, especially Black Flag, by the time I was done I felt as sick of "I make my own luck." as I was of "arrow in the knee" and "stole your sweetroll" in Skyrim.
In terms of game balance as it was in Black Flag so it is in Rogue, the various poison darts can completely dominate the majority of challenges the game puts in your path.  Berserk darts allow for methodical zero combat clearing of ridiculous numbers of enemies, and this time you're limited to two pistols.  Speaking of pistols, to get what seemed to be some of the better pistols in the game you have to collect all of an item in the real world / abstergo portions of the game, but these can only be accessed towards the very end of the story, rendering them a little pointless.
Similarly the better swords are locked behind the naval campaign which is a slow steady plod of waiting half an hour then starting the next mission then waiting slightly longer to start the next etc and ultimately is pretty unrewarding since the primary rewards are money.  Money is absolutely no issue in this game once you pass the point where you access the bank and renovations, in fact I wasted money deliberately by buying the vast majority of the animal items I needed for crafting and still never felt a lack of it, meanwhile I was scrounging for basic materials for ship upgrades and wishing I could just buy them to diminish my ridiculous fortune of tens of thousands of british pounds in the 1700s, likely equating to millions in modern terms.
The ending felt a bit rushed, we get the final abstergo sequence, a short story ending which is a bit dull and pedestrian by the standards of the rest of the game, and then credits roll (and roll, and roll, and roll if you let them, lot of people worked on this game) before you're dumped back on a dock to freeroam and finish collecting things for achievements if you so wish.
Overall it is good, but not great.

Hey, if you're wondering if AC Rogue is worth it I might be able to help.
Before anything I'd like to state that this is my opinion but I'll try to remain neutral despite my personal likes.
I'll go in depth in some points but if you want the TL;DR version just read the last lines.
So what is it? Another AC with boats?...                      Well... Yes... But with templars and a new story!
Here's a pro's and con's from my experience:
Pros:

- Great and enjoyable naval fights and commands in general.
- Various customization options
- Great lore and really catchy story.
- Loads of exploration
- Enjoyable stealth and agressive play-styles.
- Lots of collectables
Cons:
- No online mode
- Only one ship available
- After completing the main quests the game feels repetitive.
- Some bugs.
So, in my opinion it's a great game, a 7/10 with really rich story-telling and amazing naval system. I feel a bit biased since I've always dreamt about a game that gave us the power to sail and wreck havoc in the seas like a true pirate and even tho Assassin's Creed Black Flag captured that essence this game feels new.
Also being a lore-geek the plot was well done and immersive in terms of giving you some insight into the templar side of the AC universe. There's a lot of exploring and side quests to do and this can be a good thing or a bad thing. I do enjoying hunting down every last piece of content but that's me. Once the main quest-line is done you're left with side objectives that drag you from random place to random place with not much else to do. With such an amazing system I'd like to see some online action but there's none at all so don't count on that.
Would I recommend it? Yes! It's a great game, a 7/10 even if you're not an AC fan but you are into naval fights and exploring, there's no online mode tho, but it's okay since there's so much to do and the lore is very catchy.

I simply love this game, and it fills such a unique niche. Even years later, I can come back to it... and it's even better than I remember. Very few games actually impress me like that.
But most importantly, the devs really went the right way with their free-to-play/microtransactions route. It feels entirely optional, unnecessary for gameplay or progression. There's no horrible slowdown or paywall, pay-to-win advantages compromising competitive play, and best of all, no lootboxes.
Most games rely on dragging out the gameplay with hours of grind in order to maintain current players. While Warframe does admittedly have plenty of that, the reason it shines is because the basic core gameplay is inherently fun (as hell), and then on top of that there's oodles of warframes and weapons to collect, planets and locations to see, companions to collect and level up, and not to mention customizing everything (best part.)
And it caters to multiple styles of gaming, whether you enjoy cooperative team-oriented PvE, or various modes of PvP. And while most people don't seem to be a fan of Archwing (the controls could've used a little work), I absolutely love the concept of it and think it's amazing. For people who love exploring and treasure hunting, there's Ayatan treasures, Orokin secret rooms and puzzles. For people who love rich story and lore, this game has plenty of it, and I will wholeheartedly recommend that anyone who tries the game at least needs to play until they see the Second Dream. Very few games get me like that did.
What other game lets me do all these things, with such a unique theme? Hats off to DE for accomplishing a perfect balance that even AAA publishers can't nail.

100% OJ is a really weird and unique game.  It plays like a boardgame with the story and characters of an anime.  Throw on top of that a collectible card system and you have a wild hodge podge of different elements going into the blender.  This game has a lot of great ideas and on its surface it is a playable game.  Yet somehow it seems everything that went into this game was poorly executed.  As you'll soon find out, 100% OJ heavy reliance on luck and limited player input is its downfall.
This game is designed to play a lot like a tabletop game.  Its feels a lot like a Mario Party game without the mini-games (and yes, it is as thrilling as that sounds).  Every turn you roll a dice and proceed to move that many spaces.  Some spaces add/subtract stars needed for leveling up while others let you fight various monsters or reward you with cards.   There is even the option to fight other players as you pass them on the board.  You can choose to level up your character by setting goals for reaching so many stars or by winning a set number of battles.  First to go up to level six wins the game.
You go into each game with a small set of cards aimed to aid you in your endeavor.  These let you lay traps, deal a little bit of damage, or shuffle around various components.  Others cards will give you a boost in battle, usually these boost have some kind drawback as a balancing mechanic.  You only start with one card and even if you happen to land on a tile that rewards cards it might not be one you choose for your little deck.  For being the biggest element of choice this game has to offer it certainly seems like the card system is very limited, this is especially evident seeing as you must buy cards with the in game currency.  You're rewarded coins after completing missions but to really get a collection going requires tremendous time investment.
For all the lacking mechanics this game looks really clean.  The colors are vibrant and the anime characters are adorable.  The little bits of banter between missions make up the story line.  They tend to be quite ridiculous but can be kind of fun and silly.  The music is pretty catchy as well but can get a little annoying as the tracks end up repeating.  I have to admit the sound design is great.  The absurd bounce of the dice and crashing of attacks is wonderful.  If the aesthetics of this game are enough to make you want to play just make sure to set the gameplay speed to super-fast or turns will drag on FOREVER!
Playing this game feels a lot gambling.  Luck is a huge factor, there is very little that you have control over.  Everything in this game is stacked against you, even on the lowest difficulty setting.  However, like with gambling, when you finally beat the system you feel great.  You want to jump right back in and show the game who is boss.  Yet while playing, in just a single turn, you can lose practically everything!  Its a miserable feeling that you'll get over and over again playing this game.  There was so much potential here, it looks and plays like it should be a better game.  The problem is beneath the surface there are countless gaps in the design.  As much time as I put into this game, stuck in its feedback loop, I couldn't be more happy to finally move on.

Of all the games to make me rage, this probably wasn't on my list.
But unfortunately, the holy RNG gods aboved decided my my horrendous luck wasn't bad enough, and bestowed me the game that is 100% Orange Juice.
Initially, the game is simple enough: whoever reaches the final level first (5 or 6) wins. It's a bit like Mario Party, except to level up, you have to meet a condition that you have chosen after each level up.
Players can also use cards that are obtain by a specific space, and work similarly to items in MP. They also have a RPG-stunt, where players can battle enemies or each other, rolling dice to determine the amount of damage dealt, defend and evade.
While I've never played any other game but this, the characters are cute and the artstyle is pleasant to look at. I'm not far into the story, but that's cute too. I have a soft spot for cute things, if you haven't guessed.
Unfortunately, as some of my friends have put, the RNG gods are rather...erratic. More often than not, you'll be crying about your luck as you watch your CPUs (or friends) run ahead thanks to a roll of a dice. I'm playing it on Casual, and even RNG isn't too nice to you either. I can't imagine what the hardest difficulty is like.
I'm also not a fan of the music set-up. Why does it have to keep changing for no reason? And the fact that you can't skip cutscenes is also fruastrating, especially if you've played that board multiple times but lost.
But I do enjoy the game, even if it makes me a little mad. I can't say its a unique concept, but it's certainly new to me. If you think you're lucky enough, go ahead and try.

Now that the Denuvo outcry seems to have died out, I think I can re-post my review without getting slammed. Denuvo sucks but I just REALLY want to talk about how Mania is as a game and what it offers as a game.
STORY:
Sonic Mania is essentially the true Sonic 4, without a doubt. The story is simple and follows from where Sonic 3 & Knuckles left off; Sonic and Tails pick up an energy reading from Angel Island that isn't the same as they get from chaos emeralds. But, Eggman has already sent a group of Eggrobos out to the location, which excavate the jewel known as the "Phantom Ruby" just as Sonic and Tails arrive. The jewel gives these Eggrobos new powers, thus becoming the "Hard-Boiled Heavies", and they then use the Phantom Ruby to send Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles throughout different demensions, both old and new. And as always, they must travel through various, unique levels and battle with Eggman and the Hard-Boiled Heavies to foil his plans. The story is told through in-game cutscenes played out with all the sprites, just like S3&K.
ART & SPRITES:
Jesus Christ I could go on all day about how much I LOVE the spritework in this game. As I mentioned prior to this, there are in-game cutscenes told by sprites and their animations. All of their movements and expressiveness really just pop, such as Eggman for a primary example. Sonic's sprites are a mix between 2 and CD and the color palletes on all the sprites and levels is just gorgeous and everything just stands out so marvelously. All the movements and animations are as smooth as can be. It's all animated so perfectly yet you just zoom through the levels. Take Studiopolis for example. As VideoGameDunkey pointed out in his video review, there is just so much going on in both the foreground and background but stopping to admire the scenery is really just something special. I also really love the idle animations and expressions this time around. Sonic's as impatient as always, Tails looks♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when dashing forward at high speeds, and Knuckles throws some punches and
. And lastly to save space for more about this game, thank you to Tyson Hesse, artist of the Mega Drive comics, for the wonderful trailer/pre-order trailers. That Toei/CD-style rendition of Sonic is by far my favorite and you made it even better.
ZONES/LEVEL DESIGN/BOSSES/ENEMIES:
I haven't felt this satisfied running through Green Hill and Chemical Plant since Generations. I was worried about seeing these stages again but once I started playing for myself, I fell in love all over again. Mania currently consists of 13 Zones, five of which are brand new, and one of the five only being reachable by obtaining all the emeralds as Sonic. Playing through the old Zones manages to feel very fresh. The first act is typically a remix of the first two acts of the game it's originally from, some first acts have some new elements in them as well. And the second act is it's own original thing. Such as the ziplines in Green Hill or the bouncy gel/helix elevators in Chemical Plant. These levels are designed perfectly, in my personal opinion. There was maybe only one time I was hauling♥♥♥♥♥and wound up getting squished between some set pieces I didn't see coming (Chemical Plant act 1 to be specific.) The new Zones are so god damn good you'll be wishing that the whole game consisted of them (Praying for DLC one day). Studiopolis is like Hollywood meets any of the casino zones. Press Garden takes place within a serene, Oriental propaganda factory and I'm guessing it's outskirts (and even features a cut enemy from Sonic 1  *fun fact*). Mirage Saloon takes place in a Western frontier setting and has Sonic running through, you guessed it, saloons. Titanic Monarch is the "final" Zone and is basically just Eggman's fancy new headquarters and man, I really like it. As for the true final zone, you'll have to see for yourself. I can't pick a favorite zone though, sadly. Each act ends with a mini-boss for the first act and then another boss for the second. The boss fights are either familiar or brand new. While they're not all challenging, they most certainly are fun and fresh for the most part (I'm looking at you, Chemical Plant Act 2 and Hydrocity Act 1 <3). And most zones also come with their own unique enemies, the newer zones specifically, and that's pretty rad as well. A Knuckles playthrough will present you about 2 bosses special to him only, and one whole act as well. Including a cutscene (maybe two, I'm not sure.) Also, these zones and their branching paths both heavily encourage and reward exploration. Whether it be big rings leading to an emerald, items/shields, ring boxes, there's never a lacking moment when you take the time to explore.
MUSIC:
Tee Lopes proves that he is Sonic Christ himself and composes some beautiful tunes for our ears to jam to. Like S3&K, Zone music changes for the second act. Take Green Hill for example; Act 1 gives us a faithful remix of the classic, changing few things. And Act 2 slams a fresh remix down our throats. I love each and every track in this game but ones that I think of first (on terms of new Zones) have to be Mirage Saloon Act 1 (for Sonic/Tails) and Titanic Monarch Act 2. Re-made Zones such as Chemical Plant, Hydrocity, Metallic Madness, and Stardust Speedway have my heart as well. And a special thanks to Hyper Potions as well for composing the tracks heard in the trailer/pre-order trailers that fit Tyson Hesse's art superbly. This is hands-down my favorite soundtrack in all of Sonic history, honestly.
GAMEPLAY:
So you've got three styles of gameplay here: Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles. Sonic brings his spindash and BRAND NEW drop dash ability to the table, which really helps in keeping the flow for the momentum-based gameplay. Everyone else has a spindash but Tails can both fly and swim for short periods of time, and Knuckles can glide, climb, and break through certain walls by walking into them. And as an added bonus, if you're playing as Sonic with Tails, jumping and hitting jump again causes Tails to fly and allows you to grab his hands for a boost to higher ground, which is handy as hell when you need it. Elemental shields are back from S3&K and provide new gameplay elements as well. Flame shields burn those spikey bridges, electric shields can magnetize you to surfaces in Flying Battery, etc...
CONCLUSION:
Overall this is most certainly the best Sonic game I think I've ever played that isn't tied to nostalgia or some form of bias or something. Levels all feel fresh with new mechanics, visuals, and designs, new Zones will make you wish for more, the soundtrack never disappoints, sprites and their animations are all so smooth and fluent to the point where they hypnotize me with how amazing they are. In-game cutscenes are all fun and I love the zone transitions (but hate when they're missing) and boss fights, whether they be easy or hard. The callbacks, references, and all the nods to older games are wonderful. I recommend this game for anybody who's a fan of the Blue Blur, new or old. I hope the genius minds behind this game bring us more content in the future, whether it be DLC or a whole new game. Thank you for the experience provided within this game. Also, I love the collector's edition, the statue is just 10/10, much like the game. Thank you so much, again. <3 c:

Finally a true sucessor to Sonic 3K, after the failure that was Sonic 4. Sonic Mania is a fantastic game with great visuals, music, level design and overall is full of charm. It is that much fun, it just "feels right".
It has returning stages from classic games and also new ones. Special stages are a mix of Sonic cd's and Sonic 3D Saturn(3D model and stage) and the Bonus stages from Sonic 3K are back too, although those can take a bit longer if want to do them every time it pops up at the checkpoint post, which are not hard to come by. While I like those special stages, they were a bit too easy for me, but that is just a little nitpick of mine. You still have the true ending for collecting all the chaos emeralds and of course the true final boss. And without spoiling much, i'll just say I was really disapointed by how half baked and ridiculously easy it was. It's really the only thing bad about the game to me.
The story, didn't catch me and lost interest. But that's ok, as I was interested in what it had to offer gameplay-wise, but I will say that the story is pretty confusing and disjointed. It's dificult to get a grasp of what's going on without looking into it a bit more.
Pros:
Gameplay feels right with multiple unique characters to chose from.
Level design is on point, giving you a lot diferent ways to complete a stage and each character benefits from it.
Soundtrack is superb rivaling those from Sonic Team, if not sometimes better.
Boss fights are memorable.
Low price tag
Mixed:
Story
Cons:
Weak True ending and weak True final boss.

A dream come true. I didn't like Sonic Adventure even when it was new so I kind of blocked off Sonic from my mind from then on, but still went back to replay the originals all the time. Still to this day some of them are my favorite games with so much personality, color and zany 90-isms, and wacky aesthetics. Well here we are 20 some years later and I still can't believe this exists. Christian Whitehead and this team have outdone themselves! Mania is like the Greatest Hits of Sonic mixing in elements of Sonic CD's visual detail and verticality, musical capabilities, mixed in with Sonic 3 & Knuckles' intricately complex level designs. I'm glad they went with the hidden ring warps for the special stages, since that makes hunting emeralds a little more fun and rewards exploration. While Mania has a lot of remixed levels, it ultimately still has its own personality mixing up elements in the second acts of those zones and then the new zones are amazing. All in all this seriously feels like an authentic Sonic release that could have come out on the Saturn. If you didn't like Sonic back then this isn't really any different so don't expect it to change anything, but if you're a long time fan of the old and have been craving for a follow up, this is it! I hope we get more. That said, this game is huge for a classic Sonic! Even longer than Sonic 3 & Knuckles. And there's tons of unlockables and extras. I'll be playing this for a long time and it'll be in my rotation with the classics now. Pure bliss.

What's makes an RPG? This game exceeds almost all of my expecations, and wipes away all of my fears. Engrossing writing, lovable characters, engaging combat, challenging choices, great soundtrack, and CO-OP. It's hard for me to not love this game in every aspect. And surely, it's a game that's difficult to top. Do note I will mostly talk about the main campaign, because it's what I put the most hours into.
Divinity: Original Sin 2 is a video game designed to look into your very soul, and asks a very direct question, 'Who are you?'. You can make a custom character, or one of the six origin characters (with specific dialogue, unique quests, and a generally different experience), and take part in an adventure alone, with NPC companions (with their own personality and relationship with you), or actual players. It goes back to the roots of RPG's, and gives you ultimate freedom to do and be whoever you want to be. To be whatever or whoever you want. And your choices matter, for every kill and every choice changes the world in some way. The world is real. You're in an adventure.
From the voice acted merchants, to the bustling cities and towns, you'll manage to find every nook and cranny as this game is filled with secrets only meant for the die-hard explorers. Different dialogue choices, hidden quests, OP loot, completely different outcomes; the world reacts to how you behave and what you know. Whether you decide to become the traditionalist hero, to the megalomaniac villian. The choice is ultimately up to you, and the game respects that. No choice nor fight is as black and white as they seem, as everyone in the story is both good and bad in their own rights (probably with the exception of the source king). It's a game you can't really have a "perfect run" on, choices will grant many different and branching choices based on what you do.
It goes back to the roots of RPGs from the days of Dungeons & Dragons, takes the modernism of current RPGs, and dosed with the whimsical love from Larian into a game that twists you as a whole, showing your true colors. In Co-op, it tests your relationships with your friends, as you must know only one out of the four adventurers can be Divine. It's a game that's both cooperative and yet slightly competitive, and it adds great storytelling to the entire experience.
Not only does the game contain loads of different dialogue, secrets, choices, and outcomes, it has some of the most revolutionary turn-based combat I've seen. Environmental effects from fire, rain, poison, and water. You can spend hours strategizing with your friends setting up the battlefields, as almost every enemy have their own weaknesses and strengths you must overcome. Each fight is interesting to their core, making you adapt to each situation in geography, location, environment, skills, and enemy types.
I only recently completed this game, and I realize it's one of those few games I'll have really fond moments of. It's a game where as soon as you beat it, you'll immediately start another run. I wouldn't mind paying for expansions, because the level of quality that Larian provides is amazingly superb. I don't want to give many spoilers to the game, it is full of many surprises that you must experience yourself. It's unforgettable, I tell you!
Of course, this game isn't perfect. Bugs are rather prevalent, as you literally can't get some achievements. Aside from bugs, I do wish there was more character development between my companions. This isn't an issue when all of your characters are actual people. But when they're NPC companions they don't talk very often, only during specific and important story scenes. If you play solo, there will be times when you don't notice their presence because they never have any dialogue to say, which is a shame in my opinion. I won't dabble on it much, but Act 4 is a bit lame as there isn't as much depth to it compared to Act 1 and 2. This entry of the series also messes up the timeline of the games, which puzzles many previous players like me. And the final boss isn't as magnificant as I wanted it to be (no multiple boss phases!?!).
There's also the Arena mode, which is an online PvP game mode. It's pretty dead, and it seems to be the most rushed out of the 3 (Campaign, Arena, and Game Master). You can only select a few presets of characters (no character nor skill customization), and in my experience I had trouble finding a match to play. I wouldn't play this for the Arena mode because it's pretty awful. The idea is great, but the execution just isn't there.
I also haven't managed to play much of the Game Master mode. A game mode that's quite literally Dungeons and Dragons. There's a rather small following for it, and there are custom campaigns out you can play right now. And from the looks of it, seems very fun. The combat is very streamlined, and the numbers are very easy to manage. I find it better than the use of spreadsheets, very long text documents, or literally piles of papers in my experience. But ultimately, it's personal preference.
But aside from that, everything about this game is fantastic. OST (Main theme, Rivellon, all the character theme songs), aesthetics (perhaps the humans and dwarves are a bit ugly looking), storytelling, dialogue, choices, secrets, combat, mod support, and so much more. Don't think my critiques give you the impression that they ruin the entire experience, because they don't. In the end, you'll feel like you finished an adventure. You mold the game, and yet the game molds you. The world of Rivellon reacts to your moves, with its inner gears shifting and moving. You will tell countless stories of it, I assure you.
So, what makes an RPG? The storytelling experience. And a storytelling experience that allows you to be in the eyes of a child, becoming whoever or whatever you want and having your choices matter in a significant way is an astonishing feat all on its own.
And that, is why I would easily give this game a 10/10. Simply revolutionary.

You will love this game if you have an inherent desire to write code for fun, and you have an interest in outdated, esoteric machines. If that sounds strange to you, then you may want to stay away from this one...
The TIS-100 architecture is easy to learn, but hard to master. The puzzles are well designed, rewarding, and they will reveal a mysterious sub-plot as you progress. After successfully completing a puzzle you will see metrics on your code (resources used, efficiency, etc), and you can compare your stats to other players. There is a slight learning curve, and the difficulty seems to increase endlessly, so you don't have to worry about running out of challenges.
I may never complete all the puzzles, but that won't stop me from firing up this game and hacking away at some difficult puzzles to kill some time. If you get tired of trying new puzzles, you can always go back to your old sequences and challenge yourself to see how much you can optimize them by rewriting their code.

Great fun to relax with a straightforward language after a long day battling SQL embedded in PHP (though I'm certain that the puzzles to be solved with that language will become more difficult as I advance in the game)...

It's the nuts-and-bolts yin to Project Euler's yang. It's Spacechem wrapped in three letter commands. I found myself contemplating using ADD as an OR gate as I went to sleep last night.
If you don't like coding, you will probably hate this game. Might be the best recommendation I can give.

So a puzzle game that uses multiple tiny processor nodes all controlled by a simple assembly language.  This is what programmers of old have been waiting for.  It's not quite Code Wars level of ingenuinity and programming skill, but it does refresh memories of simple accumulator-stack based simple assembler programming and will certainly appeal to anyone who knows how to use a conditional jump.  Got it in the Black Friday sale for £2.49, absolute theft on my part.
Do you like a challenge? Do you like when your computer tells you to ♥♥♥♥ off, since you programmed it wrong? Then this is a game for you.

Great game, I love programming but recently I could not get myself into it properly.  This game gave me back my passion for programming. First segments are just a tutorial (as expected) but it gets harder exponentially where you have to reasonably split the code along other nodes. It is challenging, but also very rewarding!
Game is fun, worth the money, even though you can find similar web-browser-based games for free if you dont feel like spending money on this one.
Best feature in this game: friend leaderboards, watch your friends struggle on mission you have managed to pass with best score possible on first attempt is priceless.
Fun fact: I used to hate assembler (programming language), now I love it!

Definitely recommended for those who have an odd affinity for assembly language. Though I imagine the game would be rather unplayable if you are unfamiliar with assembly. I'm absolutely loving it. The scoreboards always make you want to create better solutions.

I've found this game fun so far. I solve a puzzle a day or so. The simple command set is really deceptive as this can make solutions far more difficult than having available more complex functions, methods, or stored procedures. Try reversing a sequence without an array, or concatenation, or a vector object, no tables or pages, nor tags...
…And having a single value registry with slightly under 11 bits of memory in a single signed integer to work with as memory.
So far, so good, however difficult :)

Now that the Denuvo outcry seems to have died out, I think I can re-post my review without getting slammed. Denuvo sucks but I just REALLY want to talk about how Mania is as a game and what it offers as a game.
STORY:
Sonic Mania is essentially the true Sonic 4, without a doubt. The story is simple and follows from where Sonic 3 & Knuckles left off; Sonic and Tails pick up an energy reading from Angel Island that isn't the same as they get from chaos emeralds. But, Eggman has already sent a group of Eggrobos out to the location, which excavate the jewel known as the "Phantom Ruby" just as Sonic and Tails arrive. The jewel gives these Eggrobos new powers, thus becoming the "Hard-Boiled Heavies", and they then use the Phantom Ruby to send Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles throughout different demensions, both old and new. And as always, they must travel through various, unique levels and battle with Eggman and the Hard-Boiled Heavies to foil his plans. The story is told through in-game cutscenes played out with all the sprites, just like S3&K.
ART & SPRITES:
Jesus Christ I could go on all day about how much I LOVE the spritework in this game. As I mentioned prior to this, there are in-game cutscenes told by sprites and their animations. All of their movements and expressiveness really just pop, such as Eggman for a primary example. Sonic's sprites are a mix between 2 and CD and the color palletes on all the sprites and levels is just gorgeous and everything just stands out so marvelously. All the movements and animations are as smooth as can be. It's all animated so perfectly yet you just zoom through the levels. Take Studiopolis for example. As VideoGameDunkey pointed out in his video review, there is just so much going on in both the foreground and background but stopping to admire the scenery is really just something special. I also really love the idle animations and expressions this time around. Sonic's as impatient as always, Tails looks♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥when dashing forward at high speeds, and Knuckles throws some punches and
. And lastly to save space for more about this game, thank you to Tyson Hesse, artist of the Mega Drive comics, for the wonderful trailer/pre-order trailers. That Toei/CD-style rendition of Sonic is by far my favorite and you made it even better.
ZONES/LEVEL DESIGN/BOSSES/ENEMIES:
I haven't felt this satisfied running through Green Hill and Chemical Plant since Generations. I was worried about seeing these stages again but once I started playing for myself, I fell in love all over again. Mania currently consists of 13 Zones, five of which are brand new, and one of the five only being reachable by obtaining all the emeralds as Sonic. Playing through the old Zones manages to feel very fresh. The first act is typically a remix of the first two acts of the game it's originally from, some first acts have some new elements in them as well. And the second act is it's own original thing. Such as the ziplines in Green Hill or the bouncy gel/helix elevators in Chemical Plant. These levels are designed perfectly, in my personal opinion. There was maybe only one time I was hauling♥♥♥♥♥and wound up getting squished between some set pieces I didn't see coming (Chemical Plant act 1 to be specific.) The new Zones are so god damn good you'll be wishing that the whole game consisted of them (Praying for DLC one day). Studiopolis is like Hollywood meets any of the casino zones. Press Garden takes place within a serene, Oriental propaganda factory and I'm guessing it's outskirts (and even features a cut enemy from Sonic 1  *fun fact*). Mirage Saloon takes place in a Western frontier setting and has Sonic running through, you guessed it, saloons. Titanic Monarch is the "final" Zone and is basically just Eggman's fancy new headquarters and man, I really like it. As for the true final zone, you'll have to see for yourself. I can't pick a favorite zone though, sadly. Each act ends with a mini-boss for the first act and then another boss for the second. The boss fights are either familiar or brand new. While they're not all challenging, they most certainly are fun and fresh for the most part (I'm looking at you, Chemical Plant Act 2 and Hydrocity Act 1 <3). And most zones also come with their own unique enemies, the newer zones specifically, and that's pretty rad as well. A Knuckles playthrough will present you about 2 bosses special to him only, and one whole act as well. Including a cutscene (maybe two, I'm not sure.) Also, these zones and their branching paths both heavily encourage and reward exploration. Whether it be big rings leading to an emerald, items/shields, ring boxes, there's never a lacking moment when you take the time to explore.
MUSIC:
Tee Lopes proves that he is Sonic Christ himself and composes some beautiful tunes for our ears to jam to. Like S3&K, Zone music changes for the second act. Take Green Hill for example; Act 1 gives us a faithful remix of the classic, changing few things. And Act 2 slams a fresh remix down our throats. I love each and every track in this game but ones that I think of first (on terms of new Zones) have to be Mirage Saloon Act 1 (for Sonic/Tails) and Titanic Monarch Act 2. Re-made Zones such as Chemical Plant, Hydrocity, Metallic Madness, and Stardust Speedway have my heart as well. And a special thanks to Hyper Potions as well for composing the tracks heard in the trailer/pre-order trailers that fit Tyson Hesse's art superbly. This is hands-down my favorite soundtrack in all of Sonic history, honestly.
GAMEPLAY:
So you've got three styles of gameplay here: Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles. Sonic brings his spindash and BRAND NEW drop dash ability to the table, which really helps in keeping the flow for the momentum-based gameplay. Everyone else has a spindash but Tails can both fly and swim for short periods of time, and Knuckles can glide, climb, and break through certain walls by walking into them. And as an added bonus, if you're playing as Sonic with Tails, jumping and hitting jump again causes Tails to fly and allows you to grab his hands for a boost to higher ground, which is handy as hell when you need it. Elemental shields are back from S3&K and provide new gameplay elements as well. Flame shields burn those spikey bridges, electric shields can magnetize you to surfaces in Flying Battery, etc...
CONCLUSION:
Overall this is most certainly the best Sonic game I think I've ever played that isn't tied to nostalgia or some form of bias or something. Levels all feel fresh with new mechanics, visuals, and designs, new Zones will make you wish for more, the soundtrack never disappoints, sprites and their animations are all so smooth and fluent to the point where they hypnotize me with how amazing they are. In-game cutscenes are all fun and I love the zone transitions (but hate when they're missing) and boss fights, whether they be easy or hard. The callbacks, references, and all the nods to older games are wonderful. I recommend this game for anybody who's a fan of the Blue Blur, new or old. I hope the genius minds behind this game bring us more content in the future, whether it be DLC or a whole new game. Thank you for the experience provided within this game. Also, I love the collector's edition, the statue is just 10/10, much like the game. Thank you so much, again. <3 c:
