A dream come true. I didn't like Sonic Adventure even when it was new so I kind of blocked off Sonic from my mind from then on, but still went back to replay the originals all the time. Still to this day some of them are my favorite games with so much personality, color and zany 90-isms, and wacky aesthetics. Well here we are 20 some years later and I still can't believe this exists. Christian Whitehead and this team have outdone themselves! Mania is like the Greatest Hits of Sonic mixing in elements of Sonic CD's visual detail and verticality, musical capabilities, mixed in with Sonic 3 & Knuckles' intricately complex level designs. I'm glad they went with the hidden ring warps for the special stages, since that makes hunting emeralds a little more fun and rewards exploration. While Mania has a lot of remixed levels, it ultimately still has its own personality mixing up elements in the second acts of those zones and then the new zones are amazing. All in all this seriously feels like an authentic Sonic release that could have come out on the Saturn. If you didn't like Sonic back then this isn't really any different so don't expect it to change anything, but if you're a long time fan of the old and have been craving for a follow up, this is it! I hope we get more. That said, this game is huge for a classic Sonic! Even longer than Sonic 3 & Knuckles. And there's tons of unlockables and extras. I'll be playing this for a long time and it'll be in my rotation with the classics now. Pure bliss.

This is really everything I wanted from an indie hacking game. It is a vast and glorious sandbox brimming with opportunity. To tell its tale, let me start the story about twenty-five years ago, with a little gem from Interplay called "Neuromancer."
Neuromancer was an amazing piece of work, for its time. A point and click adventure game, yes, but with a vast collection of BBS-like "sites" in "cyberspace," which could be accessed and navigated spatially, a sea of semitransparent polygons on a sprawling grid. They called the book "prophetic" in its vision of what a global computer network might be like, but the game was similarly visionary, in that it offered a classic milestone-and-unlocked-door-driven main story, but with a vast and layered world of enriching side stories and tiny details easily overlooked, that add depth and character to the world in which your character lives. This was a level of detail and nuance and supporting gameworld-enrichment that Bioware would go on to become famous for, in its epic D&D games of the Nineties, and in its later adventure games, but in the Eighties, on computers that were much more limited in resources, this was a bigger feat, and a bigger surprise to the player. You could just play Neuromancer to win it, or you could play it to learn about it, follow the exchanges on the PAX and on private sites, the private message exchanges between AIs. You could learn so much more that way, if you were clever and patient enough to retain it, to piece it together, and to make sense of it all.
It had its limitations, though. For all that supplemental-story richness, hacking was extremely primitive and frankly, rather RPG-combat-like. There wasn't much finesse to it, and though there was some pressure to stay alert and focused, it lacked the sweaty-fingers-and-hurry-hurry-hurry aspect we associate with computer crime.
Now here's where Uplink steps onto the scene.
Uplink isn't a classic RPG -- whether or not it's an RPG at all is a very good question, and I'm not sure how to address the question without spoilers. The game starts very simply; you're a hacker with a server in a colocation facility, and through it, you can access the internet. Your employer offers you access to a database of open hacking jobs commensurate to your demonstrated ability and toolkit, and you can carry them out for money. For many people, this is the entire game of Uplink -- choosing jobs, carrying them out, getting paid. It's fun stuff! The clock is always ticking. Traces are run to try to find you. You've got that sweaty palms, twitchy-taut-nerves, GO GO GO GO GO adrenaline headspace, typing and tapping and trying frantically to get the job done and wipe logs before you're traced and busted.
But why stop there? What I feel I can safely say without spoilers is that the game is very much a sandbox, and as your means grow, you find yourself able to make decisions about the nature and purpose of your work. Who you work for, why you work, what work you do and don't do, and what you're after will determine what the game looks like, to you.
A rich and detailed world sprawls before you, full of interesting things to learn, do and find. Curiosity is rewarded. Tinkering is rewarded. Ingenuity is especially rewarded. There is a "master story," but whether or not you ever even encounter it -- well, that's up to you.
The game uses a very retro interface style; it reminded me of the turn-of-the-millennium retrofuture aesthetic, and made me nostalgic for the days of multiple Unix flavors on huge proprietary hardware. Be sure to be very, very glib with your mouse skills; fast accurate clicking is a must. A touchscreen system with a keyboard would probably be ideal, but rest assured, this Uplinker runs just fine on his non-touchscreen laptop. Speed is critical, a cool head and the ability to systemically run through a list of easy but specific tasks with a ticking timer is also critical. If you don't like to be under pressure, Uplink isn't for you.
If you're looking for great visual beauty and visual exploration as found in, say, point-and-click adventure games, look elsewhere. You'll spend all your time in Uplink staring at a virtual desktop environment. Some people will find that thrilling -- I'm one of 'em! -- and some will surely be put off by it. Uplink also enforces consequences beautifully; really bad decisions will even wipe your savegame, be warned. (Can you back it up sneakily and restore it? Yes, yes you can, you...cheating hacker, you.) But most of all, if you're looking for a game that makes it easy to understand what you're supposed to do, this is utterly not the game for you. Uplink's as silent and as uncommunicative as a bash prompt, and that's why it's perfectly suited to the right kind of oldschool-hackerly mind.
You've probably formed a strong opinion of Uplink already, just from what I've said. Good. If you're the sort who loves this sort of thing, Uplink is the game you've been waiting for, and there's nothing quite like it. This is what Neuromancer wanted to be like, I think...and might have been, but for that its dreams of electric sheep were limited in resolution and framerate by its era.

Frozen Synapse is one of those games that looks to be terribly simple... But is much more complex than meets the eye. Think of it as playing "toy soldiers", albeit with realistic line of sight and reaction times, and different weapons, with a fancy cyberpunkish story. It's turn-based so you have plenty of time to plan your moves, like move, run, kneel, aim at, and so on. Once you commit, you'll likely curse as yourself for moving the wrong way, or pat yourself in the back for having anticipated your opponent and set a trap for him. You start with just rifleman and shotgunner, but later you get snipers, RPGer, grenadier, and more. And of course, your objectives will vary, from search and destroy, to survival, to escort, and much more. Some will even have turn limits, while others would be sensor dark (i.e. only enemies within line-of-sight can be seen).
While the single player campaigns are good, the heart of the game is in the multiplayer and the online matchmaking system. Play against others, get ranked, and much more.
Not for twitch gamers, but if you relish some tactical combat where planning the right move is more satisfying than making the right shot, then this is your game.

I have spent a large amount of time in this game which implies that I enjoyed myself.  Thing is, I had for the first few hours, but over time, as I came back months after months later, the game was no longer the same.  While it is an addicting game in of itself, Awesomenauts doesn't have much going for it other than the music.
Quite honestly, the music is the best part about this game.  Everything else is just not up to par.  Matchmaking is probably the worst offender.  While they do have a league set-up, the game tends to not even match you up within the same league.  If that's not enough, even if you turn the "find players worldwide" option off, you'll still be matched with players from Australia.  Coupling the bad matchmaking with the awful, unbalanced Awesomenauts, you'll find yourself irritated as you play longer and longer.
The way that they balance their Awesomenauts is through a group of players known as the "Betanauts" who play and give suggestions on what to change.  While this may not seem too bad when you first think about it, you need to know that they alone decide the metagame.  Characters that are unbalanced are likely to stay that way as time goes on and other characters that don't need nerfs will get them to the point they're unusable.  Furthermore, the way the game is set up, it benefits whatever team does more burst damage, to the point where you can have a team that just can't challenge the other team at all because of the matchups.
Of course, that wouldn't be a problem if you could see who the other team picked and what map you were playing on.  Which you can't, of course, nor can you even communicate with your team through a chat while picking characters.  Furthermore, out of the 4 maps, only 1 is even remotely good as the others are unbalanced and make the match drag on for far too long.
In my recommendation, you should honestly pass on this game.  While it is addicting, it's not very fun and you're more than likely to get irritated while playing.

I believe this is an example of a truly great free-to-play game. The game is a fast-paced action/shooter/rpg hybrid that offers a huge assortment of characters and weapons to play with and customize, diverse misson types, and some very interesting lore driven quests and story elements. The movement and combat is very fun, smooth, and engaging. The game looks and runs great even without the most updated hardware, and a good deal of the music is top notch as well. The community is by far one of the friendlier, more positive ones I've seen in an online game. The developers themselves are very active and engaged with the community, and the game gets updates on a regular and frequent basis.
What really makes me appreciate this game though is that I feel it does f2p monetization right. No gameplay altering items or features are locked behind cash aside from inventory slots, which are cheap and not needed too early on. A feature this game has that I haven't seen in others is that the real-money currency is tradeable between players. This means you can even get the nice cosmetics you want and those inventory slots mentioned before without spending any cash, you just need to be willing to spend some time farming items.
The game does have its flaws. There are often bugs that pop up with updates, most minor, but some particularly annoying. These are usually fixed quickly, but a few have lasted some time. The farming required to get some items can be very tedious and lengthy, similar to other games with random drops.
Overall, if you don't mind some amount of grinding, Warframe is a very fun, well made game that is definitely worth playing.

This game is pretty dang awesome for anyone looking for a softer Sandbox title that doesn't revolve around PvP.  PvP is a factor, but it rewards killing player-killers more than anything, since dying as a green-name only drops one random item as opposed to dying as a red-name which empties your whole inventory and is a persistent consequence that lasts for a full hour no matter how many times you die during it.   Also killing red-names keeps your name green instead of turning it red for killing someone, so you can basically kill griefers and loot all their♥♥♥♥♥♥to punish them.
Skills are pretty varied, but the cool thing is that you gain stats per each skill level, and you only have so many points to level skills with, and each skill raises a certain stat every 1 and 4 levels (i.e. Farming raises Con every 1 level and Str every 4 levels - 20 Farming will give you +20 Constitution and +5 Strength). As a result, you can choose stuff to specialize in or be a jack of all trades if you wish to.   The skills range from crafting to combat to stuff like music and mining and farming.   No matter what you skill up though, you're benefiting it via stats.  So even if you're a hardcore Farmer and lack combat prowess, you'll still be able to take a ton of hits and still hurt enemies a good amount.
Exploration is a huge factor to the game as well, as you won't be able to find everything in one single area.  As the game adds more to find and do, exploration will be even more beneficial.   So while settling down is very smart to do (especially with other players since many hands will make the work much easier), exploring is still quite important as you can bring stuff non-native to your area and cultivate it.   For example, reindeers in the frozen regions can theoretically be bred in other areas as long as you grab a male and female one.   Crops like Lettuce, Corn, and various tree types also are scattered in different regions, so it's highly beneficial to bring some seeds or carry saplings over.
The coolest thing is that everything's persistent.  While some stuff does randomly respawn or regenerate in areas, you really do need to think before you recklessly cut/punch down an entire forest.
Survival is the name of the game here, but you're surviving more against the crazy nighttime environment more than other players.  It gives you a reason to team up with others and form pockets of civilization throughout the land.  Settlements can become cities, cities can become kingdoms, kingdoms can become empires... the potential is ridiculous.  As long as Odd One Games sticks to supporting and improving and adding to the game, I see nothing but good things to come out of Tree of Life.   If you liked stuff like ArcheAge or Rust but were turned off by the PvP-centric gameplay and wished for something more focused on cooperation and exploration in a hostile land that you need to band together to fight against, Tree of Life may be right up your alley.
I didn't even know anything about this game 12 hours ago.  But it left me presently surprised and I'm so stoked to see what Odd One Games has for the future, as long as they don't screw things up majorly.
And yes, there are bugs to be expected in Early Access.  Some people have issues more severely and frequently than others, but overall I've had a very positive first day in Tree of Savior and I strongly reccommend this game if you're looking to get lost in a true virtual world.

For it's Early Access beta nature, the game seems surprisingly polished. I've seen games with a lot more crashing after their release!
First of all, Tree of Life is a survival MMO taking cues from games such as Minecraft and Ultima Online. The community aspect is very focused on, you can build together and hunt together. Also PvP is always possible but slightly discouraged through a criminal system. It seems to prevent people from generally going around, smashing everything to bits. People can catch you at your weakest in this game. I was sitting around at night, next to my fire (because fire is the only thing protecting you from the undead a night) and someone just ran in, killed me and destroyed all my stuff.
Crafting
The crafting aspect is pretty well made. You have an inventory of items and a crafting screen. Additional to that, you can build tool benches and other appliances to make you capable of crafting more, other things. Generally this reminds me of "A Tale In The Desert", which is... delightful. Gathering is often done by smashing stuff to pieces and taking the resources with you. In the other instances it is done through on screen actions in a 4-way "ring menu" around your aiming reticule.
The aiming and movement is WASD and no-click, but full 3rd person twitch based. One thing I found strange is that running (double tap W) empties your stamina very, very fast in 100 increments every two seconds (you start with about 250 stamina), I feel that should use less of it.
Battle is basically aiming your reticule in a way to make a border around your enemy light up (targeted) and hitting the left mouse button n times. This is a very boring way to describe it but oftentimes I find myself trying to target something and it wouldn't target unless I point the reticule somewhere else on the target. This is something that I attribute to the beta (or alpha even?) state, though, so it can pass.
What I found pretty intuitive and great is that you don't only have your inventory to carry things. Things that are large and wouldnt fit in a slot in your inventory can be carried on your shoulder, slowing your movement down. I found that a great idea because it gives sense to the size of things you build. I wish I could have a donkey or something to carry more things, though.
Building larger things, by the way, is done through creating blueprints of the thing and setting that down as a building site. People can then select items that are needed and start applying them to the building. It looks neat, really gives a sense to building something and actually kind of looks like people building in strategy games like Age of Empires.
All in all, I recommend this game because it already feels polished and could turn into a great game!

Experience of the game
(+) Interesting skill tree and item discovery -
There is tons of skills to learn and leveling different skills unlock different items and objects to build, which the game does not babysit you
(+) Huge map with many places to explore -
Map is big for an early release game, with different areas consisting of different materials, which leads to a need to explore
(+) Interdependence between players -
Each player only has 400 skill points for their skills, with more than 15 available skill trees. Moreover, most of the items requires 1 or more  profession to build.
(+) Cooperative nature -
Cooperation is essential to get far in the game. Everyone, including settlers, nomads and PVPers require some sort of cooperation to get ahead.
(-) Slow-paced, grindy -
Requires grinding to gain exp for skill levels. This leads to an overproduction of items on the ground for the sake of exp alone.
(-) No chat option / friend list -
It is hard to get in touch with fellow adventurers after going off alone to explore for a while. Furthermore, guild hall is only available at level 25.
(-) Requires time and trusted friends for the initial setup of your settlement -
A significant amount of time has to be invested before you are able to setup your first secured settlement, and even so, you need to constantly rely on your friends in the same settlement for future expansion and building.
TL : DR
Basically, game is fun and interesting, with many skills to learn and many areas to explore. The game is also cooperative in nature, requiring more players to get an edge over others. However, it is sort of grindy and requires time and friends you can trust to play with you.
If you are able to get hold of some of your friends to buy and play the game with you, it would most probably be a blast if you enjoy survival crafting games, with elements of MMO. If not, you are down to your skills and luck to find a good group ingame that you can count on to commit and share the resources together.

Tree of Life is, as it stands, a good game. It's a good game. You run around, you pick up sticks, you make little houses and ride cows. What's not to like? The game's got charm in spades, and it's fun for about 12 hours. After those 12 hours, you have a problem if you want to keep your stuff. I'm not going to say it's impossible, but it's very hard. You don't get walls until Carpentry 18 and even then they're not very effective. You don't get locks until tinkering 14 and that's if you're lucky enough to find iron which, for me, took a total of four hours.
Even then, the locks do nothing. People will destroy your houses, and I've seen this pretty much everywhere. If you're not in a guild or a relatively large group, your buildings will be destroyed shortly after you log off. Don't leave any farms growing either, they'll often be taken. Your mounts? Not locked to an individual, so they can be ridden away by anyone that wanders by. But that's not the worst part.
I was attacked by reds shortly after starting the game, and that was FINE. That's a fair fight, where I'm innocent and you're the aggressor. What's annoying are the reds and yellows that work together. The reds distract you while the yellows look through everything in your town that you can take. If you attack and kill them, you get turned red, which is what they want so they get full loot rights because you're a 'murderer'. It's not the strategy that bothers me, it's having a game so poorly guess moral choices when it gives us no laws. We're not protected, so until I get locks on every house, anyone can just grab anything. My towers? Pitiful damage that red players can casually stroll through. And that's just for a handful of people that just felt like bothering someone else.
The hamlet I built will probably be gone by tomorrow, that's fine. I'll remember the fun I had before I was tricked and killed by two random people that were passing by. It's still a good game, it's like wurm and harvest moon had a baby, but I feel like will never effectively protect my belongings without being part of a much larger town, and that sucks. So I won't be playing.

I started off with purchasing the Adventurers pack, I was a little worried pre-purchase because I couldn't find any lets plays, and found only one game-play video on YouTube.
I decided to risk it, and I feel I was pleasantly rewarded.
Jumping straight into Tree of Life wasn't difficult for me, first thing I did was find some trees and start smacking the wazoo out of them. Every tree tends to drop a few apples for early game sustanance (though you need a lot as they don't regain much hunger).
My first few nights very ruthless let me tell you, I didn't move AT ALL, because I couldn't see more than 2-3 meters in front of me even with a torch, with the worry of bumping into a nasty. Nighttime doesn't really ease up anytime soon so you have to get used to it unless you have a couple buddies as backup.
The day/night cycles seem to be uneven, feels like night lasts a good portion longer than the day, its not a major and not game breaking, but you can't help but want a extra 5 or so minutes of day time to carry that last rock over.
As a new player there isn't much point in settling down, as your a long way away from crafting any sort of container/storage chest, better to go off and explore and gather stuff, use other peoples bench's etc.
So blah blah aside, i'll just start listing stuff.
---- Positives ---
* Very deep and intertwined crafting system - You will have to deal with inventory space to work your way up the different tiers of buildings, and there is a lot to build. To put this into prospective, you need to be teaming up with some others otherwise you are going to be in for one hell of a time trying to gather all the stuff you need to move up the tiers..
* Visually pleasing, its simple graphics which works well for the theme they are using (compare this to many voxel/sandboxes already out). Some say its graphics are outdated, though I feel its fine for now.
* Gorgeous ambient music track during the day, very relaxing
* Survival - its up to you to survive, you can't be lazy or you will run out of food and starve. You'll be constantly on the hunt for food until you learn to start getting some farming up and running.
* Co-Operative re-enforced gameplay - You will be able to tell after about an hour into the game that if you really want to progress you'll need a few friends to help out, this helps to alleviate greifing as people will want to work together more.
* Death isn't overly punishing - You die, I think you lose one item? if even that, anyway I didn't notice it and I died a few times (not to players). If you are a pvper, and you kill someone, if someone kills you they get all your stuff, you respawn with nothing (take that greifers).
* Good community - I didn't encounter anyone who wanted to KOS, even after running into their home towns and asking for pants.
--- The negatives ---
* Lack of instruction on the core mechanics that tie in with your survival (what to avoid, where you should start etc).
* Crafting progression is brutal - Other than a few stock basic recipes for each crafting utility, you'r left to level up your skills to obtain more recipes . You may find yourself crafting 20 torches to level up enough for the next recipe, and repeating this every couple new recipes. And some seemingly basic recipes are quite far down the line (place-able light sources as an example, other the campfires).
* PvE - Some enemies hit really hard for what you would assume should be mangeable, they can absolutely mop the floor with you until you get some really good weapons (anything better than an axe). This makes the early night-time horrors if you get caught.
* You will get lost, you will lose your base, and you more than likely will start over a few times until you figure out a way to not lose your home (co-ords help with this slightly, its still a pain though).
* Hunger - Your hunger stores at a maximum value of 500 units, it decreases about 1 unit every 2 seconds. You are spending a lot of your time gathering food / maintaining food supplies. (thankfully meats and baked potatoes alleviate this problem greatly).
* Items don't stack correctly - When you try to shift crafted items from your crafting utility to say your hotbar, it will not stack. Some other odd stacking issues occur outside of the crafting utility.
* Translations on tooltips / item descriptions - Steak is worded as fish, and some other instances where English grammar is out of order or missing descriptive words.
Overall in its current early early access state, I would recommend this game to people who are looking for a Co-Op focused town building / resource gathering survival Sandbox MMO. Otherwise, maybe wait for some lets plays to decide.

This game is incredible easily my favourite game in a long time.
As of writing this review I have 28 hours in the game and I only just got passed the first big area that i'd honestly consider an extended tutorial, I haven't been so enthralled and entwined in the lore and the world presented before me, I tried my best to get every bit of dialogue and lore that was given to me. This game really pulls you in and puts forth an amazing adventurer and world for you to explore.
To best explain this game it feels like virtual DnD, the story is driven and told from a narrator who explains character actions with great detail, i've never failed to picture perfectly what he was trying to describe. The combat is turn based however it's set in the world you explore, there's no tiles so you have the freedom of movement and often do your best to squeeze the last bit of range from your abilities. There's a lot of dialogue and exploration, more-so than the combat but it's so well written I don't think many people will mind.
One thing this game does well is level-ups and difficulty. It's never afraid to keep you on your toes or pump up the difficulty for some parts and the one boss I went up against felt like a real boss, he was actually difficult and took a few tries to pass, it didn't feel unfair or like I didn't know how to beat him it just took finer oginization and planning. Leveling up always feel rewarding and meaningful, Often I found something difficult to get though but once I leveled once it was fine and surprisingly on-top of all that it doesn't feel like the enemies are getting too hard to quick if I delve into a later area un-prepared. It's difficulty and leveling felt well done and fine-tuned and it's really comming through with it.
However no game is perfect but so far i'd say this is as close as it's come to it. Auto-saves are far and few-between though I can understand it, if I do something wrong by mistake I'd either have to live with it or go back 20 minutes of play-time to get to that spot again, which I actually like, it forces me to keep to my desicions and mistakes and not have my first playthrough a perfect run. However it becomes an issue were, as recently, after the first boss the game crashed and it made me re-play the boss fight again which wasen't fun but it's the only crash i've had.
Overall it's truely a magnificent game especially compared to recent releases, it's always nice to see a AAA RPG game that you can sink hours and hours into as it seems any game that exceeds 50 hours now are either multiplayer games or sandboxes. Looking forward to more and can't wait to try out GM mode.

It plays nearly identical to to the originals, while having some minor tweaks here and there to make the game an overall more pleasant experience. Although with this near perfect recreation, it does come with some of the old games' minor problems, but overall these small issues didn't take away from the experience one bit due to my overall excitement and joy of playing the game. I know there are people who say that Sonic is "all about going fast" but you have to remember, at the core of the game, it is a platformer, but speed is integrated into the gameplay to make it more interesting(If someone wanted to play a game all about speed, they'd go and play a racing game). This game has an exciting sense of speed, and when you go fast, you really go fast. The levels aren't as linear as say, Super Mario Bros., but this non-linear level design is there to encourage exploration and platforming, which makes those moments where you're just gunning it that much more rewarding and exciting.
This game allows you to play as the cast of the original games: Sonic the Hedgehog, Miles “Tails” Prower, and Knuckles the Echidna. Each character boasts their own unique abilities, such as Tails’ ability to fly, Knuckles’ ability to glide and climb walls, and new in Sonic Mania: The “Drop Dash”, which allows Sonic to charge a spindash in the air and release when he hits the ground. These abilities really change the gameplay up for each character and their playthrough of each zone, as you can discover new routes and secrets with each character, and sometimes there's even entirely new sections of a stage open to a specific character.
The characters and enemies are beautifully crafted with god-like sprite work. Each character and enemy seem to have their own personality, which is beautifully shown through the sprites. Animations are smoother due to the added frames of animation on top of the already existing ones from the past games, along with a constant 60 frames per second, the result is a classic game that has some of the smoothest action and sprite movement I've ever seen in a video game.
The levels are all vibrant and gorgeous, each having their own vibe and personality, which makes the environments really come to life with all the different colors and backgrounds. The games has a total of 12 zones, each with 2 acts, which all have fun and interesting gimmicks that really add to the gameplay and fun factor of each zone. These 12 zones are divided into 3 sections: The Classic stages, the extremely remixed stages, and the brand new stages. Even though the classic stages are something most fans have already played before, they all have new areas, gimmicks, and looks to really seem fresh and something worth playing again. The remixed stages really speak for themselves; old stages that have been heavily remixed to almost seem unrecognizable from the original stages. And finally, the brand new stages, which all have their own new gimmicks and flare to make them some of the most enjoyable stages in the game, which makes me wonder: what if they made another game like this, but with every zone being brand new?
This game boasts a ton of replay value, as there are so many new things to discover so many secrets to find, such as the giant special-rings, which leads you to a special stages that has you chasing a UFO in a 3D space while trying to collect rings to keep the timer going, and collecting blue orbs to increase your speed. These special stages are by far the funnest and most exciting special stages I've played in a Sonic game, as they are filled with many exciting moments that really get you blood pumping, as they encourage making risky moves to take major shortcuts so you can get the emerald faster(In the Nintendo Switch version of Sonic Mania, there seems to be a slight drop in frames in a some areas of the special stages. This wasn't much of a problem overall, but I thought I’d just mention it anyways, since I'm not sure if this occurs in the other versions). Then there's the checkpoint bonus stages, which brings back "Blue-Spheres" from Sonic 3 & Knuckles. These bonus stages, while challenging, boast plenty of extra content if completed, such as the ability to access Sonic's old movesets such as the Super Peel out from Sonic CD, or the insta-shield from Sonic 3 & Knuckles. You can also unlock debug mode, which while compared to the debug mode in the other games is a bit underwhelming, it's a fun addition regardless. There's plenty more bonus content to be unlocked, such as a sound test mode, endless blue spheres mode, which also adds new mechanics into the mode, and even a “mean bean machine" mode, which is bound to have plenty of nostalgia to anyone who's played it.
This game is overall an amazing experience, and something any long time fan of Sonic, and even some newcomers, will enjoy. The game is loaded with content and replayability, and I didn't even get to talking about the competition and time attack mode. This is the game I, and many fans have been waiting so long for, and I hope this isn't the last game to come in this style. It is a Sonic game made by fans, for fans, and this game is far from a disappointment. It was such a blast to play and experience, and I had a grin on my face the whole time I played. As of now, I feel that this is one, if not the best Sonic game I have ever played, maybe even topping Sonic 2 in my opinion. I encourage anyone and everyone who is a fan of Sonic, or even someone who hasn't played a Sonic game, to give this a try. And to anyone who has a negative opinion on Sonic overall, I insist you play this game, cause who knows, you might just change your mind.

This game surprised me. I wasn't expecting to enjoy as much as I was going to where it reminded me why I enjoy gaming in the first place.

I love the new stages and the reused stages are different, I love the little references and surprises the game throws at you in clever ways that I wasn't expecting and gave me a good chuckle, I love the pixel art and how smooth it is, and I love the soundtrack and it's remixes.
Is it perfect? No. There's some glitches like the collision detection can be off at times and the true final boss (let's be honest) kind-of sucks. Not a bad bossfight, but feels underwhelming and honestly... I'm not surprised since most of the Sonic game we've been getting don't really have that great final bossfights.
So. Do I recommend it? Definitely. It's by far the best Sonic game in recent years though, for the newcomer or someone that's somwhat new to the franchise, this isn't the perfect Sonic game to start off with. It's a great game to start off with, but the things they've thrown in maybe confusing for that specific audience. I would likely more recommend starting off with Sonic 1-3 & Knuckles before going into Mania if you're new, but hey, that's coming from my experience, so who knows.

If you've ever wanted a Free-to-Play (F2P) game that doesn't make you feel like a cash cow, then Warframe might be worth considering:
Positives:
+ Entirely free to play, all content can be obtained without any spending on the part of the player.
+ Fast, flowing movement system that allows players to traverse the world in style.
+ Good variety of game modes
+ Plenty of variety in the weapons and Warframes themselves. From the weapons and Warframes themselves to the high level of customisability both on a functional and cosmetic level.
+ (As of writing) Constantly updated with new content through patches and updates, made primarily by the developers, while cosmetic items known as "Tennogen" are made by fans of the game through the Steam Workshop.
+ One of the friendliest online communities out there.
Negatives:
- Very, very grindy, not reccomended for those who prefer all content available from the get go and like to experiment from there. Content requires players to gather varying amounts of resources, with some resources locked behind timed events.
- Crafting items has an abitrary timer behind it, post meeting the resource requirements, players must wait between 1 minute to 3 days before they are allowed access to their content.
- Can experience minor connection issues at times, particularly around events or major updates where there are peak player counts.
- Purely cosmetic items are locked behind paywalls, items include user-made "Tennogen" content, colour palettes and alternate skins for weapons and characters.
- The game has a chronic issue of not explaining things to newer players, guides are reccomended.
- Outside of getting new weapons and Warframes there isn't much to the game, there isn't a heavy emphasis on a linear story that you may expect from an RPG, although there is a storyline that can be followed where players can discover the history of the universe.
Overall:
While not without its flaws, I would highly reccomend this game, (as said at the start of the review) you can't get better F2P economies than this, and the game's combat system is a blast with or without friends, combine this with actively interactive developers and one of the best online communities out there makes for one of the best action RPGs out there.

Amazing movement, deep and complex modding system, lots of possibilities for optimization and individualization for both your Character and your three equipped weapons, fun combat and a fair F2P business model to round it all up.
If you get past the "holy ♥♥♥♥ing♥♥♥♥♥♥this game is overwhelming"-phase it is truly an amazing game. Oh and by the way: it's free.

Sonic CD is a passion project made by fans, for fans. It's a celebration of everything Sonic filled with beautiful animated cinematics, throwing back to the classic days of Sonic and his wonderful outing on the SEGA CD. However, the game has flaws, and unfortunately is at it's worst on the PC, with the inclusion of a feature known as Denuvo. Denuvo is a forced and unfair addition made to the games code by SEGA that originally forced the game to be always online. After a day they changed this "feature" to require the game to connect to the internet every two weeks. This disgusting, trojan virus has infected the game and had nothing to do with the creators intent. As far as we know, it is the sole reason for the PC releases delay. However, in the face of this tragedy, the Sonic community only seems to be stronger. I posted multiple messages in the discussion pages of Sonic Mania and some incredibly nice folks help me better understand and enjoy the game. And the amount of hilarity they provide by poking fun at this crazy situation is enough to prove that we truly are like no other community on the internet. We're like a family. A family that has been waiting for years for a true followup to Sonic 3 and Knuckles, and the fact that we finally got it is worth celebrating. For those of you who are curious about this game, here are a couple things I learned about this game from the community that you might not have found out on your own. If you have any more questions then feel free to hit them up, politely and with respect to the fact that these are really just normal people who are nice enough to take the time out of their day to help you. First, this game does not have any online components other than Online leaderboards. However, you can play with friends locally by having one friend use a controller and the other use the keyboard or both use a controller. This confused me, because this setting is marked on the screen simply as: Competion Mode. It doesn't say that you both play from the same computer. This also makes the frequent requirement to be online even more confusing and leads nicely into my next big point: If the only online feature is online leaderboards, why does the game need to be always online? You can save your own personal bests and the game will try to connect to the leaderboards when you ask it to. When you're at home, playing the game next to your router. What if I wanted to install this on my laptop and play on the go?The bloody DS has been doing this right for years. Even the mobile ports of Sonic 1 2 and CD did it. Speaking of problems, the game is still pretty buggy at launch as well. Believe me, I love this game, to death, I even have a collectors edition and it's one of my proudest collectors items, but... (at least in the computer version, I can't speak for consoles) it has some really major bugs. The collision issues are even worse than the original Sonic CD on Sega CD. If you use tails to fly and hit a spring by accident, it makes the spring glitch and think that you're constantly colliding with it and plays the sound over and over making an incredibly earbleeding beeping noise that gives me a headache. Also there are already tons of Twitter posts making fun of Hydrocity especially because so many of it's gimmicks do not work at all. If you ask me theres nothing wrong with pointing these issues out and still loving an absolutely phenomenal game, it just means that they need to look these over when they make updates. This is what patches are for. For such a small team the fact that this game is so polished already is mind blowing. Even with these problems, Sonic Mania is still miles above SEGA's previous attempts to capture the 16bit magic of the Genesis games. It spits in the face of nostalgic pandering garbage such as Sonic 4. Sonic 4 isn't terrible, mind you but Sonic Mania blows it out of the water with regards to how much effort and quality went into it's devolpment and the amount of fun, lengthy hours you will get out of this clasic game. The parts of Sonic Mania you will love and the parts of Sonic Mania you will hate will most likely be comepletely different than mine, because Sonic Mania truly is a combination of everything classic Sonic, and that means the good and the bad. I for one, like Sonic 2 the best out of the classic trilogy, I love it's special stages and have collected all the chaos emeralds countless times. Which is why I love when the game is most like Sonic 2, with it's inclusions of the classic Oil Ocean as well as Sonic's sprite ressembling 2 more than it does 3. But there are plenty of people who hate Oil Ocean and love everything in the game that reminds them of Sonic 3 and Knuckles, like the Blue Sphere special stages and Hydrocity. And there's absolutely nothing wrong with either of those opinions. I'm just telling you how I feel. I for one love Sonic CD and think it's level design is great, where as while I think Sonic 3 and Knuckles is still one of the greatest games of all time, I barely replay it because I think Hydrocity is way too hard and slow. And there's once again, nothing wrong with that opinion. That just means I didn't like the part of the game that included Hydrocity. Lastly, while this is a combination of everything Sonic, the gameplay is most like Sonic 2 with how Sonic controls. That means no Super Peel Out or Homing attack. The super peel out is an unlockable only and can only be used by selecting the no save mode, and then selecting secrets. Once again, this is another cool fact the community helped me figure out when I was lost. If you liked this review, please consider giving me a "this review was helpful" rating. That would mean a ton to me because this is the first time I've ever tried reviewing a game like this. Sonic Mania and it's community are just so wonderful even with their flaws. I've never played a game on Steam that's made me this passionate and inspired me to write a review so please consider that this long peice was a work of love just like this game. I hope you have a wonderful day and I could help you decide if you want to pickup this awesome game.

As someone who hasn't played any of the
games before, I really liked this short anime series.
Story follows a defense attorney called Phoenix Wright, who's just started his career. He's getting into a ridiculously difficult trial after another.
Now, obviously the protagonist goes on and wins every trial (no real surprises there) but what makes the show interesting is that he goes on to effectively solve each murder (the default crime) right there in court.
What's
interesting is that in each case the logic
in advance. I took a whole lot of fun out of guessing/seeing the arguments before they were laid out. In that way, the show reminds me of the excellent FMV detective game
Not only are the trials themselves ridiculously difficult ("we found this guy with a gun and he does not deny murder"), there is always a witness. These (often recurring) side characters are usually some of the weirdest oddballs in existence, ranging from dementic oldmen to talking parrots to circus clowns who insist on donning the costume in court.
Maybe the witnesses just have to be weird to contrast that the mentor of the protagonist is a dead spirit medium.
The story between the cases makes little sense but each case itself (usually spanning several episodes) is entertaining and I often found myself fascinated by the complicated plots so I had to watch the each set of trials in one sitting.
Setting is Japan (apparently unlike the games that are AFAIK based in America) with a bizarre court system that usually assumes the defendant guilty before otherwise proved. This surely makes for rapid and eventful trials.
Often I found myself wondering how with all these murders, rarely do the relatives and acquaintances of the victims bat an eye because of their lost loved ones. Even losing their sister, girlfriend or father meant nothing to the people in the show, which broke the immersion somewhat. However, later episodes paid better attention to this detail.
The animation at times was scant and the music is sub-par when compared to greater animes, although I did like the title song in the first half-season.
In the end,
was an entertaining anime series with a nice series of effectively detective puzzles to ponder. I got it at a 70% sale, making it well worth the purchase.

Simple, yet chess like in its replayabiltiy, Frozen Synapse is a turn based tactical combat game.  You control a fix number of solders armed, each with a specific weapon.  Load out varies per map and round, but they navigate a simple techno/hologramed terrain with walls and windows, in an attempt to take out the other guy.  Turns are not executed live, so you can have a slow play game with someone, simply putting in your turn when you have time, or you can be running multiple games at once.  Once your turn is submitted, your opponent gets a message and vise-versa, at which point you can view the results of that round and plan your next.
Turns are process simultaneously so you setup your mans with postures, positions and what direction their facing.  As you move around the small map, so does the other guy, when your mans see someone, they shoot (unless told not to).  It's satisfying and frustrating to see each round unfold and it's immensely challenging to attempt to get your mans into the best position to attack the other guy.
Take that simple gameplay mechanic and throw in a couple classic game modes like King of the Hill and recue/protect the hostages and an additional mode called charge where you bid on how far you believe you can get and hold a position on the map.  Each play puts their bid in at the beginning of the game and whoever is more aggressive (distance from starting point) in their bid wins the bid and must then achieve that position.
Each round is unique and challenge.  While there's AI to train yourself on (which scales well) the match making system is where it's at.  Stat tracking and ranking is very much a part of the game and it ends up pairing you for battles that don't tend to feel lopsided.
It's a small, simple game so despite being really good I'll say it's worth $10.  Add another $3 to throw it on android and you can process those turns on the go.  Worth it.

According to Steam, I played this game for 300+ hours (and that does not account for all the time I played it on a tablet...). I was – very briefly – even at the global top rank. So obviously I kinda like it. Yes, it has a very simple graphics. Yes, there are some more or less annoying bugs. Yes, the controls may be more intuitive. ...
But at its heart, its one of the greatest strategy games I've ever played. I enjoyed the single player, but be warned: if you're not into reading quite a lot of text, it's probably not for you. Anyways, its true charm comes from playing 1vs1 against other (human) players. It has a unique mix of pure strategic skill, psychology, and (some) luck. The more you play against top tier players, the more psychology enters the game, and that's something I found very thrilling (leaving me to think up to 40 or 50 minutes on a single turn). Being able to play at your own pace, using any device (PC, Mac, Tablet) is realy great.
So if you like strategy games, don't mind a relatively simple UI/graphics, and enjoy trying to find the perfect move against your opponent: give this game a try.

I've been playing the game with a few friends for the past several hours(Steam tallies 6). It's good fun, rather rough around the edges, but I think it was worth the fifteen bucks we spent on it(we sprung for that four pack, you see).
By rough, I mean that with the game basically just having come out, figuring out how to do anything is kind of difficult, and there's not much of a way to ask. Mostly I just gathered stuff and ran around shanking things with bone daggers while my friends did most of the crafting stuff. Combat is kind of clunky with how the game sometimes doesn't lock you on to enemies, letting them get in several cheapshots while you dance around him trying to get the game to lock on, and the enemies rather annoyingly circle-strafe you which, as I said, is just annoying and doesn't add any real difficulty to anything. Some materials seem kind of hard to come by; tin has been a recurring issue since for some reason instead of having rocks containing tin you can only find the stuff from the corpses of dead sailors(which are faaaaairly rare, I guess). The night is pitch black, which while realistic, is frustrating because you can often get jumped by enemies and have no clue what's going on, and you can't have a torch in your hand with a weapon, so you end up fighting blind at night. On top of that, light sources(namely bonfires) are hard to maintain through the night and don't put off all that much light anyways, making them kind of useless. A few times enemies have attacked us that didn't actually appear on other player's screens, which is mind-boggling. There's several other niggling little details, but at that point I'd just be nitpicking.
Now, it should be reiterated that we've only played the game for six hours; some of this might just be my inexperience speaking, but the whole package is rather unpolished in a number of ways. Expected? Sure, this is an early access game. But hey, if I don't list the problems I've had they won't get fixed, right? On the whole, though, I DID enjoy my time with the game so far, and will likely play the game more in days to come, and wholeheartedly look forward to what they'll do with the thing in the future. I'd say pick it up now and play it. S'only 20 bucks, and if you get three friends to pitch in for the 4-pack it's only 15. Not a bad price for what's already here, I'd say.
In summation: Yeah, I recommend the game. :D

Tree of Life is an another sandbox MMO that introduces heavy rpg elements along with base building. While base building may not be the forte, leaving only preset buildings that you can adjust position of, the RPG stats and immense world size is worth noting.
(system uses + as major element, - as minor element)

+Death when not excessively PvP does not make you lose all loot, allowing for plenty of PvE play.

Cons:
+Game is somewhat confusing on what should be done (needs better 'how to')
+Combat system is rather rough, targeting especially.
-Base building take a good amount of time to build up to.
-Sound and music is poor; repetitive.
-Some masteries take longer to get into. (Blacksmithing, Archery, Shields)

Overall, this game is at a playable state and you can get a good amount of enjoyment. Being in a group, like most times, will be more fun but is also beneficial to build up your town. Another game from my classic teenage years, where I'd rush home to go play PC games after high school until 2 am and then slog my way through the next day. Rise of Nations was released in 2003, with an expansion a year-or-so later, and this Steam edition combines both of these into a neat package with some graphical upgrades, workshop support, and some minor new features like the ability to stream directly to Twitch. A cool package, overall, and it has dipped to good prices during sales.
Rise of Nations plays like some kind of hybrid freak-baby between the Age of Empires games and Civilization. RTS gameplay is mixed in with some grand strategic elements like territory control, and if you play the campaign, you'll be treated to a big board game-esque map. Games are spread out across eight ages, from the ancient times to the information age. You'll start off slinging rocks, move on to swords and iron, eventually drive some tanks, and then you'll be launching nukes and stealth bombers. There are also a ton of customization options for skirmishes, ranging from old fashioned 1v1s, all the way to massive free for all games with special rulesets. You can dive in and customize games to your liking, eliminating certain victory conditions or even making the entire game a peaceful tech race. The nearly absurd amount of customization options are also well-documented in a simple way, making it very easy to digest exactly what each individual setting is. You can very easily set a game up in almost any fashion you want. There are a wide variety of AI options too, all of which are well explained so you know exactly what you'll end up playing against.
I've always had a special place in my heart for RTS games - a cold, dark, unexplored place, that I don't like to venture to because I'm competitive in stupid ways. I've ragequit from many a Starcraft game because I rallied my workers wrong or something. Rise of Nations, however, scratches an itch that no other RTS can seem to reach, and it keeps me coming back time and time again. There is such a wide variety of things that can occur in a single game, from skirmishes with a bunch of javelins and horses to patrolling the seas with submarines, or sending planes on bombing missions over the enemy capital, managing your supply trucks to avoid attrition damage, managing spies, decoys, exploration... it's a really deep and packed game that manages to hit all the right targets and miss all the wrong ones. There are some balance issues, such as Germany being ungodly good in all things economical, but for the most part you won't notice these things unless you start trying to obsessively min/max your gameplay style... and if you're the kind of gamer looking for a min/max competitive RTS, you are better off moving to Starcraft 2 or something.
It's well worth a purchase at almost any price point if you're looking for a unique take on the RTS genre.
Seriously though, just pick Germany. Your economy will spiral out of control and the next thing you know, you are sending infantry against a bunch of guys with spears and there's something strangely satisfying about that.

It's like 4v4 X-Com, but everyone plays just one character and plans their moves all at the same time, and you have Atlas Reactor. The roster size is decent and like a MOBA in that random characters are temporarily unlocked on a weekly basis, and you can permanently unlock with in-game currency or cash. You get a free character after 10 matches, and you earn the currency fairly quick at first as you level up.
A few characters are quite expensive though, and unlocking the entire roster would take a long time as a free player. However there is a Practice Mode where you can test out any character, so you can choose a style you like best without having to wait months to test out every unlocked character.
Overall it's a pretty fun game. There's a variety of characters and skills to keep you switching around. It feels pretty balanced as well, and the options are mostly based on playstyle. If you like running head-first into battles, pick a frontline/tank character. If you like to snipe from a distance, there are those too. If stealth is your thing, that is also a viable option. If the idea of a fast-paced online X-Com sounds appealing to you, download this game immediately.

Awesomenauts is a few things. It's cartoony, it's generally fast paced, and it's a whole lot of fun. The 2D action platformer gameplay alongside the moba-ish framework works well, leading to continuously fun matches no matter how many you play. That alongside the fact that matches usually last around 10-20 minutes, it's a great way to pass that little bit of time with some partial strategy and a whole bunch of bullets. Plus, due to the customizable item pool for each 'Naut, there are literally thousands of loadouts to pick from, bringing with them just as many different playstyles. So whether you're looking for some massive pushing power or just want to stay behind and heal from the sidelines, you'll always find some way to play the characters the way you want.
Overall, very fun, with tons of replay value.

It's decent fun if you like these kinds of games and are looking for a casual experience, or are simply intrigued by playing a 2D MOBA. I'd recommend it if you're paying a few dollars or less for it, but not for full price.
Awesomenauts feels a lot more like Monday Night Combat than any other game I can think of. Killing another player requires a ton of auto-attack hits; you can unload all your abilities and have them just round a corner or straight up run away if they're slightly faster than you. Though your team can help, there aren't many stuns and most abilities can be dodged with a bit of skill which makes a 3 on 1 ambush hardly a guarantee. The maps are small and the characters are generally fast, meaning it is easy to run behind a tower and teleport back to base. This makes you feel weak, and makes the early game a push and pull grind unless the teams or picks are unbalanced. In my limited experience that makes the late game relatively even if you haven't screwed up enough to let your base get exposed; comebacks are easy and losses are slow. If your base does get exposed there are no automated defenses, meaning if you don't have somebody defending it at all times, it is easy for two people to defend your push while one person sneaks behind you to kill it. I found a build and character fairly early on that led me to a 90% win rate solely by split-pushing and running away, which seems like no fun to play against (though it is fun to run through the whole team when they think they have you cornered).
Speaking of builds, two active abilities and zero items means that buying this game just to try out various builds is a short endeavour. No items and only being able to choose three of five modifiers for each ability means that characters seem stuck in what they're designed to do. Some of the modifiers seem far less powerful than others, which means you can quickly become limited to 'Do I want this gun to shoot slightly faster or do slightly more damage?’ Adding to the lack of items, the fact that you have to preselect your loadout before finding a match means that there's no real way to react to the way the game is progressing besides the order in which you level up abilities.
While it's difficult to call a game 'easy' when you face human players operating under the same rules as you, the balance of the game is set up so that unskilled or casual players can have a decent time. There are characters that have homing abilities and huge AoE attacks, AI fills in when there aren't enough players even in ranked modes (and they're basically suicidal), and the game seems strongly balanced towards letting people escape or survive attacks if everybody is equally skilled. There is also a level up system that prevents access to characters and skills, leading to higher level players having a gameplay advantage, though generally many people are attracted by the process of levelling up. There are no dedicated servers, which often gives the host a noticeable advantage and is terrible for fair competition in a fast moving game, though it is still very playable. On the positive side, Awesomenauts boasts a strong and fresh style, with a Saturday morning cartoon presentation, including catchy music, cool setting, and colorful characters; though some of the voice acting brings down the otherwise high quality presentation.
The game is likeable and well made, if you enjoy the particulars more than I there is plenty of replayability and you will probably have a fantastic time overall. Awesomenauts is good, but difficult for me to recommend when there are so many similar games that have systems that I enjoy more and may be more enjoyable to you.

This is an extremely niche game, suitable for relatively serious programmers or those who want to be such. TIS-100 emulates a fictional machine with an interesting architecture. It contains a 4x3 grid of modular parallel processors, each of which is a processing unit or a stack-based memory unit. Each node can communicate with the surrounding four nodes. The goal is to solve puzzles that require you to implement various simple operations using a preconfigured grid of TIS nodes, reading numbers from input ports at the top of the grid and writing the numbers to output ports on the bottom. A "visualization module" also exists for converting an output stream to a color image, and some puzzles require you to produce a particular image. The processors are programmed using a simple assembly language. The arrangement of the nodes and their types constrain the communication possibilities, and some nodes are simply damaged and must be routed around.
The puzzle solutions would be very simple to implement on a real computer, but the TIS processors are extremely limited - far more limited than any real processor would ever be. Each TIS processor has only a single general purpose register and can contain at most 15 instructions. The instruction set has only 12 operations and lacks many instructions that you would expect a processor to have, requiring multiple instructions to do very simple operations. There's no RAM, but by combining processors in clever ways you can build small memory controllers. Thankfully, the TIS-100 has a rudimentary built-in debugger that supports breakpoints and single-step execution, and displays all data in the machine simultaneously.
The puzzles start out simple, but even a seasoned low-level programmer will be challenged by some of them. The game comes with 25 puzzles and you can build your own puzzles and share them with others by writing simple text files in Lua. Completing the built-in puzzles unlocks access to a network of puzzles written by others. Upon completing each puzzle, the game shows you a histogram of the speeds, sizes, and organizational complexities of users' solutions, along with marks for where yours fits in, allowing you to see how you stack up against other programmers. Even if you're an experienced programmer, you'll probably be surprised at how fast some people's solutions are compared to your first attempts, giving motivation to go back and try to do better.
The game also includes a cryptic and very simple story told through bits of text encoded into the damaged nodes of the various puzzles. There's also a secret instruction and a secret puzzle to find.
If you think the idea of learning a miniature assembly language and trying to write programs on an extremely constrained parallel computing architecture sounds fun, then you'd probably enjoy TIS-100. Otherwise, you probably won't like it.

First Impression review with 3 hours of gameplay.
Pros:
+Interesting skill progression, You gain experience in all kinds of skills as you craft, gather and battle. This leads to opening new skills to learn and use.
+Charming Art style.
+World is HUGE. I spent my first 3 hours only on the "Starter" Island I spawned on.
+Tons of room for depth. While still in early access I'm excited to see what the devs can come up with.
+Decent Price, only 20 USD.
+Possibility for great communities. In my first 2 minutes I found a friendly group of players and joined them in creating our own little settlement. Mileage may vary for you of course.
Cons:
-I haven't had a problem with it, but people being attacked by invisible monsters is a huge problem at the moment.
-While I haven't encountered lag, monster seem to act a bit weird. The Tree spirit things in particular seem to whoosh all around including clipping into the ground a bit.
-Combat is a bit clunky and needs some work. Without a guild/friend system (Planned not implemented) to turn off Friendly Fire (unsure if the system will turn this off) the game tends to be a russian roulette of please hit the monster and not my friend.
-GRIND GRIND GRIND. You will be chopping trees, for precious apples and firewood for a long time. Not only does the games stamina system limit you, but you need SO MUCH.
-Day/Night cycle. When you start out, Night it death. Zombies and Skeletons spawn in the night and will murder you senseless. Thankfully they stay away from light, so a campfire will help keep you safe. This limits you to only gathering resources at first during the day, which doesn't last very long. This cycle end up meaning that you run out as soon as dawn breaks and gather as much as you can to run home before dusk to hide by the fire. My least favorite part of this is how it limits and terrible slows exploration.
-The only true bug I experienced was when I first logged on, none of my crafting recipes or items had tooltips. I even thought this was how it was supposed to be. Guessing at what made what. It seemed cool at first but quickly got annoying as I tried to figure out what I picked up. A quick relog managed to fix this problem after a friend informed me that, yes tooltips existed. Which leads into...
-No hand holding. The game drops you in and says go at it! I don't consider this much of a con, but when you have meters that you have no clue what they represent (Looking at you Brain thing.) You can't help but wonder if you are missing out of an entire part of the game. How do you progress your skills? What does everything do? If I build this what will it let me accomplish? All of these are left to discover, which can be fun, but to some tedious.
-Death timers. When you die, you become a ghost that gets to float about for 3 minutes unless you find the soul things. 3 minutes seems super steep, and design around PvP seige aspects. Dying to a bear that you and a few friends decided you could take results in 3 minutes of time out.
Wow, that seems like a lot more cons than pros, but honestly so many of the cons are my own personal preferences or can and hopefully will be fixed by the devs. I love the idea of what they are doing here and can't wait to explore some more in this game.

You can hijack vehicles, punch tanks, use armor abilities, dual wield SMGs and stick grenades to hapless grunts, there are even skull modifiers that increase your score. The graphics and music are very high quality for such a cheap game too.
The game follows the story of two Spartans, Davis, a newcomer, and Sarah "Eggheads" Palmer from 4, as they fight the Covenant on a Forerunner planet. You'll switch between the two to accomplish various missions ranging from defending bases, escorting transports, rescuing stranded marines and all kinds of things, there's a lot of variety.
The missions are short, and designed to be played in small bursts, but they're varied enough to keep you interested, although I have to say the story (told through mission descriptions and Terminal-style animation) is poor for a Halo title. The score attack theme and skull modifiers will give you an incentive to replay missions, although there's no horde mode unfortunately.
I have only two complaints, that the local coop present on the Xbox versions was removed in this port, and that you can't select your weapons before a mission. You may use points accrued from missions to buy a different armor ability or a heavy weapon, but you're not given the option to change your basic loadout.
I got this game for $1.99 and I feel it was a very good deal.
A very good game to play for Halo fans. Highly recommended!

Rise of Nations is an older RTS with a gimmick few others have dared attempt. Rise of Nations permits players to advance through eight "ages", representing all of human history from the classical Greco-Roman empires all the way to the modern day. Critically, Rise of Nations manages to be engaging every step of the way.
Only one other RTS I know of shares Rise of Nation's gimmick - Empire Earth, a game with an inarguably stronger focus on detail and historical accuracy (And the addition of cool future ages). However, where Empire Earth excels in its detail and its mimicry of the sweeping changes in warfare which occur between each great technological age (and the complete uselessness of obsolete units), Rise of Nations is more accessible and more streamlined for the sort of gameplay both games forward.
The traditional RTS formula is a worker unit is sent to collect resources, it collects until its capacity is full, and then it returns the load to a central gathering point. This continues until the worker is killed, resources run out, the gathering point is destroyed, or the worker is given a different order. This is the formula used by StarCraft, StarCraft II, Age of Empires, Age of Empires II, Empire Earth, Empire Earth II, and nearly every other RTS game. It's a good system - it forces players to keep expanding to acquire new resources, attaches a hard limit to the amount one worker can help the economy, and gives the OPFOR plenty of opportunities to interrupt supply shipments.
Rise of Nations breaks from tradition in this respect. In Rise of Nations, it is necessary to construct specialized gathering points for each resource - Mines for metal, Farms for food, Woodcutter camps for Timber, Universities for Knowledge, and Oil Wells for Oil. Farms, Oil Wells, and Universities produce a set amount of their respective resources per worker garrisoned in them, and each have their own unique rules. Mines and Woodcutter camps have different maximum garrison capacities depending on exactly where they're placed - a small mountain may mean a Mine can only have three workers, but a huge forest may let a Woodcutter camp have ten. Once the gathering point has been constructed and the workers garrisoned, the gathering point provides a set amount of resources every 30 seconds until destroyed or the workers are given other tasks (Resources never run out).
In Empire Earth, the core gameplay is about the military-industrial complex. It takes so long to replace dead units and destroyed buildings that the game becomes about forcing the enemy away from those things. With resources scattered across the map, elements of risk are inescapable and it's just a reality that there will be no effective central organization of any army since walling a settlement in is so expensive. Everything you do in Empire Earth relates back to protecting your military buildings because if they are destroyed you won't get an opportunity to replace them.
In Rise of Nations, core gameplay is about map control. Map control is represented by "territory", multicolored lines drawn on the land itself to show which player has control of what. Territory grants a lot of benefits - it increases the firing rate of your artillery, damages enemy units, lets you place down buildings, and can grant other abilities depending on your nation specialty. The earliest, and most significant, provider of territory are cities. You begin the game with one city, and it is by cities that Rise of Nations is won or lost. If your capital city is taken, you have a limited amount of time to take it back or every building you own defects to the player who took your capital and all your units commit hara-kiri. Needless to say, you're defeated. The city is more than just a gaping strategic vulnerability, however - it's the biggest sole provider of territory, and the biggest contributor to a player in Rise of Nations.
Cities have a radius, called an "economic radius", within which they provide extra health to buildings and can supercharge the gathering rates of resource structures by up to three times. Additionally, some buildings can only be built in cities (Universities, Markets, Oil Refineries, Granaries, Lumber Mills, Smelters, Senates, Temples, Libraries, Farms). Most of these buildings are huge contributors in Rise of Nations, so cities are very important. A city can be upgraded, with its economic radius and benefit to building health growing as more types of buildings are constructed in it. On top of that, cities heal units garrisoned inside them and themselves fire on enemy units if there are units inside the city. Accordingly, a city and its civilians can stand off military units acting alone. Cities also provide small incomes of Food and Timber.
Cities are automatically named after historical cities of that nation, but can be renamed. Everything you do in Rise of Nations goes back to your cities, back to the complicated web of buildings you've constructed in them. Ultimately, even special world wonders can be constructed in cities to provide unique bonuses to your nation.
And that brings us to the military aspect. War is very much a part of Rise of Nations, and it is the best way to win matches. In Empire Earth and most RTs games, it is necessary to order every individual soldier, but Rise of Nations offers us something called an "infinite queue" which causes a building to repeat its build orders until the building is destroyed, resources run out, or the population limit is reached. The infinite queue changes RTS warfare by letting a game as macro as Rise of Nations be about the macro. With enough resources, it is not merely possible but practical to overrun an opponent with sheer numbers or keep an airbase constantly supplying planes to a beleaguered front. But merely because I am a fan of the hammer that is a horde of thousands of soldiers charging doesn't mean there aren't other, more tactical options available. There are. Generals passively increase the survivability of your soldiers and offer special abilities useful for outmaneuvering and outguessing opponents while spies can make enemy units spy for you or actively turn them to your side and explorers kill enemy spies, blow up buildings, and snipe vulnerable military units. Missile silos can blow up any specific enemy building with a cruise missile, or devastate the economic radius of a fully mature city with a nuke. Airbases send out fighters to pick off enemy units, kill generals and shoot down bombers or launch brute waves of their own bombers to batter down enemy buildings. Attack helicopters pick off ridiculous numbers of tanks and submarines for their cost while being immune to any return fire. Ranged cavalry and armored cars can pick off generals and supply wagons to let enemy soldiers die from territory damage, or conduct deep raids to kill enemy workers and weaken their economy. On top of all this, special generals are available from the Senate who provide unique benefits in addition to game-long bonuses to your nation.
In addition, strategic resources are available which both provide additional income of basic resources but offer special abilities (Some of which are more or less overpowered). Basically, who your nation is and precisely what its good at evolves dynamically through the game based on what opportunities are available, what is exploited, what you started with, and what your opponent(s) do. On top of all this, there's a highly amusing "conquer the world" mode which serves as the game's campaigns. Basically, this mode links all the battles you fight to tell the story of a great empire from the beginning of its history to the day it conquered the world or failed to do so.
But the best part of Rise of Nations is how it all comes together. I'm about at the character limit, so take the fact that I'm not even close to done talking speak for itself. I highly recommend it if you have any room in your heart.
