Rise of Nations: Extended Edition is a real-time strategy game from SkyBox Labs and previously Big Huge Games, published by no other than Microsoft Studios. It's a perfected version of Rise of Nations and Rise of Nations: Thrones and Patriots, all with new Steam features like achievements, cloud saving and more.
Like many Microsoft games remake, Rise of Nations: Extended Edition retain exactly the very same gameplay and features from the previous 2 games, everything combined into a single game. If only like Age of Empires 2: HD Edition, the population limit is increased, this game might worth more. At least we get to see the old Conquer the World campaign along with the Thrones and Patriots new campaign such as the Cold War. For you who haven't play Rise of Nations before, the gameplay of this game is very good, start with a single city, build a library, college, market and expand your city, then build more cities and expand your empire into a great nation. Victory can be achieved through conquest, science or in this game called tech race, building wonders and there are more win condition for custom play.
Rise of Nations: Extended Edition graphics are, well, it's said that the water and textures has been improved, and there is a new anti-aliasing effect, but me personally didn't see that great differences from the previous Rise of Nations, or maybe it's just been far too long. The graphics are classic, but good, very good, I'm not saying it's bad, it's just kinda still old. The performances are good, no lags or any kind of problems.
Rise of Nations: Extended Edition however, have many room for improvements, if Microsoft really care. Maybe a DLC? Bad idea for most but at least there is an addition, maybe new unique units, new unique unit models for each nation (seriously, Russian launching F-18 Hornet from their carrier?), new campaign maybe the Roman campaign or something, even maybe new nation? Expansion Packs?
Like many other too, Rise of Nations: Extended Edition has the Steam workshop support for community made custom content like maps, scenarios, even mods.
But overall, Rise of Nations: Extended Edition is a great game, very fun and with the new Steam features, even better. I recommend this.
Rating 9/10

100% Orange Juice is a sleeper hit that is what legions of fans always wanted (but never knew).
It is the very essence of a family board game, a game fit for all ages and all experiences (casual/hardcore).
The game is mainly focused on the computer whim of a dice that strongly influence and affect the entire game. From defeating enemies, to gaining stars (which are a type of currency in this game) to the amount of spaces that can be traveled, this game puts you at the whim of the dice. Dice that you have no power and control over.
The main thing that you can do to win the games are having a good idea what cards you have, the timing, the character and your overall judgement.
It is fantastic and a perfect example of how a board game should be.
Regardless of your experience, the game is fair to new and experienced users alike.
An upset is always a viable event that may occur as long as you have a good grasp of the game mechanics which are explained in the PDF file that they provide you.
With this stellar gameplay, packed together with a variety of cute characters, artistic style, music, enjoyable game modes, online multiplayer, satisfying unlockables and more, 100% Orange Juice is sure to put a smile on your face whether you play alone or preferably, with friends.
(As a fan of board games, I would rate this a perfect 10/10.)

They even added more content and patches improving the experience for all.
It shows just how good the developers are and the community who play it if they are still updating it after all of this time.

Are you the Lord or Lady set to change the course of history at your whim or will you fall to the ranks of the constrained dukes and counts of the world without ever achieving much? Crusader Kings II sets out to ask you that question while it wonders exactly HOW ambitious you are at your very core. Will you be the one who unites the Frankish Empire, will you rule the Holy Roman Empire or perhaps lead the Byzantine from tattered remains back to its' glorious position as the cultural capital of the world? Or maybe you just want to kick back and unite the Irish tribesmen or repel the english agression into Scotland? The choice is entirely yours and Crusader Kings II provides you all the tools you need to create and expand a vast and dynamic lineage to rule your lands where political marriages and leadership values is key.
Take your place in history as you lead your people with the goals you set yourself to be realized but watch out for rebellious vassals breathing down your neck to take your spot the moment you blunder for too long! While Crusader Kings II is very open and fair to you from the start the punishing effects and details of your future lineage depends on thousands of things which is what makes the game and its' replayability so vast. No two games are ever quite the same as your first born son could be a moron or perhaps your wife or husband only offers you daughters to your name which all helps complicate and muddle your bloodline.
No king rules forever and your heir plays a massive part in how your gaming experience continues once your first ruler dies so make sure to teach your children wel, even those not intended to inherit because you never know when someone falls and slips on a cliff or wakes up bleeding from the wrong orifice in the morning..
With hundreds if not thousands of hours of gameplay and even more to add via the many enriching DLC's this game promises to give you a proper experience of the world as you wish to see it and, with some strategic and clever thinking and a ton of micromanagement, it delivers hard on its' promise for a satisfying and amazing experience time and time again.

Lemme just get the VR part out of the way.  Why sell the VR edition of this to be an Oculus exlusive...
No Vive support if you buy it from here.  You could buy it from the Oculus Home store, or just play it on Revive.  Chances are though, seeing how scummy both this dev and Oculus are, you may be wasting your money for when they decide to close off Revive support.  You aren't missing much though, other than Oculus exlusive updates.  The game's okay; got some unbalanced decisions here and there(single player is bat♥♥♥♥♥♥dumb, and you HAVE to play it if you want to unlock everything).  From my few hours in game, I feel that depending on your play style, you will find one game mode that you find more enjoyable than the others, leaving the other 2 obsolete for when you have friends over.  Which, btw you will definitely need. Online is a absolute ghost town, no surprise there.
Your choice of game modes are your regular old race, a king of the hill "stay in front" kind of race, and then Death Race where you get stomped out for being in last.  I personally find the death race to be the most enjoyable, but they all have their own issues.  Death race has an issue with a zoomed out camera depending on how far apart last and first place are.  Also, being the first one to die causes you to wait quite a bit till the rounds over, and trust me, it will happen a lot regardless of your skill... RNG plays a lot into this game, and you will have a lot of moments where you feel completely powerless.  But whatever, its a casual kart game so its easily overlooked.  The controls are a bit odd, but if you have ever played Kirby's Air Ride on the Gamecube, it plays just like the top ride view.  You point in the direction you want to go.  Not exactly a bad thing, but some people dislike that.  Its pretty clear from the screen-shots how it works, so keep it in mind if you choose to purchase.
Track designs are pathetically generic, so much so that you will never quite recognize a track when you pick it.  You could just put the game on random track selection and it wouldn't make a difference really.  I'd honestly suggest it, makes the game move faster.  The tracks are all fairly easy to drive on regardless of what racer you pick though.  The racers themselves come in 3 general types, with varying stats between them within the 3 category's.  Honestly, I feel they are well balanced.  Its 100% a matter of your play style that will decide who you prefer to go with.  But, as said before, skill has very little effect on how likely you are to win; "balance" doesn't matter when you can just win randomly.  All vehicles have same max speed, and people will rubber band to the player in first.  The only stats that really matter are mobility, acceleration, and grip.
So what of that RNG?  Well, considering the match will usually be filled out with AI, you will deal with being targeted in the free-for-all race style.. a LOT! This is what makes the single player campaign so frustrating.  Weapon pick-ups randomly fall from the sky, and you will occasionally have item drops completely avoid you.  You could be in last place in a death race and have no boosts to save you, or be in the middle of the pack and have a weapon dropped right on top of the guy behind you.  Physics for if you do get hit can be random; you could thrown entirely off the track, or barely budge at all.  Sometimes, a clean weapon hit can even throw the guy in front of you further into the lead.  You just never know.  I do need to mention, if you pick a hovercraft, you are pretty much guaranteed to be ♥♥♥♥ed up if you are hit by anything.  The added mobility and acceleration tend to not be worth the trade off.
All in all, the game isn't exactly "bad".  The devs are pretty scummy for making this Oculus exclusive for VR support, and future updates are even tied specifically to that version.  For this, the desktop version is pretty much complete.  I don't think you will miss anything as far as game play is concerned.  There aren't too many games of this style for Steam, and the ones competing with this are mostly unoptimized, pathetic Android ports.  For $10, you probably will not find the value paying for this.  If you are a fan of local games, definitely worth it on sale, if only for a few hours of casual shared screen multi player.  Otherwise, for what your paying for, you could always get something better.  For a more skilful kart game, Sonic All Stars Racing Transformed would be good to look into if you haven't already got it.  You won't miss much for passing this game up.
6/10: Good on a sale, but your money is better spent elsewhere.  Do not buy if RNG racing pisses you off.

Are you a Halo fan? Buy this game.
Are you a fan of twin stick shooters? Buy this game on sale.
Spartan Assault is basically a very professional and polished mobile title, the gameplay is fairly standard, and yet manages to reflect it's source material surprisingly well. In this game you feel like a Spartan, you have access to weapons, equipment and vehicles from the Halo world, and there are many moments that make you feel like you're playing a Halo game. You can hijack vehicles, punch tanks, use armor abilities, dual wield SMGs and stick grenades to hapless grunts, there are even skull modifiers that increase your score. The graphics and music are very high quality for such a cheap game too.
The game follows the story of two Spartans, Davis, a newcomer, and Sarah "Eggheads" Palmer from 4, as they fight the Covenant on a Forerunner planet. You'll switch between the two to accomplish various missions ranging from defending bases, escorting transports, rescuing stranded marines and all kinds of things, there's a lot of variety.
The missions are short, and designed to be played in small bursts, but they're varied enough to keep you interested, although I have to say the story (told through mission descriptions and Terminal-style animation) is poor for a Halo title. The score attack theme and skull modifiers will give you an incentive to replay missions, although there's no horde mode unfortunately.
I have only two complaints, that the local coop present on the Xbox versions was removed in this port, and that you can't select your weapons before a mission. You may use points accrued from missions to buy a different armor ability or a heavy weapon, but you're not given the option to change your basic loadout.
I got this game for $1.99 and I feel it was a very good deal.
A very good game to play for Halo fans. Highly recommended!

The game really feels and looks like Halo even though is not a FPS. It has the same atmosphere and the same graphic and artistic direction, making it a real Halo game.
These being said, the game is actually designed for mobile touch enabled devices and the first thing that gives it away is the missions length that never reaches 10 minutes. In fact, you can finish most of the missions in less than 5 minutes(if you're good enough), making Halo: Spartan Assault the first casual game in this series.
The story is interesting and it's written in such a manner that can justify the moments when the game gets really hard.
The game features and experience system that allows you to buy new weapons and abilities. You can get XP points only based on the enemies you kill and the manner you kill them. This way you can earn the Bronze/Silver/Gold star or none (this means no XP points). You can also select 2 out of 6 skulls to make the game harder but gain more XP points.
The game is really enjoyable but unfortunately it has some serious issues.
There are moments the game feels so scripted and cheap that you really want to ditch it.
The default weapons set usually feels useless so you have to pick your own custom ones. However this requires a lot of XP points and force you to pick up skulls. This makes the game harder but frustrating and cheap.
While the Covenant troops have no problem in controlling the vehicles, you struggle to.
While the need 1-3 grenades to blow up their own vehicles when you are driving them, you need 3-5 at least to do the same thing with the same vehicles. While they can blow up you vehicle really fast with mounted turrets without stopping from shooting, you need more shots and time to do it and you also have to stop firing since the turrets magically start overheating when you use them.
And you also need more grenades to blow up the turrets when the enemy uses it than they need for when you are using it.
All those aspects make some missions so hard that you have to keep on trying to finish them. Sometimes you need to replay old missions to get XP points so that you can afford the right set of weapons and abilities since you waste all those points trying to figure the right set out, making a 5 minutes mission feel like a 30 minutes repetitive hell and a very bad way to make a game feel longer than it really is.

Bought this game after reading about it and watching a few videos and got unintentionally hyped.
Just as expected, the game's graphics and engine is nothing to boast about. Sporting mediocre cartoonish designs, however, Tree of Life manages to bring about an interesting feel to the world.
What I like most about the game would be the crafting system and skill mastery system. The crafting system leaves a new player completely clueless, yet the thrill of discovering new recipes or building your first water well makes it all the more satisfying.
The skill mastery system is similar to Runescape, where you can level any stat/craft that you want by using it repeatedly. This allows more freedom when raising your character's level.
Another awesome part of the game is the fact that there are no NPCs, no quests, no pre-made towns, and no in-game developer provided guides. This means that everything you learn about the game either has to be through self-discovery or from asking and communicating with other players! Something that has become quite rare in many games lately.
Tree of Life, however, could use improvements in character designs, which includes different faces, hairstyles, body builds, etc. The game can also be pretty buggy at certain points, such as the lighting working awkwardly or monsters appearing invisible. I think Tree of Life will be a great game once it is refined and polished, it certainly has a lot of potential.

Assassin's Creed Rogue was pretty good. I actually liked it more than I was expecting to. And I think that is largely because of the varying ways you can explore the world. I can't say if I liked it more than Unity or not, as the story is pretty short. If you're not doing any of the side content, naval missions, running around and clearing areas of Assassin gangs, the story could probably be beat in just under six hours. But because it's just like the more recent Assassin's Creed gangs, where there's various side quests and all of this exploring and collecting treasures, you can spend a lot of time playing this game. I got to the point where I did tire myself from constantly going from location to location, collecting treasures, sea shanty lyrics, prosperity (raises your income), renovating buildings, treasure maps, and I think it's because they tried to fill in as much as they could. It just got repetitive after a while. It would have been nice if Ubisoft actually utilized all of these locations they'd made for the seperate worlds instead of just throwing them there and adding all of these collectables. Outside of the main story, some of these locations are completely pointless and don't require a second visit. That's my main issue with this game, the surmounting amount of locations that are ultimately irrelevant.
The story is pretty good. I liked it. I liked the different perspective of how treacherous the Assassins can be, how they'll want to stop the Templars by any means, and to secure the precursor items even if it means destroying a city. That's how Shay Cormac ends up betraying the Assassins; after he's sent to Lisbon to acquire a precursor box, the great Lisbon earthquake of 1751 happens, and the destruction is similar to how it actually did happen in real life. The entire city's infrastructure is destroyed and lopsided, and it angers Shay. After being shot in the back by his fellow Assassins, he falls off a cliff and is left for dead. But the Templars save him and nurture him back to health. Although the Templars can be ruthless, it shows that they do show sympathy and empathy. The story is also great as it covers, at least it tries to cover, the French-Indian War of the 1750's. They could have done a better job of referring to some of the missions and campaigns though. If you do take over the number of forts in the North Atlantic and the River Valley, then you do get a perspective of how it was mostly a naval war, but defeating those forts is pretty much optional. The main story doesn't require it. Still, I did nearly everything, defeated every fort, went to every viewpoint.
The world's design, well, I have complaints. The north Atlantic is okay. They at least tried to design Nova Scotia, Newfoundland, New Brunswick, and the southern shore of Quebec, and the various small islands in the area. But it's scaled down so much and the only relevant areas are, more or less, Halifax, St. John's, and Anticosti, plus some of the wilderness areas. It's not and the area is quite big in terms of square miles, not as big as the West Indies in Black Flag, obviously, but still kind of big. The textures are nice. I definitely liked the weather system. It was a lot better than the River Valley area, which was my biggest complaint in this game. I don't know who laid out that area, but they should be fired. I've never seen something so dumb. It's a stupid combustion of river valley land in a square, that ranges from Mount Vernon, Virginia, to southern Quebec. None of that makes sense. Mount Vernon is directly west of Sleepy Hollow, NY. And Sleepy Hollow is basically just west-south-west of Albany, NY. Who designed this? I live not to far from the Genesee river and have explored most of its length and I can tell you that the Genesee region shown in the game looks nothing like how it should. There are high mountains in what should be the Catskills, but the Catskills look nothing like how they do in the game. Hell, they threw in some landmarks on some made up geography in scattered locations, some of them cities that aren't accurate to history, and called it a day. This is basically the opposite of what Ubisoft does for their other games. They've at least attempted to treat cities with some historical accuracy. What they did in the River Valley was a joke. It's not like the story in the River Valley part was bad, just awful design.
Overall, this game was good, but not great. 7.9/10

First off, I'm going to point out that I am a fan of the Sonic franchise. As such, this game is a nice throw back to the Genesis/Mega Drive era of the series. It consists of both new levels and old ones with some new twists to them. Kind of fun. So what's the problem?
Well there's more than one. First off, the Blue Spheres stages return, but it feels like they're significantly faster at 60 Frames/second. Maybe it's just me though. Second, collision detection is kind of messed up. Standing on a certain platform in the second zone has triggered crushing deaths even though you're standing on the edge of a platform the two platforms where sliding past each other. There are complaints about controller issues. I can't say I know for sure what it's all about since I prefer to use the Steam controller. However, when I was checking out controller options, I noticed it did button remapping a bit differently compared to other games I've played with the Steam controller. More specifically, the controls were bound to option commands rather than keys or buttons. I suspect that might have something to do with controller issues.
Of course, what I really feel is bad is how they handled preorders. More specifically not mentioning the Denuvo anti-tampering mechanism until the last minute. Part of the issue with Denuvo is it's stigmatized as it has to ties to Securom, a form of DRM that Microsoft dropped support for with Windows 10 as they believed it posed some security risks. As such, I can't leave a good review at this time. I'm willing to overlook the delay, but I honestly feel like Sega should have mentioned Denuvo when preorders began so everyone knew about it and could factor it into their decision when preordering the game.
Overall, I do feel like Sonic Mania has potential, but it needs a little more polish and some destigmatization.
Edit: I have refunded the game. I will consider buying it again and changing my review in the future if Sega removes Denuvo and has the team behind the game fix various issues with the game.

In an age of games made solely for the sake of making money with little thought or consideration put towards fun and functionality, Warframe is a much needed breath of fresh air. Digital Extremes, while they have stumbled at times in the development of Warframe - and still do from time to time - continue to show their devotion and love towards their creation and its players in constant updates and upgrades to the systems in place while continuously working to keep the game as free of pay-to-win as it could possibly be, which is already a huge step above many other games in that it can't really be called pay-to-win to begin with. It's more like pay-to-grind.
But the beauty of Warframe is that you enjoy the grind. The liberation felt in the movement system and combat is unlike any other game out there that limits you in an attempt to keep you challenged. Warframe goes in the opposite direction and asks, "What if we didn't limit the players at all?" Being able to do everything short of flying makes battles significantly more dramatic and eventful and will keep you enjoying the action even as you use your 30th or 100th weapon. And that's not even accounting for the titular Warframes themselves, who each bear their own passives, stats, and four unique abilities a piece that can change gameplay dramatically for yourself and your squad mates.
This is the only free to play game that I have not only spent more than a few dollars on, but have not felt any regret in doing so. The cosmetic items in the game are stunning and the inclusion of some player-made cosmetics through Steam feels wholesome, contributing to what probably is the true pay-to-win: The Fashionframe.
Only furthering the playability of Warframe is the fact that the vast majority of its content is solo or cooperative PvE, decreasing any chances of toxicity significantly by avoiding pitting Tenno against one another but rather making them work together to experience the hilarity and madness of missions together. This leads to not only a welcoming community, but one of the most helpful communities of any game, willing to give tips and tricks as well as simply join you in your random voyages through the Origin System in your quest to become the strongest and most fashionable one-man army there is.

Frustrating as feck. Half the time you can't see where you're going - particularly if you're in the lead. Sure, it's nice that all the cars LOOK different with the same top speed, but whilst racing - basically all the power-ups (or at least all the ones I've unlocked so far) are for killing the player in front. Everything is a blue shell basically. Turbo's are pretty much DROPPED onto anyone in the middle ground (good luck getting them if you're in last) and if you're in the lead, you have nothing to keep you there, so it ends up being more advantageous to hang back a little, pick the boosts that you're being bombarded with, and steal the win at the last minute because 1st player is stuck with no boosts, and a projectile that can only shoot forward. :/ Another crap bit: You have to press the button 6 or 7 times to get back into the same race (if you want the points for playing that is) - there should just be a "Your place is first, you won X, race again?" screen and that's it, instead it's drawn out over several screens, a couple of which don't actually tell you anything important. It would also be nice to be able to setup the controls a bit better too. Just a swap of the "turbo" and "fire" buttons would be nice... but, no, nothing like that. :/
Other than that, it's quite fun. :)

Oculus tomfoolery aside, this game is a 10/10. It reminds me a lot of Mario Kart, Rock n' Roll Racing, Micro Machines, etc. There's an auto-boost mechanic on some tracks which ensures that no player is ever too far behind (think Lakitu), and the physics system and general balancing of the game makes it tough not to have fun even if you're losing. The controls, graphics, and music are all good. There's a nice variety of vehicles which all seem to have unique driving characteristics, yet most of them seem to be on par with one another once you learn to drive them. The game is simple, but there's enough content and the right balance of mechanics to keep it fresh and exciting each time I play. Although I received BlazeRush as part of a Humble Bundle, it's definitely worth full price and more. It's hard to find good local multiplayer games nowadays, but this one was an instant classic for me.

I stink at writing reviews but I'll try for this one.  This game is about writing small assembly language programs in a tiny instruction set with a minuscule amount of memory.  Making a working program is not too hard for most of the puzzles, but optimizing them is extremely hard.  I've apparently played this 171 hours, and I haven't finished all the puzzles yet, let alone optimized them, so there is an enormous amount of value.
This is similar to Human Resource Machine, but quite a bit harder, much much longer, less visually produced (though still very attractive), and with somewhat different instruction sets and restrictions on memory use that make programs quite a bit different.
TIS-100's main difference from standard assembly, other than the restrictions, is its quasi-parallel programming focus.  This is the game's chief conceit and it does play a huge role in the programs.  You will learn the main strategies for getting the twelve processors to work together, and to send data and signals between them, by playing the first several levels.
I highly recommend this game for anyone who enjoys programming.  It's very challenging, and I hope that TIS-200 includes a larger instruction set and a way to define named subroutines that can be accessed from any program.
If you think you'll like this game, you'll probably love it.

Great little game that has its own version of simple assembly language programming. I feel that the assembly language can be very limiting at times (only 15 lines allowed), and I'm used to using way more than 2 registers (only one of which can be directly accessed) in real assembly programming, so it's pretty challenging. But, it's challenging in a pretty fun way, and the way the computing nodes work mean that you can use other nodes as extra registers, caches or for more complex architectural things like pipelining (instruction-level parallel processing) or a multiprocessor system (albeit a very limited one).
Game is pretty short, but still worth the money in my opinion.

I really wanted to like Frozen Synapse but it just didn’t click for me. I thought the combat would be more like X-Com but while similar, it’s different in a bad way. It is still technically turn-based, but instead of each unit getting an individual turn, your whole team has a turn and you assign them moves & tasks, which all get carried out at the same time. The enemy units move all together at the same time your units do, which results in wasted turns & frustration.
Let’s say you want to move one unit, who is exposed, behind some cover. You want another unit to camp behind cover & shoot a bad guy as he moves. You have to instruct both of them on what you want them to do, then basically push the “play” button and watch events unfold.
Unfortunately, an enemy unit moves into firing range of the guy you told to move into cover. You couldn’t anticipate the enemy would move there, so your guy keeps stupidly running forward as you watch helplessly while the enemy blows him away. Meanwhile, your other unit jumps into a perfect firing position right at the start of the turn, just like you told him. Unfortunately, that other enemy unit went a different way than you thought he was going and basically gets a free movement turn while your guy idiotically sits in one place the entire time. Events like this are commonplace.
Maybe it gets better. Maybe I wasn’t doing it right. All I can tell you is that I didn’t enjoy the hour of Frozen Synapse I played. I’ve thought about going back and giving it another shot but then realize I’d have to sit through the entire tutorial again because I don’t remember any of the controls. I have zero desire to do that.

The monetization of the game is not predatory like you may find or expect from other F2P offerings.  I do wish, however, that the Tennogen customiztions were a bit more affordable (~$7 for a skin, helmet, or cape customiztion is steep, but they are high quality and community-made).
I definitely suggest trying the game (and asking questions in region chat/checking out
- there are a lot of intricacies that aren't necessarily explained in-depth in game).  If you like it, don't feel bad about spending a bit of cash - other premium games that I have paid for get a lot less mileage for the cost.  Plus you can get platinum discounts from daily login bonus (suggest waiting for a 50% or 75% off discount) or you can purchase one of the "DLC" packs during a Steam sale for a decent boost.

Overall: If you like programming, or puzzle solving this is a great game. You should be warned that you need to type out what you want to do to solve a problem. That means you need to watch out for your syntax. It is difficult, there is a steep learning curve to newcomers to programming. Don't let that discourage you, this could be an amazing learning experience.
Story: There is a cute little story line that runs through the puzzles. It adds flair to what may seem to be a pretty bleak interface. But that bleakness, along with the story add to the charm of the style of the game.
Visualization: It is a seriously fun game if you are interested in programming in any way. And while it may seem to be a "game" only for programmers, after a while you will begin to see the flow of information and realize that there is some great graphical elements that give you feedback. But you need to look for them in how the nodes communicate, and what is in the node at any given time.
Replayability: I've nearly beat the main part of the game. And at first it seems like everything goes fast, but the challenges grow. If you worry about replayability, there is options for optimizing your puzzle solutions in 3 different ways. Then you can compare your solutions performance to your friends. I think this game is best played with a friend to talk about it with and push you to work harder. Not only that but there is a whole second set of puzzles available, which I've not even touched on yet. There is also some fun challenges through achievements that in some cases require a bit of creativity.
Teachers should probably assign this game as homework. Better yet, classwork.
TL;DR: Loved it. Great for problem solvers.

This thing is raw stategy.
You have a squad of "vatforms," essentially clones into which orders can be plugged. You must provide those orders in this turn-based squad combat game. Except it doesn't feel so turn based, because after each planning phase where you meticulously plotted routes and arcs of fire for your units, all the action hashes out in real time.
The game basically does a bunch of behind the scenes math to come up with the result, taking into account cover, movement, range, wepon type, etc. After a bit, you catch on to the basic rules of who's going to survive a given one on one encounter, and you can start testing strategies by running real time simulations of enemy movements (with orders given by you based on what you think they might do) before you submit each turn.
Add to the rock solid core mechanics a compelling story, holographic computer simulation graphics style, and awesome soundtrack, and you have top notch game.
Did I mention there's procedurally generated maps and multiplayer?

If you like the Rainbow Six games, you'll love this game: It's a perfectly distilled & stylized tactical shooter.
Challenging, lots of variation, really gets your brain going.
The only downside to the game is the bad optimization (pathfinding calculations probably?), resulting in long processing times after each turn. Plus the tutorial was a bit unclear about setting up the more complex orders, but nothing a few failed tryout runs couldn't fix.

Although it may look a little lack lustre, Frozen Synapse is in fact a very deep turn-based strategy in the vein of XCOM or Heroes of Might & Magic with a twist: once you and your opponent decide your units' moves, it becomes a real-time action sequence and your strategy goes against theirs. The story became gripping and the characters very interesting. It's a mix of corporate espionage, rebellion, and a war of beliefs coming together to make a fantastic singleplayer.
On the multiplayer side, it comes with the added benefit of being asynchronous (after you setup your strategy, you can wander off for hours while your opponent decides; kind of like chess by mail). The game modes are neat and varied and seting up a match is pretty easy. Another plus, the people I played against were gratious and felt like a great community.
Finally, after listening to the trailers, I decided to buy the soundtrack, and boy was it worth it! Still in my play list today.

Unlike XCOM and other turn-based strategies, where the main resource are factors like:
cover, character states and generally chance.
This game manages to remove the "chance" aspect and replace it with "time".
Everything from turns to killing an opposing unit requires time. There is no chance, there is no blind luck, there are no 95% chance to hit *аnd then miss* moments, there is no RNGesus, there is none of that ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t.
This makes gameplay a lot less frustrating, more predictable and overall, more enjoyable.

The goal is to finish 5 quests which are updated whenever you land on one of the 4 "home-tiles". You either have to win a progressively larger amount of fights or aquire a progressively larger amount of stars. There are situations where you can loose stars.
If you loose a fight you are not done for, but you have to roll dice to determine if you are back in the game. With each round incapacitated the number you're required to roll to return to the game is decreased by one, starting from 5, throwing a 6-sided dye.
Fighting occurs when you meet another player, a boss or if you land on a "combat-tile", which will select a random player (or boss) to fight against you.
Essentially this is a mario-party-like game with alot of japanese influence. Or at least that's how it feels like. Right now the game is discounted. If you're going to buy it, I recommend 3 friends and the "4-Pack", which is 5,99 right now. I don't recommend the single-player experience, but again, this is not my cup of tea.

To keep it short:
100% Orange Juice is a multiplayer boardgame for those looking for a cutesy, anime-ish game and for an experience where you feel like you just lost friends for doing a♥♥♥♥♥♥move in a multiplayer game.
The story is nothing special, but the gameplay is where it's at.
Different boards, many cards to make a deck from to alter the course of the game, and a good pool of unique characters with different stats and Hyper Cards.
[If you really like the game and play it often, I definitely recommend getting the DLC packs.]
Cards can be obtained through winning games and acquiring the stars you get from winning, which you spend in the Store for booster packs [1 card], or if you don't want cards you can buy alternate outfits, other characters, and more gameboards. (The Store is not real money or DLC-based)
You either roll a die or play a card before rolling, then moving spaces until you get what you need to fulfill your goal or Norma, like 10 stars collected from killing creatures on Red spaces, killing other players, or stepping on a Bonus space, or acquiring 2 wins [1 per red space win, 2 per player kill].
Fulfilling Norma would require you to have completed the task and also moving back to your home space on the board.
Doing this can be frustrating as getting killed will make you lose stars, and you will have to roll a certain number (once per turn) in order to be revived back to full HP.
It's pretty much luck-based, but the RNGesus-has-forsaken-us plays and comeback plays make for great moments in singleplayer (even though it's bots) and multiplayer.
I've put in a good chunk of time in this game, and I don't regret a single moment of it.
Except for maybe the amount of time I've spent not being able to complete goddamn Tomomo Hell.
Seriously. F*ck that bonus level, man. Getting killed every three rolls...
Final Verdict:
9/10. Game's fantastic.
Honestly. Get a bunch of friends, disregard the animu graphics if you hate them, and you'll have a great relationship-breaking time with your buddies on the weekends.
Not super hard to learn, either.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

I won't be talking about the DRM or Denuvo thing that most people are talking about. I'm just gonna show my general review on Sonic Mania.
Sonic Mania is somewhat a melody of the 90’s genesis era of Sonic the Hedgehog. I would call this game Sonic the Hedgehog 4 but I’m bothered by the reused levels this game has. To me, it feels like another Sonic Generations game but without Modern Sonic and it has it’s original sprite art style. I would love this game way more if the game had new levels only. I’m not a fan of nostalgia, unlike most fans. Which is why I want something new from Sonic Mania. And yes, the game does have new levels like Studiopolis and Mirage Saloon. But they're only 4 new levels and the rest are reused levels. I am aware of the reused levels having changed zone layouts and having amazing music remixes but it still feels like another Sonic Generations game. Aside from the levels, the game is generally great. The controls are decent, the sprite art is beautiful and the MUSIC!! Tee Lopes was a fan of Sonic who made amazing Sonic music remixes and he was hired to make the OST for Mania. I cannot stop listening to most of the music in the game. Tee is proof of why Sonic music is a gift from the heavens. The bosses in Sonic Mania have some of the best boss battles I’ve seen in a Sonic game. They are some really quirky ones, like the Mean Bean Machine/Puyo Puyo Tetris boss for example. They are creative bosses like Eggman’s weather machine and they’re entertaining bosses like the Heavy Magician of how she can turn into the Team Hooligan members(Nack, Bean and Bark). Sonic Mania does have a lot of content aside from the main game. There’s a race mode which you can challenge your friends. There’s a time attack mode where you can beat a zone as fast as possible. And there’s tons more like debug mode, the special stages and a whole lots of easter eggs in the whole game for Sonic fans to be pleased. Sonic Mania is up there with the decent Sonic games. Not all Sonic games have to be good or bad. It all matters on having fun and having great memories with the games. I loved Sonic Mania and I did only played as Sonic in the main game. There’s Tails which he can fly and Knuckles where he can glide and climb. I guess Tails and Knuckles are meant for new players who would mess up with their platforming and they can fly or climb back up to undo their mistake. Sonic on the other hand, had no special abilities back then until he was given the drop dash ability where he can perform an instant dash when he lands from a jump. Amy would’ve been a great addition to Sonic Mania as a hidden playable character but instead, she was referenced as a creepy small doll in one of the boss fights. The game does have chaos emeralds to collect but I won’t spoil the rest about it. For a conclusion, I loved Mania and I’m really pumped for Sonic Forces releasing on November 7th 2017. Sonic Mania and Sonic Forces together will bring Sonic back from the flaming hate he has been through.

This review will be written ignoring the inclusion of Denuvo DRM, because I personally didn't know or care about that before completing the game and its true ending.
Let me start by saying this game is NOT a rehash of the classics, as I initially feared it might be. It's an evolution of them. Every stage, even the reused ones, are filled to the brim with exciting new mechanics, enemies and areas that will keep the journey fresh from start to end. Whilst I would have preferred all the stages to be completely new, I can't complain about the reimagined stages one bit as they are all exceptionally fun.
There were very few lulls in the game and very few things I did not like. The first Act of Mirage Saloon was a bit frustrating, as I'm not much for auto-scrollers and the boss was a bit confusing at first (because it's 2D, judging the depth of the boss in order to hit it was initially quite difficult). Other than that, I have no complaints with the level design.
Metallic Madness 2 (and its boss fight) definitely stood out as being particularly great in my book, and both acts of Titanic Monarch were INCREDIBLY good. The music sets an epic tone for the whole stage, with subtle differences in the act 1 and act 2 themes which shift the tone from grandiose to almost dark and urgent. In conclusion: if you don't care about DRM, buy this now. If you do, wait for SEGA to remove it because of the backlash and then purchase it, or just buy it on console. It's an experience you won't want to miss, and the best Sonic has been in quite some time.

One of the most gripping and engaging puzzle games I've played in a long time. Full disclosure, I am currently a computer science student, so this game is sorta in my wheelhouse already, and I do have a fair amount of programming expirience. But this game is brilliant. Contrary to most, I don't think having a background in programming is necesarry to enjoy this game, but I will admit it does help. In terms of gameplay, it's a simple formula. You get a series of levels that slowly unlock as you complete more and more. Each puzzle gives you a set of instructions, which you then design a solution for. Were that all this game had to offer, it wouldn't be nearly as interesting as it is. But, on top of that, there's leaderboards, where you compare the effectiveness of your solution with others, which adds a lot to the fun of the game, as it reinforces the idea of not just finding a solution, but the best solution. Finally, and for me what elevates this game from really good to amazing, is there's an air of mystery and conspiracy in the game. If you pay attention to cryptic hints, there appears to be more going on then just moving around numbers. As a lover of stories in games, this is the factor for me that really puts this game head and shoulders above a lot of other puzzle games. All told, since I first started this game, I've not been able to stop thinking about it in the back of my mind, wondering about optimizing my code, improving solutions, and exploring the secrets in this game. As I said, this game is brilliant, and will pull you in, and not let go, if you let it.
Also, just because it's worth mentioning, print out the game's manual. Trust me, you'll want to keep it handy. Plus, having a copy of it adds a lot to the immersion of this game.

While it's background and visuals aren't multi-coloured, it all makes up for the complex controls with a astonishingly wide variety of commands for your units to execute. This isn't one of those strategy games you have played recently, like LoL, Dota or anything: Frozen Synapse really challenges you to think and plan every move, with no time constrains or pressure dropping all over your shoulders!

I haven't played this much on multiplayer, but I know the singleplayer experience is great after playing it years ago everyday after school for months on end.
A) The game has a PAUSE button. No more clickfests in a real time STRATEGY game!  That means if the enemy catches you off guard, you can simply pause the game, build units in all your production buildings, wait a minute or two, and then you have an army to fight with... assuming you have the resources to support it and can afford the ramped unit costs.
B) The game has interesting assassination and diplomacy modes, so freeforall matches don't end up in the computer players secretly ganging up on you.
C) You can quota research as well as simply "tab" through open research buildings.
D) You don't "gather resources".  Instead, you just assign workers to resource gathering buildings, and they increase your income.
E) The Conquer the World mode is similar to the "Empire" series in that you can upgrade territories and support attacks with multiple armies into single territories.  There's also an alliance system and you have to declare war to invade not to mention the presence of unique resources which help too.
F) The game is similar to Civ with 8 ages, updated (not upgraded) units, and technologies that actually improve your performance instead of just unlocking stuff.  There are also Wonders of the World, and cities get bigger over time with improvements.  Conquering cities does not destroy improvements either unless you manually target them before conquest, and cities must have all improvements manually razed after they're annexed before the city itself can be razed.
G) Attrition damage prevents enemies from slipping into your land without supply wagons backing them up.  The French also get supply wagons that heal in enemy land.
H) You can garrison units in production buildings to heal them instead of having to build castles or towers too (although you can still build them).
I) Focus fire REDUCES damage dealt to enemy units. When you attack an enemy force, just attack-move.  Micromanagement actually HURTS your performance.  This is a STRATEGY game, not a first person shooter.
J) Dragoons and Carabineers for the win!  Never fear pikemen or fusiliers again when charging enemy artillery before the industrial age.
K) Markets don't remain stagnant or solely depend on players buying and selling resources.  They float around and stabilize over time.  You can use trade routes too for wealth, and the Dutch have a cool ability that earns interest on saved resources.  You can actually play the late game without any economy at all as the Dutch as long as you don't spend everything you have.  That helps your population limit.  :-P
L) Spies, commandos, and generals are incredible force multipliers.  They can bribe, assassinate, dig-in, force march, create decoys, and ambush enemy forces.
M) The historical Conquer the World campaigns actually have interesting battle setups.  For example, fighting for the Korean Peninsula during the Cold War actually starts with a DMZ as well as the Russians (and maybe Chinese) sending help for the north as well as the Americans headquartered in Japan.  It doesn't just plunk a bunch of cities down on somewhat sculpted terrain.  Likewise, the Americans start allied with the British against the French and Iroquois in the Colonial Campaign, but they pay tribute until declaring independence.
N) There are INFINITE unit production quotas.  That means you don't have to periodically check on a production building to see if it's still building reinforcements while you're commanding an army on the front.
O) Generals AUTOMATICALLY group with combined selected military units.  When you click the "next general" button, the WHOLE army will be automatically selected.
P) Units can cross water on their own in default transport ships.  You don't need to build transports for them, but they are very vulnerable and need to be escorted.  Otherwise, a squad of destroyers or sloops can wipe out an entire expedition.  The same thing goes for naval trade routes which can be plundered for wealth.
Q) You can ADJUST research times and costs under game settings.  Play a fast and cheap game if you don't want to spend much on research or wait around, or play a slow and expensive game if you want something more drawn out.  You can also play a sandbox game to experiment with building strategies, or play a pacifist game with a score limit.
R) Capital defeat depends on losing one's capital and not recovering it for a period of time.  That means you don't have to destroy every little thing on the map to win.  You just have to conquer your enemies' capitals and hold them for so long.
S) Territory victory doesn't mean controlling the entire map.  In fact, you can reduce the percent of land needed for victory to BELOW HALF of the map if you want players to play more according to balance of powers or if you want an easier time where you can say, "Yea, I've effectively won already.  There's no need to rinse and repeat."  This really helps with population limits too since a single player with only 200 units can't beat multiple players with 200 units each.  That said, you can still ally with someone in diplomacy mode to combine your land percentages.
T) You can win with Wonders of the World as long as you have more "points" in Wonders than anyone else and hold them long enough.  This is similar to the tourism victory in Civ 5's Brave New World expansion where you need enough influence built up over other civilizations over time.
U) Airplanes have a flight radius.  You can't fly them everywhere over the map unless you build an airport to move them to.  Cruise missiles and nuclear missiles work the same way with missile silos.
V) Unit costs change over time.  For example, when you discover oil, heavy cavalry will no longer cost wealth, but cost oil instead.
W) Land itself gives you wealth.  A bigger empire is a wealthier empire, and you get more wealth with research in the temple which also expands your borders and gives cities more health.
X) All maps don't have equal resources available, and that actually changes gameplay tactics.  A map without hills is a map without metal, so don't expect many heavy units on it.  There's probably going to be a lot of light cavalry instead which just cost food and wood (since light cavalry defeat light infantry and ranged cavalry which cost food and wood or food and wealth respectively). In turn, defensive players research civics to increase attrition damage (especially the Russians) as well as push their borders to make it harder to be harassed.  Offensive players will target enemy caravans between cities and try to destroy temples since civics boosts wealth as well.
Y) Custom governments exist in the game, and actually make a big difference.  Republic, democracy, and capitalism tend to support defensive economic strategies.  Despotism, monarchy, and socialism tend to support offensive military strategies.
Z) Workers that repair buildings under attack get hurt, and can eventually die.  If you're bombarding an enemy structure that's repaired, don't worry about being in vain.  Also, repairing gets slowed down if a worker is hit and accelerates if uninterrupted.
As you can see, this game has a ton to offer.  There are also tons of custom scenarios to download with triggers and customized units (such as fusiliers transforming into carabineers to represent dismounted cavalry or special force commandos transforming into assault infantry to represent sniper versus assault rifles if you hit an action key, or man of war ships with a range of 30 to represent gunpowder naval bombardment during land battles whereas the regular game gives man of war a range of... 11 if I remember correctly to represent fighting in naval battles.  You use bomb ketches instead to ordinarily bombard cities inland).

Divinity Original Sin 2 was the first game of the Divine games that I had tried / pickup and really enjoyed myself when getting through the game and making progress with my original party. From my personal experience, DOS 2 offers unique ways to solve different quests while also being punishing if you screw it up and not letting you get a retry button (unless you reload a save). From the character selection to the origin characters, divinity has a very vast variety of options to choose for your characters skills, do you want to be a tanky mage? or how about being an rogue who can polymorph enemies into chickens. When you get into the game after making a custom character or choosing one of the six origin characters, you are able to pick up to three other origin characters to recruit into your party and journey along together till you reach your end goal. What sets this game differently from an RPG like skyrim or fallout is that you actually get to do side quest for your companions and are able to learn more about him or her through dialog, not having bland reused dialog changing with the envoirment and how they see you as an ally or an enemy depending on if you're being rude to them. On top of all of that another part that I enjoy is that all most all dialog (except some that have been added recently to put players in the right direction and some that are just bugged) are 100% voice acted, from the Red Prince to a dog in Fort Joy each entity has its own character and appeal to them. One thing that makes divinity shine from most RPGs is that you can physically kill any NPC you want, from entire towns to some of Fort Joys residence (But killing origin characters will cause problems with the main story line so avoid doing so) allowing you to kill a trading that you might have a grudge over if you want some of their loot from their store. Finally the loot system is extravagant allowing you to have different loot while looting dungeons in different play throughs based on Lucky Charm and loot tables that were generated in the game, while also not completely dropping the NPC's inventory if killed making it more useful to pickpocket them for their better wears before killing. Overall I love DOS 2 as a game, it personally has to be one of my favorite games released this year, should you pay $45? Yes this game is worth every cent the COOP is amazing and the story and side quest will have your save be longer than 40 hours or more depending on if you go into the nitty gritty.
The very best in RPGs. The depth of the characters and the consequences of your decisions is a joy play through and the combat system is the cherry on top. Thank you to all of the team made this.

So I left the Steam community ages ago and recently returned ( had to make a new account due to forgetting my old log-in details/registered e-mail ) to try Tree of Life. While it wasn't necessarily what I expected I am currently ( or was at that time if you are reading this in the far-away future ) pleasantly surprised by the game's depth, graphics, simplicity and social aspects to the point where I was reminded ( in the best way ) of the early-middle periods of RuneScape 2. I intend to keep with this game a while longer but what I see is promising. I'd encourage people to give it a chance if they are looking for something new or something similar to the old RuneScape 2.
While I've not gone terribly far in the game ( I took the liberty of exploring the map over focusing on leveling up skills ) the depth of the game's skilling is wonderful. For crafting, cooking and construction you find yourself exploring a very large map and either dodging or fighting beats ( and sometimes players, the game has P.V.P. ) of various difficulty. You'll have to do one thing ( wood cutting, mining/rock-cutting, etc. ) to do another ( making fires/charcoal, building/crafting, etc. ) and this also applies to combat where you can up masteries with different fighting styles ( Martial Arts, Dagger/knife fighting ) to gain different character stats ( Strength/Constitution, Dexterity, etc. ) that overall improve you.
While you yourself may not look great the atmosphere is wonderful thanks to the game's graphics. The game's night sky looks wonderful and the way the areas around you darken ( they become very dark ) add an element of danger to the game that would otherwise be missing. During the day the light allows you to see the details of the game's structures, which are easy on the eyes.
The game is simple enough to learn and staying with others provides a lot of security. From what I can tell you spawn in one of three spots ( I've deleted/re-made my character several times and have spawned in three different locations ) in which resources, monster level and the like all vary. You use E to open the main menu and go about crafting your gear and digging through your inventory all from that one button press. You can collect resources by cutting, mining, fishing and fighting along with many other ways. In what seems like a lawless land the biggest challenge seems to be finding your own area to claim while getting along with neighbors while dealing with the limited resources you can find.
From what I've played so far I'd give the game 3 out of 5 stars but based purely on enjoyment the game becomes a 4 or 5 star game. No matter where you spawn ( the north-west which seems to be the easiest start, the south-west or the south-east ) you're in for a fun adventure where your pilgrimage depends on how you navigate the game's obstacles My one bit of advice is, if possible, start your adventure while you have daylight to work with and stay grouped with others at night. Thanks for reading my review; I hope you enjoy this game should you pick it up.

This review will be written ignoring the inclusion of Denuvo DRM, because I personally didn't know or care about that before completing the game and its true ending.
Let me start by saying this game is NOT a rehash of the classics, as I initially feared it might be. It's an evolution of them. Every stage, even the reused ones, are filled to the brim with exciting new mechanics, enemies and areas that will keep the journey fresh from start to end. Whilst I would have preferred all the stages to be completely new, I can't complain about the reimagined stages one bit as they are all exceptionally fun.
There were very few lulls in the game and very few things I did not like. The first Act of Mirage Saloon was a bit frustrating, as I'm not much for auto-scrollers and the boss was a bit confusing at first (because it's 2D, judging the depth of the boss in order to hit it was initially quite difficult). Other than that, I have no complaints with the level design.
Metallic Madness 2 (and its boss fight) definitely stood out as being particularly great in my book, and both acts of Titanic Monarch were INCREDIBLY good. The music sets an epic tone for the whole stage, with subtle differences in the act 1 and act 2 themes which shift the tone from grandiose to almost dark and urgent. The difficulty here I feel was perfect. I got four or five game overs attempting the final boss, and I feel that's about right for a final zone (at least given my skill level).
I really liked the inclusion of Blue Spheres, and those were really fun to beat. I have all silver medals and might go for golds eventually. The Chaos Emerald stages are quite fun as well.
My only other gripe with the game is that the unlockables don't feel like they add a whole lot of replayability, because most of them are just different ways to repeat what you've already done. I would've loved the inclusion of more unlockable stages or characters, but hey, the game's only $20. I definitely got my money's worth.
In conclusion: if you don't care about DRM, buy this now. If you do, wait for SEGA to remove it because of the backlash and then purchase it, or just buy it on console. It's an experience you won't want to miss, and the best Sonic has been in quite some time.

This is definitely one of the best 2D Sonic titles I've ever played. I love the fluid animations of the sprites, the music is excellent and I love the stages though most of them are from the classic series (Sonic 1 - 3 & Knuckles). What Christian Whitehead and his team essentially did was take design aspects of the old stages and then recreate them so you get an experience mixture of old and new. There are some brand new stages and the music in all of them is really nice to listen to. The bosses are pretty good as well (and a bit challenging). All in all, this was a phenomenal Sonic game and Christian Whitehead and his team did an amazing job. This was a Sonic game made by Sonic fans for Sonic fans. I guess the only other complaint besides this game being more of a nostalgia trip would be newcomers feeling like they're out of the loop when witnessing so many references to the Sonic franchise's history. Even then, there's still something in it for everybody and it's a solid game. I highly recommend people (Sonic fan or not) to buy and play this game.
(Edit: I don't understand all the drama over Denuvo. The game works perfectly fine for me and I've hardly experienced any problems with the game. It really seems to me that the people whining about Denuvo simply aren't able to play Mania on PC themselves, support games being pirated or they're just joining the bandwagon since they can't think for themselves.)

Pros:

- Superb gameplay.
- Superb graphics.
- Superb music.

Cons:

- Stages are somewhat disjointed, they need better transitions. The story is not clear enough.
- Only 1 checkpoint bonus stage: "Blue Spheres", which gets *very* repetitive. Missed the spinning labyrinth and jackpot, the bouncing machine, and the magnetic fields.
- Last boss felt like a normal stage boss, not epic/big enough.
- A few maps were rehashed from previous games.

Overall score:

- "Sonic 4 & Knuckles" / 10, but needs a few additions.

Uplink is a mostly text based game released in 2001. This cyberpunk title is set the near future, the year 2010, and hackers slither around the interwebs. You play as a hacker working for Uplink Corporation, a company that offers illegal hacker services to others.
The aim of the game is to climb up the hacker fame ladder and make cash. You do so by completing contracts, making relationships with others and upgrading your software, hardware and gateway. All together, it feels like a shadowrun type of game.
You're breaking into the "Knight Tech" computer network. Your mission is to locate and destroy a file. You gain access to the file storage system and your proxies fail, the tracers are going crazy indicating that you're close to being traced. You franticly look for the file and delete it just in the nick of time, avoiding a hefty fine and possibly a jail sentence. One of the most gripping and engaging puzzle games I've played in a long time. Full disclosure, I am currently a computer science student, so this game is sorta in my wheelhouse already, and I do have a fair amount of programming expirience. But this game is brilliant. Contrary to most, I don't think having a background in programming is necesarry to enjoy this game, but I will admit it does help. In terms of gameplay, it's a simple formula. You get a series of levels that slowly unlock as you complete more and more. Each puzzle gives you a set of instructions, which you then design a solution for. Were that all this game had to offer, it wouldn't be nearly as interesting as it is. But, on top of that, there's leaderboards, where you compare the effectiveness of your solution with others, which adds a lot to the fun of the game, as it reinforces the idea of not just finding a solution, but the best solution. Finally, and for me what elevates this game from really good to amazing, is there's an air of mystery and conspiracy in the game. If you pay attention to cryptic hints, there appears to be more going on then just moving around numbers. As a lover of stories in games, this is the factor for me that really puts this game head and shoulders above a lot of other puzzle games. All told, since I first started this game, I've not been able to stop thinking about it in the back of my mind, wondering about optimizing my code, improving solutions, and exploring the secrets in this game. As I said, this game is brilliant, and will pull you in, and not let go, if you let it.
Also, just because it's worth mentioning, print out the game's manual. Trust me, you'll want to keep it handy. Plus, having a copy of it adds a lot to the immersion of this game.

This game speaks to me. It says "Your programming skills suck. Why are you even here? LOL NOOB!"
It's really hard, especially once the game hands you a Stack Memory and expects you to be able to use it. But the TIS-100's weird architecture with its very limited registers and limited code length per core makes for very compelling puzzles that are challenging even if you already have a basic grasp of assembler. Once you solved a puzzle, you get compared to other players and can optimize your code for various goals: least number of code lines, least number of CPU cycles for test run, least number of cores used. Often, you need different approaches for either goal.
I now kinda want a real TIS-100, no matter what a huge clusterf*ck its architecture is. But people who don't have at least some grasp of low-level programming concepts might end up really frustrated.
Have I mentioned before that I love everything Zachtronics does? Well, I do. This follows the same general concept of his other games, yet geared towards programmers.

If you ever wanted a mind bending puzzler about programming esoteric hardware in bespoke assembly code, this is most certainly the game for you.  The highly constrained processing architecture presents a large variety of challenges to accomplish even the simplest of tasks.  You'll never take C for  granted again!

Most explain what they are doing and why. Just watch one or two and there will still be plenty of levels to solve on your own.

One of those games where you can stare at the screen for hours on end, not get anything done except lose a few hairs, but feel like you've worked so hard. It's just like real programming. It's beautiful.

What a fascinating game this is! By breaking all the rules of conventional game design and foregoing in-game tutorials and handholding, instead opting for a PDF manual that you're intended to actually print out, staple together, and keep on your desk as a constant companion piece to the game.
From the launch onward the game is incredibly sober, never breaking character or acknowledging that it is a game at all. As soon as you launch this from your library you are presented with a windowed unix-looking 'bootloader' which brings you into the fictional TIS-100. There are no fourth-wall breaking menus or tutorials to deal with here.
The manual itself is an invaluable part of the experiecne of this game. It looks beautifully authentic, the way it was typeset, printed, marked up with notes and highlights, then re-scanned to its final form.
Though taken at face-value TIS-100 seems like a game aimed solely at programmers, it is at it's very heart a programming themed puzzle game. I personally have never written any low-level or assembly code, but was able to pick up the TIS-100's simple instruction set pretty quickly.
Overall, this is a game for the patient problem solver. If you enjoy something with true 'hack-value', a challenge with no point other than overcoming it, then this is the game for you.

Most people compare Rise of Nations to the Age of Empires series, and obviously they share many similarities. Both are published by Microsoft, they all share the same basic UI, game objectives, etc. However, Rise of Nations is not just another AOE clone. There is many genuine differences between these games. In RON, the major difference is the ability to advance your nation's time period until the modern age. You start off in an ancient time period, and gradually by gathering resources and building workers and buildings, progress through time. So you start off with bows and arrows and you (hopefully) will have airplanes, tanks, and nukes by the end of the game. So although the game is very similar to AOE, there is some major gameplay differences that seperates them. Personally I find RON a better overall game, although both games are amazing.
Anyways, back to RON, I find the gameplay is solid, but looks rather dated like you may expect from such an old game.  Unit fighting animations are also really basic, so don't expect the level of detail you would see in Total War or COH. However, there are tons of nations to play as, and each has specific bonuses. Unit variety is good, each faction has special units (example Germany has MG42 squad).
The age advancing mechanic is really interesting, but unnfortunately it seems the technology gap is never very far apart between players, and despite what you do you will all get the same units at about the same time. I was hoping I would get to pit some battles between tanks and infantry vs archers and chariots, except by the time I have those units, others players are developing those units too, despite how well I had been playing. The difference between ages is generally not too far apart, although there is many custom settings you can change to make it harder to progress to new ages. Just a small complaint, but generally something that can be changed in the custom game setup.
Overall, this is a great game. For it's age it's an excellent RTS. At times I find the progession rather straightfoward, but the sheer amount of units, countries and game modes makes up for its shortcomings. Defnitely a great game to buy even if you own all the Age of Empires games, I would reccomend this to all RTS fans looking for a new game!

Pros:
+ One of the best Free-to-Play models available.  Premium currency being tradeable between players means that you can still get everything that you can't farm for without spending a dime.
+ Graphics and sounds are perhaps the best available in a F2P game.  The art team put their heart and soul into making the game look great and have succeeded in every way.
+ Potato friendly.  Despite the aforementioned above the game engine is well optimized and most low end computers can still play the game with minor difficulty.
+ Open developers.  The staff at Digital Extremes have regularly been in touch with the community, be it listening to feedback and giving regular "Devstreams" of what's in the future for the game.
+ YOU GET TO BE ACTUAL SPACE NINJAS.
Cons:
- RNG is a fickle mistress.  ~1600 hours in and even I still don't have everything in the game.
- Tutorial needs an overhaul.  There's little in the game for a new Tenno to learn about aside from just diving in and hoping for the best.  Most veterans almost immediately refer to the community made wiki for newbies to understand everything more than any official resources.
- While you CAN get everything gameplay wise without spending, it's highly inefficient.  A large chunk of hard to obtain items go for a significant amount of currency, and making money early on is kinda hard.  Thankfully there's no absolute requirement to get these items.
- Hema.  You'll understand in time.
- Be prepared to wait if you're farming all your gear.

I've only played for a couple of hours so far, but i can already say, that this game has a lot of potential. It has it's problems, don't get me wrong, but the core elements of the game are already fantastic.
In this game you have to practise your skills in order to level them up (i.e. you chop wood to raise your logging level, or you craft some tools to raise tinkering). You start with the basics and craft a working bench, but later, if your skill levels are high enough you will be able to build houses, walls, watchtowers and everything else you need for your little town/fortress.
The map is huge! And the best part about it: You actually have to explore more and more of it, because of the constant need of better material.
Fighting in this game can be quite a hassle, because of the weird camera angle and somewhat random hitboxes, but i think it's manageable. There are quite a few different kind of weapons to choose from, and you level your weapon skill by using the weapon of your choice.
As stated above, you get better at skills by using them, but they also give you statpoints, based on how high your current skilllevel is. So in the long run your character gets stronger and stronger just like in other MMORPGs.
Tree of Life also features some sort of morality system, where you get flagged as a criminal for doing naughty things like murdering and stealing. The more people you kill, the longer you get to be a criminal, and as a criminal you lose everything upon death. I do hope, that they tweak this system a bit, because defending yourself against a non-criminal nets you some sweet criminal time, if you manage to kill your attacker.
TL:DR: It's a solid Early Access game with minor and fixable flaws and if you have some friends, who like these kind of games, i recommend you to get a 4-pack and start having some fun.

Edited review after many, many hours played:
So far I am loving this game. There are tons of skills to choose from and I love the fact that you can only excel in a few of them.  Each skill also levels your stats. It seems like you can get experience from building and fighting. For example, I got fishing experience from fighting a shark monster. Also, you can build up your sword or hammer by using it to chop wood. Now, that is multi-tasking.
After the update on 5/29, getting started is a bit easier.  A few lower crude locks and towers were added to help protect your resources. Locks were made harder to pick and also fill flag you as a criminal.  Honestly, the towers are indeed crappy. But the tents are better than nothing.
So far the community isn't terrible. I built a campfire and usually others come by to chat and cook food while we wait out the night.  I have yet to be victim of a PVPer.  One person did attempt to steal from my cabin, but they got a red name all for a house full of wood. Honestly the PVP system isn't bad, but it can stand for a bit more tweeks.

I think it's just that the game experience winds up being extremes in terms of things going on. Oh, and of course, once I get a groove going and have a ruler who works well with a decent heir and am making some progress, he takes a bonk to the head and is "incapable" - but then won't die, so I spend years unable to do anything.
