Crusader Kings II is one of my favorite games in my library. I've come back to it again and again, picking up DLCs that appeal to me. I recently started playing again after about a year. With the addition of the "Conclave" DLC the game has reached its peak. Managing the internal politics of your kingdom through favors, intrigue, and nepotism is loads of fun and gives you something to occupy yourself with between wars. I once had a lunatic king who promoted his horse to chancellor, and what do you know, his equine friend was loyal to the end. (Although there was that time the king brought the horse into the royal bedchamber, although we don't talk about that).
The game offers unlimited replayability. Every playthrough is different, and every region is its own microcosm. There is a learning curve, but its rewarding once you get a hang of things.
After dozens of hours of playing I've finally reached the point where I can say I've finished the game (Finishing the game is totally subjective—there are no defined goals). Playing as Brittany, my king had a demon child, the literal spawn of Satan, who murdered all his siblings to become heir to the throne. The king dies of old age, and what do you know, spawn of Satan has incredibly high stats across the board. The church hates him, but who cares, Satan is on his side. Using his ridiculously high intrigue, he revokes the titles of all the realm lords and takes total control of the kingdom. All detractors are murdered. Half the council is replaced with witches who are 100% loyal to the demon lord. Then, in a master stroke, he seizes Normandy from France with help from the HRE and England. France, perhaps the most powerful nation in the game, is left with a broken army and split apart by rebellions. Brittany is victorious. Hail Satan!

Sonic Mania is what we would've gotten if they released a true blue Sonic game for the Saturn or possibly the Dreamcast. I wasn't around for Sonic 1 2 3&K and CD's original releases but I've played them all in a miriad of ways, including on steam, emulators, actual hardware, and the like. This game perfectly captures the verticality of 3&K, the exploration of CD, the speed of 2, and the difficulty of Sonic games in general. This game is chock full of references to not only the Sonic franchise but Sega properties as a whole.
Built on the Taxman's RetroEngine (which you may be familiar with if you've been in the Sonic fanbase for any length of time, or have played the mobile re-releases of Sonic 1 and 2 or the 2011 re-release of CD, which uses the RetroEngine), Sonic Mania has extremely precise momentum physics and fantastic controls, no matter what console you play on. (Yes, I bought the switch version too) The level design takes elements from many different levels across Sonic's history, including nods to levels not even in this game in other levels present here. For example, in Chemical Plant zone act 2, the goop you bounce on makes the same bouncing noise as the floors from CD's Wacky Workbench.
This adventure's music is provided by the godlike Tee Lopes, who is best known for remixes of Sonic music on youtube. Each zone's music is absolutely amazing and worth a listen on their own.
This game is a must have for any fan of the franchise or any fan of platformers in general. At 20 USD there is absolutely no reason not to pick this up on your gaming machine of choice, whether that be the PC, the Nintendo Switch, Xbox One, or Playstation 4.
I have precisely two issues with this game.
1.The level design is a bit long winded and some levels overstay their welcome. Specifically the last zone. Took me 7 minutes to beat the last act in the game. It went on forever. Some may not mind this kind of thing, but it's not my cup of tea.
2. There are only 4 new stages. There are 12 zones in this game, but only 4 of them are original. Iizuka wanted repeat stages, so blame him. (He's the studio head of Sonic Team)
There are a few cons associated specifically with the PC version however. On PC, load times and frame drops may happen depending on the age and specs of the machine. Though that's not really the game's fault, it is something to keep in mind. The other con, at least for the moment, is the online leaderboards for time trial. On PC people have already modified the game so they have times of __"__'__. Literally a blank time. So don't waste your time trying to get anywhere on the in game leaderboards. If you are interested in running the game I'd compare it to
or friends. I say at least for the moment because it's inevitable that other consoles will have the same issue in the future, just like the Sonic Rush titles near the end of the Nintendo wifi service, which also had this issue.
Over all I give Sonic Mania a perfect 10/10. This game is a truely fantastic game with good level design, a good difficulty curve, and godlike music.
TL;DR

so, instead of wasting time going over the denuvo nonsense, which... i really am not going to claim to care about, given that it hasn't impacted me at all in any way, i'm going to scream into the void and discuss the actual game itself here
ultimately, i've not played near as much as i intend to. i still have a few zones left with my default sonic & tails playthrough, and i'm far from finished with doing any of the other things the game has to offer, like time attack, tails' stages, and knuckles' stages. however, i've played around with enough of both that playthrough and my individual knuckles/tails ones that i feel like i can form a pretty solid opinion on the game for the purposes of giving a review
it's... i'm gonna be pretty upfront here. it's a good game. it's a game made by people who love the series,
people who love the series. unlike a lot of other games in the sonic franchise, it's basically a direct continuation and refinement of everything that people enjoyed from sonic 2, sonic 3 & knuckles, and sonic cd
the level design both provides some fun reworks of classic stages, only serving to improve what was already good, and some incredibly charming and well-designed new levels and acts. i could spend a much longer amount of time singing the praises of, say... the creativity of oil ocean act 2, or the sheer fun factor of stardust speedway act 2, or the same amount of time praising the atmosphere and solid platforming and speed factor of both acts of press garden. but i'm already going on a bit long, so for the sake of cutting things short i'll summarize
it's got a lot of older sonic in it, but in a way that makes it feel fresh to go through, even for someone who just recently finished going back and playing some of the old sonic games to get ready for this

Wow.. Sector 724 seems to have flown right under the radar of everyone on Steam! I feel for the developer here, because this game has more going for it than a large number of the other titles that were release mid-April. There are a couple of other reviews here, but these are in Russian. So I thought I'd take the chance of purchasing this game at the low asking price to see if I can help out in the form of an English review.. Please note I am still learning the game, so will update this review as necessary the more I play and the more early access takes shape..
_____
Humanity has just discovered a mysterious substance known as SOR, which has lead to a scientific breakthrough in space ships gaining warp capability. The human race has now found their first colonisable planet in the far flung reaches of space. Sector 724. However, the Human Race is still bitterly divided, and every powerful Business Corporation that is capable of space flight is now in a bitter power struggle to obtain more of the SOR resource. With Earth's resources dwindling, the Earth Council has tasked these corporations to reach Sector 724 by any means possible. So long as they follow certain rules.
It is now the responsibility of the player, a member of one such corporation, to continue to explore the territories closer to earth and fund a new colony in Sector 724 in the name of their employer. However, since every other space fairing corporation on Earth has the same mission as you. The war for supremacy will not be an easy one.
So at its core, Sector 724 is a Turn based Strategy game. Players will start as the dominant Corporation with 7 Sectors already under their control. Each sector brings in different additional resources (Ore, Silver Bullion, Gold Ingots, Research Potential and SOR) which funds the war effort in different ways per turn. Whilst Ore, Silver and research are consistent, SOR harvesting can fluctuate every turn and Gold is only obtainable in certain sectors or in battle.
Every Turn begins with a Real Time battle with a random corporation. Unfortunately however you never know exactly who you are fighting. It is pretty much you Vs the rest of the world. The core difference is more down to the fleet composition which can contain anything from a couple of fighters, upto 5 huge fleet destroying battleships. Depending on how many ships are in a sector, you can select 5 ships of your own to go into battle with, although it is recommended you have the best and most powerful where possible, otherwise you will get torn apart. And you will, often, since the enemy composition and number of ships appears random and often scales with your tech level. If you lose a battle, you lose a sector. If you win a battle, you get to choose a neighbouring sector to conquer.
Battles are however a simple affair, and control is limited to a few factors. These are speed, direction, weapon and shield energy management, Tactical nuclear missile fire rates, Ship reactor overcharge (which damages ships) and the ability to retreat. Battles last anywhere upto 5 minutes unless a fleet retreats, is fully destroyed or the designated flag ship of the fleet is destroyed before the rest. Fleets can move about their own space, but the Earth Council refuses ships to enter enemy sectors in fear of all out war and the council being overthrown.
Each victory or loss also comes with an approval rating from the Earth Council. At early stages it is +2 points approval for a win, -1 point approval for a loss. This can also dramatically impact your funding from the Council as time goes on. Therefore it adds the pressure to be victorious as much as possible early on, as early funding is crucial to the arms race you will engage in.
If you are lucky to win a battle. You will have a chance to upgrade your ships current weapon design blueprints or research new tech and ships. If you fail in battle, you are stuck with the same tech you had before the battle and have to wait next turn. Once you have done this, you can outfit your ship with the new tech to get the edge in the next turn. You also have access to the shipyard to build new ships for existing sector defence, or to replace ships that have been destroyed, or you have assigned to new sectors.
The other option open to you is Sector 724 itself. In this screen you are tasked with sending harvested SOR to the new colony itself to improve development ans supply. The more you supply the sector with SOR, the more funding in Silver Bullion you receive for the war effort. This is the most important screen as funding the colony to maximum is the ultimate goal to win the game. This is also the location for trading with Earth's Council. Depending on market prices of SOR and the laws of supply and demand, you can purchase extra SOR for additional Silver Bullion to get to your goal faster. Or instead of shipping SOR off to the colony, you can sell it for Silver to fund your war effort at home. So finding the careful balance is required in order to win the game.
You will get your money's worth out of Sector 724 with a few games played. Does it have legs to carry it in the long term? Only time will tell. However I will give this game a positive review at this point in time as the potential is there and the price is low enough to not be an insult to your wallet should you wish to give it a go. And I suggest you do.
Whilst the game isn't super amazing at the moment. It still stands as a Good one. Chances are you've already purchased a couple of games on Steam or a bundle. They are likely games that are far worse than Sector 724. It's a rough gem that does need a lot of polish. But does have the potential to be a rather unique indie title.

*~I've rewritten my entire review, as my last one was lackluster.~*
Uplink is a fairly interesting game, unlike any other I've played before. Uplink is a game where you assume the role as an agent of Uplink; a company with hackers(crackers) for hire. Simply put, you take a job, do the job, and get paid. While it sounds simple, there's much more to it than just going in, doing something, and it's over, especially when you start taking on more difficult jobs.
A majority of the gameplay consists of, as stated above, taking jobs from one of the many companies in the game and executing the desired task(s). There are many different types of jobs, all of which have their own difficulty. Jobs range from attacking a system to copy or delete one or two files to copying or destroying entire databases, attacking company LANs, cracking into bank systems and much more. You may also fuel your own desires, and perhaps crash the global system.
With the money you collect, you're able to upgrade your hardware and software. Hardware consists of the gateway *The case*, CPUs, memory *Serves as storage*, the modem, and security, all of which, excluding memory and security, have different "levels". Upgrading your hardware lets you complete tasks faster, store more data, and avoid going to jail if you ever make a little mistake and the police come to confiscate your gateway.
While it may not be clear at first, you will eventually become involved in the story of Uplink, which comes with drastic decisions and results. (No spoilers here)
Mods for Uplink exist, and while there may not be many compared to other games, there are a fair amount ot custom skins and gateways. Modding the game is very simple as well, and anybody with a painting program can make a mod for Uplink with no extra software required. While most mods may be skins, there is a completely separate game (mod, if you will) called Onlink, which is Uplink with much much more content added.  I suggest checking out Onlink for yourself, and looking at how much more it adds.
The layout of the game is fairly simple, and reminds me of Windows 95 - 2000. When playing the game, I recommend playing at a resolution of 1024 x 768 or lower. A lower resolution makes for a better experience in my opinion, as text may be harder to read on bigger resolutions, and the game is from 2001, thus the GUI is designed for smaller screens. The game is perfectly functional at bigger resolutions, however. As for hardware requirements, you should have no difficulty playing Uplink, unless you're running a system with the minimum requirements for Windows 2000.
The gameplay of Uplink may seem repetitive to some, especially after finishing a game or two. While it can be repetitive, most of the repetition is during the early stages of the game, and as you get better equipment, you have many more jobs to do, thus alleviating the early repetition. As for a downside to gameplay, *potential spoiler*
I definitely recommend Uplink, especially on sale for $2.49. It's a game where you get to live the fantasy of being a hacker in an action-packed way.
Sure it's in no way likely to teach you how to be a hacker, but it does a good job of making you feel like one.

Yeah so it's a fun game.  But I've run through it twice now and I have a major complaint.  The story line is way too short and if you just do that you miss 50% of the content, which is what I did the first time through.  The second time through I spent more time on side missions and extra story lines and still managed to end the game only finishing ~75% of the content.  Which brings me to my gripe:  the ending, which is not very epic IMO, signals the end of the game.  That's it.  No continuation if you feel like going back and finishing side quests and such, it's just over.  So if you want to see how some of those things end, you have to start all over.  Well I've played through twice and it was a good investment with plenty of entertainment so money well spent.  But I won't be playing it again as it is a bit too much like grinding to finish the quests with a lot of repetition.  How many different cool ways are there to kill the enemy before it gets old?  I'd say about 537 which is an easy number to reach in this game.  And the ship gets way too powerful in the end for any enemy to offer any real resistance so it just becomes a game of dropping a mortar on anyone you want disabled and using the puckle gun to finish them off instead of all that tedious boarding action.  I don't care how many upgrades and guns you put on a frigate, a man o' war gonna drop yo♥♥♥♥♥if you dumb enough to tangle with one.  Not in this game.  At least make it challenging.  Shae's upgrades are a waste of time, or at least not important enough to try and find all the animals you need to make the upgrades.  The first time through I forgot all about them because his defaults were sufficient to do whatever I needed to do.  I did upgrade his weapons and armor but again, once you've done that to the max (without quest weapons) you don't need to do anything else and you'll be fine.  The accuracy rating on the pistols doesn't mean anything and I can do a head shot at max range with any of them, even the default pistols.  The only significant difference I found upgrading my weapons was with my sword.  And once you've upgraded your sword 3-4 levels the killing becomes ridiculously easy.  And what happened to the Abstergo story line?  It just disappears at the end.  Anyway, good game, and worth the money if you like this franchise.

This game is a modern RC PRO AM. Isometric racer with power ups and most races rely on getting lucky with speed boosts to win.
Most of the stats are meaningless. Acceleration determines how quickly you top out in speed, and all cars have the same maximum speed. Mass determines how much weapons affect you and what happens when a boosted car rams into a player. Handling is how well once can turn though I found it odd that a land car with low speed was nearly impossible to steer while a hover car with even lower handling than the land car drove almost perfectly.
The campaign has several varieties for missions, most of them being custom races to help the player learn how to play. The problem with the campaign is the game forces the player to engage with the worst game mode in Blaze Rush: Normal Race. Yes, just racing blows because the game has a catchup mechanic that teleports racers lagging behind so they can always get lucky and pick up a speed boost to instantly win the race on the last lap. 100% crap shoot.
However, where the game shines is King Of The Hill and Grinder. Grinder is a simple and fast paced game mode where a giant machine charges at the racer and instnatly kills them on contact. The goal is to use weapons and speed boosts to either kill the other players outright, slow them down to get crushed, or outlast them after the Grinder picks up speed to take out stragglers. King Of The Hill is another game mode like Standard Race, but instead of having to drive for 3 minutes while being in 1st and hoping the teleported opponents get lucky in driving, the game ends once a player stays in 1st for 50 seconds. I like it since it requires constant use of weapons and speed boost due to players being unable to coast until the last lap and get the win.
Overall: Short game longevity with a lackluster single player campaign, but with two really fun game modes and a lot of choice in customizing party play when playing online in a party. Would recommend if on sale due to replay value.

I have really conflicted feelings about Oblivion, and most of my complaints lie where they do with other Elder Scrolls games. Let's be completely honest, the combat in these games aren't the highlight of the show, and Oblivion is far from an exception. What would be excusable for a combat system becomes laughably tedious as the game progresses since all enemies scale to your level. Levelling, as it stands, is incredibly tedious. Instead of an XP based level up system like traditional RPG's, Bethesda opted for a "skill-based" one. To level up, you must progress your seven major skills (which you can pick when you make your class). The only way to level these stats is to GRIND. and GRIND HARD. If you're not inclined to just cheat your stats with the console, you'll be stuck spamming custom made spells that use as little magicka as required to get any sort of real boost.
The major problem of Oblivion is it's scarcity in good content. The sidequests are phenomenal, and some of the most interesting and creative you'll find in any video game. They range all the way from dinner party mysteries to vast journeys into unmarked areas. The main quest is, quite simply, boring as all hell.
Many skills just seem completely useless as well. Acrobatics for example. Sure it's kind of fun bunny hopping around, but the dodge isn't that great and the mastery skill of jumping on water is practically useless. Mysticism, Alteration, and Illusion are practically worthless with the exception of a couple spells, like Paralysis in the Illusion family. The reason they are "empty skills" is because enchanting your armor will get you far better bonuses than the spells and allow you to alot your magick into vital things like Restoration. Athletics can be useful when it's mastered maybe, but running faster and regenerating fatigue quicker? Horrible. You don't really win at all with Oblivion in context to the combat. It's either a spongey mess of mouse clicking, an absolute cheesing with high level destruction or 100% chameleon/shield enchanted armor, or just a bore of sneaking around and getting an 8x bow attack.
The absolutely fantastic and beautiful thing about Oblivion however is the immersion. Books laying around referencing ancient battles, Ayleid ruins hiding powerful Liches, or mini events like the Bloated Float Inn being pirated when you sleep onboard. The little tidbits of good content are paced out well to counter the absolute chore-ish nature of the rest of the game. The relief of finishing a long questline of fetch quests like the Knights of the Nine expansion is both satisfying and underwhelming at the same time, because once you realize you just went through the same copy-pasted caves and ruins just with some flavortext to keep you interested, the expirience sours. As with any Bethesda game, mods are almost essential to the expirience. It doesn't have to be 100 different loli-maid mods either, just the basic fixes or fanpatches and graphical improvements are fine enough to keep the expirience fresh.
Overall, to somebody that has never played Oblivion or many other RPG's before, it's a fantastic game. You'll enjoy it for many hours over many characters. However for someone that has a lot of expirience with other RPG's with more polish, you'll find yourself disappointed by a lot of it's shortcomings.

A wonderfully rich game in the series and has hours and hours of content.  I remember when I first saw Oblvion at the E3 XBOX Conference I was astounded at how good this game looked.  I first played it on the XBOX 360 and have since seen it on the PS3 and the PC.
This game on PC was a hog when released, but on more modern machines, including more modest ones today can run this game looking as good as the developed had intended.  Many of the screenshots uploaded show off the rich environments of the Provence of Cyrodiil.
Like many games in the Elder Scrolls series you start the game as a no one and find yourself in fortunate circumstances which enables you to wonder the world.  Upon the first part of the character creation where you have a myriad of options to taylor your character exactly how you want you do find just how deep this game can be.
Game play for Oblivion has departed a little from previous entries as it is now more action based, where your states do not determine IF you will hit the enemy but how much damage, if they block and so on.  So it is not the TRUE RPG experience that many might have expected if you love Morrowind.  But it enables a player to quickly get into the swing of things and as you progress through the story you find yourself sometimes feeling more powerful than you are and will undertake some foes that are just out of your reach, BUT, with the mechanics of Oblivion it is not beyond impossible, creative ways to get objects between you and your enemy, knowing when to run, are all options if you find yourself in a sticky situtation. Many of the objectives in the game are leveled to your character so none of the quests seem too difficult and other than a small handful of quests you can do most (the others will not unlock until you reach a specific level).
Leveling is easy, you have major and minor skills, get your Major skill up a level and you will level yourself.  Minor skills level up as well, at a slower rate.  This is where it will be a good indication as to how you will want to play your character since if you pick a warrior load out but find you want to sneak around then sneaking skills will take longer to level.  So to increase a skill you use it, fight enemies with a sword to increase your blade, hit them with damaging magic and your destruction will increase, sneak around the dark corners of the world (and there are many) and you will get better at doing do.
The music by Jeremy Soule is one of the best sound tracks he has done and I even love listening to it as I find myself looking over the vistas the game presents.  The music dynamics do over an insight if you have annoyed an enemy, but it is a good indication especially when you do not know from where they are coming at you.  The biggest let down with an unmodded version are some of the sound glitches that happen, where audio will cut out, it will come back after a period of time but you will find yourself wondering the wilds and making no footsteps, but the most difficult one is the weapon strike and knowing when you have hit your enemy as it can disappear to.  But I believe there is an unofficial patch can fix many of these issues.
Under newer operating systems this game might just crash from time to time, I have found when the in-game dialogs display as white and not textured it might be a good time to save.  Save often, make sure the auto saves are also set, on PC this takes no time and you will be welcoming it after a few crashes.
All in all this is a top addition to the series and would highly recommend it to anyone who enjoys a solid RPG experience and a game that will sometimes make you just want to sit and enjoy the view.

Sonic Mania is what we would've gotten if they released a true blue Sonic game for the Saturn or possibly the Dreamcast. I wasn't around for Sonic 1 2 3&K and CD's original releases but I've played them all in a miriad of ways, including on steam, emulators, actual hardware, and the like. This game perfectly captures the verticality of 3&K, the exploration of CD, the speed of 2, and the difficulty of Sonic games in general. This game is chock full of references to not only the Sonic franchise but Sega properties as a whole.
Built on the Taxman's RetroEngine (which you may be familiar with if you've been in the Sonic fanbase for any length of time, or have played the mobile re-releases of Sonic 1 and 2 or the 2011 re-release of CD, which uses the RetroEngine), Sonic Mania has extremely precise momentum physics and fantastic controls, no matter what console you play on. (Yes, I bought the switch version too) The level design takes elements from many different levels across Sonic's history, including nods to levels not even in this game in other levels present here. For example, in Chemical Plant zone act 2, the goop you bounce on makes the same bouncing noise as the floors from CD's Wacky Workbench.
This adventure's music is provided by the godlike Tee Lopes, who is best known for remixes of Sonic music on youtube. Each zone's music is absolutely amazing and worth a listen on their own.
This game is a must have for any fan of the franchise or any fan of platformers in general. At 20 USD there is absolutely no reason not to pick this up on your gaming machine of choice, whether that be the PC, the Nintendo Switch, Xbox One, or Playstation 4.
I have precisely two issues with this game.
1.The level design is a bit long winded and some levels overstay their welcome. Specifically the last zone. Took me 7 minutes to beat the last act in the game. It went on forever. Some may not mind this kind of thing, but it's not my cup of tea.
2. There are only 4 new stages. There are 12 zones in this game, but only 4 of them are original. Iizuka wanted repeat stages, so blame him. (He's the studio head of Sonic Team)
There are a few cons associated specifically with the PC version however. On PC, load times and frame drops may happen depending on the age and specs of the machine. Though that's not really the game's fault, it is something to keep in mind. The other con, at least for the moment, is the online leaderboards for time trial. On PC people have already modified the game so they have times of __"__'__. Literally a blank time. So don't waste your time trying to get anywhere on the in game leaderboards. If you are interested in running the game I'd compare it to
or friends. I say at least for the moment because it's inevitable that other consoles will have the same issue in the future, just like the Sonic Rush titles near the end of the Nintendo wifi service, which also had this issue.
Over all I give Sonic Mania a perfect 10/10. This game is a truely fantastic game with good level design, a good difficulty curve, and godlike music.

This game...this game right here.
This is one of the
few examples of free-to-play done right.
I first hopped on at around January of 2016 - nothing compared to an actual veteran of the game - and played for a bit. Didn't seem all that interesting to me at first and put it down for a few months. Once I got back into it, I went in with bitter pessimism on how this game could be limited in some way, shape, or form.
Turns out that those limitations are really based on how far the player's willing to go. There are no artifical gatekeepers other than timers for components, no sudden stops and begging for the player to shell out cash to proceed, none of that facebook game bulls*** here, none at all.
No hinderances, no handicaps, no baby-step handholding, no throttling
. None.
The only thing that could hold players back from progressing is themselves.
Everything, and I do mean everything, can be unlocked with enough actual effort. Yes, there are shortcuts in the form of people using Platinum - the games premium currency - to get stuff or to cut times, but unless they're event-exclusive items, cosmetics, or weapon skins, legit players can get them as well in due time. The main form of experience in the game is 'Mastery Rank', which is achieved by leveling equipment to rank thirty, which steadily fills up one bar beneath the players name when they view the Esc menu. Once the bar's filled, players can do a 'Mastery Test' that, once passed, will elevate them up one MR and thus unlock more features of the game, like wielding better weapons to progressing with the games story.
One rather prominent side of the game, the one that nets the game 'Grindframe', are the Relics. Relics on their own are the games 'lootboxes', using that term rather lightly, but they are ridiculously common to earn in general from several of the 'endurance missions', missions that technically have no end and last for however the player can manage before heading to extraction, being Defense, Interception, Survival, or Excavation. Unlocking them requires the player to hop into 'Void Fissure' missions and collect enough of one resource that drops over the duration of the level, which will unlock the rellic with a chance for one of six items that the relic contains; Three Bronze items, two Silver items, and one Gold item, the last being the most rare. Players can actively tweak the odds of getting items by refining the relics, how far depending on how much they want to change the odds, the highest refinement tier effectively making every item in the relic have an equal chance.
The main reason for those relics are for the always-sought-after 'Prime Equipment'. These items are often upgrades compared to the originals they represent, with the warframes almost always a straight upgrade. If one goes to a wiki though and looks up the whole list, they'd notice that a number of these primes are 'Vaulted', which means that they're taken out of the active loot pool and will not drop no matter the farming. This isn't really a con though per-se, as players can use this fact as a means of not only getting into the trading scene, but also get some platinum in their digital purse. There are people who are willing enough to shell out hundreds or even thousands of platinum for that one prime component, set, or rare mod that they're looking for.
In terms of actual gameplay, it starts off slow for the more newer players as per the usual MMO shtick. Around...MR six or something is when it ramps up, since Jupiter and past that is when the players build will really factor in on how quickly they can nail the foes, who can and will lay an unprepared player out flat if they do not keep moving. It's around that point that players will be quite aware of one of the lesser-popular modes, but I'll refrain from explaining that and let players see for themselves. There are moments where stealth is key, but more often than not, it's so that one can get to an objective without raising an alarm. If they do, they would have to rush before a timer runs out, failing that portion of the mission.
The kicker to this game? People and various other groups were expecting this game to fail within a year after launch, with games like Planetside 2 among others taking its place, yet here it is. Four and a half years after launch and it's going strong, especially so due to the Plains of Eidolon update having released a couple of months or so back.

What is this? another RTS from 2003? This isn´t age of empires II, why is this on steam? well, let me tell you all, that this, it is an awesome game. although my play history on steam shows a pity amount of time spent on this game, I have played the hell out if Rise of nations on the cd fromat, since it was only recently added to steam.
What is this "Rise of nations" then? well, Rise of nations is your usual RTS game (Real time strategy) and it is the old "gather materials, Make people and soldiers, advance and conquer" quite the normal rooster of mechanichs. what really differs this game from other games I have played (keep in mind i haven´t played all RTS games) is that the game has alot of mechanics and features that make the game really feel like you´re creating and advancing.
E.g. is that the game has a feature with reasearch, basicaly, there are multible routes to develop in, economy, warfare, popuation and sience . this really changes the way you "advance through the game. that means you don´t just upgrade your army and then destroy the enemy base in one go with only kind of troops, instead you might find it better to upgrade your economy and simply "starve" the enemy out by being able to consistently attack the enemy.
A very nice feature that i found amazing, was the idea, that when "creating" a offensive unit, it gives you a platoon instead of a single unit, which makes the end game end (lol) in a enoumrus fight against highly numbered armies.
Going back to the advancement, the game lets you advance from the culture age all the way up to modern age where you fight with rockets, tanks and jets.
also, the game has a feature, where you have a relation to other nations/players. this means that you can be netrual, allied, friendly or in war with other nations and you can, during a game, ally with another player.
The game, of course, isn´t flawless. E.g. is that the game is from 2003, which means, that the game has it´s limits, althoug the steam version is better, so the grapichs isn´t explecitly amazing. futhermore,  the terrain might seems a bit dull and it is quite easy to do a fast rush if you play a certian nation.
All in all, this is, imo, a really great RTS game and it hold a certian nostalgic fealing to me.

It's a shame that this game was overshadowed by Unity. It's definitely worth a playthrough if you're a fan of Assassin's Creed. The best way to describe how this game fits into this story would be like how Revelations was fit into Ezio's Story: It's a thing that's there and it's kind of nice to have but it doesn't have much pertinenece to the story as a whole.
I like to say that while Unity got all the programmers, Rogue got the story writers.The gist of the story is that you're an assassin that went rogue and now fight for the Templars. Woo. Though the premise is simple the characters actually have more depth than a brick wall and it makes for some really interesting sequences. At some point in the game I was emotionally attached to a person I would eventually have to kill, and the dialogue really helped to drive those feelings.
I do have to note though that all of the assassins are ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s to you even when you're on their side, and the first  friendly character in the entire game is the guy that recruits you to be a Templar.
So the engine was beefed up a bit as the water actually ripples as things fall into it or whales breach the surface, and these ripples can be used to damage enemy ships. The addition of Icebergs gives more strategy to naval combat, but the higher success rate of pointing all your cannons at the enemy ship, kind of nulls that.
Like most Assassin's Creed games, you are armed to the teeth  and there's more weapons than there are number buttons on the keyboard. Although I appreciate having variety, the pistols, sleep darts, berserker darts, and shrapnel gernades were more than enough to get through most obstacles.
Something they added that I liked at first was a new enemy that would sneak around and try to kill you from stealth. Whispers creep in as you get closer to them, the whispers get louder. If you get too close they run up to you from across the map and almost kill you. So you stab them. And they die. and if you happened to get hit by them, you regen health immediately. Which is why this became more of an annoyance as the game went on. I caught myself just seeing what direction they were using eagle vision, took an educated guess on their position and avoided them. It's a good idea, but it definitely needs improvement so it isn't just annoying.
It also has the usual collect all the goodies missions. I gave up on trying to 100% this game when I saw that there were 8 number of collectables: animus fragments, shanties, templar maps, templar artifacts that you find from the maps, letters, Viking swords, treasure chests, and prosperity. At some point I realized that I wasn't having fun collecting stuff and would rather be doing stuff that was more action packed.
Overall, I had fun playing it. While AC4 was a pirate game with assassin elements this is definitely an Assassin Gae with Pirate elements. Definitely worth a look, but do remember that it does have its flaws.

What is BlazeRush?
Genre: fun racing game with weapon pickups
Setting: racing league on different planets until taken away by a corporation --> defeat the boss
Difficulty: 6/10 --> AI gets tougher in endgame, lots of luck-based races
Length: 5-15 hours for a single playthrough (depending on luck)
Mode: singleplayer campaign, multiplayer
Similar games: Death Rallye (which is from a top-down perspective)
The positive aspects:
- Different cars with different abilities (acceleration, resilience) and looks
- enjoyable racing modes (normal race, time trial, last man racing/ escaping a roller, boss races)
- quite entertaining multiplayer
- winning a race is possible until the end --> you can't fall back much, off-screen cars are teleported back into the screen
- game runs perfectly smooth, no crashing
The negative aspects:
- only five weapons (Gatling, rockets, slime, sawblade, sonic waves)
- weak weapon impact on AI drivers, especially in late game
- driving and aiming skill is not rewarded - you can't be far in advance or fall way behind, the game will always teleport those "fallen ones" back into the screen area
- over-sensitive controls (depends on chosen car)
- the camera perspective (isomorphic-like). You can't change it, you get used to it, it sets the tone of the game, but it also makes you go crazy. As being in lead, you sometimes can't see where you have to go, blindly maneuvering around with only little help of a HUD road map. This leads to numerous annoying situations, making the otherwise solid campaign unnecessarily hard and your result depending on luck too often.
Result (and summary for those who have no time reading):
It's hard what to think of BlazeRush. It is basically a good fun racing game unless you're talking about the camera perspective. being ok in multiplayer for a short game of party racing, the singleplayer campaign becomes a real pain. If you like being rewarded for driving and aiming skill, hands off. If you're looking for a little, competitive fun racer, give it a try.

Very good, but very hard. It shows the real pain of Assembly Programming.

10/10, would "PARALLELIZE" again.

The TIS-100 makes computing visceral, and I think everyone should experience it. Both the pain of learning to do *anything* with very little, and the joy of getting so much more done with even less. I think this is what the greybeards reminisce about when they talk about squeezing every last drop of utility out of a system.
There's a strong feeling of nostolgia, of being a 10 year old in front of an inscrutible console and nothing but an afternoon to kill. I'm not old enough to remember the old terminals, but I did have a 286 with just the DOS command prompt and no manual or clue in the world; the TIS-100 recreates that feeling of intellectual exploration. Where a task looks insurmountable or impassible and you just don't have enough memory, or space for code, or just the wrong node is broken... But you know it can be solved. Or if the solution is obvious, you know it could be *better* - faster, smaller, simpler.
So you just tinker with it, test ideas, and a solution forms. And then you refine it, and try newer ideas. Break things up, reinvent a few wheels. And while the computer cycles through your program watch what each algorithm does (espcially if nodes feed back to each other - you can literally watch execution bounce between chunks of code)!
If You like Challenging Programming, this is your Game... You may pass Hours trying to squeez every possible Cicle out of a Program...

This is my favorite strategy game, probably ever. Even though I'm horrible at it and don't play enough.
It's a simultaneous turn based game in which you have soldiers and give them orders for the next 5 seconds of the fight, both players input orders, and not just move and shoot, move, crouch, aim direction, target priority, target ignore/fire on sight and time based things, so you can do "Move to this wall, take cover behind it, in 2 seconds, get up, look in front of you but do not engage anyone and crouch back down half a second later".
What you do then is try to simulate what your opponent would do, because yes, you are in control of enemy units during the planning phase so you can order them to do what you think the opponent would do, or even move the units around anywhere in the map if you have fog of war and they aren't seen.

This game already has tons of positive reviews and hardly needs mine to be shown as a success. But I've sunk over 400 hours into it and I'm sure many, many more will come in the future. As such, I feel obligated to give another thumbs up here. Plus, I just want to talk about how much I enjoy it.
100% Orange Juice is a mash-up of several Orange Juice game characters in a board game setting, along with a couple of made-for-this-game ones. Before playing this, I only knew of Sora, and only because I had heard the soundtrack from her game. So this is coming from someone who was totally exposed to Orange Juice games because of this one.
You can get this for single player use. Campaign modes exist, five in all, and if I were to get the game just to play those, I would consider it a worthwhile purchase. That being said, campaign mode severely suffers for one major reason: the AI cheats. I don't mean that in an "I get so unlucky that it feels like they're always doing well" way. The game's code has shown that difficulty levels going up causes it to be more likely that the AI will get the rolls they need. This is artificial difficulty at its finest, and if that was not a part of this game, I would have nothing else to complain about.
However, multiplayer is where 100% Orange Juice shines. There the luck is truly random (no matter how you might feel otherwise), both for players and any AI you have filling in the slots. Lag is almost nonexistant from my experiences, and it is very easy to link up with friends to play. There is a lot of hilarity to be had, and I have gotten so many hours put into this game simply because it is so much fun with other players.
There are a variety of boards, almost all of which are fun for different reasons (I loathe Farm, but that's the only exception for me). The cards used in the game are of a good variety, and since each player contributes ten cards, it makes for a good mix. Most impressive is the character balance. Yes, there are tier debates, and yes, some characters are simply better in some ways than others. But overall, it is a game where you can win with any character, with all of them having their own strengths, weaknesses, and powers.
DLCs usually give more characters, with one giving more cards. DLCs tend to be a pain in the rear end for most games. Here, I like them. They are not expensive at all, the characters given are great, and it shows how the developers are still helping the game evolve. They are released at wonderful intervals, waiting just long enough so players can go, "Okay, I've had a lot of fun with these characters. Are there any more coming? I'm ready to try someone else." Falling back on old favorites is enjoyable too. I personally use Saki, Krila, and Alte as my top three, and while I love playing with new characters, it feels great to go back to them as well.
Speaking of the developers, they are constantly working to improve this game. When balance issues are brought up, they work to make small changes that keep the characters closer in varying strengths to one another. They release new maps as free content. They give out holiday specials that you can earn simply through playing. Their other games have bonus characters that are not necessary for here, but really nice for those who support said games. And perhaps most importantly, the developers are constantly asking how to improve 100% Orange Juice, and watching the discussions to weigh in when needed. This type of devotion is something a lot more games could use, and it really shines here.
As this is a Steam game, I feel obligated to remark on achievements and trading cards. The achievements are, for the most part, reasonable and fun to collect. The ones that were frustrating have been toned down by the developers, which I think is a wise move. The trading cards are quite cute. I cashed them in for a badge and have enjoyed the wallpaper and emoticon I got as a result.
To wrap up, here are some various comments. The art is adorable and the sprites are great. The music is fantastic (for the most part; I still am a bit meh on three or so character themes, but out of the vast number of characters, that is a very small amount). The methods of winning make for a fun mix. The learning curve is very nice; I played one game and then knew enough to go through the rest of the game. I have never experienced any glitches with it. The price is ridiculously cheap for how good it is, and getting it on sale makes it an absolute steal. It does come in bundles, but I wouldn't bother waiting for those if you want it, unless you are particularly stingy or uncertain if it is your type of game.
So yes. I highly recommend 100% Orange Juice. If anyone wants to have a game, I'll be around and ready to play!
EDIT: 750 hours in and still going strong! DLC keeps coming and the game keeps improving. It's never too late; if you're interested, grab it and hop online!
A great game for Halo fans, something new and fresh from the beloved franchise.

Game's surprisingly good/lengthy for its price point.  It is pretty hard to mess up a a top down shooter after all. Controls are responsive, and there's enough difficulty (and you can turn it up if you so desire with handicaps). It has enough content and polish to make it fun, but not enough to stand out really. While Halo's artstyle and music is nice, don't expect anything neat storywise besides a blurb to go with it between missions. No voicing in them, nothing. Levels are also fairly short, with a general length of 5-10 minutes long (Not to say that is necessarily a bad thing). The game can be finished in a day, though it'll take all day. After you're done there's going for gold stars for replayability, some grindy achievements, and Steam leaderboards.
Overall, not a bad title to pick up if you're looking for something cheap or have someone to compete with in the leaderboards. It was a little over a dollar in the winter sale.

With a theme that is mostly missing from the FPS multi-player genre, Gotham City Impostors shows a decent effort in attempting to make it all work together, but falls short due to some serious problems. The amount of customization and game modes is comparable to, but not nearly as polished as Team Fortress 2. You can choose between different body types, faces, clothes, calling cards, voices, etc. There is definitely something for everyone when it comes to personalizing your character. You are also able to choose from a variety of weapons, sub-weapons, special abilities, and items. All for the price of DLC or grinding to unlock them. The gunplay takes a bit of getting used to as some weapons seem to fire in a weird burst fire mode, which makes you feel like you have a limited control of aim and accuracy. The firing and movement in general feel slightly unresponsive and very floaty. The game's biggest flaw comes from its netcode. There is no server browser, no numeric ping counts, and it often takes about five minutes or longer for the game to place you in a match. The matchmaking lobby puts you in a queue and makes you wait without allowing for the people waiting to chat. All of this waiting in the matchmaking lobby does not make the game worth playing, as you will be spending most of your in-game time in the matchmaking lobby menu rather than actually playing the game. If you are patient enough and willing to put up with long waiting periods after each match, you might have some fun playing the game, but you will eventually become tired and bored of waiting in the matchmaking lobby.
Gotham City Impostors is okay.

Basically, the bottom line is that there is simply no game like Chivalry. It's game mechanics are so simple, yet there are not used anywhere else.
Games like mount and blade, or war of the roses, and even for honor rely on your mouse movement, for the direction of where you would swing your weapon. But the problem is that that system never registered very well. Put 100 people up and make them do a certain combo, and you will see how varied results would be in those games.
In chivalry, all you have is LMB for your basic attack, MMB scroll up for an overhead swing (which is a stronger attack) and MMB scroll down for an thrust (which gives range).
RMB is for blocking. Shields can block indefinately but drain stamina, other weapons only block for a second or two. You can kick and break someone's block (that's used against shields).
Finally, there are lots of weapons. Some providing range, some providing more damage, some only allowed for duel hand wielding. And running builds up speed and allows you to do a charge attack that does more damage.
At the same time, not only does the mechanic work, but it also is very aethentic, realistic, plausible.
Look at this gameplay footage from war of the roses:
Look at how you have this UI for your direction, which just stands out of place. Every time you get a hit, you get "notified" by a red slash. All this "numbers" telling how much damage you did.
In chivalry, you  have no UI basically other than the basic bottom line requirement (health, stamina). Full immersion.
Now, onto the game modes. There are about 4 of them: team deathmatch, free for all, last team standing (2 teams, 1 life each), duel, and objective based.
All are integrated well into the game. You can find all of those being played at a regular basis. The game supports up to 16v16.
But the main mode of the game is the objective based mode. It's pretty much attack/defend mode. One team attacks a castle, first burning the village, killing the peasants, and then moving onto the castle itself, until finally in the main hall of the king. The defenders are there to stop them. Once the attackers reach the king's hall, the MVP of the defenders becomes the king. Attackers win by killing the king. Defenders win if they manage to hold on until the timer runs out.
This is it. The game is still very alive (unlike say the expansion or the sequel. The lag compensation is also very good, if that's what you are worried about.
As for the performance, the game uses unreal engine 3. If you are able to run a game that uses this engine, you most likely can run this as well.

As a preface, I have next to no programming experience, but a vast and technical understanding of hardware. Programming has always been my weak point, due to its seemingly impermeable complexity; I don't think like a computer, and real programming language's mnemonics often make very little sense without researching and understanding a much deeper and intricate reason.
This game is, simply put, QUITE AWESOME. It takes an extremely limited set of assembly mnemonics, and gives you an extremely limited, highly multithreaded enviromnet, and offers a clearly defined objective to achieve. The puzzles are not easy; in fact, these are some of the hardest puzzles I've had the pleasure of solving. The difficulty doesn't arise from the complexity of the task or obfuscation of the methods; no, it comes from the fact that you have such limited resources to achieve the goals. A normally simple and trivial multiplication program can easily become extremely challenging when you can only add, subtract, a stack memory (automatically pushes and pops), and a handful of conditionals. VERY fun and engaging!
I highly recommend this game for anyone who wants to be able to break that initial impermeable layer of programming. Make no mistake, it will not teach you programming, at least, not in the normal sense; but it will help you to wrap your mind around the methods and semantics of programming within an extremely limited set of resources.
A++ all around!

This is a difficult recommendation to write, because I really enjoy this game, but have a friend who is rather indifferent to it, and finds it hard to learn.
On the point of education, I found it straightforward to learn with the tutorials and intuitive controls, but multiplayer has a good way of showing you how little you really know about strategy. I have to think though that you have to like turn based strategy enough to *want* to learn.
Assuming you 'buy in' on the turn based strategy bit, I think Frozen Synapse is great because it condenses a lot of action into these fixed moments of time, so you are forced to make the most out of every microsecond. Your opponents decions are unknown to you, and while you can run through all the possibilities of their response, you're eventually going to have to commit to a course of action, or die with mediocraty.
There are few games that really seem to distill a genre down to its pure essence, but Frozen Synapse does the trick. On top of it, the one technical problem I had was answered promptly and by a team that clearly loves and takes pride in their game. Personally, I offer it an enthusiastic recommendation, but possibly contingent on someone having at least some interest in turn based strategy.

If you've got the people this is an amazing multiplayer experience. BlazeRush is a top-down racer with a few different game modes and plenty of pickups to fire at your opponents. There's a singleplayer campaign as well but you'll be finding most of your fun with the multiplayer options. All the racers share the same screen so you get pulled ahead (or destroyed) for falling behind. There's a standard lap race mode, a mode where the person in first the longest wins, and Death Race. The last mode is by far most fun I've had with this game. A giant machine chases all the racers around the track until everyone is eliminated. The person that survives longest nets the most points, and it starts right back up again until you reach a set number. This leads to plenty of hilarious moments as players struggle to stay far ahead with boosters or sabotage the competition with firepower. I'd say it's a definite buy. Online multiplayer's dead though so grab this with 2 or 3 friends.
Super fun in local multiplayer at least, that's pretty much all I've played so far. And that alone is well worth it.

Fair warning: This is LONG. Also not particularly well written, because I don't write particularly well. If you need a TLDR, then here it is:
First off: Ignore my hours on record, I've played the game for hundreds, if not thousands of hours since it's closed alpha over a year ago outside of steam.
I find Atlas Reactor rather difficult to describe well. Genre wise it would be a simultaneous turn-based MOBA (for all the meaning left in that term). Simultaneous turn-based, for those who are unaware, means that the game is broken into turns where you plan your moves, but everyone plans them at the same time. MOBA in that there are two teams of 4 people who each pick a character with a unique set of skills, then procedure to try and kill everyone on the opposing team. To be honest, every description I have heard of Atlas Reactor makes it sound mediocre-to-boring. It is not.
As the big thumbs up icon suggests, I like this game. A lot. It is not a game for everyone though, if you want twitch mechanics, skill shots, snowballing, or just flat out hate anything turn-based then this is not for you. One pitfall(?) of many turn-based games this does avoid however is length. This is NOT a casual, slow-paced game. Matches have 20 turns, maximum, of which you have 20 seconds to plan your turn. This is not a lot of time, especially for people new to the game, and you should expect to mess up a number of your turns early on because of it. Nevertheless, once you get used to the game it does make it nice and fast paced, and matches last for an average of about 20 minutes.
People can (normally) use one ability a turn, then move. Each turn of the game goes through several 'phases'. The first phase any ability placing a trap of giving buffs/de-buffs goes off. The second phase any ability that moves you character goes off. The third phase the damaging abilities go off, and finally everyone moves.
The game is confusing at first, and the tutorial... was not amazing in my experience. I have played through several iterations of it, and while each one was better than the previous, they all failed to explain several key aspects of the game and were slightly unclear on others. It has since been updated, again, to which I cannot speak to, but judging by past experiences it is probably still not perfect. It is fast though, and if don't you don't want to play with others while unsure of the game you can always play a couple of matches with bots (which also gives you the option of having longer turn timers, allowing you to take more time to work out what the hell is going on).
So, enough for me trying to explain how the game works:
Being simultaneous turn-based, one of the core aspects of the game is bluffing and predicting others. As everyone plans their own move at the same time (secret from the other team, of course), this means predicting what you think the opposition is going to do and accounting for it is a key part of the game. This also means that as you get better at the game you're going to have a lot more turns where you both look and feel very stupid, firing your attacks off into empty space while that character at 2hp you expected to dash there stands still right next to you.
I know this sounds like a negative. It is not. Because on the opposite side of that you have those amazing moments when your prediction is accurate and you kill that character off in the fog of war who thought they were safe because you couldn't see where they were standing.
Helping you with those predictions is the fact that Atlas Reactor is a game of full-information, meaning that at all times you can check what moves everyone has available to them, what their energy is, what buffs/de buffs they have, what their cooldowns are and what mods they are running.
Mods are another nice aspect of the game. Outside of matches you can select from a number of different modifications to character's moves, which while not changing the core of the move can make changes to it that can seriously change their play style, allowing you to customise them to suit how you want them played.
Onto the characters themselves, (almost) all of them have their own unique concept and playstyle, from placing walls to block attacks, to firing grenades that turn into mines, to turning invisible and sniping people from the other side of the map. The characters, while all very different, do not differ so much that you have to relearn the game every time you change character, and are all quite impressively balanced for this type of game.
As for the community, although that's rather hard to rate as a whole, my experience with them have been overwhelmingly positive. Playing this sort of game (i.e. a MOBA) you expect to have insults and rage flying at you almost every match, particularly when they go badly, however in the thousands of matches I have played I can count on one hand the amount of times this has occurred to me, and this is including ranked play (and yes, there have been a large number of matches where I have played incredibly badly I am sorry to say). Now, as the game has just gone Free-To-Play, theoretical this could mean a lot more unhappy people joining the game (don't worry, I still love you), but I have yet to encounter this. While the community is relatively small, queue times for normal matches tend to range from 30 seconds to 2 minutes, which is perfectly reasonable, and hopefully the move to Free-To-Play will only increase the playerbase.
Finally, and I'll admit this is the reason that finally got me to write this review, the Devs. I have become aware that there are a lot of people who are hesitant about trying this game because it's developed by Trion Worlds. People have been (rightly) upset with a lot of the things Trion have done in other games that they have developed/published, and I'm not going to defend those decisions. What I can say is that the Dev team for Atlas Reactor have engaged with their fan base throughout the development process, both taking on feedback and clearly explaining the reasoning behind any changes made to the game. If you join the official discord you will see a huge list of friendly Devs who will all (okay, mostly all) respond to any questions you have of them. Throughout the year I have been playing they have demonstrated a strong passion for this game and delivered quality new content at a consistent rate, and there has been no hints of anything even remotely resembling Pay-To-Win. If the only reason you are not giving this game a try is because you dislike Trion Worlds, I STRONGLY encourage you to reconsider, as the Atlas Reactors devs have so far proven to be exactly what you would want from a dev team.
In conclusion, I have played a ridiculous amount of games in my life, and normally get bored of them incredibly quickly. This has not happened with Atlas Reactor. It is an incredible game which is impossible to do justice without playing it yourself, so if you have any interest in it whatsoever I strong recommend you give it a go.

Review:
100% OJ is a board game that lets up to 4 people play at a time with the goal of achieving 5 normas first. Normas are achieved through gaining stars or defeating enemies (both npc and players).
The game has a fair bit of RNG, but is not completely reliant to it. Lots of factors come in deciding an event's fate such as Suguri's Accelerator, Sora's Extraordinary Specs and Nanako's Deploy Bits just to name a few.
Each character gets a deck that they can customize and bring to the game, ranging from healing cards to traps.
The DLC content for the game are mostly characters, but they aren't necessarily overpowered, as well as there are quite a lot of unlockable characters that can be bought by stars, which is obtained by playing the game. There is also another DLC pack that gives you a whole set of cards to collect, but I don't really find them as staples in the deck. The default cards are definitely much, much better in my opinion, the dlc cards give you more alternate playstyles that suit various characters (both dlc and non dlc). DLC that doesn't affect gameplay is the starter character voice pack, which gives QP, Suguri, Marc and Kai voices when they are being played. It also gives you access to the 4 characters as your announcers.
Overall, 100% OJ is a nice, comfy game that you can spend an entire evening playing and still not get tired of it.
TL;DR
100% OJ is a board game with a fair bit of RNG that you can influence and has lots of star collecting, costumes, and cute chibi characters. Cute, fun game :]

This is hands down the nerdiest game in existence, and I absolutely love it.
For anyone who actually has any programming experience, the hardest part of this game will likely be the way the nodes work. There is no addressable memory in this game. Each node has a space for you to put code in, an accumulator (ACC), and a single register (BAK, which cannot be addressed directly) to save and swap to. Storing and moving data around consists mostly of passing it between nodes using the MOV command and the "LEFT, RIGHT, UP, DOWN" keywords, which can get incredibly complex and confusing later on, but it's the primary challenge of the game.
Anyone who wants a unique, interesting, and difficult challenge will likely be satisfied with this game, especially those who have some experience or interest in programming. However, this is not for everyone, and if the trailer doesn't remotely interest you, it's probably not worth it.

There is so much strategy in this game, that sometimes it's too much.  Frozen Synapse is a favorite of mine that puts the player into scenarios with differing obstacles, resources, and goals.  There is no chance in this game.  Either you make a solid strategy and execute it well, or you make mistakes and pay for it.  That is what makes this game great, as well as frustrating.
In each level, you are given a goal (e.g. hostage rescue, survive for X turns, send a unit to a certain location) as well as a set number of units to complete it.  You will see all of the level; there is no fog of war, though you may not be able to see your enemy's units if they are not within the line of sight of a unit you control.
The controls are so-so.  You will need to give each unit a set of complex commands that usually looks something like this:
Ignore all enemies while traveling to a point, engage enemies while aiming in a direction and moving to a second point, stand at a window and wait for 2 seconds, cancel aim and ignore all enemies while traveling to a point, crawl from a point to the next, then stand up and aim in a direction.
That may not make much sense to someone who hasn't played the game, but the point is that setting up a long set of commands like the above example takes time.  If you are not a patient person, this game will probably feel like work instead of being fun.
In the end, I enjoyed this game a lot.  It takes time, but watching your commands unfold and completing a level was very gratifying for me.  I played both the base game and the Red DLC, but did not try multiplayer.  The DLC wasn't much special.  It introduced a new unit, which was cool, but the levels were too easy.  Oh, and the story is bad.  Don't buy this game if you're looking for a compelling story.

I backed my Portugese ally's attempt to repel an invasion by a neighboring lord. After winning that border dispute, my ally usurped my kingdom from me. After a few years, I was able to assassinate him through a manure explosion. Seriously. Upon learning of the successful attempt, my character quipped a very clever, very 80s action flick, response. These little details take a large, complicated game and make it engrossing.
Make no mistake, this game is massive and complicated and frustrating. You will lose.
The game does an amazing job of immersing you in the realm of intrigue and stagnation that was the Middle Ages. Blood lines, succession wars, usurpation, superstition and a serious lack of technological advancement. The real time aspect is a nice touch as it adds a sense of urgency bordering on the overwhelming that isn't found in something like the Civilization series. The pause button is a lifesaver.
The complexity of Medieval politics is the games strength and focus. This isn't a game about medieval warfare or empire building. This is a game about building a dynasty. Once I stopped comparing it to Total War or Civilization, I found myself enjoying the intrigue of court life. The complexity is also the games downfall. It's difficult to keep track of the who's and the what's, and at times the game seems arbitrary in it's nature. I found the tutorial to be necessary but lacking a full enough explanation on the finer points of the game. For example, while duchy's around my kingdom seemed able to field large armies I was left with a few hundred men. I appreciate the imbalance of the game, but something about this bothered me. With similar holdings, they were able to field much, much larger armies than my pitiful band. This I believe is the one downside to this game is the combat. It's too simplistic, too arbitrary and lacks feedback.
With the Portugese usurpation of my throne, my powerbase dwindled. Left with no heir or family members available to be married off, the disgraced grandson of Fernando the Dragon succumbed to his dispair and commited suicide.
I immediately restarted the game.
EDIT:
I decided to try a different era, of the five listed two were locked behind DLC. Mildly annoying but I pressed on. The Mongol era had the option to play as a few muslim characters, that would be interesting. Locked behind DLC again. This is getting a touch repetitive. Oh look, in the Late Middle Ages I could play as an Indian lord vying for control of the sub-continent. Let's do tha...
LOCKED BEHIND DLC!!!

I don't say this easily, but I must admit this is one of my favorite games ever - along with Witcher 3
Here are some things that I would recommend to new players:
1- Do the tutorial. It will help you get familiarized with the many game features and it will give you money to help you with your journey.
2- DO NOT give up. There is no actual winning here, it's all about survival and how long you can carry your characters' legacies. You will lose quickly quite a few times, but that's normal :)
3- The personal traits you should develop first, in my opinion, are:
> Stewardship: Better perks for realm management, especially the increase in demesne limit.
> Marshal: More efficient and bigger armies.
> Intrigue: Makes you better at plots and politics.
> Diplomacy: Your vassals will like you more.
> Learning: While advancing your science quickly is desirable, it is better to do it by having your
spymaster steal it from other realms. I think this also makes bishops like you more,
but that barely matters.
4- Do not send your characters to battle if your succession is not ready to go. If you die, things can get bad.
5- Watch out for religious wars, sometimes your enemies will team up and literally screw you up. If this happens, always keep a good amount of money so that you can strategically buy mercenaries and take your enemies out when they're all teamed up. (Be careful as the mercs may attack you instead - joining the other side - if you run out of money and can't pay them).
6- If you have a small kingdom, hold as many counties as possible. If it is a big kingdom, strategically give duchies away, but keep your core counties/duchies for yourself. If it is an empire, then give kingdoms away, but be very careful.
7- Try not to hold too many duchies. There is a pretty ugly opinion penalty for this, give them away to people who like you if you need to (preferably from your family).
8- Baronies are also your friends, but counties override them in desirability. I usually keep the most important ones (especially the one in the capital county), but give the rest to dynasty members that have a good opinion of me and are not envious (watch for this trait).
9- Do not hold any cities or religious buildings. The game will give you a warning about this, do not ignore it. Also, be careful on who you give them to.
10- Take out titles from your enemies when there is no penalty (when they act dishonorably). This is usually when they are in a plot against you or your close family as well as the times when they lead factions against you.
11- Use minor titles on people with slightly low opinions of you (to make them slightly like you).
12- Keep the pope semi-happy at least, especially if you have nearby enemies who are favored by the pope.
13- Do not let neighbors get too big and powerful, they could and will take you out eventually - or at least put up a fight. If you do have a huge neighbor, send your chancellor to make his vassals angry (forgot how this is called). Also make alliances with other neighbors to defend yourself should the need arise.
14- Change your succession law to primogeniture as soon as you can (your main heir gets everything you have). Gavelkind succession can be a nightmare.
15- Push for having children as soon as you can (look for a wife with good fertility bonuses). If you don't have a male heir yet, push for having ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ children with anyone you can and legitimize them. Also, your female children should be married matrilineally so that their children will be born to your house (if not, then try to get an alliance out of the marriage).
16- Do not waste your time in naval military advances, it won't matter for a long time. This is, of course, unless you are in an island nation. For example, Ireland can get to anywhere in Brittania without a navy and even if you wanted to get to the continent's mainland, your realm's ships will be more than enough.
17- Increase tax income from city vassals as soon as possible. This is what will give you the most money. You want to watch out for very low opinions though - they will still pay you, but significantly less.
18- Have at least small county vassal taxes and aim to increase it when they somewhat like you. Bribe the heck out of them to keep em happy too.
19- Always look for oportunities to expand your empire. This includes creating claims on neighboring counties, waging religious wars, and creating a duchy so that you have a causus beli on a county that the duchy covers but is not under your control.
20- Watch out for angry neighbor alliances. They could overrun you, so you need to play some politics here.
21- And finally, enjoy the game :). Remember that you will lose a few times, but that's what makes it fun. Experience also matter a lot here, so you WILL get better at this the more you play it!

This game is completely insane.
I don't mean that this game is quirky, or frantic, or random. I mean that this game is absolutely certifiably mad. It has the insanity of a well-spoken schizophrenic, who presents a compelling, logical, and well-reasoned theory of the world in which the true masterminds are carrier pigeons.
The TIS-100 is a beautifully crafted piece of virtual hardware from a world very different from ours. It's something that could have been made in the 80's, if we had fundamentally different assumptions about hardware design. Luxuries like multiple registers and programs more than 15 lines long are discarded in favor of easy visual debugging and a baffling degree of parallelism. Tasks that are trivial on reasonble hardware take careful consideration and lateral thinking on the TIS-100.

TIS-100 is a game unlike any other I've played. For one, it actually requires you to think. This is not a game where you can just jump right in and make a program right away. With the exception of the first program, you have to make all the programs from scratch. Secondly, it actually feels like you are writing actual programs. Yes, the program language may be made up, but, to "debug" the puzzles, you need to use the same exact skills needed to write real-life programs, such as troubleshooting, program organization, and critical thinking, just to name a few. And to add to the feel, there is no tutorial. There is only an owner's manual on pdf. All of this added together really makes you feel like a genius after you solve a puz - uh, I mean - debug a program.
All in all, if you are looking for a game that is fast-paced and action-packed, go look somewhere else. But, if you like to think through a puzzle that makes you feel good about yourself afterwards, or if you are ever interested in programming at all and would like a taste of what it takes, then this game is PERFECT for you.
