Let me just get this out of the way first, the DRM is terrible and needs to go. Not only is it extremely sketchy to include it without a warning on launch day, and with a bug that prevented offline play, and give out Sonic 1 to those who preordered two weeks prior preventing anyone from getting a refund (refund policy is two weeks after acquisition, and Sonic 1 counts for some reason), it's rather ironic that the DRM is of the "Anti-tamper" kind, despite the developers getting their experience literally from tampering with previous Sonic games. This is very hypocritical of whomever decided to include the DRM in this otherwise fantastic game, and there really is no benefit to be seen from including in a $20 game, no less.
That said, once the DRM situation has been sorted out, since the game is otherwise perfectly playable as it is, this is absolutely a game any fan of platformers or Sonic in general should pick up. Anyone who had enjoyed any of the previous games in the classic series (1, 2, 3&K, CD, and even 4) will certainly find something to enjoy, and the dedicated followers have probably already bought this but that's because they will certainly gain the most from this in terms of the references and attention to detail that has been lovingly weaved into this experience "By the Mania, for the Mania". Even so, those unfamiliar or skeptical about the blue hedgehog ought to find something to be pleasantly surprised about, this franchise did have real appeal that wasn't reduced to just memes and glitchfests, particularly during the 16-bit days, and Mania is a just as fine place to start as any of the originals to see why this franchise became popular in the first place.
Worst case scenario is that this may seem too similar and doesn't do enough original, but truthfully, it's been so long since a game that is this close to the classics that chances are what's here is more than enough, at least until the inevitable follow up with much more original content. The game's zones I would consider to be divided into thirds, the first third are remixes of past stages with some new twists thrown into the mix much like Sonic Generations, the second third are stages that borrow the names and general settings of previous stages but with a lot more interesting twists and mechanics from other past zones as well, and the final are completely original zones that are where the game's identity and charm really resides, where the developers could go all out with their creative energy and it really does show.
The final verdict: add this to your wishlist. Keep an eye out for news of when the DRM is removed. Then buy, buy, buy. Or buy it for consoles in the meantime, but chances are there will be a modding community that should make the PC version the version to buy. Don't worry about buying it twice or more times though, this game deserves it.

At this point, Sonic is best summarized as being a string of broken promises. After many attempts to bring the franchise back to a "return to form", it's almost poetic that this promise was finally delivered not by Sonic Team themselves, but by fan developers being given free reign over the Sonic license in this retro callback. Not only does Sonic Mania live up to the hype of being "the true Sonic 4", it's arguably the strongest title in the series, dethroning Sonic 3 & Knuckles as the often-heralded "best Sonic".
This shouldn't come as much of a surprise to anyone who has been following the Sonic fangame and rom hacking scene over the years; Taxman and others in the community have been recreating classic Sonic gameplay through fan projects for at least a decade and a half, perfecting both the mechanics and the complex level designs that define the Genesis/Megadrive titles. With a conglomeration of indie developers, artists and musicians all sharing the same passion for the blue blur, it becomes obvious that the end product is a labor of love, and not just a retro cash-grab.
The game's sense of style is clear the moment you let the title screen run. The intro animation, menus and credits harken back to colorful and abstract aesthetic reminiscent of Japanese Sonic commercials and box art, while ingame sprites and backgrounds are vibrant and detailed -- the characters themselves brim with personality thanks to the game's cartoon style and ultra-fluid animations. Tee Lopes takes the reign of the sound design to create a soundtrack that reflects classic Sonic's iconic melodies, upbeat pacing and compositional complexity.
The gameplay comprises primarily of remixed zones with some new zones occasionally thrown in. You would expect to be exhausted of revisiting old zones after Sonic Generations and the umpteenth recreation of Green Hill Zone teased in Sonic Forces, but Mania executes this tired concept rather effectively -- Act 1s of old zones typically consist of old zone ideas completely restructured into new levels and remastered with crisper and more detailed graphical designs, whereas the Act 2s of those zones redefine those zones through the introduction of new gimmicks that completely twist and distort how the level is played. These levels could very easily have constituted as new zones themselves, and I often found myself forgetting that I've technically "been here before". That being said, the NEW zones are incredible for Sonic standards, and in spite of the solid execution of the remixed zones, the old to new ratio left me wanting a bit more.
That being said, the stage designs are great whether they're reusing old gimmicks or featuring new ones. Somehow, the game manages to match the sheer complexity of Sonic CD's layouts while still managing the sense of flow provided by Sonic 3&K. Cheap hits and cheap deaths can still occur, but they're much less frequent than in previous titles. This is also thanks in part to the game's 60 FPS limit and the wider screen resolution permitted by PC monitors.
Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles are all here and bring with them many of the same game features that were present in Sonic 3 & Knuckles, such as character-specific abilities and Knuckles-only routes. Sonic's insta-shield, however, has been replaced with a dropdash, which is a little less intuitive at first but ultimately a very addictive maneuver. Dropping into a spindash has obvious usages in speed running and is a nice way to keep the momentum going, but it also happens to be invaluable in combat, allowing Sonic to quickly strike at bosses or dodge incoming attacks. It pains me that Sonic Mania doesn't hint at this mechanic anywhere ingame, and pressing then holding the jump button WHILE in midair is too deliberate of an action for the player to find it out by accident. A simple cutscene showing Sonic dropdash would have been enough to remedy this.
The special stages are without a doubt the best in the entire series. The gameplay is similar in concept to Sonic CD's UFO-busting stages, except that each stage is built on a race track, and you must collect blue spheres to build up speed and catch a single UFO before your ring counter depletes -- this creates a clear sense of momentum in the gameplay that most of the other Sonic special stages never really captured. The magic of course is in the execution, as Mania's special stages lack the cheapness of Sonic 2's halfpipe or the headache of 3&K's blue spheres, offering tight controls, clear obstacles, and unique challenges in each stage. But really, my favorite part of the special stages is marvelling at the Saturn-era 3D aesthetic, which is unlike anything I've seen from other games in recent memory. Honestly, this portion of the game could have easily passed off for a sick arcade title in the 90's.
Checkpoint bonus stages are back, but they are all Blue Spheres now.... and good grief, there must be a thousand of them! Thankfully they are all optional, but you will need to complete some of them in order to get certain special campaign unlocks, and doing several stages back-to-back gets really exhausting VERY quick. While they make a nice side addition, I would have prefered to see something simpler take its place in the campaign, akin to Sonic 3&K's slot machine stage, gumball machine, and... whatever the ♥♥♥♥ that third one was.
The game's main problems come down to a few miscellanous design decisions that make the game more punishing that it need to be. The return of Time Over is an obvious one -- with how expansive these levels are, you really just want to be exploring every possible nook and cranny for rings, powerups, and special stages. But for some reason you are still capped at a 10 minute counter, which directly punishes this. Lives is something I don't have as much of a problem with, as my save files are usually in the double digits anyway... but a less able player gets sent back to the beginning of the zone if they run out. This doesn't sound that bad, considering that Sonic 3 & Knuckles did the same thing, but Sonic Mania's acts are at least as big as 3&K and can get even longer while looking for special stage entrances. When you factor in some of the game's Act 2 bosses, occasional physics glitches, and the annoyingly strict player-crushing rules against moving terrain, sometimes this can become a bit overbearing. I once bailed out of a boss fight simply because I had so many lives but I was too tired to play anymore; would have been nice to leave off at the beginning of Act 2 instead of the entire zone.
Speaking of bosses, this factors into the game's uneven difficulty curve. Some levels, and especially some bosses, simply feel out of order in terms of challenge and punishment. The first few zones aren't too bad about this, but after Flying Battery, the Act 2 bosses are all over the map. It's nice that we finally have some Sonic bosses that are both creative AND challenging, but I feel like some fine-tuning was needed on this front.
All that said, Mania is not perfect, but it's probably the best Sonic game we've ever had. It's a treat for anyone who's been itching for a new classic Sonic title for the past two decades (like me!), but it is also an excellent platformer in its own right and a good first entry for anyone looking into the franchise.
Before buying, a couple caveats about the PC release: the Steam version of this game uses Denuvo DRM. I don't know much about anti-piracy software other than that Denuvo is apparently fairly controversial, but it's worth disclosing. Also, the Steam version currently does not allow you to play Sonic Mania unless you are logged into your account even if you are using offline mode. (EDIT: Apparently this is fixed now.)
That all being said, I would still recommend Sonic Mania; I would simply prioritize owning this on a console first if you already have one and you're concerned about DRM for one reason or another.

After a year's worth of hype, a 2 week delay, and a backlash against the DRM: Sonic Mania is here.
Sonic Mania is NOT is remake of the original Sonic The Hedgehog Series of the Genesis Era. As one of the developers described: Sonic Mania is a project, that pretends to be a game released in the Sega Saturn (I know. I didn't even know this console existed either.), and you know what? Its not bad and its not good either.
Its amazing!
Sonic Mania is great, because it identifies itself as a succesful classic game. The brightest minds in the Sonic modding community build this game (Christian Whitehead, Pagoda West, and Headcannon etc.), and I kid you not, this people have more tha 10 years dedicated (as a hobby if I am allowed to say) in building fan-based Sonic games and programs that have tried to emulate the classic Sonic experience. After much experience, I'd be lying if I told you that: this game is full of bugs, incomplete, and something that fails to captivate what a Sonic game should include.
The game itself runs smooth on my gaming rig, but also in my 3 year old low-spec laptop (btw: Thanks for NOT making this game resource-intensive!). A solid 60 FPS (not always on both systems, but most of the time) and Full HD resolution make this game a full-fledged Sonic game of its on caliber. I've been playing this game with an F310 Gamepad, and I have NOT had any issues with the gameplay. The characters a very responsive, and you sometimes think the game is to blame for your accidents (in my case, I find it difficult to react fast).
Sonic The Hedgehog is marketed as an all about speed platformer. I guarantee you, this game is so fast, you may lose track of Sonic (maybe the zones too) due to the speed, but that is what defines Sonic. Despite being fast, Sonic is still controllable. While playing, I never had an issue stopping Sonic, or making Sonic go fast.
The only problem I had with the gameplay, was that Tails and Sonic stop holding together when flying, and this can something be troublesome when you just want to get to higher ground. In no way, does this interrupt the game quality.
As a long time fan, I expect A LOT from this game. Remember: A years worth of HAS to be worth something.
This game does not fail my expectations. Some levels are redesigned, while others are new zones created out of the creative minds of the devs. Each level had something different to show case, but nevertheless, I enjoyed the attention to detail and quality applied by the developers.
In the end, I can sincerely say that I WOULD RECOMMEND this game to anyone. Besides the technical issues behind this game, it is difficult NOT to enjoy Sonic Mania. Sonic Mania is a masterpiece by itself, and also a rebirth of the franchise (after much of its recent turmoil). Plenty of love and care went into the production of this game, and as a long time fan, I can say I am proud of Whitehead, Headcannon, and Pagoda West. They really went all out in creating this game, and they really exceeded the quality (in my opinion) of ANY game in the entire franchise. I am glad I purchased this game.
P.S.: I know I have not unlocked everything, but could you include a "Hardcore Mode," to give the option for long time fans to increase the difficulty of the game? I honestly think this game is somewhat easy, and I'd sure enjoy a bigger challenge.

BlazeRush is a third-person perspective, arcade racer that combines simple controls with brilliant physics resulting in one hell of a good time. This is the type of game that you may look at and ignore, or you obtain it somehow and let it sit in your library. Well let me just say that BlazeRush is worth your time and money, here's why.
BlazeRush is a primarily single-stick controlled game with power-ups. Think of Mario Kart but at a fixed camera angle and without any real complex driving mechanics whatsoever. Simply point the controller stick in the direction you wish to go, and your vehicle will go in that direction (also indicated by an arrow at the front of the vehicle). I'll say it now that this game requires a controller for precision; I would not recommend using KB+M for it. Now, you may not be into that sort of thing, that's fine. However, neither am I, yet this game managed to actually capture my attention on multiple occasions.
Thanks to power-ups, it turns a pretty standard game into one hell of an explosive, speed-fest. From rocket boosts, to actual (semi) heat-seeking rockets, racing and combat collide in a desperate struggle for first-place. Just as power-ups make Mario Kart highly entertaining, power-ups are absolutely amazing in BlazeRush. The system for obtaining them is also a bit unique. Items simply fall from the sky at random, and people can drive into them to collect them. They fall a lot more frequently for the people further behind the leaders but leaders can continue to collect items that they may need in the future to maintain that lead.
Now due to the fixed camera angle, obviously some cars may fall too far behind and then no longer be visible. As a result, there is an automatic catch-up system in the game. Fall too far behind and the game will automatically move you close enough to the rest of the racers without giving you any advantages. The system here feels fluid and balanced and never takes away from the flow of the game.
Each type of vehicle has their own strengths and weaknesses. Tank-type vehicles will do excellently on cornering, but drifting is horrible on them, and their top speed is pretty limited. Racing-type vehicles are great at speed in all aspects, and can drift, but their handling is pretty weak and can easily be pushed out of the stage with various weapons. Flying-type vehicles are a bit balanced in most aspects but don't expect them to shine in any particular aspect.
The campaign is one of the best ways to actually get into this game. Levels progress in difficulty slowly, introducing you to different environments, weapons, vehicles and power-ups. The AI provides a healthy challenge while not being too over-the-top or rage inducing.
The graphics of BlazeRush are well designed and attractive, combining a semi-cartoony look with over-the-top explosions for an insanely fun experience.
Vehicle sounds, weapons, power-ups and other elements of the game sound very good and really give the right effect at the right time. The soundtrack is fairly well varied and entertaining. For an arcade game such as this, it felt right at home.
I didn't expect much from BlazeRush but after playing it on so many occasions I have to admit it is quite fun and addicting. It's even more so playing with other people, but the campaign is highly challenging and worth playing too. I'm quite impressed that this game has captivated my interest this much and I would highly recommend it to anyone who likes arcade racers in general.
8/10 -

Hollywood hacking, the game. The learning curve starts off not too bad, then goes pretty steeply up, then levels back off once you figure everything out. There's not too much to it, but pay attention and a small storyline opens up that puts pretty much everything at risk and leaves it to you to decide what to do.
All in all, this is a great game to kill a bit of time with, especially if you're without internet access for some reason. A word of advice, if I may? Robbing banks is extremely hard to do, but totally worth it, so try and figure out how to do that. Other than that, just screw around. Hack random stuff and play with it, see what happens.

There's no other game out there that captures the feeling of being a (Hollywood-inspired) hacker. It may look simplistic, it may be more than ten years old but once you've completed your first successful hack and experienced the adrenaline rush of constantly having to look over your back, doing everything right and hoping that you won't get caught, you want more -- much more. To the point you risk everything just to get into even the most secure systems.
Ive played every Assassins creed game except Syndicate and Rogue has been by far the best AC game there is hands down.

If you loved Black Flag you surely will love this. Freeroam aspect is alright, but more loading screens than Black Flag. Combat is very similar to Black Flag but the ship battle has been tweaked a little bit. The game takes you to different places to New York and the pacific ocean you travel as Shay Patrick Cormac once an Assassin in training now a fearsome Assassin hunter. But this time around you travel with your ship the Morrigan. I won't say anything to spoil, but if you loved Black Flag this is a must have.

Without a shadow of a doubt my favourite Assassin's Creed game of all, and my favourite protagonist of perhaps any game out there, not just this franchise. You feel for Shay throughout, and if you're as open minded as myself, you may find you agree to his ideals. You're eyes and mind are opened to a new reality which sometimes begins to make the previous games feel like 'Assassin Propaganda', where you are blinded by the Assassin point of view.
In the present day you play an Abstergo Entertainment employee within the familiar environment of Black Flag. The employee is a nobody (or 'numbskull', as you're often dubbed), exploring the memories of another nobody called Shay Patrick Cormac - an Assassin in the 1750's. As you find out just how important Shay is to both the Assassins AND the Templars of the present and the past, you find that certain decisions you make reflect that of Shay himself: you view the world "as it really is".
In Shay's memories, he is sent on a mission which has him unexpectedly and uncontrollably involved in the literal destruction of a city. With the guilt and disgust of the innocents killed, he confronts those that sent him on the mission only to find that they won't listen. After confrontation, and events following it, Shay finds himself allied with the same people who share the same view on protecting the innocent and doing what is right. However, these allies were once his sworn enemy. Ultimately Shay must end the threat, even if he must kill those he once saw as his family.
Overall, the stories of both times are short, but rich, and almost every character has some kind of interesting backstory, with reference to previous games, and future ones (Unity & Syndicate). They definitely could have filled certain gaps in the story where time passed such as explaining how Shay got to where he eventually gets to in the final sequence. However, everything ties in so well in an almost flawless fashion, filling the interesting gap between the transitioning protagonists of Haytham and Connor in AC 3, as well as a key moment in AC Unity. The present day is 'marmite' - a term used to describe how you either love it or hate it. I found it interesting, mainly because the unknown protagonist rises to importance in parallel to Shay as he explores Shay's memories.
Naval Combat is slightly more flushed out and feels much more satisfying than Black Flag (and Black Flag had it spot on at the time!). The biggest and best difference is the upgrade to your round shots which fires a double volley of cannons! Another key thing is to watch out for those Bounty Hunters ramming into you. It's not something to take for granted this time around. Otherwise it's essentially the same badass naval combat unrivaled in games in my opinion.
Melee combat and stealth kills are also essentially the same as previous games as well, so don't expect much of a noticeable difference besides the new (and cool) grenade types that have different effects. Ubisoft definitely didn't see the need to revamp the combat in this game due to doing so in Unity.
There is a lot to do for side content, about as much as Black Flag, with Hunting missions, Assassinations, Fort and Gang territory controls, Shay's Fleet missions, and the ever-awesome (and much improved) Legendary Ship Battles.
There's a number of collectibles to find across 3 maps; Animus Fragments, Chests, Prosperity gems, Shanties, Templar Maps, and more. And depending on DLC's, there is also even more to find and unlock cool content.
You can also earn money from a bank account after performing activities that increase your generated income. One of these activities is Renovation, which was seen in Black Flag at the Pirates Hideout. Renovating public buildings will raise your income, as will taking over Forts, Territories and collecting Prosperity gems as a new collectible.
= Final Opinions =
Essentially the biggest grip in this game, though, is the intrigue of the Templar point of view. At first I thought 'Yep, I'd love to be a bad guy for a change'. Sometimes bad guys are more fun, right? Well as the story hit a certain stage, I found myself seeing the Templars as peacemakers, just trying to do what's best for people and having the Assassins constantly meddling in their affairs and destroying their plans.
But most of all, they were being careless. Shay saw it this way and allied himself with those he was meant to kill. The very first character you meet when you try to set things right appears good-hearted and honourable, a man of a heroic and kind nature, wanting to do whats right for the people in the colonies as much as Shay does. He becomes Shay's role model, and, perhaps, you're own (if doing what you feel is right, is you're sort of thing). For me this was the biggest and most important thing; the ultimate change of opinion not only in this game, but the entire franchise.
Also, I find that the key requirement for atmosphere and immersion in all games is it's music and sound design. Let me tell you, at least 80% of the music is perfect. Elitsa Alexandrova is brilliant! The main theme feels so... Shay. The Legendary Battle theme (David and Goliath) is almost as epic as the track used in the Legendary Battles in Black Flag (let's face it, ya can't beat that). Chase and combat tracks are also really nicely composed. I personally found that this was the last game with a great soundtrack - Unity and Syndicate just got repetitive and annoying for me.
So now I ask myself something. Forget Jedi or Sith, that's so 2016. The real question to be asking is this: Assassin, or Templar?
Templar. Definitely Templar.
But then, I could just be an unknown employee from Google, my hands forced into a secret oganisation, and now I'm just spreading Templar propaganda.

The beginning of the US were (mildly) interesting in AC III; pirates were awesome in AC IV; ships were something new in both; however, they were cool because they were something different. Now, they feel like something seen again and again. When you expect to play an assassin and actually spend most of your time attacking ships, it gets old pretty soon. All of this said, the story is definitely better than its immediate predecessors, and if you liked Black Flag you will love this too. I still feel like recommeding it because it is a good Assassin's Creed, but as a game in general it has many traits of a missed opportunity.

A really original simultaneous turn-based tactics, set in a cyberworld of a distant future.
Even if usually I'm not too much into this kind of games, I really enjoyed it for its simple yet complex mechanics. The rules are really basic, but since the whole game is about predicting opponent's moves, and you can never, never know for sure what another human being is thinking, and that's why it shines in multiplayer more than anything else, even though it has a lenghty and worthy campaign.
Multiplayer is really versatile too, since you can just leave your turn and play another match (or even another game altogether) while you wait your opponent's; you can even set the game to send you an email when a new turn is awaiting you.
Also, is worth nothing that replay of your matches are automatically saved on the servers, and you can watch even other's really easily; and there's an amazing little option that uploads your matches to your YouTube channel.
Graphics are really simple, but they do their job, and the soundtrack is astonishing good.
Just try the demo and complete the tutorial, you'll get an idea if this is or not a game for you, you could be surprised.
I also recommend St. Ives Apricot Scrub for blemishes and black heads.

Full of annoying fixable bugs.
It's one of the games with the "devs don't play their own game" syndrome.
For a game where you're sort of supposed to parkour all over the place, there's a crazy number of places where you cannot simply wall jump upwards or even run along the wall, because there's a tiny protrusion of the collision box that stops you.
There's a "ledge grabbing" mechanic that basically never works when you try to jump somewhere, but are a bit too short, and instead triggers every time you try to walk into a small hole, resulting in climbing out of that hole.
Waypoints often work the other way than they should - in big open areas, that you are able to easily jump over, they show you a path to go as if you were glued to the ground, and on the other hand, in some complex multi-floor tunnels they appear at the very end, without showing you the way there.
Full of unnecessary grind.
As far as i know, it doesn't use any kind of progressive RNG drop system. Technically it's possible to grind for something infinitely, and that sucks.
Basically all high level missions have a significant chance of dropping useless newbie-level junk. Of course, even when you drop the proper reward tier, you still need to be lucky to get the specific one you want.
Quite often, when a new weapon/frame gets added to the game, you're forced to grind for some new resource, or one that disappears after ~2 days from your inventory, so your hundreds of hours in game and countless stacks of all other resources are meaningless.

Let me just get this out of the way first, the DRM is terrible and needs to go. Not only is it extremely sketchy to include it without a warning on launch day, and with a bug that prevented offline play, and give out Sonic 1 to those who preordered two weeks prior preventing anyone from getting a refund (refund policy is two weeks after acquisition, and Sonic 1 counts for some reason), it's rather ironic that the DRM is of the "Anti-tamper" kind, despite the developers getting their experience literally from tampering with previous Sonic games. This is very hypocritical of whomever decided to include the DRM in this otherwise fantastic game, and there really is no benefit to be seen from including in a $20 game, no less.
That said, once the DRM situation has been sorted out, since the game is otherwise perfectly playable as it is, this is absolutely a game any fan of platformers or Sonic in general should pick up. Anyone who had enjoyed any of the previous games in the classic series (1, 2, 3&K, CD, and even 4) will certainly find something to enjoy, and the dedicated followers have probably already bought this but that's because they will certainly gain the most from this in terms of the references and attention to detail that has been lovingly weaved into this experience "By the Mania, for the Mania". Even so, those unfamiliar or skeptical about the blue hedgehog ought to find something to be pleasantly surprised about, this franchise did have real appeal that wasn't reduced to just memes and glitchfests, particularly during the 16-bit days, and Mania is a just as fine place to start as any of the originals to see why this franchise became popular in the first place.
Worst case scenario is that this may seem too similar and doesn't do enough original, but truthfully, it's been so long since a game that is this close to the classics that chances are what's here is more than enough, at least until the inevitable follow up with much more original content. The game's zones I would consider to be divided into thirds, the first third are remixes of past stages with some new twists thrown into the mix much like Sonic Generations, the second third are stages that borrow the names and general settings of previous stages but with a lot more interesting twists and mechanics from other past zones as well, and the final are completely original zones that are where the game's identity and charm really resides, where the developers could go all out with their creative energy and it really does show.
The final verdict: add this to your wishlist. Keep an eye out for news of when the DRM is removed. Then buy, buy, buy. Or buy it for consoles in the meantime, but chances are there will be a modding community that should make the PC version the version to buy. Don't worry about buying it twice or more times though, this game deserves it.

At this point, Sonic is best summarized as being a string of broken promises. After many attempts to bring the franchise back to a "return to form", it's almost poetic that this promise was finally delivered not by Sonic Team themselves, but by fan developers being given free reign over the Sonic license in this retro callback. Not only does Sonic Mania live up to the hype of being "the true Sonic 4", it's arguably the strongest title in the series, dethroning Sonic 3 & Knuckles as the often-heralded "best Sonic".
This shouldn't come as much of a surprise to anyone who has been following the Sonic fangame and rom hacking scene over the years; Taxman and others in the community have been recreating classic Sonic gameplay through fan projects for at least a decade and a half, perfecting both the mechanics and the complex level designs that define the Genesis/Megadrive titles. With a conglomeration of indie developers, artists and musicians all sharing the same passion for the blue blur, it becomes obvious that the end product is a labor of love, and not just a retro cash-grab.
The game's sense of style is clear the moment you let the title screen run. The intro animation, menus and credits harken back to colorful and abstract aesthetic reminiscent of Japanese Sonic commercials and box art, while ingame sprites and backgrounds are vibrant and detailed -- the characters themselves brim with personality thanks to the game's cartoon style and ultra-fluid animations. Tee Lopes takes the reign of the sound design to create a soundtrack that reflects classic Sonic's iconic melodies, upbeat pacing and compositional complexity.
The gameplay comprises primarily of remixed zones with some new zones occasionally thrown in. You would expect to be exhausted of revisiting old zones after Sonic Generations and the umpteenth recreation of Green Hill Zone teased in Sonic Forces, but Mania executes this tired concept rather effectively -- Act 1s of old zones typically consist of old zone ideas completely restructured into new levels and remastered with crisper and more detailed graphical designs, whereas the Act 2s of those zones redefine those zones through the introduction of new gimmicks that completely twist and distort how the level is played. These levels could very easily have constituted as new zones themselves, and I often found myself forgetting that I've technically "been here before". That being said, the NEW zones are incredible for Sonic standards, and in spite of the solid execution of the remixed zones, the old to new ratio left me wanting a bit more.
That being said, the stage designs are great whether they're reusing old gimmicks or featuring new ones. Somehow, the game manages to match the sheer complexity of Sonic CD's layouts while still managing the sense of flow provided by Sonic 3&K. Cheap hits and cheap deaths can still occur, but they're much less frequent than in previous titles. This is also thanks in part to the game's 60 FPS limit and the wider screen resolution permitted by PC monitors.
Sonic, Tails, and Knuckles are all here and bring with them many of the same game features that were present in Sonic 3 & Knuckles, such as character-specific abilities and Knuckles-only routes. Sonic's insta-shield, however, has been replaced with a dropdash, which is a little less intuitive at first but ultimately a very addictive maneuver. Dropping into a spindash has obvious usages in speed running and is a nice way to keep the momentum going, but it also happens to be invaluable in combat, allowing Sonic to quickly strike at bosses or dodge incoming attacks. It pains me that Sonic Mania doesn't hint at this mechanic anywhere ingame, and pressing then holding the jump button WHILE in midair is too deliberate of an action for the player to find it out by accident. A simple cutscene showing Sonic dropdash would have been enough to remedy this.
The special stages are without a doubt the best in the entire series. The gameplay is similar in concept to Sonic CD's UFO-busting stages, except that each stage is built on a race track, and you must collect blue spheres to build up speed and catch a single UFO before your ring counter depletes -- this creates a clear sense of momentum in the gameplay that most of the other Sonic special stages never really captured. The magic of course is in the execution, as Mania's special stages lack the cheapness of Sonic 2's halfpipe or the headache of 3&K's blue spheres, offering tight controls, clear obstacles, and unique challenges in each stage. But really, my favorite part of the special stages is marvelling at the Saturn-era 3D aesthetic, which is unlike anything I've seen from other games in recent memory. Honestly, this portion of the game could have easily passed off for a sick arcade title in the 90's.
Checkpoint bonus stages are back, but they are all Blue Spheres now.... and good grief, there must be a thousand of them! Thankfully they are all optional, but you will need to complete some of them in order to get certain special campaign unlocks, and doing several stages back-to-back gets really exhausting VERY quick. While they make a nice side addition, I would have prefered to see something simpler take its place in the campaign, akin to Sonic 3&K's slot machine stage, gumball machine, and... whatever the ♥♥♥♥ that third one was.
The game's main problems come down to a few miscellanous design decisions that make the game more punishing that it need to be. The return of Time Over is an obvious one -- with how expansive these levels are, you really just want to be exploring every possible nook and cranny for rings, powerups, and special stages. But for some reason you are still capped at a 10 minute counter, which directly punishes this. Lives is something I don't have as much of a problem with, as my save files are usually in the double digits anyway... but a less able player gets sent back to the beginning of the zone if they run out. This doesn't sound that bad, considering that Sonic 3 & Knuckles did the same thing, but Sonic Mania's acts are at least as big as 3&K and can get even longer while looking for special stage entrances. When you factor in some of the game's Act 2 bosses, occasional physics glitches, and the annoyingly strict player-crushing rules against moving terrain, sometimes this can become a bit overbearing. I once bailed out of a boss fight simply because I had so many lives but I was too tired to play anymore; would have been nice to leave off at the beginning of Act 2 instead of the entire zone.
Speaking of bosses, this factors into the game's uneven difficulty curve. Some levels, and especially some bosses, simply feel out of order in terms of challenge and punishment. The first few zones aren't too bad about this, but after Flying Battery, the Act 2 bosses are all over the map. It's nice that we finally have some Sonic bosses that are both creative AND challenging, but I feel like some fine-tuning was needed on this front.
All that said, Mania is not perfect, but it's probably the best Sonic game we've ever had. It's a treat for anyone who's been itching for a new classic Sonic title for the past two decades (like me!), but it is also an excellent platformer in its own right and a good first entry for anyone looking into the franchise.
Before buying, a couple caveats about the PC release: the Steam version of this game uses Denuvo DRM. I don't know much about anti-piracy software other than that Denuvo is apparently fairly controversial, but it's worth disclosing. Also, the Steam version currently does not allow you to play Sonic Mania unless you are logged into your account even if you are using offline mode. (EDIT: Apparently this is fixed now.)
That all being said, I would still recommend Sonic Mania; I would simply prioritize owning this on a console first if you already have one and you're concerned about DRM for one reason or another.

TL;DR: 4/5 - Give it a try, especially if you like optimising and fiddling with code.
I've played a fair bit now and, to me, this is one of the best puzzlers I've ever played.
A few words about the gameplay in case you wonder: The game consists of 48 levels, each a programming task. Looking at the first screenshot here on Steam should show you the level SEQUENCE COUNTER. In the upper left corner you have your task. The 12 squares that take almost all of the screen are "nodes", independent CPUs that you can program freely with up to 15 instructions each. The arrows between them are "ports" that allow you to move data between nodes. There are also input and output ports at the top and at the bottom of the screen, respectively. Your program has to stand four tests, three with predefined inputs and one with random values. You can see the given inputs and expected outputs on the left in the screenshot.
The programming language used is some very basic form of assembler consisting of just 13 opcodes (compared to the several hundred of a real Intel x86) . If you got prior programming experience or even worked with assembler, then this should be quite intuitive. For me it was definitly easier than the geometric approach of SpaceChem, Zach's previous game. Without any knowledge of programming the learning curve might be a bit steep as there is no tutorial, just a short manual. However, this should in no way discourage you. Pressing F1 brings up a quick reference of all opcodes and this game might actually enable you to understand the inner workings of a computer on a basic level so the educational value is immense.
There is another aspect to this game, beyond merely completing the tasks: Of course you can solve a level in many different ways but the real challenge is to find the "best" way to do it. This is where your wet OCD dreams come true. Each solution gets a score consisting of the number of CPU cycles your program took to complete, the number of CPUs you used, and the length of your program. The game keeps track of the minimum you achieved in each of the three categories separatly. So naturally you start coding up optimised solutions for each category. This is where the only shortfalls of the game become apparent. First, you cannot really see the exact world records (it's a histogram view) so you cannot tell if your solution is already best possible. Second, you can only save three programs per level. With three variables to optimise this leaves you no space to try out new things. The first issue is remedied by a reddit thread (see
and the second can be worked around with manually copying and renaming solutions. But honestly, it's 2015 not the nineties, this shouldn't be necessary anymore.

After a year's worth of hype, a 2 week delay, and a backlash against the DRM: Sonic Mania is here.
Sonic Mania is NOT is remake of the original Sonic The Hedgehog Series of the Genesis Era. As one of the developers described: Sonic Mania is a project, that pretends to be a game released in the Sega Saturn (I know. I didn't even know this console existed either.), and you know what? Its not bad and its not good either.
Its amazing!
Sonic Mania is great, because it identifies itself as a succesful classic game. The brightest minds in the Sonic modding community build this game (Christian Whitehead, Pagoda West, and Headcannon etc.), and I kid you not, this people have more tha 10 years dedicated (as a hobby if I am allowed to say) in building fan-based Sonic games and programs that have tried to emulate the classic Sonic experience. After much experience, I'd be lying if I told you that: this game is full of bugs, incomplete, and something that fails to captivate what a Sonic game should include.
The game itself runs smooth on my gaming rig, but also in my 3 year old low-spec laptop (btw: Thanks for NOT making this game resource-intensive!). A solid 60 FPS (not always on both systems, but most of the time) and Full HD resolution make this game a full-fledged Sonic game of its on caliber. I've been playing this game with an F310 Gamepad, and I have NOT had any issues with the gameplay. The characters a very responsive, and you sometimes think the game is to blame for your accidents (in my case, I find it difficult to react fast).
Sonic The Hedgehog is marketed as an all about speed platformer. I guarantee you, this game is so fast, you may lose track of Sonic (maybe the zones too) due to the speed, but that is what defines Sonic. Despite being fast, Sonic is still controllable. While playing, I never had an issue stopping Sonic, or making Sonic go fast.
The only problem I had with the gameplay, was that Tails and Sonic stop holding together when flying, and this can something be troublesome when you just want to get to higher ground. In no way, does this interrupt the game quality.
As a long time fan, I expect A LOT from this game. Remember: A years worth of HAS to be worth something.
This game does not fail my expectations. Some levels are redesigned, while others are new zones created out of the creative minds of the devs. Each level had something different to show case, but nevertheless, I enjoyed the attention to detail and quality applied by the developers.
In the end, I can sincerely say that I WOULD RECOMMEND this game to anyone. Besides the technical issues behind this game, it is difficult NOT to enjoy Sonic Mania. Sonic Mania is a masterpiece by itself, and also a rebirth of the franchise (after much of its recent turmoil). Plenty of love and care went into the production of this game, and as a long time fan, I can say I am proud of Whitehead, Headcannon, and Pagoda West. They really went all out in creating this game, and they really exceeded the quality (in my opinion) of ANY game in the entire franchise. I am glad I purchased this game.
P.S.: I know I have not unlocked everything, but could you include a "Hardcore Mode," to give the option for long time fans to increase the difficulty of the game? I honestly think this game is somewhat easy, and I'd sure enjoy a bigger challenge.

A 'Hollywood hacking' simulator from 2001, and Introversion Software's first game. Simple systems with interlocking complexity and great music combine to make a tense cyberpunk experience. Hack systems, complete contract jobs, earn bucks to upgrade your system, repeat. The story jobs are technically optional, which lets you do other jobs in between - and earn more money, which is nice - but you'll run out of other things to do eventually.
Unlike some of the more recent games it inspired, Uplink's totally 1337 haxoring is mainly GUI-based, which means clicking all the things, although knowing how to use a command prompt will help a lot. Once you know what you're doing, the initially rather steep difficulty curve levels out pretty fast, but half the fun comes from pushing yourself as far as you can without screwing up anyway.
The biggest problem with Uplink is the lack of variety. It's more fun if you play it in bite-size chunks or have an appetite for grinding, because that's what you'll be doing initially to get the gear you need. Even if you plan to rob banks, you need certain tools to do that without getting caught.
The typing field UI is also quite finicky, which is anathema to a game centered around...you know, computer hacking. It's not immediately clear that you need to tab to a field to type in it, which is necessary because merely mousing over it only activates the field for as long as your mouse is over it.
Uplink's game world is also relatively small in scope for what's supposed to be a corporate subnetwork of the Internet, but hey, it's a mild dystopia. And also an indie game from 2001. These guys were literally pressing disks in their house to start; that's worthy of respect, if nothing else.
Recommended if you're a GIANT NERD like me.

If you think that StarCraft is some sort of chess, but APM and multitasking aren't your strong side…
If you like jukes, predictions, positioning and teamplay in League of Legends, but don't have enough micro to play on ADC…
If you mastered risk management in XCOM and get bored…
… you'll fall in love with this game.
But there are some peculiarities.
First of all, it's turn based game with 20 seconds limit per turn. Most new players (including me a few months ago) struggle with it. Later you'll accommodate, but still sometimes you'll find yourself getting out of time. This limits your ability to calculate all possibilities and make optimal move coordinated with teammates. IIRC this was deliberate design decision based on play tests. So this game requires a little bit different skill from xcom — ability to make the best decision in limited time. In xcom you playing against rng and AI patterns, and here — against time and enemy mind.
Secondly, because of the time limit, you can't sit and read skill description during PvP match. So to play PvP you need to learn how every freelancer works (because you'll newer know against whom you'll be playing). That's why you forced to play a few games against bots before you allowed to play PvP. Of course, it isn't enough to fully understand what's going in a game. Yet sometimes even your opponents will explain your mistakes and how to avoid them (btw many thanks to people that do that).
So I'd say that it's an awesome game with a pretty bad learning curve. But it is definitely worth it.
PS My actual playtime should be probably around 300 hours, but I prefer to use glyph launcher to not know it. =)

Atlas Reactor is a simultaneous action selection game where your team tries to kill the enemy team 5 times before they do the same to you. In Atlas Reactor, each round is played over 4 phases. The 4 phases are Prep, Dash, Blast and Move. In the Prep phase, you can set traps and use buffs. In the Dash phase, you may move to avoid attacks that may occur in the Blast phase. In the Blast phase, you attack. In the Move phase, you do a movement that you set earlier. If there is a conflict, supposedly the faster one gets there first and blocks the other.
Januarly 2017: You can rotate among 7 different heroes in Free Mode, though you may demo all heroes in Practice mode. This is basically Pay To Win as you lock out essential core mechanics behind a massive paywall. Lockwood costs 10,000 Flux to buy. Other heroes such as Helio costs 20,000 Flux, Oz and Pup costs 35,000 Flux, Su Ren costs 50,000 Flux and Bryn costs a whopping 75,000 Flux.
Conclusion, I believe this game tried to combine XCOM's tactical success with a MOBA. However, the design just isn't good. It reduces the tactical choices that XCOM and MOBAs bring to the table. So, no.

1. 25 different Characters to Use
Small but very interesting lineup like Rampart and Pup.
1. How do you differentiate who gets the same square?
There is no explaination in the tutorial.
2. Massive Paywall
Lockwood costs 10,000 Flux, Helio costs 20,000 Flux, Oz and Pup costs 35,000 Flux, Su Ren costs 50,000 Flux and Bryn costs a whopping 75,000 Flux.
3. Why are you limited to shoot first, then move?
Why can't I move first then shoot? This form of combat is limiting choice. By locking in the phases, you've removed a lot of choice.
4. Visual Bugs
I found a bug with Bryn's Impale which caused the arc to show up in a reversed manner.
5. Pay To Win
Sadly, game mechanics are hidden behind that massive paywall

Frozen Synapse is a true tactical masterpiece, albiet one that suffers from an overuse of randomness. Frozen Synapse offers a modern take on chess (in a sense), and simple yet complex mechanics. The campaign is a well scripted, addictive and interesting experience, but what shines the most is the extremely intuitive online play. Each online match is played in steps: The planning phase, and the action phase, and with the proper player - you could play a step a day, as you can pick up said match over the course of a week, rather then log in, play, quit - lose the game, etc. Unfortunately, online is relatively dead, although you can always find the rare match to test your skill. The visuals are mediocre, but fitting for the type of game it is. The OST is absolutely fantastic, and is well worth the purchase! Frozen Synapse is well worth your time and money, especially for fans of tactical turn based isometric games.

I've been a huge Halo fan since the very first Combat Evolved on Xbox. This was mainly due to the epic story line. The game in itself, the back story, the history of your main character. Just the whole thing. I even guessed that the humans were or interacted with the forerunners in 2003 (not hard since 343 recognized our species). I've even read 2 of their many  books. I've owned and played every Halo game even the somewhat lame ones (Halo ODST & Halo Wars, not bad games just nothing compared to the rest). I was very happy to find Halo Spartan Assault on Steam.
If you're a fan like me then this game is a must have and since it's only $4.99 there's no real reason not to get it. I traded a game for it, a game I earned for free so even if you don't have money this is still obtainable.
I like top down shooters and this one runs incredibly smooth. The story takes place in between Halo 3 and 4 and focuses on the newer batch of Spartan II's. The game is a challenge if you try to obtain gold for every level and there are over 30 levels.
You play one of 2 Spartans back and forth as you complete missions. You only control your character but I think that's part of the fun (more like Halo 1-4 except not FPS). Board any vehicle and take your pick from nearly all of the UNST and Covenant weapons we've come to know in the previous games.
This isn't a long game and the replay value is moderate if you're a fan, but its a great arcade style of game play. Not complex and easy to learn.
If you're not a fan but you're looking to spend $5 on a decent game this is a good choice and it has trading cards that are selling in the Steam marketplace for a good amount at the moment compared to other cards.
If you're a fan then this game is a must have. Great visuals and more Covenant domination at the hands of the Spartan II's.
My only wish is that they made the game longer but for the price and the style of game that it is the length of the game isn't a surprise. Also even if they made the game with 100 levels I'd probably still want more... :)

OLD REVIEW. Will update in-time.
--------------------------------------------------
-Short, first time experience review (2 hours played)-
I'll be going through a few quick things I've experienced this far into the game. Both some positive and negative ones.
-------Positive-------
-On the positive side I find the game very charming to it's current surrounding environments. There's a lot of different kind of places in this huge world to explore. Making it interesting to see where and how communities will grow up along the world later on in the long run.
-I haven't progressed too much with the skill system this far. But I see that reaching different professions will take a good while and a lot of time spent on each skill. An interesting way to go about the development of your character.
-Sadly enough I haven't manage to get much further with the game to experience and learn about other positive things, and I'll tell ya why.
-------Negative-------
-Oh boy, here we got a few negative things to worry about. First off, I see that the developers wants the players to figure out pretty much.. everything through their first hour into the game. And yes I know there's a few guides to read to help ya out. But even the help of the guides can still make things seem confusing to understand. Especially when you wanna start out right away. There's no simple way to indicate what you exactly have to do to start making that.. that.. that and that. You get my drill. Once you start experimenting, you eventually start to understand how things works. Tho it's not an easy guess at first and can become a little frustrating for some.
-I found myself at the end of my first game session very frustrated and somewhat disappointed. Throughout my session I found myself constantly being attacked by invisible creatures. Both under day and night time. Most of the time I heard skeleton rumbling noises approaching and then the situation would proceed with me losing tons of health, one hit at the time. Forcing me to leave my current settlement... forever. I experienced this on the EU server and from the little I read in the discussion thread not long after the end of my game session, other people had experienced the same problem. It's a very huge issue that must be dealt with immediately! The game is practically unplayable at this time. As you can't see or attack these invisible creatures! Very disappointed to see an NPC being bugged. Perhaps? Especially at this time at the launch on Steam.
-And of course, just as I spawned in at the very beginning, I were attacked by another player. Not saying it's a complete negative issue. After all, it's a mix of MMO and PVP. Perhaps it's just me who doesn't like being attacked just as I spawn in, into a new game that I've never played before..
-------First experience conclusion-------
So far the game feels promising and it has potential to improve a lot. Tho, the major issues such as the invisible creatures must be dealt with as soon as possible. 50% of the experience is being ruined due to this problem and making it somewhat unplayable right now. Especially if you wanna settle down somewhere.
Tho, as I have looked forward to this game for some time now, I can't go too harsh on it. It's still in development and I hope the developers fix and update the game often to improve it's current.. minor issues.
-That's all I had to say, hope this little review helped!-

SLAMMED! calls back to a simpler time in my childhood watching John Cena take on Triple H for the Wrestlemania title match. Though I didn't quite understand what I was watching at the time, it was entertaining nonetheless to see two musclebound guys tell a story, enthrall an audience, and all the while duke it out in equal measures of athleticism and finesse. It wasn't until recently did I ever appreciate what went into professional wrestling - this addition of the "Choice of..." anthology only cements pro wrestling place as a form of entertainment and an art.
Well written with much thought put into the consequences of one's actions, SLAMMED! puts on a spectacle while also showing what goes on beneath the surface. Its author, Paolo Chikiamco, shows his love for the sport very clearly in the span of 4-5 hours to get from beginning to end - only to entice to you read again and see how things could play out differently. For a choose-your-own-adventure that urges its readers not to think of the "what ifs" and to not focus on the future, I certainly look forward to reading through again and exploring those what-ifs in detail.

I don't know any game like Atlas Reactor. It's a mix between the turn-based strategy of the XCom series and the mechanics of a fast-paced MOBA. The turns will be played simultaneously so there's not much time to waste. You need to think about your next actions, your positioning, your cooldowns, etc, while predicting the enemy's next moves.
Now that Season 2 is drawing near I decided to delete my first review from back when AR was still in Early Access. The reason for this is the biggest and best change they could've made: Atlas Reactor is now fully F2P. You can still buy the three different editions but it's not necessary anymore to be able to choose freely between the Lancers (You could only play the free rotation).
"Then why should I buy the packages?" Well, it's nice to support the devs of a great game, right? Additionally you can unlock all the freelancers at once, get special cosmetic items and some in-game-money.
Another thing that came with the F2P announcement is the dramatic drop of queue times. Sometimes you you'd have to wait up to 10 minutes to get in a game, because there weren't enough players. Now it's only around 30-50 secs.
As a conclusion: Probably my Atlas Reactor review is the one review I changed the most, just because it developed in so many different ways. And after all these changes it always keeps looking better and better with Season 2 as it's current max. Lancers feel balanced and just right. It's Free-to-Play. It's great. Excited to see what the path ahead holds for us.

Part of what I loved about SpaceChem, one of Zachtronics' previous puzzle games (and probably their most well-known game), is that it captrued a lot of the problem solving skills inherent in programming. TIS-100 is a programming-themed puzzle game of the same ilk, by which I mean it gives you a goal and tools and lets you figure out how you want to solve it. Will you go for least number of cycles spent, making your solution the most time/resource efficient? Or will you go for the solution that uses the fewest lines? Maybe you'd rather a more balanced solution? If you liked SpaceChem, chances are very good you'll like this.
One thing I like about TIS-100 is that instead of feeding you story in between levels, it's hidden in the manual and "corrupted" nodes for you to suss out as you go along. Assasins Creed is an action-adventure game that was released in 2014, and is the follow up to Black Flag. People are known to slate the game for its similiarities with Black Flag, but I honestly believe that the combat and naval mechanics in Black Flag were too good to throw away. I did indeed play Black Flag and loved it, and despite the mechanics being very similar to Rogue I still loved it to bits and there was no part in the game where it felt boring.
The graphics for Assassins Creed Rogue are of an A rated standard, but there are a few issues that I came across. As with Black Flag 2560x1080 was not supported despite being in the options, so I had to install a quick fix to begin playing the game, but apart from that I experienced no crashes whatsoever whilst playing this game. The only graphical issue that I had with this game was the lack of anti-aliasing that this game had. In Black Flag you had a selection of anti-aliasing options to choose from to smoothen out those jagged edges, but you only have the option to enable FXAA, which leaves rather noticeable jagged edges on objects such as rope and fences, but this isn't too noticeable on characters and will not effect your experience to a high degree. The game runs smoothly however and no stutters or lag spikes were detected.
Now time to talk about the good 'n' juicy bits of the game. New combat mechanics were implemented such as new ship upgrades and customization options which weren't featured in Black Flag. You can have a nostalgic trip by purchasing some of the iconic ship customizations that were available in Black Flag, but other than that all of the customization options are unique, and they haven't just dumped old content into this lovely game. New naval mechanics have been added such as the ability to leave oil trails in the ocean and set fire to them to roast your enemies (Water+Oil=Fire?) and the pucker cannon can now be freely aimed, allowing you to take out poor old icebergs and take out drunken pirates who try to oppose you.
Enemy ships can now ram into you, and begin to board your boat, so you get a taste of your own medicine in a sense, as you will be forced to defend yourself.
You are also not able to go to the harbour master and reset your wanted rating like you were able to in Black Flag, so the only way to escape those blasted pirate hunters is by hit and running.
Some new weapons have been added to the game such as the shrapnel, beszerk and sleep grenades, which gives you a larger variety of ways to take out your enemies.
For those players out there who are into helping out lil' NPCs then you can now renovate buildings all around the world to let pirates have fun and commit debauchery.
The world itself is of huge scale so theres plenty of ocean for you to trek around in whilst singing shanties, but I felt that the world was rather monotonous, and besides the naval combat there wasn't really much purpose landing the anchor and exploring the world, unless you were interested in crafting. The world is beautifully designed, but the lack of interactiveness around the world and side quests meant that the only compelling part of the game was the story.
The story completely made this game for me, as it allows you to have a perspective from the Templars side, and their understanding on the world. The story was exhilarating to play through and the compelling protagonist made the game a delightful experience to play through. The Abstergo plot was also interesting and gives you a better insight on the Assassins Creed lore.
This is the second game in the AC series that I have played through and I will most certainly be playing through the next game in the series. Ubisoft definitely know how to produce a game and I respect them for putting time and effort into their games and producing content that their fans want to see, which is rare for game developers to do these days.

Warframe, or Grindframe, or Bugframe, or ... well, you can say many things about this game.
It is to this day one of the best-updated games out there. No matter if you return after a long time, or constantly play it, they still manage you show you something new.
I don't want to pretend like you can achieve everything in a short time. It takes hundreds of hours to even get close to end-game status.
Still, the path is the game, not the goal. Warframe is what you make of it. For some it might be a challenge to see how far they can go on an endless mission, others might want to complete a raid as fast as possible and some might just want to have fun with their friends.
Warframe has one of the most helpful communities you will ever find on the internet, but once in a while you meet the elitist idiot that tries to tell you how to play, my advice, just ignore him unless everyone agrees with him.
The new player experience is..rough to say the least. The mechanics are plenty and you will not learn them by just playing the game. I recommend looking for a veteran in one of the chat channels and ask them if you do not get what the game wants you to do next.
If you ever want to explore the hardest content in the game, there are groups out there that will teach you all you need to know. There is much to learn and even you read the wiki to get bits, the whole picture is gigantic. If you do not how to approach something like raids, just google were to learn it.
One last point: Free-to-play or Pay2Win. I will not pretend like you can easily play this game without spending anything. A decent part of increasing the power of your stuff is highly time-gated or extremely hard to get. But it is not impossible to just invest like ten bucks and be happy for a few months. The prices are mostly fair and if you talk to a veteran, they can tell you how to spend your money responsibly. Trading for premium currency is a thing in Warframe, so if you are invested into playing the game without spending anything, it is possible and usually done so by long-time players.

Slammed! is an interactive story based in the world of professional wrestling. You don't need to know or understand professional wrestling, although some terms are crucial to understand (ie, the concept of kayfabe) and a quick google search every now and then will help as you go along. At its core though, this is a story about your journey and the personalities that you interactive with - the wrestling is the backdrop for the most part.
The story's pacing is excellent, and the blurring of the line between real and kayfabe (which is broadly the same concept as the "fourth wall" in acting) is really well done. The quality of the writing, purely from the point of view of the storytelling, is also excellent. For me, the best example of this is the section that features the "promotional video" for the grand finale, where the writing got me genuinely pumped up for the big climax.
There is a reasonable amount of replayability - there are enough branching story arcs for you to play several times and not get bored of it. The choices feel meaningful, and there are several possible finales and many different journeys you can take on the way to them.
Highly recommended.

BlazeRush is one of the games you get in a bundle, activate the key, idle the cards and leave it in your library to collect dust, but trust me this game needs to played by everyone who like arcadey top down racing games.
BlazeRush is about racers who like racing (great story right ?) and there's a corporation that tries to stop them racing by taking over every planet they race in.
Of course you are not in it for the story and for the gameplay and let me tell you it's quite a treat.
There are  main events and I'll go through each one. The regular races where you need to finish first and try not to get destroyed by the enemy drivers, king of the hill where you try to stay in the lead for 50 seconds and a deathmatch where there's a steam roller behind you and you try to be the final person alive, a time trial mode where you need to finish a lap in a certain amount of time and there's a boss battle in the final mission where you need to use the weapons you used in the game to destroy the "Boss".
Each of these events are very chaotic and they are incredibly difficult so don't expect to breeze through all the events. The enemy AI is violent and every chance they get they will take you out and trust me you need to play dirty to win.
The soundtrack is really great as well and is awesome to listen to when you are playing this game.
The graphics are alright for the most part, and I love the cell shaded look for the tracks.
The track designs range from mediocre to pretty good. Each track has certain points where you can jump out of the track if you use boosters, but those parts are marked on the map, but it's still sometimes frustrating.
Now for the bad things for the game:
The one thing I hated was the fact that when you die you are set back so far back that there is almost no point in competing and the only solution is to restart.
The controls if you are using a keyboard takes a lot of time getting used to and I highly HIGHLY recommend using a controller.
The difficulty comes off as really difficult even in the early stages and not to mention the final act in the volcano planet has a massive difficulty spike and the final boss is quite tough, so be prepared for a challenge.
The camera is atrocious, it only follows the leading car at all times so if you are too far behind and too far ahead you will have to use the map to navigate the entire map.
Overall BlazeRush is a really fun game and it's pretty difficult as well, while I don't think it's worth the full price, it's worth it if it's in a bundle or on a discount.
Final Rating:
7/10 - Worth checking out

BlazeRush is an arcade style race-battle game designed to keep everyone in the race as much as possible.  The balance is just right to reward skill but to also allow a little luck to pop in now and then.  The game supports both single-player and mutli-player.  And it does not short change the single-player mode as it contains many maps/levels and includes a final boss battle.
The controls are slick and the motion could be described as having exaggerated physics.  Note that some people in the reviews here have complained about the controls as the car moves in the direction you point your controller which is not standard in overhead race games.  It took me a few races to get used to it and then it felt quite natural.  Another popular complaint from reviewers is that when your car falls too far behind or goes off the track, the game advances your car to the end of the pack.  Some do not like this "catch up" feature but I find this feature keeps the race exciting.
There are three race modes -- normal, leader of the pack, and out run the grinder.  Leader of the pack requires a racer to be in the front for a total of 50 seconds.  Out running the grinder is my favorite as it involves a giant grinding machine chasing the racers.  This mode will keep you on the edge of your seat as an unstoppable monster nips at your bumper.  All three race modes have random power-ups that fall onto the track such as weapons and speed boosts.  The speeds boosts though only fall to the car not in first place thus once again causing exciting lead changes in this game.
Get this game if you enjoy the fun of back-and-forth battle-oriented races.  It's a little gem!

Aside from a few minor flaws, this is the best Sonic game I have played in a long time and if you grew up playing Sonic on Sega Genesis you will enjoy it.

SO. It's unfortunate that Sega was rather dishonest about the reason for the PC delay -- specifically to add a rather questionable form of DRM that they didn't even get the implementation right on. They used Denuvo, which is a rather overkill DRM program that sometimes gets flagged as a false positive by your antivirus (because the multiple re-encryption the program uses is something that malware developers like to use to avoid detection). While they were committed to fixing the most egregious issue with the DRM -- that it required a continuous internet connection to play the game on launch -- within a day or so, it's still frustrating that the game's launch was tainted by rank dishonesty and questionable administrative decisions like this. Note that Denuvo requires the publisher to send the game executable to them to build the DRM-encrypted version; the Steam version was likely done at the same time as the other versions, with the additional lead-time likely used primarily to have the Denuvo version coded up. I haven't had any issues with offline play since the patch was put up, but between the bad communication and such a strict form of DRM, I couldn't let the issue go, even if my review is positive overall.
Game itself is good, though. Levels have familiar designs but are greatly expanded to the point where most of them are 3-4 times (or more!) larger than their original sources, built with mechanics found from throughout the stage. Production values on sprite art, animation, and music are all, frankly, impeccable (the synth horns in the music would normally feel cheap, but here they work especially well in the context of mid/late-90s CD game audio). The bosses are somewhat unpleasant though, several of which are overcomplicated affairs, some of which have next to no connection to the stages that they're part of (the Metal Sonic boss is the most egregious). Even so, the joys deeply outweigh the frustrations. Worth a look.

This game is essentially Black Flag 2.0. If you liked Black Flag like I did and this is at least 15% off, I highly recommend it. The engine is the same, and a lot (actually all except 1 that I can think of) of the mechanics were kept. As such, Rogue doesn't bring anything new gameplay wise (except the grenades and the air rifle, which are pretty neat). However, it's still a good game that wraps up the North American chapter of the series nicely.
Pros : Naval combat was kept from AC4, with the addition of a ram dash.
Protagonist is more interesting (at least IMO) than previous AC heroes.
Story-wise, there are nice hints to other AC titles, like AC4, and a clever easter egg to the beginning of AC Liberation.
Combat feels fluid, controls are well optimized.
Sword and dagger combo replace the ol' sword from past AC titles, bringing a breath of fresh air to combat.
New feature - Assassins' HQ, which are a nice addition to the franchise
New feature - Stalkers, who use assassin tactics that can give you the ol' one-two if you're not paying attention.
Cons : Older target hardware is evident - Rogue doesn't look bad at all, but the animations are somewhat clunky.
Story feels a bit rushed particularly towards the end.
Dialogue writing is completely telegraphed and breaks away from Edward Kenway's pirate swagger in AC4.
The game doesn't really give you an incentive to explore the world - most of the story missions are in the same few places, so you can fast travel through most of the story.
TLDR ; This game is halfway between a new game and a Black Flag DLC. Buy it if you have the money and / or if you liked Black Flag.

I wanted to refund this game so bad at first, but I realised because I was playing a character I knew wasn't me was central to the experience of pro-wrestling. I'm not an active fan but this made me want to return to my childhood days and enjoy it all.
This game was made by a master of terminology and theory of the genre. I played a heel through almost the whole game and just twice I broke kayfabe, once to sign a fan an autograph [if they said I was a jerk about it haha, I was nice to them.] and also to a woman who had some problem with family or something.
This is a great story and I only played once. It certainly levels with the standard highest bar I place for CoG, which is Choice of Robots [my fave story wise and sheer "yes you can do that, and it will have a real effect."]. I might not like pro wrestling as much as Robots, I love this game for the same reasons.
I can't quite figure out some stats, maybe they effect wording or story path with no choice involved [except the choices that gave you those stats.] My story path definitely satisfied even if there is only one main path. I felt the sting of every revelation and the confusion of "Is this kayfabe? Or do I have to kick some♥♥♥♥♥" I got so into it that in game I started to accidently handicap myself thinking I'd end up having to seriously fight bloody.
If you don't know wrestling terms, the game makes them sorta contextual, but if there isn't an in game dictionary of terms, there is a good free online one.
Good weaving in and out of the timeline to help have you choose things and establish in-game reality. Since at times it'll weave forward or back through time There aren't many, or any, awkward sudden choices to make.
Finally, now and then you get to read a news type blog post about you and what's happening in your corner of wrestling.
Just a lot of fun. Damn good story, you don't just choose how it goes, but like wrestling.... you tune it like a song also

Just the concept of kayfabe as a stat and a mechanic is amazing, and it works great here. The writing is solid all around, and it's worth noting that it attempts to be accessible to non-wresting aficionados too by providing little explanations of wrestling lingo at times, though it's probably not quite enough for the entirely uninitiated. Keep your search engine of choice at the ready if that is the case for you, and you'll be a-okay.
It branches plenty, about as much as you'd expect from a
game. If I was left wanting more, it is more a testament to the quality of the game (and my fascination with the sport, to be perfectly fair) than a judgement on how much content there is.
Very much recommended; it's the wrestling adventure most savvy fans dream of, and unique in what it does to the genre. I wish "traditional" wrestling games were more like this.

Uplink is a great and fun game about the universe and life of a computer hacker. Despite being more than 10 years old, the game is as much fun as when it was lauched, a great advantage of the indie games. The game premise is that you are an agent of the organization Uplink, and as such, you are available for big companies, jealous neighbor, political enemies, mafia and all sort of questionable social elements for tasks that involve stealing of destruction of data from a rival company, framing innocent people, forging fake curriculum, cleaning criminal records, and much worse acts. You choose what missions will you undertake of not. You succeed of fail by your own competence, you live with your own conscience and the choices you made. You may make money by stealing it from someone else at a bank, or by missions, or by sock market. Ultimately, you will have to choose between protecting the internet from a terrible anti-tech group virus, or help destroy the internet for once and all.
