Chivalry is a pretty great game. At least it WAS a great game, but now it's kinda gone downhill. Ever since players chose to flail their bodies around in a blind attacking flurry, the game has gotten a lot less enjoyable. And it isn't so much the gameplay itself, it's just the abilites some people in- game can have that are kind of cheese. For instance, vanguards. These guys are everywhere. And it's almost annoying the amount of times everyone dies to one. Their range is extravagant, as well as their damage output. sure, they don't move very quickly, but enough to screw anyone over if they need to escape, or if they have low health. Other things that can be pestering is the formentioned 'torso-flail'. People who do this usually make a duel very monotonous. The physics and real- time combat is thrown out the window, as well as parrying and blocking.The way this works is that one player moves their upper body around in a way to confuse the opposer. This eventually leads to the flailing player to throw random strikes that are completely unavoidable when it comes to dodging, blocking, parrying, and counterattacking. This is due to the unknown direction of each attack, and the power of it. High- tier players usually do this, and it can be horrid against new gamers.
All in all, I reccomend this game if you wish to play a good hand- to- hand medieval game. Or, if you're still waiting for Mordhau.

Some of the most entertainment I've ever had for £5. The learning curve does have a little bit of a sharp turn on node 6, but it does continue to build on what you've learned before that and introduce more complexity as the game continues. The language is wonderfully simple, containing only the most basic of required assembly instructions. The limited program space in each processor contributes significantly to the difficulty of more complex programs, requiring the use of multiple processors to implement an algorithm and thus encouraging the use or parallel processing for increased speed. The display of statistics relative to other players after each successful run really inspired me to revisit completed nodes to improve efficiency, either of processor cycles or total instructions - definitely encouraging the traditional hacking mindset! Definitely recommend to anyone who likes logic puzzles, and especially to programmers or aspiring programmers.

Micron is a fun puzzle game consisting of 51 levels (plus 12 bonus); the objective in each level is to guide a stream of balls towards the exit by placing some special obstacle tiles that change the stream’s direction: there are vertical/horizontal blockers, diagonal ones and teleporting gates (that are unlocked during mid-game levels).
The first half of the game is fairly easy, the puzzles are not very complicated and have nice solving ideas that sometimes can seem to be repeating a bit too much, but this wasn't an issue for me. However, the last few levels are pretty difficult and the bonus levels are extremely challenging to the point of frustration because you might find yourself trying to come up with a solution for hours and you simply can’t find any. For those that want to obtain all the achievements in this game, this might be a bit annoying unless they resort to consulting a guide.
Also be warned that some of these puzzles are timed; you need to coordinate to the second the timing of placing the special blockers on the board. This again requires a lot of trial and error.
I’ve also tried a few levels from the workshop and they’re nice and enjoyable; I appreciated that the game automatically downloads the workshop items that I’ve subscribed to, without needing a restart.
Very enjoyable game for a good price!

Micron is a decent game, short and reasonable. I would consider it purely average, providing good gameplay with fair polish, but treading familiar ground.
I was expecting some rhythm elements, but they really don't exist. Each level has sounds associated with bullet reflections, which helps to generate the music. Nothing is really based on moving to the beat, and some puzzles require actions between the beats. Most levels don't require speed, but a few require timed actions to catch bullets at the right time. The difficulty curve varied widely due to these timing-based levels, forcing several restarts to complete. Still, the game is quite easy.
The music is fair, but is not a real gameplay element. Most levels are short and can only be solved in a certain way, so replayability only comes from Workshop levels. Puzzles were interesting but not hugely satisfying. Later levels became more frustrating, as one mistake meant a full restart. Once levels feature over 10 objects, I was wanting an Undo button instead of a full restart. Granted, it didn't take long, but the short game length could mean that 20% of your time is spent restarting and rebuilding levels.
Micron didn't do anything bad, but didn't inspire me much. It's a decent game at a fair price, a nice way to spend a few hours but not really compelling you to challenge your mind. I would recommend a sale above 50%, below $2.50 USD is a good time-value. If you are looking for rhythm gameplay, keep looking. But puzzle fans should find some entertainment here for a couple hours.

Excercise your critical thinking skills in this fun puzzle game.   With its simplistic design and musical sound effects I found it quite enjoyable and would highly recommend it.  The concept is simple.  Balls are shot from an opening and you must place angles and or portals to get it to open doors and get them to the end.  The difficulty is you must put them in the proper spot at the proper time to achieve your goal.
It is a great game for all ages however those under ten may need help to finish it unless they are unusually patient.  A great game to play with your children though.  Get their little problem solving wheels turning!  The game has some difficult levels but not overly so in my opinion.  I did however cheat on one of the bonus levels and look for the answer elsewhere.
There are a number of free levels for download in the steam workshop as well.  Just subscribe to them and they will be downloaded the next time you start the game.
I did not find any bugs and was not able to complete any level using less than the full complement of pieces provided.   Note: This is edited because I could not find the level editor. I did find the level editor it is in your steam files.
In my opinon it would be worth the full price of $4.99 or even better to purchase it on sale!  However I prefer to let the gamer decide how much a game is worth as it is a subjective matter.  Hope this review helped.

I bought the All Freelancers Pack on Steam but play and still play on Glyph since why would I need to go from steam to Glyph when I can go just through Glyph. So the review.
Played the game since the early Alpha. I've seen this game change from F2P to P2P to P2P + Free Mode and now finally to Fully F2P. And I will say this to everyone who think this game is cancer, p2w, lame, or whatever, you can now stop reading this review because you won't like it because I'll say the real aspects of the game not some superficial nonsense you guys say everywhere.
So the gameplay is great. Trion Worlds made a superb effort in making the game fun and reachable for everyone. Like every game it has minor visual bugs like flying dead bodies once or twice glitching themselves out of existence but nothing gamebraking.
F2P
The game is now fully free to play. Which means you can get any Freelancer just by playing and gaining in-game currency(Flux). So I tested it out on my f2p account how hard it is to grind for flux if you are just a fresh new account. It took me less than a day to get 10k flux.... 10k. It was faster than I've expected. Freelancers cost from 10k to 50k flux. So most players will be able to get atleast a few of their favorite freelancers quite fast other onces will take some more time. Overall the f2p model of the game is top notch. For e.g.: Heroes of the Storm to get a hero takes(without taking in account lvl rewards) takes alot longer than in Atlas.
Also there isn't at all any p2w mechanics in the game. Sure there are microtransactions which also give cosmetics nothing more.(It's used only to support the game for those who want some skins faster) Also skins can be gotten from lootmatrices from leveling up. So pretty much currently a great f2p than some other games out there.
Community
Sometimes happens toxic players if you do something stupid. Sure noone is safe from that. But overall the Atlas community is incredibly friendly and helpfull(especially when giving their referral codes).
Gameplay
A completely different way of playing a MOBA. If you played XCOM then you wil know how it is played +/-.

Death Ray Manta is an intense twin-stick shooter game in the style of Robotron:2084 released by Williams in 1982. It follows the tradition of other classic games in the genre by giving it a psychedelic inspired makeover and casting a peculiar animal in the central role - in this case a manta ray with the ability to fire deadly laser beams from its head. The game is extremely colourful and eye-popping visually and has an electro sound track. Rapid reflexes are required to avoid an instant wipeout, and levels are cleared in just a few moments. In fact, you may not play the game for very long as there's only one life and when you hit something, you have to start from the very beginning again.

Bought this game as it seemed to be the only half-decent racing game for SteamOS, plus it had baked in VR support... I'm so impressed!
The VR support is superb, right from the get-go, it's dynamic and immersive. A few times I found myself flying through an over-track sign, but I suspect I was probably too close to the head tracking unit - you want to be sat back about 6ft with this for best effect! (Controller recommended therefore!) Having the ability to chose where you look on the track is an amazing benefit (and experience!), as when playing in non-VR, you sometimes find your FOV a bit limiting when you're leading the pack. Being able to sit forward a bit or look around other cars for the best view of your own car and/or the track is just bonkers. Not to mention the machine gun fire and rockets flying around :D
Even in non-VR on a SteamOS (Read: Ubuntu with Steam on it) machine it runs flawlessly - A lowly Intel Pentium G620 and an AMD R7 250 (1GB) is more than sufficient to play this at decent frame rates at 1080p - which looks beautiful on my TV!

I'll start by saying I recommend this game
the bugs/flaws.
For a little while, I was playing this with the gf probably 2-4 hours a day, often more than that on weekends. We'd probably crash midgame every other day or so. Fortunately, the workday cycle is a relatively frequent autosave, so we never lost a ton, but it's obviously still annoying.
Crashes were also highly likely if we left the game paused by inactive for an extended amount of time (eg. finish the workday, leave it on the summary screen while making dinner).
We would also randomly get varying amounts of slowdown. Most of the time, it wasn't unplayably bad, and lasted for maybe two minutes at a time. The last level was an exception. There, we got probably 80% slowdown, and it was persistent. That was awful. Trying to fulfil a in-level goal hinted during the stage intro made it worse. We completed the level, and couldn't bring ourselves to go back and try for that side goal again.
There are achievement pins. For some mind numbing reason, only the P1 actions get counted. In my play, I was generally focused on building the factory and setting up automation, and my gf was exploring/hunting/etc. I happened to be P1, so that meant pretty much any "kill X blahblahmonsters" pins saw nearly zero progress, even after killing dozens of them. We're both kind of anal, so we were fully exploring every single map. Knowing that there were kill based achievements, we were making a point of killing pretty much all monsters/nest before completing any level. Also (this one might be poor design rather than a bug), for the kill X nests achievements, only some nests count. The game never tells you this, we found it only through trial and error.
There were many questionable design choices. You get "gum" as consumable short term boost items. We got them by the truckload, and honestly didn't use them much. That said, there are maybe half a dozen types, and three or four strengths (duration) for each type. Rather than have a list of these with a quantity shown, each one got treated as an individual item. The inventory screen for these was not sorted (I assume they were just in the order we got them, which is presumably random). So trying to find any specific type of gum to use often involved scrolling through page after page of random other gums.
Another example: You can place blank soup machines, which will lock to the first ingredients you add. Once you've created a pairing for the first time (let's say ingredient A + ingredient B = Soup AB), you gain the option to place a soup machine which is preprogrammed for Soup AB. These are a bit cheaper than blank machines, and since a Soup AB machine only accepts those ingredients, there's no possibility of accidentally placing ingredient C in the machine and locking in a recipe you hadn't intended. Well, there are probably 15-20 ingredients, and again, EACH preprogrammed soup machine is shown in a single massive list (which is maybe kind of organized, but I didn't bother trying to figure out how). This means there are again several pages of machines to scroll through. I felt it wasn't worth the 15%  or so cost reduction, and just about always used blanks.
All that said, none of these make the game unplayable (except that last level), and we legitimately had fun with the mechanics. I often enjoy "bulid the machine" games (Leap Day, Factorio, SpaceChem, etc), and my gf liked the exploration component (also, terraforming each world until nearly everywhere had oxygen).
Most levels were pretty easy, so if you're a challenge seeker, this game might not be fantastic for you. A lot of out fun came from the sandboxy element, as my playtime probably suggests. We could probably rush to a win in 15 min or so on most levels (which I occasionally did by accident). We were often instead putting in a luxurious 45-60 min each. I enjoyed finding a good recipe on a given level, then working to build out a large sustainable production line for that particular soup.
If your playstyle is to just crush the goal as quickly as possible, and move on to the next fight, I'm not entirely confident this game is long enough to warrant your attention. As a playground where you can kind of mosey along and take things at your own pace though, it's worked out pretty well for us.

Echo Tokyo is the name of a city located high in the sky, at and around the tops of skyscrapers and various towers, and presumably above the site of "old" Tokyo. Below a certain height, radioactive fog blankets the Earth, a result of wars that devastated the world and made the surface uninhabitable. As far as its citizens can tell, Echo Tokyo might be the last remaining gathering of humanity. Regrettably, government and justice have become functions of money in a manner typical of cyberpunk.
The game consists of two completely separate short stories. It is my understanding that it initially only contained the Shizume route. And that Keiji's route was added at a later time, not even as a "free DLC" but as an integral patch to the main game, in an effort to expand the content available. A justifiable notion, considering that the whole thing can still be read in under an hour easily. This is also probably why Keiji's route is of noticeably lower quality than Shizume's in just about every aspect.
The writing is average at best. It's correct, but uninspired. It tries to hide this lacking of substance behind flowery flourishes that had me raise an eyebrow more than once
. It tries to be
at times but doesn't do a good job of it. I appreciated and enjoyed the darker themes present in this title, where the majority of VNs tend to be more "sunshine and rainbows". But then, the protagonists' insistence on not killing becomes even more absurd, doubly so if you consider their backgrounds. There are more mundane issues with the writing, too - Shizume's name is sometimes spelled Shizumi for no reason, and Keiji's route has a lot of typos.
The art starts off decent, pretty good even (in the Shizume route, at least) but it's calibre quickly worsens, to the point where I had a hard time acknowledging it as a commercial product. It was almost as if the first few shots were commissioned to an outside, better artist. Or there was a single artist who suddenly understood how much time would be needed to fully illustrate the whole story at that initial level and ended up winging it for the sake of budget and/or time. At least in Shizume's route all of the pictures are of the correct resolution, in the sense that they use up the whole available screen space. In Keiji's route the images are sometimes squares of various sizes, leaving black space around the edges and indicating a scarcity of graphical assets. In one case, such a square is actually a part of the previous image cut out and zoomed in, pixels and all...
I imagine the creators were aware of the inadequacy of the visual side of things, and thought they can balance that out with above-average audio. This would explain why "full professional voice acting for every line" was considered important enough to go in the game's intro blurb. And while the music is indeed good, I can't say the same for the voice acting.
Echo Tokyo: Intro is supposed to be the first part of a series, but it's a bit of a false-start; let's hope the overall quality improves in subsequent installments. The asking price of 3 EUR is not too terrible at first glance. But then, if you compare that to the likes of Written in the Sky, which is free, only marginally shorter and with better art... that's where the picture turns sour.

It's too bad this game has no community. It's one of the most interesting real-time/turn-based hybrid strategy games I've ever seen. It's still plenty good for matches with friends. The single player campaign is super hard, so don't get it just for that.
The ability to have multiple matches going, visiting them whenever time permits, is extremely convenient.
The way you plan your moves, simultaneously, while trying to predict your opponents movements, is just so pure and tactical. You basically strive to maintain an advantage any time your soldiers engage the enemy. Whether its stance, steadiness, cover or aim, you try to give your soldier the best; he pulls the trigger and does the rest. For example, you might crouch while checking a corner or face a certain way while passing through a doorway (so that your soldier is more ready to fire accurately at an enemy, that might not be as ready or steady, in that moment).
It's like rainbow six if it were a turn based strategy game.

Keiji's story is almost completely out of his control from the beginning, and is a bit more compelling and horrifying.
This VN retails for about $3 and I wouldn't really recommend it for that price, not just because of the length, but because it doesn't tell a full story. Note: My actual playtime is far less than what my displayed playtime is. I accidentally left the game running for two days, so my real playtime is probably around 3-4 hours.
Micron is a puzzle game where the goal is to guide streams of bullets towards the exit by placing pieces that the bullets can bounce off of. It's a very simple concept that is immediately understandable, but it turns out that some very interesting puzzles can be created with it.
A number of obstacles present in the levels create the challenge of the game. Present in every level is a barrier that requires four bullets shots to destroy. These do not make much of a difference in the early levels, but create much of the challenge in the later levels where you are forced to cut off the source of your bullets in order to complete the level.
Gates which are initially closed also appear, and they must be opened by a bullet hitting the correspondingly colored switch. In levels with multiple switches of the same color, bullets must hit the similarly colored switches at the same time in order for the gate to open. Finally, there are barriers which only bullets of the same color can pass through.
Later on in the game, portals which the bullets can travel through are introduced. These are a nice addition that add further complexity to the game, but they also make you wonder whether there is anything else that could be added to the game, as they are the only pieces you can place that aren't ones that the bullets bounce off of. Why not have a "vortex" piece that always makes a bullet turn left or right? How about a "splitter" piece that duplicates a bullet? There is a lot of potential for the concept of this game, and I feel that it is not always realized fully.
The game is also rather short, with only 51 main levels and 12 bonus levels. Most of these are easy and can be solved within a few minutes, although a select few of the later levels are quite difficult. Steam Workshop support helps alleviate this a bit, but currently there are not many user levels available.
Despite this, for $4.99 ($1.49 in the current holiday sale), the game is cheap enough to warrant a purchase for any puzzle game fan interested. The game seems to take a "quality over quantity" approach, and for what the game is, that's perfectly fair.

I've been playing hardcore strategy games since I picked up a copy of Russian Campaign in 1978.  The same year I began playing roleplaying games at summer camp by tearing up little pieces of paper, writing numbers on them, and pulling them out of cups to generate random numbers.  Two years later I was playing Ultima I.  Since that time, I have spent 80% of my personal free time playing games.
I had thought I was simply having fun.  But I am now convinced that all of that time was an extensive training program to prepare me for this game.  I have been richly rewarded.
Play this game.  Get all the DLC (maybe not music and such).  Play only on Ironman.  Understand that you will make many catastrophic, dynasty killing, history altering, vein popping mistakes.  Let it all roll off your back.  Keep learning, keep developing new strategies, and keep pushing yourself.  It's a fantastic game.
Don't play this game to 'win'.  Play it for the experience.  It's a rollar-coaster ride, not a go-cart race.

TL;DR - It's fantastic. Game of the year material. Writing is fantastic, gameplay is solid, graphics and art direction are nice.
Writing is fantastic. Some places are better than others, but I haven't come across anything particularly bad. When you think it's gonna be kinda bad, it firmly places it's tongue in it's cheek. Whether or not that's a good enough excuse for overly cliche writing, that's up to you (it is to me). It takes an Elder Scrolls route and allows you to talk to everyone you come across (minus the characters that physically can't) and even all of the animals (if you have the perk). Not every character is a shining example of the writing, but they're serviceable at least.
Combat is old school. Table top rules. Turn based, initiatives, action points. Generally not my cup of tea so this is where I lack any experience to say what sets this apart from other turn based isometric RPGs.
Graphics are fine and serve the purpose for an isometric game. Art style is nice. Characters are varied looking, the world is familiar enough and very pleasing to explore.
Exploring an get you ♥♥♥♥ed pretty hard (it did me... many...many times) but its still rewarding and fun. This is a game where the main quest isn't a ♥♥♥♥ing chore (Witcher 3 I'm looking at you) and when you get lost doing other stuff, it's because you genuinely want to and not because the main quest is so boring. The game is a bit tight lipped on what the ♥♥♥♥ you're supposed to and where to go at times, but a quick look in the journal will get you on track (unless the game just straight up doesn't plant a marker for you like it did to me... twice).
The camera can kindly ♥♥♥♥ itself. You can barely see in front you which make moving a chore. The UI gets in the way of targeting at times making moving long distances and combat a tad frustrating.
Conclusion! If you like fantasy RPGs, don't mind tabletop rules, and have a PC (requirements aren't too bad and can run on a low end machine) I absolutely recommend playing this game. It's frustrations are limited and its charms are vast.

One of my favorite games. The magic of this game is in how it doesn't have one big feature, but rather a dozen (or more) little ones that give it a depth that I've never seen before. Want to assasinate a rival? Go for it. Need to take control of a neighboring county? Just send your Chancellor over to manufacture a claim for you. Have a vassal who hates your guts? Buy his friendship by granting him a title. Is your neighbor a bit hostile? Send him a payoff...I mean 'gift' of gold and arrange a marriage between your son and his daughter to keep peace. Just be careful whom you marry, because the traits of each parent carry over to the couple's children. Taking a craven, slothful, sickly, idiotic spouse may be a bad idea--even if the pairing is politically advantagious. And, by the way, these things are all happening at once. Then your spymaster informs you that he has uncovered a plot to kill you. Worse yet, your ungrateful son is the ring leader. What to do. What to do...
This is just a fraction of what this game has to offer. Because of it's considerable width and breadth, the game does have a steep learning curve. YouTube has some great walk-throughs to help you get started. It takes a bit to get the hang of it, but once you do, this game sinks it's teeth into you and doesn't let go.

I was skeptical at first about Atlas Reactor. Then I gave it a shot when I saw someone on the Steam Community Hub was giving it away.
Atlas Reactor is basically a timed turn-based PVP arena-type game. In essence, it's an SRPG with a decision timer of 20 seconds to keep the game flowing. It gives four phases which is Prep Phrase (for prep skills), Dash Phase (Dash skills), Blast Phase (Attack skills), and Move phase. Each phase everyone's character does simultaneously, though it does show them in sequential order during Blast Phase (except for knockback, pull skills, those seem to always go last). Which makes for an interesting PVP-type game. Course, you aren't getting any action besides planning the moves for your character and seeing them in action once the decision-making segment has ended.
So far, it's a 4vs4 turn-based PVP arena. That's all it offers for right now as far as I can see.
While, it is fun, groundwork seems solid. Like another one of my friends, and I can't seem to think of any ideas that would help improve it, is that sometimes it just seems... impactless? Neither of us know how to really word it, but it feels like it's missing something that could make gameplay more impactful.
All-in-all, it's actually kept me surprisingly entertained despite how skeptical I was at first. If you're a person that needs a lot of time to plan of strategies for your moves, this game will need you to think fast within 20 seconds. If you need more time than that, you might not enjoy it too much unless you really wanna push it.
On another note, this game could use more cute girls. Or perhaps just more interesting characters. The human ones are kinda, mostly meh? But that's just my opinion.

Echo Tokyo: Intro is a fully voiced visual novel intended for older audiences. Comprised of two stories, Shizume's novel plays out similar to a choose your own adventure providing roughly 6 choices that lead to various endings. Keiji's story is a kinetic novel (linear - non-interactive novel) with one true ending.
I definitely enjoyed the voiced narration. Although the chosen actors could probably have been better, their story telling compelled me to continue through the novels. What differs from this game to most other (cheap) VN's is the fact that the story actually shows a progression in graphical assets (scenery, characters etc.), exactly like a graphical novel. Most (cheap) VN's tend to re-use a handful of backdrops to progress the story. The artwork isn't anything praiseworthy, just sufficient in getting the point across. A few environments were really well illustrated however.
I definitely would have enjoyed the game more if there were more game options for personal tweaking. The only game options provided are Fullscreen options. No text speed, font size, menu opacity or dedicated saves/loads (only qs/ql) options.
I enjoyed my playthrough of both stories (~30 min total) and feel like it could have been much worse. There aren't that many VN's on Steam anyways, so this is definitely worth a shot.

I could have sworn I had written a review for Warframe previously, but lo and behold, after playing nearly 4000 hours, I had not.  But I am not going to delve into the graphics, the gameplay, the gunplay, etc, which all has been done before (though I will vouch for those reviews that state how awesome all of those aspects are, since it is true!). Instead, I am going to tell you why I continue to play this game after over 4 and a half years.
I have played since 1 month into Open Beta, and was witness to the birth of the Glaive, Fusion Moa, and Vauban ("all hail King Booben!"). While it is hard to believe that it has been so long, it is really no wonder at all why I am still playing. The fact that I am is, in and of itself, a testament to the quality, the depth, and the continued developer involvement in this game. While not all players have always agreed with the choices that Digital Extremes has made over time with the direction that they have taken the game, one cannot deny that they have been, and continue to be, heavily and deeply committed to this game. By now, they could have easily and simply wiped the slate clean and cashed in on releasing a Warframe 2 and even Warframe 3. When one considers the changes that have been made (completely overhauling the UI several times, reworking bosses, and overhauling the entire damage and movement systems), it boggles the mind that they didn't do just that.  Rather than making their playerbase have to restart and reinvest with a new iteration of the game each time they decided to make a big change (like most developers do), they have decided instead to keep evolving this game, and bring everyone along who wishes to continue the journey.
And while it is 100% correct that you can play this game without spending a dime on it (esp. once they added the ability to trade the premium currency, Platinum, between players), this game is so good that I have willingly given several times since I began playing. And spending money in this game (contrary to other F2P games where "whales" dominate the leaderboards and take all of the good rewards) really only grants you three things: 1) the ability to buy more slots for frames and weapons so you don't have to make hard choices about which ones to keep and which ones to sell, 2) freedom from farming or grinding gear that can take a chunk of time to obtain, and 3) lookin' good! The first is obviously the biggest draw to obtaining and using platinum, but once you do get it, the third inevitably comes into play. "What? DE just released an awesome looking Deluxe skin for Nekros, my favoritist frame of all time?? Must... have!!!" While I have indulged in the second once or twice, you really want to refrain from doing so, as the few times that I had I soon after regretted (buying the Elytron Archwing, when on sale, since I was having trouble finding the component blueprints, and then DE decided to move them into the Tenno Research Lab where they could be purchased for credits... CURSES!!!).
You know the age-old interview question of "Where do you see yourself in 5 years?" If anybody had asked me back in 2013 if I would still be playing Warframe in 5 years, I would probably have said that was a silly question... games don't last that long! I mean, TF2 is an anomaly. But when one considers what Warframe actually is, and what DE has accomplished in these past 5 years, there is no question in my mind if I will still be playing 5 years from now. And this is way, way more than a hat simulator. No offense, Valve.

This game is so in-depth its insane. But it's so good. Frozen Synapse is an odd blend of turn based strategy and squad tactics. Turns don't play out like in Civ5 for example, they play out in 5 second intervals. Both you and the enemy will act out the moves you both planned whenever the end turn button is pressed.
The way the multiplayer works means games can be both casually played one round a day over the course of a week or you can become a full on fanatic of the game if you wanted. The soundtrack is also one of the best I have ever heard. Very ambient, but in a good way. It suits the setting and atmosphere of the game really really well, the setting being very cyberpunkish and is done very well.
Overall I would give it a big recommendation. I would only recommend it though to slightly more hardcore audiences, casual players might be put off a bit.

As a programmer, this game is a wonderful mind-melting experience. If you are familiar with assembly language, you will feel right at home, but the operator set is so limited that anyone could pick it up within an hour.
That limitation is also what makes this game so difficult. The puzzles would be trivial with a more complete form of assembly, but with only one register (+1 non-addressable storage slot) per node, you are forced to rethink how you store and look at the input. I've caught myself obsessing for hours over puzzles, looking for the optimal solution to a problem that would take me seconds in C++.
I would recommend this to anyone with an interest in puzzle games, regardless of their programming experience. Quick to pick up, difficult to master, and incredibly satisfying.
Long story short, if you enjoyed Black Flag, you'll enjoy this one!

Blazerush is a top down, isometric racer, very similar to games like Rock n' Roll racing. It's got fairly solid gameplay for its type, about 4 different racing modes. Definitely feels like a micro machines game, in a really good way.
Like any kart racer, the game can be chaotic, and when it doesn't go your way, it can be very frustrating. When it does go your way, you feel awesome pulling out of the explosions unscathed. The game has a good balance of this and a skillful player can get through most challenges, though sometimes it can feel as if your opponents are snatching all the powerups.
The strength of this game is the death tractor races, which periodically eliminate the racer in last over several rounds. You can have a lot of fun boosting just out of the tractor's reach, and timing your shots perfectly to put an opponent behind you for the one moment the tractor appears.
However, the other game modes were not fun for me. In one game mode, you must be the leader for 50 seconds. Seems fair, right? But for some reason, in this mode, it always seems like one AI is a lot harder than the others, and pulls ahead quickly. Then you can never reach him because your stuck behind the other ones who all seem out to stop you from winning. The only way to win this mode is to get ahead immediately and dodge all their shots.
All in all, its a fun, short, kart racing game. If you're interested, this game will deliver for you.

As I work on my backlog, it seems the more of these cheap shmups I play, the simpler they become. Opening DRM (which is a silly acronym) launches a fullscreen game with a brightly colored logo, credits, background and epilepsy warning (which is more than Hyperspace Invaders II can say). Press the Fire/Accept button and you're swifly launched into Level 1 after a short Level intro screen with no plot/story or explaination of controls. It plays like every twin stick shooter though, so move with the left anolog stick and directionally shoot with the right. Suddenly you see a crapton of neon colored enemies, enemy death effects, triangles, level borders, and rainbow bullets from your own "manta". You will probably die pretty quickly with in the first few scenes, which takes you back to the title screen. Press fire and repeat again.
That is all there is too it, but apparently, there are 32 levels. Because the game is so fast paced and visually polluted, I thought these were randomly selected, but it is always the same sequence of levels. Someplayers will enjoy the "1980s themed" appearance and retrowave/synthwave/darkwave soundtrack - think of games like Hotline Miami and Far Cry: Blood Dragon.
Unlike most shumps, score is counted purely on the amount of levels you complete and the single gem on every screen, which disappears after about five secounds when you start the level - forcing you to make the gem a "risky goal" if you want to increase your score, which will probably never exceed more than 64. The border of the arena won't kill you, unless you run into the missles lining it. Turrets on the border can also shoot projectiles that you can destroy easily. Some chasing enemies and in-arena turrets shoot the same kind of projecttiles. There are stationary triangles that will kill you upon contact, but are easily destroyed. There are objects that move on a track and can be easily destroyed. Your standard shot has a wide spread and medium range, which kills enemies and destroys objects objects (besides wall turrets and missles) VERY easily, but one hit and you loose your ENTIRE RUN - I once died on level 30 of 32 because of a simple dodging mistake. This game is both easy and hard and can possibly be finished within anywhere from 15 minutes to 15 hours depending on how many times you fail.

Echo Tokyo: Intro is a short adult game introducing players to the world of Echo Tokyo, a near-future Science Fiction setting that so far seems inspired by anime and Cyberpunk.
The game contains two short visual novels, both of which are quite dark and violent, with similar themes. There are only a handful of choices in the first story and none at all in the second.
The presentation of Echo Tokyo is generally very good. The game has a number of great landscapes and areas and a good art style, drawing heavily from science fiction anime.
There are a couple of re-used images with minor modifications in the first story (Shizume) that would have been better re-done for the second showing, and I did notice some images that didn't quite seem to fit the story. (Does any woman actually sleep in suspenders and stockings!?)
There are no sound effects in the game and only one music track, which plays throughout (albeit with mostly appropriate increases or decreases in volume in certain places). I didn't find the music annoying or anything even after almost two hours of listening to it.
Both stories are fully voiced, although the voice acting is a bit variable. The female voiceover in the first story (Shizume) was excellent -- perhaps not quite as good as Khari Wahlgreen as Elika in Prince of Persia, but close! I hope to hear more from the woman who voiced this story. The male voice acting for Keiji in the second story, however, was nowhere near as professional, sounding somewhat mumbly and with a few lines that really should have had another take.
The gameplay is minimal, even for a visual novel, with only a very small number of either-or choices in Shizume's story, and none at all in Keiji's. Just turn off your screen saver, press the auto-forward button, and watch, listen, and enjoy.
Pros:
+ Truly excellent voice acting for Shizume, let down a little by the voice acting for Keiji
+ Great setting, with interesting stories and ideas, let down a little by the quality of the writing
+ Achievements -- an easy 100% for anyone into that sort of thing
Cons:
- The writing is okay, but not great. It really could have done with a pass or two by a professional editor, not only to fix the moderate number of grammar errors, but also to give some advice on re-working some of the more awkward sentences.
- More choices would have been nice
- Auto-forward is a tiny bit slow for the speech, particularly in Shizume's story
- Too short: I want more! :)
Echo Tokyo: Intro introduces us to a very interesting science fiction anime world that I want to see more of, and has some of the best voice acting I've heard in a while. It's let down by some not-quite-so-good voice acting, and could do with a bit more focus on the quality of the writing.
I'm really looking forward to reading/watching/listening to more.

As a programmer, this game is a wonderful mind-melting experience. If you are familiar with assembly language, you will feel right at home, but the operator set is so limited that anyone could pick it up within an hour.
That limitation is also what makes this game so difficult. The puzzles would be trivial with a more complete form of assembly, but with only one register (+1 non-addressable storage slot) per node, you are forced to rethink how you store and look at the input. I've caught myself obsessing for hours over puzzles, looking for the optimal solution to a problem that would take me seconds in C++.
I would recommend this to anyone with an interest in puzzle games, regardless of their programming experience. Quick to pick up, difficult to master, and incredibly satisfying.

* The Bad
- too short

The note on the store page about combining puzzle and rhythm gameplay doesn't make much sense though since the music has no effect on gameplay, it is just generated by how you place blocks.
While the game is short, comprising 63 levels plus workshop support, it has a small price tag to match.  Definitely recommended for anyone who likes puzzle games.

I've been playing hardcore strategy games since I picked up a copy of Russian Campaign in 1978.  The same year I began playing roleplaying games at summer camp by tearing up little pieces of paper, writing numbers on them, and pulling them out of cups to generate random numbers.  Two years later I was playing Ultima I.  Since that time, I have spent 80% of my personal free time playing games.
I had thought I was simply having fun.  But I am now convinced that all of that time was an extensive training program to prepare me for this game.  I have been richly rewarded.
Play this game.  Get all the DLC (maybe not music and such).  Play only on Ironman.  Understand that you will make many catastrophic, dynasty killing, history altering, vein popping mistakes.  Let it all roll off your back.  Keep learning, keep developing new strategies, and keep pushing yourself.  It's a fantastic game.
Don't play this game to 'win'.  Play it for the experience.  It's a rollar-coaster ride, not a go-cart race.

Want to assasinate a rival? Go for it. Need to take control of a neighboring county? Just send your Chancellor over to manufacture a claim for you. Have a vassal who hates your guts? Just be careful whom you marry, because the traits of each parent carry over to the couple's children. Taking a craven, slothful, sickly, idiotic spouse may be a bad idea--even if the pairing is politically advantagious. And, by the way, these things are all happening at once. Then your spymaster informs you that he has uncovered a plot to kill you. Worse yet, your ungrateful son is the ring leader. What to do. What to do...
This is just a fraction of what this game has to offer. Because of it's considerable width and breadth, the game does have a steep learning curve. A simple projectile deflection puzzler with nicely integrated music. Micron is advertised as a "fusion of puzzle and rhythm gameplay", but the rhythm portion of the claim doesn't really hold water. The game has a nice, laidback feel and very clear, simple graphics. The 60-ish levels don't really ever become frustrating, and can all be solved in a reasonable amount of time. In fact, clearing the game 100% only took me a couple of hours. If you're looking for a mellow diversion for a few hours, this might fit the bill. Micron didn't really impress me in any singular aspect, but sometimes just a solid execution can be enough.

What is Micron?
Micron is a 2D puzzle game where you have a grid of tiles and need to set diagonal or horizontal/vertical tiles in a way that balls - shot out by non-movable cannons - reach the exit. While this is easy at first, the puzzles get harder continuously, although only few are really difficult. Some can however be described as tricky - if you don't pay attention to the setup and pieces you have, you can't solve them, as you might need to use pieces for more than one purpose.
After all, it is a nice little game I would recommend for a price of maybe 1.50 to 2 Euro, as it will take you around two hours to solve everything, unless you get stuck on difficult puzzles.
A smaller version of the game is available for free on Kongregate.
Recommended: For puzzle-fans.

I have a lot of these "mini racers" or "top down racers" now, both combat (Burning Cars, Death Rally) and non-combat (Bang Bang Racing, MiniMotor EVO, Little Racers Street, Real World Racing), and while I have only gotten into a few of them, I think I have seen enough of Blazerush to say that it's the best one on Steam.
The controls feel spot-on from the moment you begin, and they even feel pretty good with the keyboard. Works well with Xbox360 controller, does not work with directinput gamepad. Acceleration with the 360 controller is "push in the direction to move" instead of say a throttle trigger or button, which felt odd at first, but I quickly grew to like it.
There are a lot of cars to choose from, all with a cool sort of Micromachines-meets-MadMax type of style. They have only 3 attributes each (acceleration, mass, and handling) but some feel different based on their wheel config (two or 4 wheels, tracked, hover, etc).
There seems to be plenty of tracks to unlock, with quite a few different themes, but maybe too many of them have the same "wasteland" feel to them.  I know it's supposed to be that way, but it actually makes some of the tracks too similar. Amazon and the snow ones are nice standouts.
The main drawback to the game as I have seen (only a few hours played so far) is the lack of upgrades & customization for the vehicles - there are none. No skins, no engine or weapon upgrades to buy, no garage to manage, the only thing to do in this game is pick a car and race. Not a big deal but it is a bit one-dimensional.
The game could definitely use more weapons as well,  so far have autogun, saw, missle, slime, & sonic; perhaps I haven't unlocked them all yet, but I havent seen any others in any screenshots.
In quite a few ways this game reminded me of Cel Damage, with the wild comebacks and last-second heroics, or knowing you were blasted off the track to oblivion but getting in that last perfectly-aimed kill as you fall down a cliff. It could have taken another page from Cel Damage by including more weapons, and my number one request would be a mode where you choose exactly which powerups are available in a given skirmish race. In other words, maybe you feel like all rocket boosters and buzz saws, so you could make it so only those populate in that race.
The game runs at like 300 frames per second, which ran too hot for my gpu, but it has it's own FPS limiter in the options*, so I won't have to remember to change my fps limit manually on my gpu every time I play. Nice!
*for some reason when I limit the game to 120 fps, it runs at 111 fps. When I had used my gpu's limiter, I ran at 90 fps and it ran 90, idk why the in-game limiter runs different but it doesnt matter much).
The one time I went to play multiplayer, it was a lot of fun but only one round was going on, with about 6-8 people playing. It was a little bit laggy but very fun.
All in all, I really enjoy this game, and the mix of challenge vs casual fun seems about right. A good choice if you are looking for a top down mini racer, even without a sale price.

Atlas Reactor is execellent combination of XCOM Turn-based strategy and dota 2 style hero mechanic. There are many good points for what it game can be considered as unique and fun:
1) Pick your own playstile.
There are big enough hero pool, each hero with abilities that can be adjusted to your own playstile creating you own view on hero and making him more comfortable to playing with.
2) Fast paced turn-based
Time is limeted here and it aslo affect gameplay. You must thunk clear and fast to win.
3) Different maps, cover system.
Maps can affect your gameplay in interesting way.
4) Team play matter.
If you really want to win you must constantly contact with other people in your team to make right maneuvers and help each other to survive/focus target to eliminate.
5) Discord integration
Through it is not guarantee that there will always be people in the room it is certainly appreciated that they make it simpler to people from the same team to gather and communicate with each other.
Problems that this game have at this moment:
1) Ranked matchmaking was death last time I checked. It's hard to find people to play with within reasonable time.
2) Too few maps. They are too concentrated on level surroundings that most people do not look at instead of play zone and it seems to affect speed at which new maps are added. This parametr I think quite affect game population.
3) Bad marketing. They've started promoting the game as a free to play game, which actually looks like a demo version. And, they should've advertised it like it, because many people raging on game now thiking that this is like normal free to play when it is not.
4) Prematch. I think that even in standard pvp there should be hero picks instead of pick even before you found match.

Echo Tokyo: Intro is a EVN developed by Dharker Studio  and published by Dharker Studio  themselves, as the name suggests it is more of an introduction.Echo Tokyo is the last bastion of humanity. A nuclear fog has made street level uninhabitable. Now hundreds of years later Echo Tokyo lives on, by building bridges and platforms between the skyscrapers to create a new city in the sky. This cyber punk city somehow manages to function without government or law, where the companies rule and order is what people make it for themselves.

Shizume Misaki – Origin
The first graphic novel story introduces Shizume Misaki, in this fully voiced interactive graphic novel, telling her tale as she begins working as a Fixer within Echo Tokyo.
It is said that a fixer will take any job as long as the price is right. Though many act mainly as private investigators, many others will do any job to pay the rent.
What will become of Shizume on one of her first big jobs as she visits into the most dangerous area of the city… The Slums.
Keiji Light – Origin
The second graphic novel story introduces Keiji Light, in this fully voiced Kinetic graphic novel we learn of the origins and trials Keiji went through as a child in the slums. As well as how he was groomed and abused after being abducted and experimented on, leaving him where he is now.

As a long-time fan of the Halo series (I bought Halo: Combat Evolved when it came out, and have bought every Halo upon release since then, excluding this one, as I thought a mobile game wouldn't be anywhere near good for the series), this game was actually quite enjoyable. The music felt nice and didn't bore me, which lives up to my expectations since Halo has always had a kick♥♥♥♥♥soundtrack since forever, basically.
Picked this one up on sale for 2 dollars, and honestly it was worth it. I wouldn't be as likely to have bought this particular game but I did and don't regret it.
One thing I particularly like about this is that by expanding the platforms upon which Halo is available it opens it up to a wider audience. I do however have the desire to see The Master Chief Collection on Steam, as while this game does the series justice in the sense it lived up to what it promised, it doesn't do the series justice in the sense of bringing the feel of the rest of the games to PC. Yes, I know Halo CE and Halo 2 had PC ports (I own both), but it would be nice to see Microsoft pay attention to their fanbase in modern time as well. I'd gladly dish out money to play any Halo game on PC.
I'm a huge fan of Halo's lore, so it's a nice touch to see what went down between Halo 3 and 4. The story wasn't as overly convuluted as say, Halo 4's. In addition, it was nice to see things featured in Halo Wars pop-up again (Another game I feel is underrated among the fanbase as a whole).
Over all I'd rate this an 8/10, but if you're looking for the classic Halo experience, make sure Microsoft knows you want The Master Chief Collection on PC.

A really good visual novel, if currently rather short as only one of the stories is ready. In Shizume's story you play as a 'fixer' (private detective) who infiltrates the slums to find a missing girl. Of course it's not as straightforward as that.
The game is set in a very visually appealing setting of a post-disaster Tokyo, where everyone lives far above the clouds. The story is told through static images, a lot of them, which are very skillfully drawn and it's all set to soothing music.
Every line of text is voiced by the voice actress, sounding very professional. My one criticism there would be that she seems to be holding back a bit in scenes where more emotion would be required.
Echo Tokyo: Intro is a visual novel I can definitely recommend. It's one of the best on Steam currently, making up for its current short length with its low price -- and more content to come soon in the form of a second chapter.
//Edit: Chapter two is out now as a free update.
It does not feature any choices, but does provide another half hour of story. It is much darker in tone than the first one. Like the first chapter, it is fully voiced and told through static images -- all new art -- set to music.

This is a very short and very limited interactive graphic novel. Some of the art is good but the art involving characters is obviously less quality than the background images. The backgrounds are very nice and detailed but the characters look as though they were drawn using MS Paint while being rushed. The quality of audio for the voices is very good but the dialog isn't.
There are really only 4 different options you can select with the game in its current state (and that's if you make it far enough to get those options but you can always start a new game). That is the entire graphic novel, there is nothing else to it. You click one of two options for each time the opportunity presents itself and repeat that process at most 3 times. I spent about 24 minutes interacting with it and was able to unlock all of the achievements and complete the novel. That is too short in my opinion.
There is one good feature I like about it though, there is a skip button that will allow you to skip past dialog you've already experienced and go directly to selecting one of the two choices you are able to pick. So if you've already experienced the story with one option, you can start a new game and skip the the point where you wanted to chose a different option and hope it changes the story. There is also a quick save option but one round of the story is so short it doesn't have any real use from my perspective.
I bought this game on sale for $2.24 and I'm not upset about the money I spent but if I knew how short it was, the iffy story and art, and how little interaction I would have with it, I would have passed. Maybe the additional content that will get added later will help but as the game is now, I would not recommend buying it.

I really enjoyed this game. In my opinion, this was better than Unity. Unity took until the end-game to actually grow on me, but this gripped me right from the start.
The ship battles from AC IV were a nice touch, now set in the Atlantic Ocean, with colder climes and freezing waters, and it was interesting to fight alongside the British against the French in the colonies. My only complaint is the lack of actual side-missions, as the closest you get to that are the Assassin Interceptions which is just basically killing targets to defend someone before the timer ran out, nothing like the narrative based experiences you had in the older games such as Brotherhood with the mercenaries, courtesans and thieves guilds, for example. The main story could also have used some beefing up; at only 6 sequences it's rather skimpy, fortunately there's plenty of exploring to do (and you'll spend a great deal of time collecting resources to upgrade your sloop).
All in all, a very enjoyable game, and I'd hope to see a full-fledged Templar AC game in the future.

I wish the game wasn't quite so garish; if you ever thought Geometry Wars' color and special effect sensibilities were too tame and conservative, DRM might be more your style. I played this game back when it first game out when I was pretty young. When I saw this on sale I was pretty excited for a trip down nostolgia lane. But unfortunately this thing has not aged well, and it has revealed that it isn't a game so much as an chore to be optimized.
Its overly complex in what you need to keep track of, you need to simultaneously be researching key technology at a library while expanding new cities, keeping your military updated with the newest weaponry, building resource-efficiency buildings, researching efficiency upgrades at said buildings, building new workers, building a military to begin with, and expanding your commerce with trading with your other cities. This isn't even taking into account the building of wonders or tactical combat, or the specialization of what troops to build in what quantities.
It's a massive headache to play, even on easy difficulties. And even when you win, it's unsatisfying. In my most previous game, I ended up building wonders to boost my empire, and appearently that starts a timer which at the end of you just straight up win. And then you're back to the main menu. Now I know you can probably turn that off as a setting, but the anti-climactic end to about 45 minutes of pretty intense micromanagement of a realtime empire is frustrating.
It's just too complex. Too much. I recognize that the individual features of the game are probably solid, but its inpenetrable. I do like other turn-based strategy games like StarCraft II, Civilization, and Age of Wonders 3, so its not the genre, but this particular realtime strategy game is getting a pass from me.

I haven't played this game since it was in Early Access. I heard about this game when it was first annouced as PixelJunk, Inc. I have played PixelJunk's other games on the PlayStation platforms - PixelJunk Monsters was my favorite. I bought this game early, based on their previous work. I played for this game for a little bit, but never really got hooked. I loved their distinctive art style, but didn't really have much fun.
Updates came and went, but I didn't go back to the game.
Fast forward a couple of years. The game has been released, and patched several times. While looking at Factorio and Rimworld, I remembered that I had this game already. Loaded it up, and started a few levels. This game is a lot of fun!
It is like a lot of other crafting/base-building games. Crashland on a planet, start building a base. Mine resources for money to expand your base. Use the native flora and fauna to make soup, and then launch the soup in a rocket to feed the hungry citizens of the galaxy!
There is a more compelling gameplay loop now. You're trying to make soup faster than an off-screen rival company and put them out of business. Add more soup machines to make different flavors of soup. Variety increases market share. Add more rockets to ship the finished product faster. Start growing more ingredients to make sure your supply chain is feeding all your machines enough raw materials. Automate your production with robot workers and conveyor belts to shuttle around ingredients and soup cannisters.
As your market share increases, the rival corporation will send coporate raiders - literally. You will need to create base defenses so the aliens don't come and destroy all your hard work.
Instead of being thrown in the deep end with endless menus of tools, the game gives bite-sized chunks so you can learn and perfect your infrastructure. The "aha!" moments from getting conveyor belts and robots right is really rewarding.
At first, I thought that restarting my base from scratch was annoying. However, I quickly realized that there were more efficient layouts. A base layout that might work on one planet may not work on another. Building a soup empire from grasses and vegetables will be very different than building a base from mushrooms and underground creeper vines. Killer tomatoes make great soup, but you'll need to create a herd of them that will sustain your soup production without overwhelming and kiling you.
There is also a sandbox mode if you want to just keep adding on to the same base. I am still progressing through the levels, so I haven't started a sandbox-mode planet yet.

This game is an obvious economic repackaging of the main mechanics of AC4 Black Flag and AC3, and features a lot of the classic Ubisoft tropes and carries over many details from AC4, such as almost identical combat.
That said, what is added is the most cohesive Assassin's Creed game since II, or at least Brotherhood. The wide sprawling naval and land areas are absolutely full of not only boring collectibles, but interesting activities, that stay interesting far longer than you'd expect.
They obviously took the oppurtunity of developing a second-rate AAA sequel alongside AC Unity to experiment with the mechanics and formula that has defined AC for a long time, the reversal of roles as a Templar opposed to Assassins means being stalked by Assassins, having to prevent them carrying out Assassinations (a reverse of mission types such as in Revelations) and helping the British fight the French (the Ten Years war is the backdrop to the story as it is technically a prequel to AC3).
Slight changes in the way you do normal mundane Ubisoft open world collection chores means it's a less tedious for a while, and the additions to sailing, mainly the ice breaker ram and the ability of enemy ships to ram and board you makes the naval part of the game feel very different whilst the regular gameplay loop of firing cannons repositioning and firing remains exactly the same.
It's my opinion that the executive figures of Ubisoft will always demand the focus of their developers be on the graphical aspect of their games above all else (focus groups aside, graphical fidelity is visual and extremely easy to sell as a major plus in an otherwise mediocre program), but AC Rogue is a window into what would happen if the developers of these games were given some freedom. Turns out it wouldn't be bad.

After having played this game for 2-3 hours, I was ready to call it near perfect. And for some, it probably still is after 20 hours, but for me it just got too darn random.
I think it's very subjective - I believe the developers probably succeded in implementing exactly the game they had envisioned: Pure chaotic, explosive destruction around a racetrack. But I feel the near constant rain of random weapon drops makes luck the supreme factor in winning pretty much any race.
The forgiving nature of some of the game modes where you're simply teleported forward to catch up should be replaced by more frequent nitro boost/weapon drops. Imo the leader should hardly get any drops. When I'm in the lead I've often practiced firing whatever weapon I had every time I saw a weapon drop I could reach, just so that I could grab it and prevent my opponents behind me from getting it. That's just a flawed gameplay mechanic right there.
Technically the game is perfect - runs absolutely smooth, and the VR implementation with Oculus Rift DK2 is unrivaled. Awesome stuff!
Tweak the gameplay to reward skill over luck somewhat, and it's a friggin' classic. (and a bargin too!)

Very fun and simple racing game, with decent graphics, a kicking soundtrack that I can only describe as mixed techno/dubstep [probably the best part imo], a fun assortment of weapons and vehicles/characters to choose from that once all are unlocked create a great deal of chaos in the later levels, and some interesting tracks set on a few different fictional worlds. Its a fun mindless game [as with most racing games, dont expect much from the story] right up until the last level of the campaign.
I only really had 2 issues with the game. One was that in some game modes, the game will port racers who are lagging behind, back into a closer position to the others. This was annoying as it felt very hand-holdy and quiet often it would port me straight over some pickups that otherwise would have won me a race or two.
The other issue, was the final boss. At the end, the 'corporation' from the back-plot sends its 'president' to deal with you. he comes in a spaceship that looks like it was made by mercedes-bens, but armed by the military. He is almost impossible to beat - while most levels took only a few minutes to beat and were the kind of challenge that felt good to redo a few times until you beat it, I had to keep on reloading this mission tirelessly for the better part of an hour. [I'm not exactly one to give up easily, but I swear by the end of it I felt like throwing my controller across the room. XD] He has alot of health that you have to slowly widdle down, and if he knocks you off the track - which is extremely easy for him with his massive assortment of weapons that he spams you with - you loose immediatly. This might have been less of an issue if they gave you a couple of lives to beat him with, but you loose once and its game over. It was, for me, quiet frustrating, and didnt feel at all rewarding when I finally beat the game.
All in all, its a super fun simple racer, probably better to play with friends then to play the campaign, really. I personally bought it through a BundleStars bundle, and dont feel its worth the full price on steam. But if you see it in a bundle or on sale, somewhere, I would highly recommend it for a night of pointless chaos.

In brief: Great game, tough learning curve. If you are a fan of simulators and/or strategy, give it a try!
In depth:
For those new to grand strategy games, Paradox Games are what you would call the ultimate strategy simulators, trying to base the games in facts and more realistic gameplay rather than action. What you would call the ultimate "Risk" with dozens of layers of depths. You do not manage single units or squads, as in a RTS, but an entire nation or dinasty. The games are played in their entirety in what seems to be a campaing game from the Total War series; and you will approach it from the point of view of someone in command.
And then, among the different games from Paradox, you have this true jewel: Crusader Kings 2!
In it, Paradox has really fun a nice balance for newcomers and oldtimers alike, mixing into their classic Grand Strategy style more RPG elements and tons of twistings and fun: in the game, you do not control a nation or a kingdom, but the family dinasty! This makes the game so much appealing in different levels and works best in the Medieval context:
-You will have to manage the basics of the Kingdom - taxes, levies (armies), royal titles and subjects' loyalties.
-You will have to assured your dinasty continuation - through procreation, laws, wars and plots.
-Develop your characters through the game, and laugh at yourself at how things turned out.
Thus, the fun of this game is to "live" it:
-how do you manage your most powerful vassals to be loyal to you? Money? Titles and adulation? Support their interests? Or be a feared ruler with a tiranic rule? What about the church opinion of you? Or the cities?
-what about your heirs: find the right woman, but... is the kid yours? Or are you having lil' ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s around and you are afraid that acknowledging them may bring future troubles for your heir? What if your heir is a jerk? And... which law governs for inheritance?
-Now, all good and all, but you want to expand your Kingdom... same as your neighbor who might be your second cousin... maybe fake claims in each other lands and invade? Or have a wave of murders to drive the inheritance to yourself? Or maybe a combination of both?...
...However, you might own too much land and titles, and your own vassals grow wary of your power and reclaim their share. You might want to hold to it, but are you gonna risk a Civil War during your next crusade? Or just create new trustworthy vassals... that might turn arrogant when your heir takes the crown...
It is one of best experiences on games I ever had. YOU GOT TO GO THROUGH THE FIRST ONE OR TWO GAMES (40-80H) TO ACTUALLY LEARNT ALL THE LAYERS OF THE GAME, but don't worry, you'll have a lot of fun. And after that, you'll just want to repeat with different kingdoms or time periods; and probably would like to add some new flavors with the tons of DLC available. For my own taste, I'd recommend in the following order:
-Way of Life (+ characters features)
-The Old Gods (+ VIKINGS!)
-Charlegmagne (+earlier starting time period and the Charlemagne events)
-Legacy of Rome (+new content on the Byzantine Empire)
-The Republic (+if you want to try to play as a Merchantine Republic)

You will notice similarities to AoE games and Civilization games while the priniciples they pioneered are put to the test to provide a unique civlization building military real time strategy game that to this date has no equal. On sale or not this game is worth every penny, and if you ever finished playing Age of Empires 2, moved onto AoE 3 and felt that game was lacking, I suggest you try out Rise of Nations. I gaurantee It will be a satisfying experience.

will take almost any video but also comes with correction presets for all the popular brands of action cameras and their generic clones and you can easily create profiles for any camera and lens you use. (Built-in profiles listed at the end of the review).
As there are a lack of reviews for this little app I thought I'd add my two-cents.
Probably best right away to answer the three obvious questions:
1. Why would you want this when you can get free video tools which do the same?
2. Do you lose quality?
3. Why use a fisheye in the first place?
1. Why buy it at all?
eg. If you use a GoPro they have their own dedicated app. There is a vast difference in the fisheye effect between the hero2 and 3, and until they and the other makers come to their senses and include the fisheye correction apps in-camera for some people it's still easier to pick up one  pocket-change app like this on steam than download various other apps and plugins for Vegas or Adobe or whatever video editing suite you use.
2. Does it distort?
Yes, and No.  It alters the video you put in, but that video has already been distorted into a fisheye which makes it a hard one to answer. its like asking someone if he still beats his wife, whatever answer he gives is going to sound dubious.
Just look on it as swapping one type of distortion for another and getting the choice of the one which you like the best (or which is the least distracting).
For example Take a look at any panned video image on in a real TV programme, discovery channel make huge use of fisheye action cameras, half the time the edges have been corrected in the same way this programme works, but you barely noticed at all because you were looking in the centre. If that had been a rounded fisheye it would have distracted you from what was going on in the centre at first.  That's about all there is to it. If you do notice the blurry edge at all, it's far less distracting than the fisheye effect.
3. Why use a fisheye lens at all?
Soon there will be some troll, usually the one leaving a thumbs down as a negative review of a review (the irony of that) asking us all why we use fisheye lenses in the first place.  On behalf of all of us who do use action cameras with fisheye lenses, I think I'm speaking for us all in saying get a life, there is nothing for you here. If you don't know why you sometimes need fisheye correction, then why are you reading a review about a fisheye correction app anyway? If you have popped in to troll us for buying an app that other various apps do for free, may I refer you to the the previous two paragraphs above, indicating that  the review is for helping people decide whether the software is any good, and not inviting judgement of our video equipment choices,  which you probably haven't read anyway, before you jog on.

If you're a fan of board games and/or turn-based strategy games like Xcom, you need to try Atlas Reactor!
What's Great:
- Gameplay. Simultaneous turns means all players on both teams choose what to do at the same time. That creates a lot of depth at a quick pace. Better strategy still trumps how fast you are at the controls.
- Great Characters. I love the diversity and design. They're also well-balanced.
- The free mode / trial. You get several characters to use and they rotate weekly. It gave me time to understand the gameplay and decide if I liked it enough to pay up. Way better than F2P.
- Discord integration. It's effortless to jump into group/team voice chat in Discord.
What's Not:
- Learning the basics. It took a few hours to begin to really understand how things work. I watched the videos, read online, and ultimately resorted to trial and error before I understood most of the core concepts.
After a few weeks on the trial, I picked up the Ultimate Edition because I like what they've done here so much.

The first time I played Oblivion, I hated it. I thought it had the worst character models of all time, and the combat took too long and felt unnecessarily difficult, I immediately developed the opinion that Skyrim was the best game in every regard. That was probably one of the biggest mistakes I've ever made concerning a video game. The thing about oblivion that makes it the polar opposite of Skyrim is that, the more you play Oblivion, the better it gets. Meanwhile Skyrim is magical at first, and then progressively gets way too easy and tedious. So heres why you need to play Oblivion in 2016:
1) The combat
As mentioned antecedently, Oblivion combat system is ♥♥♥♥ing ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ at first, but then, very similarly to Morrowind, you feel yourself getting progressively more powerful. You start as someone less dangerous than a native american toddler with cerebral palsy, but turn into one of the most epic warriors on the face of Tamriel. It also requires more skill, you need to strafe and blocking actually consistently makes a difference in who falls first in an engagement. Although there are no fancy decapitation animations, it still rewards more of a sense of completion, since you know that you have to be powerful to slay this person or creature.
2) The Story
Oblivions many storylines, particulary the Dark Brotherhoods, blow skyrim out of the water. The characters have so much more depth than, "I came from X and I'm gonna hostile to you now but after one ♥♥♥♥ing quest I'm gonna worship the ground you walk on" They will start to like you more after every few assassinations, depending on how well you perform them, and when its done, you wont just be their favorite warrior, you will be their leader. Same with the main quest, rather than just running around dungeon to dungeon, killing the draugr "boss" at the end. There are many different types of quests within the main storyline, and honestly it feels like a complete movie at a certain point.
3) The quests
You know whats better than having to go into a tunnel fight the draugr minions, fix a puzzle with the directions right in front of you, and have it be the same puzzle every time? EVERYTHING is the answer to that. Oblivion has such a vast arsenal of different variations of quests that it can throw at you, poisoning someones food, chasing a unicorn, etc
4) The world
The final point I'm going to rant about is that the world of Oblivion is more interesting than Skyrims in almost every regard. The people have their own conversations, and the game somehow manages to give personality to all of the random conversations as well. For example, when a nord and an imperial had a conversation, the imperial said, "those nords sure are hostile" and he immediately said goodbye. That sort of discomfort in the face of racism adds so much personality and says alot about the world itself, and the bigotry is hurled in every direction from every direction. It also, despite a weaker engine, still looks prettier, due to its bright colors rather than white and brown.
