Warframe is a game based around space ninjas and other fancy junk where you go around killing everything with a huge variety of weapons. "But how can you have so many weapons and have them all be unique?" They all have their own special ways of playing with. Newer weapons tend to have special gimmicks with them that make them more fun. "A bow that shoots an ice globe and destroys anything within that? Sign me up!" That doesn't mean that older weapons aren't as fun, however. You also choose a frame of your choice (okay maybe you have to build him/her first) but once you do so, you can use the abilities which are massively fun to use
.
The game itself revolves around grinding. In order to get better, you grind to get stuff. Sometimes it will take a while to get what you want, but the grinding itself isn't too difficult provided you have the right stuff and know what you're doing. A lot of people find this pretty fun, but that doesn't mean everyone enjoys it. The beginning of the game is fun and all, but sometime later, there's a lot where you either stick with it, or leave the game due to it's grind. That is up to you.
What if you don't want to kill? Well, Plains of Eidolon just released. You can play No Man's Sky (mine rocks) or go fishing. You can also choose to sit in the market and try to make a profit. What most people do like however, is the fact that you can customize yourself and your weapons. Most people call this "fashionframe", but you can call it whatever you want, really. It's kind of limited if you're a free player and can't buy any skins, color palettes, syandanas
and other junk that'll improve your game. Not to say that it's required as it's not necessary, but people in this game tend to base books on their covers.
As for the premium currency of the game, they do it amazingly well. Only thing that I can complain about really is the fact that you need premium currency to get weapon slots and frame slots, but other than that, everything is cosmetic only for the most part. Not to fret, however, because you can farm stuff and trade that stuff for plat. I do wish that we didn't have to rely on other people to buy our stuff to get inventory slots if you don't choose to spend money on the game, however, as that gets kinda boring as you absolutely need it but no one's looking to buy your stuff. What can you do about that though?
All in all, the game's pretty fun. I'd say give it a shot as there's no risk, but there is a slight one. If you have a family to take care of, work to deal with or anything that requires your time, I'd advise you to stay away if you get dragged in. Not to say that it's a guarantee that you'll get addicted, just there's a pretty high chance if you like grinding. Or destroying things. Or talking to people. Or marketing. Or fashioning. Or- Look, you get the point.

A great game for anyone who knows some assembly programming or wants to get started learning assembly, TIS-100 is a game about creating systems of small pieces of code to perform a task, such as multiplying a number or counting the length of a sequence.
The TIS-100 system is very different from any real CPU, only supporting 13 instructions (including conditional jumps). One TIS-100 program includes code for each different "node" within the system. Regular processing nodes can pass data between them using registers, and each node has just two internal registers not used for passing values. There are also memory nodes wchich store data in a stack.
The format of numbers within the TIS-100 is very strange: values are from -999 to 999, which must require at least 12 bits but wastes one bit. It is impossible to do bitwise operations on these values. Additionally, there is no support for input or output of text characters within programs, but the OS does this somehow.

It's called Bug Frame for a reason, only some of these problems within the game, clearly aren't bugs.
Warframe is an example of problematic issues within a game and how, despite these problems, it can become a success. On one hand, Warframe has succeeded in almost every way big name game designers have FAILED in recent years with most games. On another hand, their work is an example of how find viability and profit without (in MOST cases, 99%) trying to cash grab/scam and use pay to win in either cash shop format or the extortion of a monthly fee, regardless of your own satisfaction or how well the game is performing and other facts that can affect someones enjoyment of the game.
Warframe has NUMEROUS pros. When people ask if you like games of this type and suggest Warframe, listen. Give it a try. The graphics are beautiful. It's populated. It's packed with quick action. There are mini games within the game, and Fashion Frame is a running joke because of all the dozens of different stylization choices for your frames. (Note, most of the more elabroate are made by people selling them through Steam. This will cost real cash.) You can chose to buy things within the game, or actually just farm for it. Buy in game cash or just sell rare loot to other players. The game is so flexible, and deserves high praise for that.
However..
As much as it is known for the Fashion Frame aspect, it's known also as Bug Frame. The bugs are epic. Forcing many aspects of hosting off on players computer instead of having dedicated servers for anything but a few in game nods can result in entirely lost game sessions, being booted back to square one in the middle of difficult mission, or lost event credit or loot. Networking problems have been insane at times. Submitting a bug report, complaints, customer service etc. cannot be accessed in game. Accidentally hitting capslock or even posting something into general chat with a word or two in caps for emphasis will result in a kick, meaning when your in a rush to get a group for an alert mission or trying to sell things in the heavily flooded trade chat channel, your just out of luck. Not so much a punishment for those in big guilds, but for small time clans or solo players, it's a petty, annoying swat in the face. For a small indy compnay that sometimes hides behind 'beta' status (for how many years now?) and claims they just don't have the people for many things, it's even sillier someone wasted the time on coding the bots for this. Not to mention the 'police' they have added to general chat sometimes litterally go to far, censorship at times can become draconian. Prepared to be laughed at and reminded it's a canadian owned game if you mention anything about censorship, freedom of speech or having a right to debate, communicate about anything other than your warframe colors, OR even respectfully critique a problem within the game. Boot.
Game balance is often out of whack. The feel in the beginning of the game is one of a pleasing struggle, while mid to high end you might end up feeling an overwhelming sense of forgoding (errrr...forboding..) due to the competiton between you and players with all the bells and whistles who can level THE WHOLE MAP WITH ONE BUTTON CLICK. As this reults in lack of opportunities to max your xp gain or trigger powers that say, require kills by headshots etc. it is a source of frusteration. Cooperation is not always the name of the game.
There are other things that throw people off too. PvP is, well, bad. The flying Arc Wing element of the game can still be annoying and has only now been made good enough to be bearable, depending on the missions you run. The third person aspect gets in the way of your vision, can't be switched to first person, can't be zoomed in or out.  In game notices block your vision during combat. The game lacks day and night cycle clocks for regions in game where it is important, and has no real in game auction house. It's all handled by old school chat or a third party web site thats totally unaffilliated. DE has apparently completely lost track with the mindframe of new players and left them in the dust until the unfororseen success with the PoE expansion, and now are desperately scrambling to play catch up. The new player experience is still iffy.
Many people struggle to find a direction in the game after having collected most of the frames and unlocked the map. There are choices, but none so important that you can't simply walk away and skip them, leaving things... well,  on one hand, up to the players choices, which can be good! But it many times seems to be leaving players feeling lost at the 'end game'. It's one reason why many leave Warframe between 'expansions', which are usually just a small quest and the release of a new warframe.
Rating this game a straight up yes or no really doesn't reflect some reviews, and this is one of them. It lacks the huge sins of developers like EA, does several things right,  yet has glaring flaws DE seems comfortable in simply leaving unaddressed.

Nom Nom Galaxy is an interesting game that doesn't quite fit into the expectations you may have of its overall genres. It's a platformer mixed with a real-time economic component, and it's incredibly engaging. The basic setup is that you run around a 2D world harvesting ingredients from plants and animals (kind of like Terraria), and turn those ingredients into soup, which you then fire off into space in rockets to try to out-compete other companies. The ingredients have their own ecological relationships, too - some animals attack you or eat plants, the resources all spawn and reproduce differently, some are hazardous and others provide you and plants with oxygen, and so on.
Most of my time was spent rushing around a level, digging and harvesting resources, desperately trying to out-produce my competitors while keeping in mind resource ecologies and market trends, and it was a blast. Tinkering with your factory, trying to figure out how to invest your money and resources and time in order to get the optimal return on your soup business, is something that easily devoured several hours at a time if I wasn't paying attention. Most games felt like I was struggling to compete at first, only for victory to sneak into reach so I could pounce on it. Good times!
There are really only two bad things I could say about this game. First, a few of the controls are kind of weird and poorly explained - it took me way too long to realise that where my mouse was relative to my character controlled which direction my character threw or deposited objects in. Also, whenever I placed objects my character punched or swung their sword, meaning I often accidentally punched or chopped ingredients or my own robots or equipment. Yeah.
Second, most levels decide to throw combat events at you. Your "competitors" will throw goons at your base, forcing you to spend money on defenses and rush to fight instead of harvesting. That entire part of the game felt superfluous and unenjoyable; it detracts from the skills you're practising in the main game and draws thing out, and all for what? The combat isn't very fun at all, in no small part because the controls just aren't as snappy and crisp as they need to be for combat.
Besides those, though, the aesthetics and core gameplay of Nom Nom Galaxy were enough to pull me in for hours at a time. If Dota and LoL are RTS offshoots without infrastructure or resource exploitation, then Nom Nom Galaxy an RTS offshoot without much combat. It's great fun, and I want more games in this genre!

Well, where can I start?
Crusader Kings II is probably one of the most addictive Grand Stratergies i've ever played. With over 100 hours on it, I can proudly say i'm addicted.
I came to this game, hoping that Paradox had made a good historical game and they exceeded my expectations.
Here are my positive and negative views on this game:
Pros
-----
- Addictive
- Different combinations of gameplay
- DLC Mechanics [I'll come to this later]
- Playing your favorite nations.
- Playing important bookmarks in history
- De Jure Wars
- The Council
Cons
-----
- Bad Multiplayer [I'll come to this too]
- Assassination Attempts
- Not many Cons
The DLC in the game is quite bountiful, it spins the whole mechanics you have learnt in the vanilla and makes you spend more hours on the game trying to get how the game works.
A good example is Conclave DLC, which provides a whole new set of laws for you to toy with and a Council which you have to always please.
The thing that I am disappointed in the most with this game is the bad multiplayer, where your friends go out of sync randomly. My solution for anyone finding this problem is to use LogMeIn Hamachi and go to Documents\Paradox Interactive\Crusader Kings II\Maps then delete the caches there. You will have to do this every multiplayer session you do, have fun!
Verdict:
Crusader Kings II is a game that is worth your money when it is on deal or not. It can entertain you for hours on end, wether you get home at 3 oclock in the afternoon and want to unwind on a Friday night sweating on this game, or if you're just going to play an hour or three with your favorite country. There are many ways to toy with this game.
My advice is to purchase the game and any DLC that changes your gameplay in an Autumn Sale or Christmas Sale, it is worth your money.

Miner Meltdown is a multiplayer battling/mining game - although let's be honest, there will be more battling than mining when you play because that's where the fun is. There are several game modes: Deathmatch (what do you expect), Diamond Dash (deposit the most diamonds - get them by mining, killing mutants or killing other players) and Crazy King (variation on King of the Hill with a constantly moving zone that you have to chase around the map). Diamond Dash is the best, as it strikes the right balance between gathering loot and frantic battling. And battling is definitely where it's at in this game, it's the fast pace of it that makes it really fun, it's like Towerfall crossed Terraria and Starbound, with the vast array of weapons and items that is in the spirit of Worms.
The pixel art is really cute, you can choose some funny and silly characters to be your mine and the music is fun and bouncy as well, which makes all the DIAMONDS OR DEATH!!! feel fun rather than mean or brutal. Although you wouldn't know that by the way me and my friends ended up swearing at each other (all in good fun of course) as we played it.
I did a video review of the game here:
All in all, Miner Meltdown is really, really fun to play with friends. I hope that more people play it so that the online servers are busier than they currently are. Let me explain what a revolution this game was when it was released.
Morrowind was a fantastic game, offering you an open world with the choice to do just about anything but Oblivion offered a far more cinematic tale with amazing graphics(at the time) to boot.
In morrowind, you could only see a portion of the map at any given time..then oblivion came around with it's white gold tower that could be seen from any distance. This was mind blowing to me back then..it let you know exactly where you were in the world and turned up the immersion completely.
Another huge step was voice acted NPCs, to actually have a conversation instead of just reading their words made a huge difference in the lore. You could hear their emotions in their words instead of just guessing off their text.
Other additions: Horses, realistic combat, wider variety of quests
However this game was the turning point for a lot of whats wrong with TES and FO today.
I feel that these additions should have either been left out or tuned way down.
Quest markers - mixed with compass..there is no guessing
Compass - Could of been a great addition by itself
Fast travel - really kills exploration
Immortal quest NPCs - kills immersion
Closed cities - open cities were better
I don't know why Bethesda decided it necessary after morrowind to hold your hand so much but it seems to be the trend in their games now.
Overall, this was a great experience in my earlier years and I would recommend this game to anyone.

That thing warped my brain to think and process problems the way a computer does, while LEGO provided the hands-on problem solving.  While a debatably cruel thing to do to a child, TIS-100 is the CARDIAC modernized.  These tools are engineer-makers.
Now I can pass along the brain damage.  Thank you!

Well, I'm having fun anyway.
For people who enjoy programming, and exploring systems, this game can be a great challenge and a lot of fun. Since it posts a rudimentary sort of leaderboard, it can be competitive, too, as you try rewriting your solutions in various ways to achieve optimum performance or minimum number of instructions.
Of course, you can probably achieve a similar thrill by finding and exploring a _real_ new/unfamiliar system or coding language... but what the hell, I'm having fun, that's all that matters.
I can't really imagine someone getting into this game who's not a programmer, or interested in programming. Because that's really what it is - programming in an extremely limited assembly language, while potentially dealing with parallelization issues (if you want to minimize your cycles... you don't have to if that particular optimization doesn't interest you).  You only get two registers, one of which only lets you swap it with the other, so if you need to use two variables at a time you end up using another node (CPU core?) just to read/write the other value.
So yeah, anyone with even a small amount of experience with an assembly langugae will find it easy to get into this game, but someone whose never played with assembly before will likely be lost.

Sonic Mania is the newest entry in the long running Sonic the Hedgehog series, this entry is a part of the Classic 2D Sonic era (rather than the Modern 3D Sonic or Modern 2D Sonic ones) like the original Sonic 1, Sonic 2, Sonic CD, and Sonic 3 & Knuckles.
After a disasterous attempt with Sonic 4, Sega recruited popular Sonic ROM Hackers Taxman & Stealth to create this game, and well what can I say? The end result is
and they achieved their goal of trying to make a Sonic game as if it were made for the Sega Saturn perfectly.
Saying this is a love letter to Classic Sonic is understating just how good this game is, the returning levels are familiar yet new, bringing mechanics from previous Sonic games back in new ways while still fundamentally understanding what makes these levels tick. The new levels gorgeous and integrating brand new mechanics that feel like they could be mechanics Sega would have done back in the early 90s.
Really that is what makes this game work: it understands Classic Sonic. Sonic isn't just about pure unadultered speed (something Sega themselves have seem to forgotten), because what's the point in a rollercoaster that just goes down big slopes really fast non-stop? You need that slow build up as you climb up the slope before you get the exhilerating speed boost. The blend of exploration, fast moments, and fast-with-zone-knowledge moments are perfect and display a mastery of understanding how the Classic Sonic games were built.
With all 3 main Classic Sonic characters available (and Knuckles having his own areas and story just like S3&K), Sonic Mania is a return to form that this franchise hasn't seen since 1994.
The music by Tee Lopes is also very well done, and while I wouldn't go as far as to say it's better than Sonic 3 & Knuckles OST (there really isn't any Sonic as catchy as S3&K's boss battle music), it's really close.
Sega opened every single trailer of this game with "Sega proudly presents", and you know what? They should be proud.
Verdict: BUY. (now)

Okay. Here we go. No, this is not a "DENUVO DRM SUXXXXX" bs review. Instead, I'll get to the point.
This game. This MOTHER♥♥♥♥ING GAME. I just beat Stardust Speedway Zone in my Sonic & Tails playthrough, so this'll be short and probably missing a few points.
I've been waiting for this since the first announcement last year, and lemme tell you, my hype did NOT go down the drain. Just by booting this game up, I was already squealing from nostalgia. A nostalgic feeling I haven't felt in like forever. I mean okay fangames are a thing and I enjoy them just as much as the next person, but this is different. VERY different.
Sonic Mania feels and plays exactly like a classic Sonic game. In fact, the physics are easily comparable to that of 3/& Knuckles. Starting in the fresh Green Hill Zone Act 1,
I already felt like I was back with my Mega Drive when I was 5 years old, even though I'm playing on a keyboard. Gameplay is polished enough to the point where you can easily compare this to the original trilogy, which is fantastic. I've only faced a share of bugs, but nothing gamebreaking.
The soundtrack is, of course, what you'd expect from a Sonic game: Nothing but greatness. In fact, I think the weakest parts are the remastered level tracks (GHZ1, CPZ1, FBZ, etc.). But lemme tell you, getting to the Act 2 remixes feels GREAT. ESPECIALLY SSZ.

The difficulty is where it gets tricky: Levels have been tweaked and drastically gone harder, especially Flying Battery, so expect a challenge truly worthy of a Classic Sonic player. I can't say I recommend this to newcomers. (Besides, Mania is a direct sequel to 3&K, so definitely play the original trilogy first. Go for the Sonic 1 & 2 ports for mobile devices and emulate the Sonic 3 Complete romhack, which is currently the best way to play S3.)
If you're a Sonic fan, or at least loved the classic games, I CANNOT recommend this enough to you. Get it.

Alright. I'm gonna update my review because the devs updated their business model and kindly asked me to give it another try:
"We have heard the feedback from the community and now are full free to play. We would love you to come back and give Atlas Reactor another look now that we are full free to play."
Well that sounds nice. My initial thoughts are down below if you want to read them for some reason.

So yeah, I gave it another try and to be honest these changes are actually pretty good. The free rotation of - I believe - 6 freelancers is still in but in addition to that you can unlock your favorite freelancer with the ingame currency called flux. If you are familiar with the way how League of Legends handles this then you are ready to go. It is basically the same model.
There are 4 currencies. Flux, Iso, mod tokens and a violet one. With flux you buy chamions, with iso you buy cosmetic stuff, mod tokens are for your freelancer abilities and I have absolutely no idea what the violet one does.

Freelancers cost either 10k, 35k, 50k or the newest one I believe 75k flux. To be honest I am not 100% sure about pricing because this menu of the game is really clunky. I can't sort the freelancers by how much they cost and if I wanted to check every single one I had to go through the same menu everytime. Some QOL changes would be really nice.

It varies because you get flux by daily missions and challenges. I played 6 games and had around 3k flux. I think you can get around 10k flux after 10-15 games. In addition you get a "chose the freelancer you want" token after 10 games.

Yeah absolutely. I was ♥♥♥♥♥ing about the f2p model because it felt weird. You had this currency but you couldn't spent any of it. It just wasn't well thought. Now as a f2p player it is a little bit grindy but you can play the way you want. Heck you can even play ranked if you have grinded enough.
:
Atlas Reactor is pretty cool. A lot of people described it as a multiplayer XCOM which I totally agree with and it works really well. A fast paced roundbased multiplayer strategy game. The biggest issue however is the free2play model. I got limited time access to all the heroes (freelancers in this case) and 3 days later they were locked behind a paywall. Let me explain what a revolution this game was when it was released.
Morrowind was a fantastic game, offering you an open world with the choice to do just about anything but Oblivion offered a far more cinematic tale with amazing graphics(at the time) to boot.
In morrowind, you could only see a portion of the map at any given time..then oblivion came around with it's white gold tower that could be seen from any distance. This was mind blowing to me back then..it let you know exactly where you were in the world and turned up the immersion completely.
Another huge step was voice acted NPCs, to actually have a conversation instead of just reading their words made a huge difference in the lore. You could hear their emotions in their words instead of just guessing off their text.
Other additions: Horses, realistic combat, wider variety of quests
However this game was the turning point for a lot of whats wrong with TES and FO today.
I feel that these additions should have either been left out or tuned way down.
Quest markers - mixed with compass..there is no guessing
Compass - Could of been a great addition by itself
Fast travel - really kills exploration
Immortal quest NPCs - kills immersion
Closed cities - open cities were better
I don't know why Bethesda decided it necessary after morrowind to hold your hand so much but it seems to be the trend in their games now.
Overall, this was a great experience in my earlier years and I would recommend this game to anyone.

Devil Daggers is the best pieces of quake made into one whole endless level. It's minimalism and arcade style pacing is masterfully crafted for a pleasant learning curve that will keep you in this strange and hellish platform for quite a while.
Aesthetically it seeks to replicate the look and feel of the very firt 3d polygon games and the low res capabilities of machines at the time of their conception. The pallete is greys, reds, oranges, and muted borwn on a black canvas. The sounds are purposefully low res. The mechanics are simple. The physics are enchanting. The ai is predictable but the games focus on movement is so crucial that you are always learning new techniques.
The best part of the game however is the championing of score by time videos that you can watch and learn from. The tutorial is built into the failure. As you continuously fail you are lead to leader boards with the ability to watch the scores of those just above and below you as well as those of your friends.
It is a game that has brought out the best of the old school 3d shooter, and yet it has no map, its just a blank plane with spawning enemies.
Super impressive, would love to see what Sorath has next.

Miner Meltdown:
~~~~~~~~~~~~~

So, let’s check our equipment, shall we? We have pickaxes, dynamite, guns . . . flamethrowers . . .  bazookas. . .  Are you sure we need those? I thought we’re going to dig for gold and diamonds. What? There is another group of four miners that will enter this mine at the same time as us. On second thoughts, what else can we take?  It’s OUR gold and specious stones and I’m sure they’re thinking what we’re thinking. It’s going to be a Miner Meltdown!
Miner Meltdown is an action /online co-op game where you and three other players (or bots) will face another group of four opponents in fun and fast battles through randomly generated mines.
There are three types of modes in Miner Meltdown. In Diamond Dash, you collect diamonds by killing mutants and opponents and make your way to the drop zone to score points. In Deathmatch, you’ll receive ten points each time you kill an opponent and three points when you eliminate a mutant. In those two modes, the team who accumulates the most points will win the battle. In the Crazy King mode, you and your teammates have to be in the king zone to score points; you can’t miss it, a large blue circle which moves around the mine. The first team to reach one hundred and fifty points will win the round.
You can join or host a game. As the host, you can select the duration of the game. It could be five minutes (or less), twenty minutes, or even a few hours if you wish. Plenty of fun if you play with a group of mates.  You can also customize your miner by selecting one of several skins available before starting a game. Additional skins will be unlock as you level up.
In terms of the game play, it’s fast and really fun; either you play online with your mates or against bots. You can select the bots’ level of difficulty (easy, medium or hard) when you setup the game. At the end of your wagon ride, you’ll be greeted by a character who will show you what he as under his coat . . . and by that, I mean weapons, guns, machine guns, flamethrowers, grenades and other great goodies. You will be allocated a certain amount of gold before entering the mine and I would advise you to choose your items carefully.  The mines will have existing paths to follow but as a true miner, you’ll start digging your own path with a view to collecting gold which you can use to purchase new weapons or equipment when you see the man in the long coat. You’ll be given five coins each time you manage to collect gold nuggets. You might find additional gold when you find and open a chest. However, you’ll probably receive additional weapons and gadgets rather than gold. With all that digging going on, you’ll still have to fight the miners from the other team.  Great fun!
Graphically, the pixel artwork is well done but I must admit that I am not a fan of the soundtrack. I find it pretty annoying. The good news is that you can disable it. Control-wise, I preferred the keyboard and mouse option which gave me better gameplay.
Positives:
~~~~~~~
-	Good pixel artwork
-	Randomly generated mines
-	Fast and fun gameplay
-	Miners customization and skins to unlock
-	Achievements
Negatives:
~~~~~~~~
-	No trading cards
-	Not a good soundtrack!
A fun game to play online with your mates! It’s a Miner Meltdown!

GAMEPLAY
RATING: 9/10
Miner Meltdown is a 2D team-based online competitive multiplayer game.
Players must scour the map for minerals, upgrade their gear, and attempt to blow up
the opposing team all the while avoiding monsters, traps, and environmental pitfalls
along the way. Oh and did I mention? There's grapling hooks and jetpacks - I think thats a good enough
reason to buy this game. There are 2 gamemodes so far - Deathmatch (typical team vs team - whoever gets the most points wins)
and Diamond Rush (you collect diamonds and bring them to your base).
It's very easy to pick up and learn and it's actually really fun -
when there is someone playing it. Yes, the game has a huge problem, and that is its playerbase
which is almost none existant, but that can easily change because this game is really fun when
playing with friends, so if you're looking for a party game - I totally recommend this
STORY
RATING: 0/10
The game doesn't have a story, but it doesn't need to have it, it's not meant to be a story driven game.
It's meant to be an action shooter and I don't see the story being of any relevance here.
VISUAL PRESENTATION
RATING: 7/10
Miner Meltdown has that retro game feel and it's really satisfying and works really well with the gameplay.
You will rarely mistake your teammate as your enemy and other way around. Overall I really like the pixelated
2D graphics.
AUDIO PRESENTATION
RATING: 4/10
Ok, so... I don't really like the audio in this game, it gets annoying after some time - especially the music
but maybe it's just me so don't hold me on this. Weapons sounds are good and all and mining sounds sound like Terarria.
FINAL SCORE 7/10
It's a hidden gem for sure and it's leaving early access in 2nd of August and I heard there will be
many changes implemented into the game - new gamemodes, weapons, enemies etc. So there is no reason
why you shoudn't try this game out. It's cheap, it's fun, it's great to play with friends.
So buy this game and make the playerbase active because this game deserves it!

When I played SpaceChem, I was impressed that someone had made a such a great game out of basically just parallel programming. TIS-100 takes this a step further: it is precisely parallel programming, and in an assembly language, no less. It's the purest of puzzle games.
A game like this is necessarily rather narrowly targeted. I had, myself, created a little limited virtual machine (though not parallel) for playing with fake assembly before, so TIS-100 was just the thing for me. Programming in assembly can be a very fun challenge, since it requires you to really look at the very basic steps of a problem in order to orchestrate a solution.
If studying a puzzle under a microscope and writing a solution following fairly harsh restrictions sounds like fun, then you'll probably enjoy TIS-100. I certainly do. If that sounds like mindbending drudgery to you, then I suggest looking elsewhere.

I've played every Assassin's Creed game since the first, and enjoying Assassin's Creed 4, I decided to pick this one up.
It's very similar to 4, first off. If you liked the sailing and piracy of 4, it's practically the same in Rogue. However, there is substantially less content in this game than the last few Assassin's creed games, and apart from some minor gameplay changes and additions, it's just more of what made Assassin's Creed 4 tedious. The endless collectathon of chests and Animus fragments continues, although you aren't required to do this for anything but 100% completion.
This game is also very short, the main story is much shorter than the other Assassin's creed games in recent memory. Not that this is necessarily a bad thing; it took me about 9-10 hours to complete the main story, and that's a leisurely pace. By comparision, Assassin's creed 4 took me about 20 hours to finish, and it really started to drag on at some points.
Story spoiler:
Nothing of any interest happens in the main story; Shay doesn't really have an arc. No significant developments take place, really all Shay does is set up other Assassin's Creed games, namely 3 and Unity. The characters are not engaging, although they don't get any screentime anyway.
This game is really not worth your money. Pick it up if it's 10 bucks or something if you REALLY liked saling around collecting chests, and can't get enough of boring stories.

Awesomenauts is quite a unique game, maybe the only unique game I have played yet (on Steam and not).
I recently got the game and played roughly 12 hours at it, you can really get the hang of it within 2 or 3 Practice matches against bots offline. You have a really large selection of characters to choose from before the start of a game, some of them will be locked until you level up to a certain level which will unlock them (leveling up is relatively easy, an average of 2-3 per session). Not only the characters, but you have an even larger variety of Upgrades to unlock and choose from for each character, each character with his own unique upgrades and special abilities and attacks. Still in the character region of this review, I would like to point out a flaw in this game that has got it quite a lot of hate which is Overpowered characters and abilities. Taking Ayla for example, she may seem hard to get the hang of and quite weak, but her Rage ability wrecks havoc everywhere she goes, a good way to nerf her ability is to increase the damage she takes while the ability is toggled ON. Leaving the characters aside, another flawed section of this game is the Community and match making. The people do not accept defeat and are sometimes disgusting to talk with, going from trash talk to insults and even more. The Community of course is the only flaw in this game that cannot be fixed, or should I say, is hard to fix. From the Community, we go to match making which is a huge pain when searching for a battle to join in, players are not matched equally and you can get, most of the time, put in a game alone with bots. Despite all of that, I still recommend Awesomenauts as it is a wonderful concept in terms of gameplay, soundtrack, characters and much more. I highly recommend this game if you're into 2D platformers, action-packed, fast paced games. It is a real time killer, really fun to play. And I would like to thank Joost for being a great Ronimo team member on the forums.

A fun twist on the MOBA genre, adding platforming skills to the set of skills required in the genre. While lacking as big of a roster as other MOBAs, each individual character is unique and offers an approach for almost every player. The gameplay is also more geared towards a wider audience, with there being only two lanes to attack/defend and only 3 types of attacks for each character to use. Setting up a controller is a bit of a pain, but for the most part the controls work fine if you desire to use a controller.
Overall, it's a really well-polished game! Almost everything has a distinct outline to it, most notably the colourful character sprites. The polish patch adds a few extra shiny things as well, updating some particle effects and more visual confirmations on damage and solar (the in-game currency) picked up. Each map is well-designed, each offering enough variety to set them apart. All of them are a blast to play on.
And the sounds of the game are also top-notch. To add to the already stylised look of the game, each character has his/her own theme song, which does a good job at giving them more of a personality. These theme songs are then given remixes (for the most part) that play whenever that character goes on a killing spree, rewarding the player for playing well and making them feel awesome! The stages also have their own themes, matching how they look very well, and the theme song of the game itself is nothing short of spectacular!
My verdict would be a 'Yes, totally worth buying'. The game especially enderes to those who may not be that familiar with the MOBA genre and want to start familiarising themselves with it, so if that is you then I'd highly recommend checking Awesomenauts out. Even more advanced players can find enjoyment from the game, with the ability to team up with two other friends and offer a tough co-ordinated fight to the other teams.

This is not a review for S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Pripyat. Instead, this is a review for the fan-made modification S.T.A.L.K.E.R.: Call of Chernobyl.
Call of Chernobyl (CoC) is a mod that combines the maps of all S.T.A.L.K.E.R. games, and allows you the choice of playing as one of the nine in-game factions. Each faction has their own starter weapons, and offers their own different experiences. Some are hostile to most, others are neutral, but there will always be someone out there with a sight on your head. Since I’ve never had an original thought in my head, I went with the way that Raycevick had his set up, subtracting the modifications that were supposed to add more atmosphere.
Let me tell you, this game does not lack atmosphere. Every encounter in this game is life or death on harder difficulties and with the Increased Weapon Damage mod by Pavolpi. To add to that, Arsenal Overhaul 3 by E.Nigma42 is a great addition that helps diversify the weapons on offer. These two mods were recommended by Raycevick in his video, and both can be found on ModDB.
In order to convey the feelings of this game accurately it is best to share experiences. Every single person who plays an open world game like S.T.A.L.K.E.R. will have a unique experience. The orders of events will never line up exactly with someone else’s playthrough, which adds to the feelings you get in the game. Once I got to grips with the controls, some of the environment, and the fact that playing it on Veteran is probably the best way to play, I started a new game as the Military. Partly because I guessed that I could get some good weapons, and partly because teaming up with a few guys seemed like the best way to not die.
I started at a small checkpoint at Rostok with only a pistol. That was usual for starting out in the sandbox mode, as knifing hounds would be a bit of a hassle. One of my comrades said that he’d give me his rifle if I assassinated a target that wasn’t too far away, and I got him to come with so I wouldn’t have to walk all the way back there in the event of me succeeding. I also got a shotgun wielder who said he wanted something called, “Hercules.” I don’t know what that is. Now is a good time to mention that I am playing on Ironman mode, meaning when I die all my saves tied to that character are deleted. I was playing it safe; using my binoculars to scan for people and animals from bushes, keeping an eye on my PDA and the road ahead of me so I didn’t run into any anomalies. That’s when I heard something I hadn’t heard before, a bloodsucker. It would constantly rush us, darting in and out of bushes and going completely invisible to ambush us. It had its young with it, I believe. That was the easy one. We took it down, and I heard the body of one of my friends hit the grass. I rushed over and took what I could, his pump shotgun and a few extra rounds, and turned to face the bloodsucker. Two spent shells and one first-aid kit later, we were in the clear. I took the rest of the ammunition off my fallen Hercules lover, and took the patch off of his uniform to remember him by. I would later use the patch to trade for some 9x19 FMJ rounds. We closed in on the back of a dilapidated shack where the target was staying. One bad step, and they heard us. A crack of bullets- shotguns and pistols- came at us. Luckily there were only two guys, my target and his buddy. They went down easy enough. My friend handed me his rifle, well, his SMG. A Heckler and Koch MP5SD. Very useful for what was to come in the future.
Our celebration was short lived, as the noise brought over more bandits. They were probably upset that I killed their friend, and fired at us from a distance. My friend was hit in the head by a 5.45 round. I took his
gun and loaded it. Good old Kalashnikov. It replaced my pistol. Once I had finished off the small counter-attack, I took a look around me.
The Great Swamp, my PDA said.
By this point, I was engaged. I was feeling why this game was respected, and it was amazing. I swept through the marshes and cleared encampment after encampment of bandits and looters. I found AK’s, M16s, M1911s, a couple MP440s, all of which I stripped of ammunition. By the time I made it to another Military checkpoint, I had 30 kilograms of my 50 kilogram inventory filled with ammo for weapons I didn’t need. So I sold it for ammunition I
need. I went East, unknowingly headed for the Neverending Forest. I never made it there. There was an office building between me and the forest, filled to the brim with survivors who weren’t too keen on my presence. I had picked up another soldier at the checkpoint who fell quicker than the bloodsucker’s victim did. I was trapped behind enemy lines, stuck on a rooftop. Luckily enough for me, I had stolen a VSS with a few extra rounds of ammunition. I was completely silent. Unfortunately, the suspected me and began to search the complex. Once someone was shot from a rooftop, it was all over. For stealth, I mean. They all fell to me, and I barely wasted any ammunition. I wasn’t the greatest shot in The Zone, but I was fierce guerrilla who’d show up everywhere. One enemy remained, the SOB who killed my partner. I put a burst in the back of his skull as he sat by a fire. It was around 21:20 by that time. Pitch black. By that time, I had heard gunfire from the forest. 22:05, it was closer. 1:50 closer still. Until I caught sight of someone walking towards my location. He hadn’t seen me, so I flanked over a hill and shot at him with a Mosin, because my VSS had run dry.
That’s when I heard the siren. A Psistorm. I should head inside. I was out of breath and scared. I felt actual fear. I ducked into a bathroom and attempted to waited it out. By 3:30, I got curious. I slowly crept out of the bathroom, lit only by a distant flame and the light show going on outside. It was oddly beautiful.
Shouting insuede. More gunfire. Unknown amounts of enemies. One rushed me with an RPK, and it was over.
Rest in peace, stalker. You tried your best and made a dent in your world. Unfortunately, suicidal gopniks with machine guns are more dangerous than you had hoped.
Alternatively I could’ve just written: “Drank a bunch of vodka and rushed B like true Russian. Cукa Blyaт,” but that would’ve taken a lot shorter.

Putting all that DRM stuff aside, I've seen people complain about how the 2 weeks weren't used at all for the "optimizations" and bug fixes that SEGA promised it would be used for.
The truth is, they were used correctly. The DRM was one thing. The PC release was much better day one than console releases as it does fix many of the bugs that were found in those two weeks, helping the game stabilize, and issues that other people experience are just because of the fact that there's so many types and varations of computers that it's hard to make a product work for everyone on PC. But that's besides the point. Here's my actual review.
Sonic Mania is an AMAZING game which references the old Genesis Sonic games, while adding SO MUCH more to the mix. Of course, it starts off normal, but it throws a curveball and remixes the old zones in ways that most people wouldn't expect, adding brand new elements and many brand new branching paths within levels that they'll feel so different in new runs.
On top of that, the new zones are amazingly unique and original, and the art style and such assets of these levels manages to match the old Genesis/Saturn feel perfectly in an already amazing Classic game.
This is still a Classic Sonic game. A FULL Classic Sonic game with perfect controls, amazing replayability, amazing cleverness and level design, and it's just an all around masterpiece.
A must have if you're a Sonic fan. 10/10

Another great addition to the AC franchise, while the gameplay is definatly nothing new and basically a complete copy from Black Flag and AC 3, Rogue brings us a new perspective through Shay's eyes as he walks the path of both assassin and templar.
This game benifits alot from his personality and story, along with several other characters that make your game experience totally worth the time.
The story was somewhat short for a stand alone but really enjoyable to go through, meeting new characters each with their own motivations and some characters from previous games that enrich Shay's journey.
The gameplay hasn't changed a bit. from combat to travel and naval battles, there's little to no changes, aside from a few new weapons and the always enjoyable naval battles now with burning oil available aswell.
The territorial disputes could have been better if they brought along the territorial wars from Revelations, but oh well it is well made and it is definatly interesting to play the templar side of things.
It really shows that this game suffered from Unity's release, it could have used some more attention, all things considered, Assassins Creed Rogue is still definatly a better game and experience than AC Unity, even if the graphics aren't as shiny it profits from better FPS, overall superior optimization, solid and fast gameplay without the random bugs and crashes.
Assassins Creed Rogue is definatly worth the purchase, hold on buying it until a sale arrives since most of the gameplay if nothing new but the story will be worth the money, a solid title with a good story, a pity that the developers didn't give it the attention it deserved.

Perhaps my favourite installment in the franchise. Rogue is the first AC game to finally offer a(n in universe) Templar perspective, giving the player a different viewpoint into the the realm of AC and an opportunity to consider the motivations of a group that is typically portrayed as a mob of clandestine sycophants hellbent on ruining the lives of the poor schumcks outside their clique. Although some of the plot and dialogue are a little wearisome (I find this to be the case with ninety percent of video games ), the main story arc is engaging and brings a fresh take to the typical AC narrative. First impressions of the game were solid as well: just about anything beats playing through the first twenty minutes to half-hour of a game as a prepubescent goofing around in bushes or stealling things... While the gameplay is virtually identical to Black Flag, I didn't mind too much; having to learn new keybindings for every bloody game (pun intended) they release gets a little wearisome. Additionally, since it's set in North America, the boreal landscape is a pleasant deviation from Black Flag's lush West Indies, while still retaining a good sense of adventure. Most of the gear is the same, with a few minor exceptions, and I personally feel the available outfits and the ship design are infinitely preferable to BF. I recommend it most to diehard fans of the series, but I believe most people would be able to get something out of Rogue, provided they aren't bored by playing a game overly similar to its predecessors.

This is Black Flag 2.0.
This is a worthy successor to one of the best games of the franchise.
Rogue is described as many things; a cheap lower-end alternative to Ubisoft's attempt to pander to both generations of consoles, a short story set in between games in a similar manner to Freedom Cry or Liberation, a simple sidestory given better quality through asset and game mechanic reuse.
It's kind of all of those things, and also none of them. Yes, it was slid under the rug when Unity was first released, but it ended up being more critically acclaimed for better story and gameplay. Yes, it does reuse assets from Black Flag, but the assets are used in ways that seem new and interesting, and the change in scenery really does make this game work. Finally, it is true that it is rather short for an Assassin's Creed game - less than eight chapters long - but the Kenway Saga that it concludes makes it more than worth it.
In conclusion, if you don't mind the familiar tinge from Black Flag, Rogue is an excellent all rounded Assassin's Creed game, and is definitely worth the price.

Oh boy. The Elder Scrolls IV: Oblivion. This game blew my mind. Possibly one of the greatest open-world fantasy games of all time.
This game is rich and wonderful. Each quest is unique and exciting, from working for the brawny Fighter's Guild to helping solve a mystery of a suspicious merchant. I'm serious--every quest is a brand new, unpredictable adventure. From slaying vampires, to carrying out morally gray tasks for evil gods, to robbing the Imperial Palace itself, this game takes you almost everywhere you dreamed of going in a fantasy world.
The voice acting is solid albeit they re-use a lot of voice actors. The writing is pretty decent with some really memorable moments.
The combat is a little lacking but it's bearable.
Now the environments are really exciting and fun to explore--the first time. But after playing for a few hours, you start to notice "Oh, I've been in this cave before." (As in, they literally copy and paste a cave design and re-use it somewhere else. It's terrible.) Or you think "Oh God, ANOTHER Oblivion gate." (Yes, SOMEHOW they made breaking into Hell and killing demons on their own turf into a boring chore.)
Now for some more bad: the game is also incredibly simple despite how fun and vivid it is. Short swords, long-swords, two-handed swords, and daggers are all ONE skill, simply titled "Blade." 1H axes, 2H axes, maces, warhammers, are all just "Blunt." Really? Like... really? How do you compress that much into two skills? At the very least, give us "Short Blade, Long Blade" and "Axes" and "Maces." Like, please? Also the "Speechcraft" skill is pretty useless and the concept of Speechcraft in this game is a total joke anyway.
Also one beef I have with the game is that it doesn't restrict you at all--which is a good thing for some, but not for me. I like my ROLE-PLAYING GAMES to be, you know, role-playing. Does it make sense that a vampiric assassin from the Dark Brotherhood is welcomed with open arms by the Nine Divines in their temples and churches? Or that a barbaric daedra worshipper is allowed to become Archmage of the Mage's Guild? The game just doesn't seem to care who you are, except that you're the "Hero of Kvatch" and let's you do whatever you want. Which is good, because it allows you to play as a "one character fits all" sort, but it's a little immersion-breaking.
Also the game's leveling system is totally crap. The game levels up with you, so you're never in over your head if you know what you're doing. You can literally become the Arena Grand Champion at level 1.
But those issues still aren't enough to stop this game from being amazing. I mean it. The Guild questlines are absolutely THRILLING. The Daedra quests are unique in their quests themselves and the quest-givers. Of course, every quest in Oblivion is really different but there's a whole different flavor with the Daedra that make them special and really stand out--of course, when you're doing the dirty work of evil gods, how could it be anything but special?
So, seriously, buy this game. Pick up your sword. Chop up some vampires. Serve evil gods. Become a mercenary. Save the world from hellish monsters. Save a man from a cursed painting by jumping inside it.
Even with all of its faults, absolute 5/5. The good parts outshine the bad, without a doubt.

It's not a bad game by any means, but it just doesn't measure up. I've played the first couple of Halo games, and I feel like this game just doesn't have the polish of the originals. I was having a hard time telling, at first, why I got the "Mission Failed" prompt, because it's hard to tell when you've died. You die, and before you can tell, the prompt immediately covers the screen.
You don't earn things by accumulating experience, either. You spend it like money on items on a mission to mission basis, and you don't retain the weapons or other items you've previously purchased. Each level has a specific loadout it wants you to use, and you have to spend kind of a lot on items. On top of that, you don't have much of a choice of what you actually CAN purchase. There are three total guns, three boosters, and three shield items, and they are the same 3 options, it seems, throughout the game.
The game is very one-dimensional, as well. You are almost exclusively running and gunning all the time. There is no need--or opportunity, really--to be stealthy at any point. Melee is a delayed attack, and it's also quite weak. The auto-aiming is not very consistent, and manually aiming with an analog stick is inferior. Driving vehicles around is fun, especially with a tank, but you are quite limited in how much you can use vehicles most of the time. There are large roadblocks almost guaranteed whenever you drive a tank that prevent you from continuing with it. There are almost no opportunities to take an alternate path in the game, with or without a tank or other vehicle.
You pretty much run or drive from point A to point B for every single mission. Occasionally you have to sit and guard one area, or blast your way through a remarkably durable but ultimately destructible door. Other times you run around a slow-moving escort that you must protect from destruction. These are basically all slight variations on run-n-gun gameplay, because of the lack of strategy. Most weapons work the same way, they just look different (basically, either bullets or a colored laser/plasma projectile). The shotgun is a terrible weapon, the plasma pistol is shameful, the spartan laser is devastating, but there's little other variation.
If you want a comparison to another similar game, let's take a look at Killzone:Liberation for the PSP. It's not a GREAT game, by any means, but there's at least a little variation in the gameplay, and you unlock things that you get to keep throughout the game. There were also several different challenge modes, though most were filler. The survival mode was easily the most fun once you completed the game, because you could use the things that you continued to unlock in a Crimsonland-esque challenge. It's true, I've only spent a few hours on Halo: Spartan Assault, so maybe I'll change my tune. Personally, though, I find that a game with as little depth as either this Halo title or the Killzone title has, I should know if the game is good in a couple of hours.

Oh boy, this game is something else. I've only played it for 104 minutes as of writing, but I can tell this will be another rogue-like that I can easily sink several more hours into. The game mechanics are well laid out for you to get the hang of the basics right off the back, but has some slighter things it doesn't tell you about, such as using recoil to move around in the zero-g environment. As for weapons and equipment you start out each game with the same default loadout, and through each of the ships you can find random assortments of new weapons and consumables for you to use in your loadout. Through the 104 minutes of play I can't say I have gotten a repeated weapon or consumable drop which drives build variety, to a point.
The big learning curve about this game is that you have to purchase your equipment loadout everytime you start a level, and if you die you lose the money you spent on that loadout. This then comes to going into a level with a barebones loadout with the last of your money, hoping you can scrape by with the cheapest gear you can. This game is risk vs reward to a high degree, but even if you win a level you can still effectively lose money if your starting loadout for that level was extremely expensive. So plan appropriately, and if needed you can lower your health as a cost savings measure.
In short:
Good game, worth the $5 I spent, look forward to beating it and then playing an unreasonable amount.

Problem difficulty curves nicely, starting out with problems which introduce the architecture of the machine and ramping up from there to some rather tricky puzzles. I wasn’t much of a fan of Alientrap’s first release, Capsized, but they more than redeemed themselves with Apotheon. While both featured impressively detailed 2D art and floaty, chaotic combat, Apotheon was where they refined the formula into something satisfying. CRYPTARK then represents a further refining of their style, focusing the combat down to hectic yet manageable firefights and constructing a mysterious and threatening world for them to happen in. If not for a few technical stumbles it would be just about perfect, but almost perfect is never a bad place to land.
Drifting out in the vastness of space is an immense alien fleet, thousands of derelicts devoid of life or purpose. At the center of this fleet is the CRYPTARK, a vessel said to hold an artifact of immense importance. A mega-corporation is prepared to pay your salvage crew mega bucks to bring it back, but finding the thing is the tricky part. By capturing other craft in the fleet it should be possible to triangulate the CRYPTARK’s position, so long as you can blast your way past their automated defenses. Customizing your rig’s loadout is key to surviving these incursions, as is taking risks to secure more weapons, more funding, and the strange artifacts hidden among the derelicts.
CRYPTARK has an excellent hook for its action, and an equally excellent structure for it. For each stage of your journey you’ll select an alien ship to invade, each one procedurally-generated and filled with security systems and drones to contend with. Once you select your loadout you jet into space and into one of the ship’s many hatches and get to work. It’s entirely up to you where you enter and how you proceed to your final goal, the oddly-cerebral central core of the vessel. The combat is pure twin-stick shooting, challenging you to weave between foes and bullets while you blast back with your own ordnance.
You don’t have to fight, either. Stealth is an option if you can stay out of detection range of drones and security sensors, and some weapons are silenced to help you avoid drawing too much attention. This ability to pick your battles extends to the ship systems you’re up against, as the only one you MUST destroy is the central core. But you’ll encounter drone systems that pump out enemies, alarm and sentry systems that control security measures, lock systems that seal important passages, and plenty of others that will massively complicate your incursion. Some systems even cover for others with shields, repairs, failsafes, or cloaks. The makeup of the ship’s systems is shown when choosing your next target, and is pretty much always the most important aspect of that choice.
Money is also going to be a concern, at least in the campaign. You score cash for every derelict you seize, along with bonuses for optional objectives like leaving certain systems intact or not using supply pods to heal or gear up during the mission. That cash is spent to outfit your ship at the beginning of those missions, and some of it is lost when you die, so it’s both a resource that allows for better gear and a measure of how close you are to failure. This goes out the window in the game’s brutal Rogue mode, where your only gear is what you can scrounge from research nodes and death is final. The two modes play very differently but you’ll need to master both to find all the artifacts in the game, interesting bits of lore that serve as the true goals of your adventure.
The strategy is the big draw of the game, especially when you factor in bonuses for sticking out optional objectives or trying to score the rare artifacts which are only rewarded for completing special feats. Pushing yourself in those areas can heighten the tension and tax your problem-solving skills, but it can also frustrate due to certain aspects of the design. It’s entirely possible (and probably intentional) that situations can get completely out of control if you trip certain alarms or allow enemy factories to crank out foes. You might also run afoul of the the wicked environmental hazards which are often far too dense to navigate and battle around. And on one occasion I actually got stuck in the walls of the ship I was exploring, forcing a VERY costly restart of that mission.
These are pretty much all issues you can get past by being patient, careful, and just plain good at the game. It’s a gratifying title to work at as well, with plenty of rewards tucked away for talented explorers. The art style does it plenty of favors too, featuring vibrant colors and exacting details. Even the sound design helps immerse you in the grim, alien technology with a moody soundtrack and meaty effects. It’s a challenge to master but not hard to find the fun in, especially once you start blasting away with heavy ordnance. CRYPTARK gets a lot of mileage out of its hook and offers plenty of action and secrets to enjoy once you’re there.

This game is worth buying as long as you're aware of the multiplayer issues.
At the time of writing I've played the majority of this game with my partner who is on a different computer in the same house. The connection is very stable, with no other games demonstrating problems. I'm assuming the game is remotely hosted (no LAN), based on the problems being encountered, but if not then there's really no excuse.
Fundamentally the multiplayer works, but suffers from numerous problems. It's laggy, up to a one second response time for input in some cases. Almost unpredictably the game will pause, process for a bit, then reload the level as if a day transition had occurred. Neither of these problems are as bad as the third though.
The third problem is the desynchronisation between players. You could be playing a different game and not know it, as there's no way to know if you're out of sync. I've played for an entire in-game day not knowing that the game on my screen was different to the game on my partner's screen. Very frustrating.
If you want this for multiplayer, don't buy it yet. For singleplayer it's fine.

I wanted to like it. I tried to like it. I gave it a shot. It's just fighting me every step of the way.
First, controls aren't really great. You dig with a huge buzzsaw that carves out wide areas. Great for tunneling, terrible for constructing a factory. Then you dug a little too far? Sorry, you can only jump two blocks. You can grab an edge to pull yourself up... sometimes. Unless you're holding a crystal. So alright, build some vertical shafts to climb up, but then you run into the building trouble: Zoom.
The game zooms in and out whenever it wants to and it doesn't stop zooming quick enough. So you can stop moving, pull up the build menu, pick a room type, rotate the room on the map, hover where you want it to go, and then click to place it. Oh no, right as you clicked to build it, the screen zoomed out more, moving where you were hovering the room, so now it's built somewhere else! Ok, let's erase the room and rebuild (eating the cost). Nope, that was now a load-bearing segment, so your entire base collapses. Reload an earlier save? That's not a thing, sorry. You lost the entire day's work.
Then the actual game hits. Find ingredients (in limited quantities, farmable but very, very slowly) and shove them into soup machines. Then shove the finished soup into rockets. Get enough to have a monopoly at the end of a day to win the level and start over on another stage. There are robots that help carry some things either side-to-side (If you have perfectly level ground and don't mind waiting an ice age for them to walk) or throw things straight up (if you build the entire factory around that being helpful). Otherwise, you're on your own.
Constantly getting stranded, or having ground collapse, or digging too much with a terrible buzz tool, or building and having it shift by a square... just so I can grind for soup ingredients for brainless robots to shove into the two machines until it tells me that I beat a level. Shallow, tedious, and plagued poor controls. And that's before the unexpectedly bad performance and laggy multiplayer.

Right, Atlas Reactor is a simultaneous turn based team deathmatch like MOBA. Phew, that's a lot to say all at once- but yes, Atlas Reactor is ALL that.
The game's rules are pretty simple, first to 5 kills before the 20th turn, wins.
A variety of maps with different cover and powerup spawns help break the monotony of the same map over and over again.
The game revolves around 4 phases: "Prep", "Dash", "Blast" and "Move".
Players have around 20 seconds to make plan their moves before the phases above carry out sequentially.
In the Prep phase, certain moves can be used before anything else, these are usually skills that heal or buff/debuff players.
In the Dash phase, moves that displace either by teleportation or "running" will happen. These skills are usually used to either close the distance between yourself and the enemy, or used to dodge attacks if you think they are going to hit you in the Blast phase.
In the Blast phase, all attacks will be carried out- moves that displace targets such as Big Bang will all happen at the same time after all normal attacks are completed.
In the Move phase, players may reposition themselves if they wish, or they may choose not to move at all.
As it stands now, this game plays wonderful. A few visual bugs here and there aren’t game breaking, just a little funny. However the UI does take a while to get used to- but once you do, be glad that it gives you as much information as it can without taking up too much space.

Some of the remaining puzzles are pretty hard, and I didn't feel inclined to solve them because:
There is no space to write any comments.  There should be space on every single line to write a comment.  I'd walk away to get something to eat and come back and it would take a while to remember what I was trying to do.
Just trying to swap 2 numbers to solve e.g. the sorting puzzle is next to impossible because of the very limited instruction set.  An insert sort can be done in 3 lines of C code, but forget trying to do an insert sort on a TIS-100.
The multiple CPUs running in parallel is interesting although you only ever get to use 12 at most.  Most of those 12 will be running idle though because in many cases you will be using them merely as memory storage, since there are no OP codes to access RAM.  So in the end you only ever write 1 or maybe 2 threaded programs that can only use a couple of variables,  There are real computers out there with a similar architecture to the TIS-100 (e.g. Adapteva Epiphany) and solving the given puzzles on one of those would be a lot easier, and you'd be learning a real computer instead of a fake one.

This is a fantastic game. It's obviously inpired by programming for old processors like the Z-80. But there are a few things that make this something very different than a Z-80 simulator.
1. The instruction set is *very* limited, mainly because there's no numeric "representation". So no rotates or shifts; no bitwise instructions. It's all just adding and subtracting integers.
2. There are just two registers that you can store values in -- and one of these you can only access indirectly. Not a lot to keep track of.
3. The machine consists of multiple processors that send numbers to each other in a very simple way. So a lot of the problems are ways of making numbers flow around. I feel like I'm only starting to grasp how this can be exploited to solve the problems.
My only complaint about the game is that I'd like to be able to see some kind of global leaderboards or metrics, so I'd know if my solutions were decent. The leaderboards in the game apparently include Steam friends, but if you don't have a lot of friends that are into this kind of thing, it's kind of lonely ;).

Honestly, you should know already whether you want to play a game about writing code to pass unit tests in a minimalist (but not strictly minimal*) assembly language for a stream processing architecture with no physical implementation or professional utility. Therefore, I will primarily address the few remaining issues.
No, the developer is not running a scam or otherwise objectionable.
* Specifically, it does have more jump instructions than strictly necessary, both subtraction and negation, and some pseudoports. These improve the optimization possibilities drastically and the "power" of the language quite slightly. It also has comments, labels, and human-readable names for instructions and ports because it's an exercise in cleverness, not cruelty.
: The game has no time pressure ever. The interface uses both the keyboard and a pointer. The interface doesn't require great precision with the pointer, but it does require entering a fair bit of text. There are no vital sound-only cues. No lines are voiced; all dialogue is presented in text. Only the puzzles involving the graphics module rely solely on color for identification; specfically, there's a single shade of red in addition to white, black, and two greys. It's visible in one of the screenshots on the store page. As a non-expert, I see only minor problems except for the blind, who could only possibly play with both an OCR-capable screenreader and immense patience.

This game has one of the best Free to Play models out there, all the premium currency really is for is fashion, speeding up crafting, getting fully built items & frames from the market, and trading. Some people will look at this game as another typical MMO cash grab game, but it's a lil more than that.
The lore can be vague at first glance, but if you dig a little deeper, you can see what it all reveals about the factions, history of this golden empire known as the Orokin, and other aspects of backstories. That's if you're willing to look into the lore of Warframe and not just play it for the gameplay.
Speaking of which, the gameplay itself is pretty fun. There are many weapons to choose from to annihlate your enemies with, such as assualt rifles, pistols, shotguns, swords...you name it. With even more weapons added to the arsenal to this day.
Customization is pretty up there with cosmetics for your frames, companions, and weapons. The ammount of color to choose from is vast, but you will have to unlock those palletes via Platnium. Fear not though, there are seasonal color palletes that appear on certain holidays, downside is you have to wait for those holidays.
Missions vary by a few, such as Exterminate, Capture, and Defense to name a few. After awhile on playing the same mission type over and over again, you'll get bored, that's why you can create challenges for yourself. Such as melee only stealth Exterminate.
That's as much as I can say, the rest you'll have to look for yourself, but overall, this is a great game to try out by a great company of developers.

Warframe is one of the most successful free to play game at the moment. Everything in the game, excluding Tennogen cosmetics (player created items that can be bought through Steam with real money only) can be acquired through gameplay. The ingame currency, Platinum, can be freely traded among players for almost any kind of items, and one can never put a dime in Warframe and still have thousands of Platinum through careful trading (and thousands of hours of play, lets face it).
Although a bit repetitive, the game being essentially doing and redoing small missions over and over (even though the mission types differ, after the first few hundreds it starts to lack interest, and I have done more than 5000 as I speak), it shines through its pristine controls, with perfect movements.
With the new area released, Plains of Eidolon, Warframe adds a bigger and more open world map to its content, hopefully  trying to fix the repetitiveness of the game (although bounties are essentially miniature missions and is definitely boring).
Probably the biggest incovenient of the game right now for me is the lack of super high level missions. Sure, you can get that level 80-100 Sortie mission each day, or you can stay 60+ minutes in a starting level 40 defense or survival mission to start seeing level three digits enemies, but we want a whole planet full of different kind of missions, all at least 100. When you play for quite some time, have finally gotten most of the good weapons's rivens with godlike stats, can rip through level 145 enemies in a few shots in Simulacrum, we want to test field these weapons in actual missions. Level 120 defenses, level 150 exterminates, this is what we want. A challenge.

If you liked Assassin's Creed 4: Black Flag, here's more of it!
In a way similar to what Brotherhood or Revelations were to AC2, this game uses the exact same engine and gameplay mechanics as AC4, but takes place elsewhere and also adds a lot of new gimmicks and side activities. For example, since you play a Templar, you have sidequests to protect assassination targets instead of killing them. You get a silenced rifle for the sleep/berserk darts, with an extra dart type to detonate explosive barrels or attract attention to where it was shot. You also get a grenade launcher that has explosive/sleep/berserk grenades. All of this is fun to use to fool around with the enemies, who mostly aren't a challenge (unless you're always trying to not get spotted).
Piracy, whaling, hunting and crafting are back, diving is gone, those super ships are in again, there's a lot more areas to explore and convoys to raid, ship weapons are mostly the same, there's more types of collectibles, and the British soldiers are your friends this time (sort of).
Like AC4, it's not a game that's very concerned with stealth. There's the occasional (side) objective to not get spotted, but you can generally kill a whole street worth of dudes to escape.
One annoying addition to the game: hidden assassins. You'll hear whispers growing louder as you approach an assassin who's hidden in the bushes, on the roof, or in a crowd. If you come too close, they'll dart out and stab you, then run away again. There's a LOT of these dudes, but fortunately if you kill them, they stay gone.
Story-wise, it takes place between AC4 and AC3, and uses characters from both. I assume it would be pretty hard to follow if you hadn't played both AC3 and 4 before. There's a visit to another AC game later on, but it's more of a cameo. It's an absolutely non-essential story if that's all you're here for, but then they've all kind of felt like that since Ezio's trilogy ended. The way the main character defects from the Assassins and how steadfast he is in remaining with the Templars are kind of wonky, as is the main character's Irish accent. Thematically it's a new spin on things, with you hunting down your old associates, but not enough time was spent with them beforehand to really have that make an impact.
The meta-story takes place in the same setting AC4 did; Abstergo Entertainment - a Templar front company. I don't think you're the same character from AC4, but it's not that clear. While AC4's meta-story had hints of what happened to the First Civilization, this one doesn't. It's honestly not essential either, but the documents you find do flesh out the backstory somewhat.
So if you want more AC4, here you go. If you want the next evolution in Assassin's Creed mechanics, or a story that feels like more than a stopgap, look into Assassin's Creed Unity (pretty underrated from what I've played so far).
