Snagged the game from a recent humble bundle, and I'd say it pretty well was worth the entire cost of the package from the fun I've had. The gist of the game is it's a twinstick shooter through procedurally generated levels with the only requirement to beating each one being to destroy the level's core.
There are, of course, obstacles to keep you from doing that. Shields that you need to destroy the generators of, monster factories, turrets, and locked doors, to name a few. You can disable or destroy each of these by blowing up the system controlling them, making the rest of your time in that level easier, though apart from the shield generators they can usually be ignored if you wish.
The other obstacle-in the main mode, at least- is your budget. Everything costs money. Having a higher max HP, however much ammo you want to bring with you, extra items like health packs, turret drones, or spare keys, all cost money, and if you aren't careful, can go over whatever reward cash you might get from completing a level. You can increase the reward money you get from a ship by either completing various optional objectives, which can range from destroy/keep certain systems, keep your max HP under a certain amount, don't use a certain weapon type, or keep your expenses for that level under a certain amount. What's more, if you can complete all of a level's side objectives, you get even more bonus cash.
Apart from that, there are also artifacts which spawn in different types, or difficulty level of levels, and are usually harder to complete than the normal side objectives. Doing so however unlocks a small bit of lore, and can be used to unlock different types of suits to use while playing, or different paintjobs for those suits.
There's another game mode apart from the main campaign called, appropriately, rogue. Instead of choosing and planning your attack on each level and equipping for it, you run a marathon blitz through them from start to finish, scavenging weapons you find to replace the ones that run out of ammo, and making what you have work. There's another "game mode" after rogue, but it's only a single level than an actual campaign or anything.
Difficulty-wise, the game is rather easy to complete. Even in rogue mode where you have less control over your equipment once you learn what to attack first and what weapons you're best off using, it's relatively simple to systematically go around and take down each level piecemeal. The biggest challenge I had was with some of the artifacts in campaign mode, since they required a very bare-bones loadout, or left me with practically no health. But planning those levels out and winning by the skin of my teeth was some of the most exhilarating fun I had with the game.
Overall, the game is amazing. It's fun to play, it's fun to listen to, and it's certainly worth the fifteen dollars if you want a fun twinstick game to sit down and play.

First, I like this game.
Second, it goes against my principles of F2P so I can't recommend it.
You see, I don't agree with the idea of a F2P game with a PvP focus causing an imbalance between players to make money. In this game new players only have a short-medium range cannon, no support weapons, an incredibly weakly armored hull, and almost no chance against anyone who's been playing for more than a few hours longer.
Now their idea is that you eventually win enough (or participate enough if your team's new too) until you can afford all the shiny gadgets that let you compete with the people who've been playing longer. Or you pay $20 to get it. I don't agree with that system because it gives new players a big visible wall between them and everyone else and makes them more reliant on the gear than on their own skill levels.
They could've avoided most of my criticisms by giving new players a balanced starter hull and the machine gun support weapon (okay slight bias here cause I love that thing). That would give players something to work with and shift the focus of failure from the gear to the player's skill level. More importantly they'd stick around longer.
Other then that I feel like this game needs an early access tag. Too few game modes and maps.

Windforge is a pretty interesting game in 2D exploration/building genre, which could be great if it didn’t suffer from bugs, certain annoying mechanics, and general feeling of unfinishingness.
The main unique feature of Windforge is that you travel around the world in entirely customizable airship. Everything you add to your airship in Windforge affects its performance: propellers determine its speed, balloons help the airship stay afloat and rise, turrets are used in combat, engines are required to power other devices, and even blocks and cosmetic furniture matter in that they weight your ship down.
Unlike games like Terraria or Starbound, Windforge's focus is almost entirely on exploration and fighting rather than building: in fact, you will likely only build your airship, as there’s no point of building a house. Windforge also has almost no decorative items, and most of decorations it does have are not actually available for player to make or collect and place on their airship or house.
When it comes to combat, the challenge is average at best. While enemies can be dangerous during early to early-mid game, the AI is terrible, which is particularly noticeable in ship combat: it is too easy to outmaneuver and destroy even much stronger AI ship. But certain enemies, like krakens or large dragons can still present a danger to you or your ship through mid-game. Bosses are also a disappointment: they generally have similar attacks and attack patterns, and like most enemies suffer from terrible AI.
Aside from poor AI, another glaring negative is that the world design is rather bland. Random locations are very similar: they are all just collections of floating islands, occasionally with ruins on them. The only reason to visit them is to mine ore or collect recipes from the ruins: you won’t be visiting a new location wondering what you might find there. And it doesn’t help that you spend much of the game travelling through these similar locations, typically having to travel through over 10 locations to get from one quest location to another.
Also, unfortunately, there are a lot of bugs and glitches. Officially Windforge isn’t in Early Access, but it certainly feels like it is – with exception that the work on it has stopped. Most notable is that blocks can glitch through each other during collision, like when airship falls atop another, or to the ground, making it hard to dismantle fallen airship. Physical model is also glitches sometimes, making an airship or whale’s body suddenly fly up or sideward, or bounce on spot. And game’s save/load system also has a number of bugs and exploits, like player’s ability to replenish breathing air by saving and then loading game, or how freshly killed enemies revive after loading (with minimal HP, that allows easy double kill), though these can mostly be avoided by the player.
But overall, I’d say that Windforge is quite an interesting game, despite its bugs and other shortcomings. If you are looking for more combat/adventure-orientated take on Terraria/Starbound, you may give Windforge a try.

The very existence of this game proves that European developers are no pushovers. I have played through the fallout games and the only one that comes close to the level of enjoyment S.T.A.L.K.E.R: CoP is Fallout: New Vegas (This is only my personal opinion, so dont take it as solid fact). This game focuses more on realism over the crazy over the top features like some other games. Your not going to get a death ray that kills everything in one hit or a tactical nuke launcher, but the game doesnt need it and it might be even better this way. Their are of course downsides for a game as great as this, so I will list off what I have found in my 100+ hours of gameplay. Some things you should know before playing: There is player storage at Skadovsk, Yanov Station, and the Pripyat main area. Make sure to keep your guns and armor in good condition. Offload your loot often, when you get overencumbered it will take a lot longer to get to somewhere far away. one shot to the head doesnt always mean dead. be prepared for new enemies that are rediculously powerful and hard to kill, so bring grenades and a shotgun if you can.
Pros:
-The graphics are good enough so that even those who can't stand anything under HD could still find the game enjoyable
-It has a host of weapons that cater to different playstyles (Pistols, Shotguns, Assault Rifles, Sniper Rifles, etc.)
-The gunplay is enjoyable and the enemy AI is good enough to keep you on your toes even after multiple encounters with them
-The replayability of the game is high, especially with the Complete Mod
-The environments are varied and nice to look at
-different faction choices can lead to different items and characters available for the player to experience (i.e: the Friend of Duty and Friend of Freedom achievements)
-the game does not serve items to you on a silver plater, it's not going to tell you how to kill such and such or who can give you what. Their is no "tutorial level", you are dropped in and it's up to you to learn what is what.
-The difficulty curve is "comfortable", if the game is just a little to tough, the lower difficulty settings soften up the game a little
-The atmosphere is immersive and will manage to unnerve you at times. Even with a 12 gauge and grenades, you will still be hesitant to enter a dark building with growling noises coming from inside.
-If you like the Cheeki Breeki iv Damke, you will not be disappointed.
-Most glitches are hilarious, such as the stalker in the medical office in Skadovsk randomly floating in and out of bed, or having people randomly walk in rapid circles, once a feral dog even managed to get inside Skadovsk after I slept.
Cons:
-The game can be a little buggy, I recommend saving every so often (about once every 5-30 minutes). The game is by no means unstable, but it will crash every so often. (Note: it could have just been my computer)
-Their is a lot of information to digest at the beginning, especially involving the controls. If you assume the game will play like a modern fallout game, where you basically have shoot, reload, throw grenade, and aim (not including hotkeys), you'll have another thing coming to you. S.T.A.L.K.E.R: CoP has: A button for reloading, switching ammo types, switching fire modes, firing, aiming, pulling out your detector, using a bolt, using a knife, and switching Night Vision on and off. This may seem daunting, but if you play enough you should be able to get used to this, maybe an hour at most. A mouse with more than 2 buttons will definitely help with this if you can afford one.
-some sections of the game may take more than one try to complete, if you like to play on a medium to high difficulty level, but expect to coast through the whole game, you may find the game a little difficult or annoying to complete. If some parts are a little to hard, there is no shame in reducing difficulty to enjoy the game more.
-Unlike the modern Fallout games with their radio to help curb bordom on the road, S.T.A.L.K.E.R: CoP has no such thing. The closest you will get is the occasional hostile encounter, or Stalker campsite. This does not explicitly make it a bad game, it can just feel like much of the same when you have to go from point A to point B multiple times over a long playthrough.
-Enemies can encircle a "safe zone" you are in, which can seem like a cheap trick when you have to jump off of the top of Skadovsk or sprint away to avoid roaming packs of Feral dogs or other mutants surrounding the area. It can get a little annoying if you are underpowered and you have to wait for the stalkers and bandits patrolling around the ship to finish them off to avoid losing half your health.
-If you expect the game to help you take your first baby steps and tell you what to do, this is probably not the game for you. You might actually find the game aggravating if you are not prepared to learn from scratch.
-Owl will get annoying fast, real fast. Hearing him say "What are you, a statue?" or "Dont let the door hit you on the way out!" will get annoying after you hear it for the first time. It gets no better the millionth time as he says it almost if not every single time you approach and leave.
In general, I give this game a 10/10 as it has not failed to bring enjoyment every time I play, and it surpassed my expectations. This is a hidden gem of a game series and is woefully far from the mainstream. If you like fallout, or games with decomposing environments, good gunplay and an overall challenge, this is probably the game for you.

The S.T.A.L.K.E.R. series is all good, but this one is my personal favourite. I'm really into the quests this game has, they're all pretty interesting and fun for the most part, even if to a degree they usually boil down to 'go here kill these guys take this loot'. This is one of those 'budget' games which can be hard to get past if you're one of those weirdos who can't take a little jankiness in a game.
Call of Pripyat is just kind of flawed, like the rest of the series, but it's an honest flawed. It's a little hard to describe, but the issues with the game are mostly the dated graphics, the awkward animations and FPS combat, and perhaps the occasional crash. I've had my saves corrupted in the past, leading me to have to start all over again but I really don't know the cause of those.
One of the most impressive parts about the S.T.A.LK.E.R. series is that these guys made their own engine. They're not just hawking another Unreal Engine 3 game or something like that, they actually made their own engine, while building games with it all the way. I don't know if it's that good of an engine, but I sure do like that it doesn't seem to much have loading screens, it does open worlds very well, and I can tell you right now that despite it being made by a group of slavs with spit, prayers and duct tape it's even still a better engine than that Gamebryo crap Bethesda is still using.
Pick it up some time if you can get it on sale, I wouldn't pay full price for it I don't think since it doesn't ooze the polish that would make it worth $20 USD to me, but $10 USD? Definitely. I've spent a lot of time playing this game, though my Steam hours might not reflect it.

There are games with mixed reviews that are meh, or bland, or generally bad.  Windforge is not one of those.  You will either hate it because you don't connect with it, or you'll love it and wish there were more of it.
This is one of my favorite games of all time.  I picked it up in a bundle and didn't look at it twice for months, but when I finally did play it I got sucked in for a week and a half.  It ate my entire holiday break in winter of 2014.  Why am I only reviewing it now?  I noticed some screenshots I took back then and got nostalgic for it again.
Don't get me wrong; it's not a big-budget game from a professional game studio, or even a highly-polished indie offering.  It's a first solo project from a tiny game contract house (I think maybe one developer?).  It's a little awkward, imbalanced, has some pretty major engine flaws, the AI is pretty weak and large parts of the story feel missing or unfinished.
But if you can get past that, it's a very satisfying little crafting adventure game sandbox with a side of RPG with a power curve that's pretty satisfying when you earn the upper ranks.  It's a slow build, first teaching you how to build and repair a ship, then sending you on some quests, but by the end you'll be a swashbuckling pirate ransacking enemy airships or a spelunking archaelogist digging up treasures in the murky depths of an ancient temple, or taming flying beasts to ride into battle, or an armed-to-the-teeth space marine, or most likely all of the above.
I really wish the game had more success; it's a hidden, underrated gem with a lively steampunk world that deserves some DLC to fill it out, or a remake or a sequel.
If you get a chance to pick this up in a bundle or a sale, it's well worth it.  Or if you like weird, unpolished indie games like Valley Without Wind, or even the early Minecraft Beta.

If you're looking for a game review you've come to the wrong place. But if youre looking for a fantastic ravioli recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients
- To Make the Dough
375 grams (3 cups) plain flour
1/2 teaspoon salt
2 eggs
1/4 cup (50 ml / 3½ tablespoons) olive oil
1/2 cup (120 ml / 8 tablespoons) water
Extra flour for dusting
- To Make Cheese Filling
15 ounces (425 grams) container Ricotta cheese
5 ounces (142 g/about 1/2 cup plus 2 tablespoons) "3 Cheese Italian Blend" (Parmesan, Romano & Asiago)
Note: grate these cheeses yourself and create your own custom blend.
1/2 cup cheddar cheese
2 eggs, lightly beaten
1/2 teaspoon salt
1/2 teaspoon pepper
- Extras
Your favorite sauce for the ravioli (i.e. marinara/ marijuana)
Parmesan cheese
Basil
Fried vegetables
Shrimp
Fish slices
Chicken pieces
Make the Ravioli filling.
- In a small mixing bowl, add the ricotta and mash with a fork.
- Add in the 3-cheese blend, Cheddar cheese, eggs, salt, and pepper.
- Mix all ingredients thoroughly until you have a smooth, paste-like consistency.
- Cover the bowl with plastic wrap and place it in the refrigerator for about 30 minutes.
Make the Ravioli dough.
- Crack eggs into a large mixing bowl and beat them with a fork. Add water, oil, and salt. Mix.
- Add 1 cup flour to the bowl. Use a fork to mix the flour with the eggs, water, oil, and salt. Repeat with the rest of the flour. Mix until a smooth dough is formed.
- Clear and clean off a large work surface and dust it with flour. This is where you are going to roll out your dough.
- Take the dough out of the mixing bowl, shape it into a ball, and place it on your work surface. Knead for at least 10 minutes or until it becomes elastic.
- Dust a rolling pin with flour to prevent the dough from sticking. Roll out the dough until it is about 1/8 inch (1/3 cm) thick, or about the thickness of 2 stacked quarters.
- With a cookie cutter or upside-down water glass, cut out circles in the dough (will make about 15-20 dough circles).
- Ball up the unused dough and either roll it out and make a couple more raviolis, or wrap it and put in the freezer for another time. Dough can keep for weeks when frozen. Just make sure to wrap well so that it doesn’t suffer from freezer burn or absorb freezer odor.
Fill the Ravioli shells.
- Take the ravioli filling out of the refrigerator and place a tablespoon of it in middle of a dough.
- Fill a small bowl with water, dip your fingers in, and moisten around the outer edge of the dough circle.
- Fold the dough in half over the filling, making a half-moon shape. Be sure all the filling stays inside. Pinch the edges together and then seal the edges of the ravioli with a fork. Make sure to press firmly and go all the way around. This will add a “homemade” touch as well.
- Repeat this process for all your dough circles.
- Dust the finished ravioli with flour to keep them from sticking together.
Form the Shells and Fill Using a Ravioli maker.
- Roll the dough into two sheets
- Place one sheet on the ravioli maker, and form the filling cups.
- Fill with the ravioli mixture.
- Lay the second sheet of dough on top, and roll it out. This will seal in the filling.
- Remove and separate the finished raviolis.
Cook the Ravioli.
- Fill a large pot with water and bring to a boil.
- Place the ravioli in boiling water for 5-6 minutes, or until they float. You can also test for doneness by nibbling on the edges to test.
- If you don't want to make all the ravioli at one time, you can freeze the rest
- Take ravioli out of boiling water with large slotted spoon and place on warmed plates
Serve it up.
Top with your favorite sauce, grate some fresh cheese over it, and enjoy!

After having a not-so-pleasant experience with an early access game purchased earlier this week, I was very delighted to find that this game was extremely well-polished for still being in early access. In fact, the only thing keeping this game from being released already is just more puzzles -- note, this doesn't mean there isn't enough content to purchase the game already; the puzzles are not easy puzzles that can be completed within a few minutes. In order to play through this game, thinking is crucial. While many other puzzle games strive for this, TIS-100 is the only puzzle game that I can say truly forces you to think outside the box. Although this game might not be for you if you're not a fan of hard-thinking, concentration, and patience, it's really great fun for people looking for a challenging puzzle game that will have them stumped on every level. The developers have taken a very minimalist concept and created a fantastic game out of it. Throughout the game you'll find yourself trying to figure out how you've botched up the current level, only to realize that you completely overthought the entire problem and that the solution was right under your nose all along, which leaves you with a wonderful feeling of success as soon as you've finished it.
For you programmers out there: I cannot recommend this game enough. It teaches you great debugging skills and complex logic, as well as how to hack the crap out of such a simple machine.

An absolutely brilliant work. Simple, but brilliant.
The problems are inially easy, simple to solve. However, they become harder, and you must be prepared to spend a lot of time coming up with solutions, and fixing them when you inevitably discover your soluion contains countless bugs! There are many different ways to solve a problem, but some have lower cycle time, some have lower instruction count, and some are simpler but slower. This inherintly means even if you solve a problem, you have plenty of reason to go back and ... optimize.
This game's not for everyone. There are no flashy graphics, or cool music, and the story, although reflective of your experience playing the game, is nothing to write home about. All this game contains is logic puzzles, albiet in a nicely presented way. If you like those sorts of things, you'll like the game, otherwise, all you'll find is headaches and frustration!
Conclusion : For 6 dollars, it's a good pickup if you like logic puzzle games.

This game appealed to me because not only is it cheap, it has a style that isn't made too often nowadays.
Abduction Bit bills itself as an NES-style arcade platformer, somewhat similar to Ice Climber and Bubble Bobble.
However, if you know your gaming history, this is nothing like a NES game at all. If you grew up with consoles, this is much more like what you'd find on a Colecovision. Or if you were more into 8-bit computers, like something you'd find on an Atari 800, MSX, or Commodore 64. In other words, think of this as a pre-NES platformer.
The best way to describe this game is that if you put Donkey Kong, Montezuma's Revenge, and Bubble Bobble in a blender, this is what you'd have. There's one touch deaths, precise jumps needed, and a particular sense of timing.
You are an alien who must incapacitate some humans with lasers -- you have to be very careful with your laser because it takes time to charge. After they're incapacitated, you must touch them -- which will get them transported to your flying saucer. You have to freeze them up when they're close because the humans are only incapacitated for a few seconds. If they touch you or shoot you, you die.
This game uses a basic colour palette with black background overlaid on a 4:3 TV approximation with scanlines. The game it resembles most is Montezuma's Revenge.
I have mixed feelings about the approach. The 4:3 approximation actually reminds me of what I'd see on 8-bit computers when they were using an FM modulator. However, the scanlines look nothing like what I'd see from a CRT display. Ironically, most modern games have a hard time emulating CRTs of old -- there's a reason I still keep a 15-year-old TV for my Sega Genesis.
Be that as it may, I do like the graphics. Pixel art is a big fad right now, but developers always seem to dip into the well of NES/SNES allusions. So I'm happy the developer was inspired by an earlier era of gaming, one which younger generations may be oblivious about.
This is the worst aspect of Abduction Bit. The sounds effects are shrill. Just the act of walking is annoying as hell.
I don't know why the developer went with such a basic approach to sound effects. 8-bit machines of this era had great sound. Take a listen to the SID chip of the C64 or the PoKEY chip of the Atari 800. Even the Colecovision was capable of playing decent chiptunes.
Frankly, I feel this was a missed opportunity for Abduction Bit. A good soundtrack could have taken it over the op. Instead, I had to mute the whole thing.
The game advertises itself as having full controller support but I wasn't able to get it to work with either a Steam or Xbox 360 controller. So instead I used a keyboard.
Thankfully, the keyboard is a breeze. You use the arrow keys for movement, "z" to jump", and "x" to shoot.
All the same, you're going to have to be extremely tight with how you move because this game is unforgiving. It's easy to make the wrong jump or shoot at the wrong time. This game has one touch deaths, and if you run out of lives, you have to start from the very beginning. There's no checkpoints in a game like this.
One of the great myths about PC gaming is that you need an expensive rig to play new games. What isn't often mentioned is that PC is the best format to play indie retro games -- and these games don't require high end hardware. For those of us who want to play new games that utilize a retro style, PC is the promised land.
Abduction Bit is one such game. It isn't exactly authentic. The art is accurate, but the scanlines not so. As for the sound, it's awful.
However, the gameplay is wonderful. If Abduction Bit had existed in the 80s, it would have found a good home on my C64. Or hell, if it was an arcade game, I would have welcomed it in my local pizza shop.
This is recommended if you love early platformers.

I will say this first, the gameplay is solid but I can't recommend the game myself. Personally, I can't enjoy a game that is "Pay for quality of life." Want to simply be able to store items? Want to be able to color your vehicle a color other than a few basic ones? $10. I can look past the color limit, however stupid it is, but the fact you can't store items means you better enjoy playing one type of vehicle as long as you play the game. On top if this, you can't use loadouts which is 100% pay-for-advantage. People can pull a gun to counter you and you can do nothing about it. There is also no "Try" option for parts so you'll buy something to find out you hate it and really hate the game for it, even more so when you're new with very little stuff.
It also doesn't help that the new player experence isn't very good. You're given vehicle and one way to play in a game that's about being able being able to make many different ways to play. What? Point is you'll be grinding it a lot until you can get something you want. On top of this you're given 0 support weapons so players with a real load out are about 2x as strong as you are.
Now as I said at the start, the gameplay is pretty solid, though I don't see it as a long term game myself as rounds started too feel a little too similar, but playing with just one type of vehicle feels a little boring (Which you will basically have to do if you want to play for free).
Overall, is it bad? No, but the limited gear space is what's really holding the game back. If it was $5 for unlimited parts, I'd maybe give it more of a shot but I can't see myself spending $10 on this when I could get way better value.

this is a hell of a hidden gem of a game - it's a twin stick shooter style game done in a nice nin offensive 2D style that works well with this type of game - the basic premise is you salvage old and wrecked spaceships using your upgradable suit to enter the derelict crafts and turn off their security sustems so the plebs can go in and salvage it - once the central core is shut down - job done -
except it's not job done really - the game actually has a lot of depth to it - and if you just try to play it like a bullet hell game firing all cylinders then you will die - a lot -

This game got a bum rap when it first came out. There were bugs, and game review sites were not kind. But the devs kept at it, and did a good amount of patching in the months following the game's release. By the time I got it, everything seemed to be in order and I had a blast with it. The guts of the game are that you're an airship captain trying to figure out why the sky whales (yes!) are disappearing. It falls solidly into the Terraria 2D crafting genre, but rather than building a base, digging like crazy, and exploring the depths, you're going to spend a lot of time flying around, desigining ships, and getting into lots of air combat, which is both fun and hilarious.
That's not to say the game is perfect. The animations are a little weird, and clicking on things is sometimes inaccurate because of the faux three-dimensional appearance of the game. And combat can get frustrating sometimes. But the world is interesting and has a neat backstory. And the setting is so cool, with different layers of the cloud world having different styles and effects, and the flying whales are just awesome. The whale fat adds bouyancy, and can be added to your airships, allowing for truly bizarre ship designs if you're so inclined.
For the price, there's plenty of fun to be had here, and it's markedly better than a number of other entries that came in the wake of Terraria's success. And it has a real story that can be completed, giving some structure to what's normally a formless sandbox genre. So if you're looking for a Terraria-like game with a unique twist, try this one out.

Atlas Reactor is complex, and has a steep learning curve, but it is fun once you get into it. It's a bit like X-COM, so I'm told, In that it's turn-based and you control a character with a set of abilities that have their own cooldowns, but you only control one character at a time in an evenly matched, compettitive-style setting that reminds me of MOBAs.
The character design and music is great, as is the asthetic of the maps you play on. It's intriguing and makes me want to know more about this funky, futuristic world these characters exist in.
One thing I didn't find in this game (you might want to look into it on your own) is any sort of in-game economy to purchase heroes (or freelancers as they're called in Atlas Reactor). I guess you have to just rely on the free rotation or pay about $30 to unlock all heroes in perpetuity. If you play it and find this is the sort of thing you're looking to spend a lot of time with, I'd say it's worth it.
Also, it's more fun with friends. You can plan and coordinate attacks on each turn, which is really important as you have to predict a lot of what the enemy is doing in order to be effective. There's also provision for voice chat if you want to integrate Discord, so you can strategize with strangers you are matched up with, if they've done so too.
I had fun, and will likely return to this. Try it out at no risk and see what you think. GLHF

Probably one of the best works of Paradox. Contrary to the other titles in the Grand Strategy genre, Crusader Kings II puts emphasis on personal relations, instead of the usual inhuman/transcendental/immortal figure of nations.
This can lead to fun (YMMV) situations such as preparing for an heir to claim a kingdom, by accumulating gold for mercenaries, building up keeps and hiring the best generals... only to have him die of a disease at the last minute. I pesonally like this style for being the best representation of how human politics worked in medieval times; history being full of examples of situations such as the one I described.
Although this difference from other games is very well responsible for a slightly (again, YMMV) steep learning curve, where the meaning of archaic terms such as "demesne" need to become part of your vocabulary, and in the beggining you may have a "how the heck am I supposed to use marriages?" attitude. An honorable mention must go the subrealms mechanic, in which your vassals are sort of their own countries - sometimes growing so powerful they can conquer foreign realms by themselves.
Although the game's mechanics aren't really difficult to learn, this does mean that the game isn't for everyone, in the sense that not everyone has the patience and time to learn the nuances of the game. In my opinion, though it is all worth it, and the game is very fun to play once you know what the heck is going on.
Bonus is the fact that the game has a huge replayability factor, with many different cultures and religions with differing mechanics (most only accessible with DLC, though) and that is without mentioning mods. Owning the game gives you access to the Paradox Forums, where most mods can be downloaded from. I can personally attest to the the Game of Thrones Mod and the After the End mod (which takes place in post-apocalyptic, feudal North America).
In conclusion, the game is good, and definetly worth the money spent. However even for Grand Starategy games it can be weird, so be aware you'll need to get used to unusual mechanics.
*YMMV = Your Mileage May Vary

Why do I like this game?
It is something that feels completly new and polished at the same time. I like games like Overwatch and LoL and XCOM so this mashup here is exactly up my alley. You have memorable characters (some derpy, some serious and most of them something in between) which all feel different to play and they are still releasing new ones. But what I love the most about this game: they follow the monetization-model of overwatch: buy once and play forever. You want some more cosmetic stuff? just level up to earn crates or buy some to get cosmetics faster. It is one of the fairest models in my opinion.
Gameplaywise I love that you only have 20sec to decide what you do. For this decision you should think about what the enemy will do and try to predict and meanwhile need to watch what your teammates try to do so you dont mess up their idea. That results in mistakes in many cases which leads to the feeling that this game is easy to learn and hard to master without being unfair to anybody. It is just one of a kind for me.
Things I think schould be improved:
Right now there are only 5 maps. Every single Map is great and has a different layout and needs different strategies but all in all some more maps would help greatly to spice things up. As you can see from my playtime: 4 maps are still good enough for many hours of play but I still wish for more.
Regarding variety: right now in ranked it feels like there are 2-3 freelancers/heroes you see in every match either banned or picked which indicates to me: heroes are not completly balanced right now. They are balanced enough that none feels completly useless but some need more effort to play well then others. But thats something LoL did not achieve in years...

I'm a huge fan of hacking/programming games.
This one? It's one of the best I've played. I'm no assembly programmer; hell, I barely ever even write in C. This was all new to me, and it is extremely challenging. The reward from accomplishing the challenge is immeasurable. Maybe it's just me, but that is what I love about programming, and this one goes in all the way, allowing you to rethink your code, optimizing it for higher scores. Writing a comparater in assembly is something that is far more difficult than what I would normally do, but just learning a method to do it based on the manual is exhilirating. Naturally, this game is not for everyone, if you can't read a brief documentation manual while you play, or can't stomach programming, I honestly can't recommend this, you won't enjoy it. However, if you feel rewarded by completing something you previously did not understand, I highly recommend this. What I'd love to see is a game like Uplink with incredibly in depth programming, kind of like this. This game is absolutely fantastic.

tl;dr: A must have for any future developer and current developer. Incredible value for the price.
Without a doubt one of the best early access games I've spent money on. TIS-100 is the game I've wanted for quite a number of years and a good introduction to low level programming. For non-cs people, low level means closer to machine language. Assembly is the lowest level language you can effectively program in. If you can't program I would very much say this game is likely not for you to be completely honest. You'll need to think like a programmer in order to complete these challenges but it is still by far the best video game to combine real programming with puzzles and should be a mandatory part of all C.S classes in the future. If you're someone who is fluent in a higher level interpreted language this should also be a mandatory game to play as you'll get a deeper understanding of how your conditional statements and programming logic work under the hood.
I'm extremely excited for any future update and will be following Zachtronics	closely as they develop more unique games.
Feature requests/notes for developers:
1.) Adding an instruction pointer
2.) Real world exploitation techniques in some levels. i.e buffer overflows, building simple ROP chains, etc. Adding the instruction pointer somewhere would make this much more feasible.

This is a 2d platformer/shooter.  The general theme is one of violence and comedy, with amusing dialog and bizarre weapons (a magic toaster?).  Kudos to the devs for not making it "retro pixel".  Unfortunately, while retro pixel graphics remove the need for developers to hire competent artists, that doesn't mean you can go without both artists and decent graphics... to be successful, you have to have both.   The art looks like it was done by someone fired by Seth McFarlane for illustrating the characters in Family Guy poorly.
The control scheme is bizarre and really doesn't help gameplay much.  It's a bit stiff but I found it playable enough, but the gameplay is not compelling enough to maintain any interest.   Bonus - the devs forgot to translate some of the language so you get a bit of the Russian alphabet thrown in from time to time.
I'd probably give this a 4/10, there's a lot worse platformers out there, but there's also better ones, and it's a crowded market.

I want to like this game, I really do. But it is too unfair and buggy.
For example, there are several things that can happen ingame that can put you in an unwinnable state due to no fault of your own. (level generation for example, some systems interacting in a way that locks doors again (this is not mentioned in the game, levels can be generated with multiple systems that you cannot defeat ever. The distance between the systems is too large).
Several things in the game make no sense in-universe wise, but are clearly intended only to make the game harder.
- Enemies can move through walls and closed doors at times.
- Certain big explosions only hurt you, not the enemies (one of those things you can only know if you read the forums, no ingame warning). Other explosions do hurt enemies. Both look the same on the map, and why stuff isn't hurt is unclear and feels very unfair.
- The game over state is not having negative money, but dying if you have less than 100k left. For some strange reason you get fined for death (this is in addition to the cost of your loadout) which makes no sense in universe wise. Otherwise, going into negative money is no problem. You simply don't need to die. Which is unexpected and stupid.
- You pick your loadout before going in, and you cannot go back to change it while the game is running nor can you reload. While your main supply ship is still there. This makes no sense. And is annoyingly 'game hard'. Pick a wrong loadout? The only way to try again is to die, ow wait. Then you can't try at the same level again, no the game randomly generates a new level. So you have learned nothing. (makes no sense in universe wise, and bad gameplay).
The game has bugs. Many bugs.
Examples I encountered:
- Only get the option of skipping the tutorial after having played the tutorial 3 times.
- Game crashes a lot. Esp when alt tabbing.
- Saving in rogue mode doesn't always work. (Yes, after the dev said it was fixed).
- All kinds of various small gameplay bugs, javelin bolts dissapearing in certain cases, enemies who normally can project a shield around themsleves can suddenly project a shield in a random spot. Levels generated unwinnable. Corridors marked as passable on the map unpassable. Etc.
And the biggest problem imho, why I think you shouldn't buy this game. I had a problem where the game relocked some doors, and that caused a gameover. (this was unexpected, and basically ended my run). Somebody had posted about this problem on the forum. Reaction from the dev: "I'll look into this and see if I can reproduce (and also decide if it's something I wanna fix or not)".
Buy Starward rogue instead. Might look less good, but not as buggy, and at least it respects your time.

Pros:
+ Extremely vertical and varried world. If you fall, you could end up falling for miles
+ Decent exploration. You never know what you will run into.
+ Airship battles
+ Abandoning your airship to sabotage another from the inside.
+ Fire system. It can spread, and take out your entire ship if you're not careful.
+ Sky whales. Enough said?
+ The most terrifying underworld I've ever seen. Honestly, I don't think I can ever go down there.
+ Grapple hooks. Better swinging mechanics than most spider man games.
+ Using animals as parachutes. Not that I would do something so cruel...
+ Allowing you to attempt to fix your airship while in free fall, instead of just saying game over.
+ Allowing you to get stuck in areas if your ship gets shot down and you don't have another
+ Hijacking other ships.
+- Ship Ammo at first is hard to come by, but it did lead to the most epic demolition derbys ever so I'm not sure thats a con
Cons:
- optimisation is a bit meh. It dropped into the single digits on my nvidia770 during a few of the scripted sequences. Specifically the ones where a lot was happening, buildings turning to sand and such.
-  Loot system can be a bit mean when I spend forever shooting a crazy armored guy with my weak gun and he drops a walnut to congradulate me.
- Camera doesn't zoom out as far as I'd like when flying airships. I've hit more buildings than I can count because of this.
Overall: Way better than they get credit for. Not many games let you fail as hard as this one, and even fewer let you manually climb all the way back up every time you do.

Doing just that is by no means an easy task as the average play session (at least for me) lasts only about a minute to a minute and a half (if even that, might feel longer with everything it throws at you). As soon as you die, you are met with a leaderboard showing how long you lasted that time as well as others, which is of course, standard. BUT, it also gives you the option to watch the replays of all the players on said leaderboard, so if you find yourself getting stuck in one particular section you might be able to learn how to better deal with a scenario from studying the higher ranked players, i absolutely love this feature. Overall, if you enjoy games you can play in short bursts, and also love the feeling of quake esque shooters this might just be worth your five dollars. 8,5/10

Devil Daggers is ONE HELL OF A GAME! Me and a friend both bought it at respectively the same time and must I say it's been an adventure! We both started out, running around on the playing field just trying to see who can stay alive the longest and beat each others scores. But as time went on, we slowly started to see that there's multiple tactics to really survive.
Devil Daggers is a challenging game with a interesting learning curve, yet features awesome/satisfying gameplay elements like perfect jumping, shotgun shooting, and Rocket Jumping! You'll feel so much momentum and power in this game!
As you start to get farther and farther, more challenging enemies like spiders, bigger skulls, more spawners and even centepedes come out of the abyss to kill you. But there is a learning curve to this game because the same enemies will appear at an allocated time.
So as you make it to (120 seconds) a centepede appears, and at first you'll think to yourself (HOW DO I EVEN KILL THIS THING!) But the more you make it to that time the more you'll be able to practice that segment. It's like a system that pulls you in because you have to work hard to even be able to practice and I assure you the reward of progression is so satisfying!
Another very cool feature is that you get red gems that increase your firepower, making both your machine gun and shotgun shoot more daggers at a time. And once you get the 3rd upgrade, (70 Gems) you can fire homing daggers that OBLITHERATE everything on the stage. (Almost everything)
The game lets you keep track of your friends scores, with results being uploaded in real time, and you can even watch replays of your friends instantly.
Me and my friend are probably trying to beat each others scores as you're reading this review.
Just get this game please, it's an awesome time waster that is so addicting. Best 5$ you will ever spend.

So, Atlas is a pretty good game, and one I would reccomend to any PvP-focused strategy-lovers out there. Here are some things to consider:
1) As of time of writing, the developers are very responsive and interact with the community a fair amount.
2) Again, as of time of writing the community is fairly small, which can be a plus or a minus. You'll get to know some names if you play enough.
3) Pretty good balance. No game is perfect, but the balance in this game is as good as PvP titans like DotA, despite its young age.
4) Engaging turn-to-turn decisions and prediction-based core gameplay. If you like the idea of getting into your opponents' heads to try to think one step ahead, you'll like this game.
5) Relatively few ways to play. There's a Co-op vs bots mode, and PvP (ranked or unranked.) That's it. The core gameplay is good, but if you're the kind of gamer that constantly needs new experiences to enjoy a game, this isn't for you. It's very much like other PvP-focused games in that way: you're essentially doing permutations of the same thing, so if you see it getting old for you quickly, it's not for you. If you enjoy MOBAs or TCGs or even online shooters to an extent though, you're already used to this and you'll be fine.
All in all, I reccomend this game to anyone interested in the idea of a turn-based arena.

I like to think this game is like a really cool version of chess. When watching gameplays, you may think that this game looks too "slow" and "boring", but you really have to play the game in order to appreciate it. I, for one, am pretty damn addicted to this game, and if you decide to take the time to play and understand the game, you'll find that this game is not so slow, and hopefully not boring, haha. At the start, the game may look pretty confusing at first, but try to get past that. This game puts your brain to work and you really have to strategize with your teamates.The game can get crazy intense, and winning is super satisfying. Games are about 18 minutes long on average.
Playing this game for free allows people to play 6 freelancers (characters) that will rotate every week, I believe. So TECHNICALLY you'll be able to play every freelancer.. eventually. However, you must purchase the game if you want to unlock every freelancer, and ranked matches won't be available unless you purchase the game. Custom games can also be made upon purchase.
That being said, the game offers enough if you want to play for free, but I find myself deciding to spend the 30 dollars to unlock all the freelancers, ranked matches, and custom games. (Or hopefully this game goes on sale... maybe during a winter sale? PLEASE!)
NOW FOR THE CONS:
Several things I can think of that makes the game a bit discouraging to play:
Since this game is quite new, I understand that the game is not fully optimized yet. So the game feels a bit laggy and buggy. However to me, it's not too bad, and I'm able to enjoy it pretty comfortably. The game is actually quite smooth for the most part.
Also, the servers would have sudden crashes from time to time. In 2 days, I have gotten about 3 server crashes, and would be forced to exit out of the game, but I'm able to log right back on quickly after exiting out.
Hopefully they fully optimize this game for a much smoother experience, but I definitely recommend giving this game a try.

If you think it'd be cool to solve programming puzzles in some simplified assembly language, then you are going to love this game. The puzzles are not too hard, but optimizing can be really challenging and multple solutions can give correct answers with different tradeoffs. The language is easy to learn but tough to master.
If you have no idea what this is about, imagine trying to combine simple building blocks (in the form of written computer instructions) to make a computing node then combine multiple nodes to do some calculation. You can build some surprisingly complex functions this way. If you are not at all familiar with programming you will need to read a tutoriall and some help. All that is required is the desire to solve this kind of puzzle and some curiosity.
10/10, worth your money and your time!

I love Sonic Mania, I really do. I think it's an all around great game and the developer's passion can be felt from start to finish. That said, this is not the ideal version of the game. If you own a Switch then consider picking it up for that.
Like many other people I have some frustrations over the inclusion of DRM, especially for the fact that it's Denuvo of all things. If you don't know what makes Denuvo so bad then I encourage you to pull up Alta Vista and do yourself a search, because there's so much to get into that it's not worth wasting a bunch of time here. The fact that the game was delayed for two weeks because SEGA wanted Denuvo to be included is terrible. It's inconvenient, anti-consumer, and actively makes the game run more poorly than its console counterparts.
Mania also suffers from controller recognition issues, currently. This may change, and honestly I don't know how much of this problem is the game itself or the DRM causing issues. Throughout much of the lead up to Mania's release, fans were assured that USB saturn controllers would be supported. However, Mania lacks native d-input support, meaning you get to mess around in Big Picture mode to get anything that's not an Xbox controller to be recognized. This is a pretty good game with lots of perks. I've been playing this game for 50 hours without buying the 29.99 premium pack. So if you're concerned about this game being pay to win, you have nothing to worry about. In less than 3 games that take 10 minutes you will already have enough for a new part. The credits are easy to earn and parts are fairly cheap.
I did end up buying the basic pack however. Not becuase I had to but because it made the game much more enjoyable. While you get a slight advantage over people who are free to play in the access to 3 quick slots to save 3 diffrent builds. I say advantage because it saves a significant amount of time from switching items out.
The next reason I bought the basic was you have unlimited item storage. This isn't a necessity by any means. Your storage increases with your rank and really it takes a while before you max out your parts. All the parts themselves are easy to collect completely free.
The gameplay itself is very solid actually. The parts are pretty well balanced for the most part. For example, if you want to use a missle launcher over a heavy cannon you'd trade 5 damage for slightly faster firing speed and a diffrent type of projectile. Or if you want to use 6 wheels instead of the tracks you get less weight and slightly better max speed. There are a lot of turrets and hulls though that in my opinion are a waste of space so bear that in mind.
As other posters have said the autoblance is a little funky where red team always gets the first person. This creates some very unbalanced games naturally. Since you can leave the current game without penalty there are *some* players who leave the game. Putting you at a further disadvantage. However this has never been a huge problem for me at least as the cases the games get terribly unbalanced is few and far between.
The maps spawns are a little obnoxious at times. There seems to be a trend where when someone spawns alone the enemy team waits to spawn on top of them, all at once. This makes some skirmishes very unfair becuase it feela like the second you spawn you'll have to fight for your life. However it's only in deathmatch and team deathmatch game modes. In the other game modes it's a lot less of a problem in my opinion.
The controls are difficult to get at first. Once you start having a few hours under your belt though it starts getting much easier to control yourself without spinning out. How you can move really is versitile in you can climb on walls, hover over water, or just roll around. In some builds jumping, hovering, and to some degree gliding can be fun to catch people off gaurd.
The game is very stylized in a good way. It has both cute and cool attributes that make it visually nice to look at. The game is also fairly good looking full optimized as well so if you play on a toaster like I do than you'll not have to worry about it looking like a pixelated discolored mess. However there seems to be some kind of bug internally that does create massive frame drops. I'm sure in time it will be fixed.
The map designs themselves range from really enjoyable to wanting to stab yourself with a dirty spork. I'm talking of course about 2 maps in particular which happen to be water levels. This forces ryou to either drive around obstacles in a small path to fall off and drown if you're not careful OR use the hover parts to get across water safely. The other major water map is just a giant putting people on top of the hill at a huge advantage. Now forcing you to either use legs to climp annoying walls or hover to sit on the bottom. While some of the maps are boring at first they really grow on you overtime. For example there is a map that is built more like a king of the hill game mode while everything else is just hills and empty space. At first it seems boring but once you get the hang of movement you'll appreciate the simplicity. The maps are very diverse from each other but there are so few you start getting a little bored of them.
Overall I like this game. It's fun, charming, and a little nutty. I feel like it needs more dynamic part choices though to extend potential play styles. I also would like playing support to be more rewarding to do. Seriously you only get an achievement for playing medic, but get bonus points for getting more kills. Some of the hulls and turrets also need slight rebalancing to be more viable as they're great in concept but poorly executed. Once you kind of see the major meta builds, you start realizing how few options there really are for actual parts/non weapons/non support. Also for how high some of the maps can be having a max aiming hieght can get really annoying sometimes.
I suggest this game becuase dispite its faults and shortcomings it really is a solid choice to play for a while. It's easy to get caught up in playing the game before realizing just how many matches you've played. Playing around with new builds to find what works is very enjoyable as well. Solid gameplay, visually good to look at, and overall an 7.8/10 from me. It would be higher if the game had more maps, parts, and gamemodes. would like to see some king of the hill or payload style games.

Having just beaten all three modes as of today, I must say 'til I'm blue in the face -- this game is not impossible, this game is not impossible, this game is not impossible.
Difficult, hectic, fun -- not impossible.
You're an underfunded but over-weaponed privateer using 'pioneer' suits to board dangerous alien derelicts that you will rip apart piece by piece until you can strip away the Cortex Core, which ... looks like a brain, and functions as you might expect (except that it also shoots brainwaves at you). You'll need to overcome shield and alarm systems, disable drone factories and sentry controllers, bypass locked doors and dismantle repair systems that threaten to undo your hard work.
There are actually two gamemodes in this - campaign and rogue. (There is also a local 'coop campaign' which I can't comment on because I've only played solo, as well as a final Cryptark Excavation mode I won't go into because spoilers. It's neat, though.)
Campaign allows you to carefully plan your moves, overviewing different missions and deciding which one looks most doable. Though you're stuck with the same pioneer suit you choose at the beginning, you get to swap out your weapons before each mission if you so desire - you're on a tight budget, though, so be careful. Overdoing it and/or having to evac on a mission will lose you precious funds, and if you go into the red you'll have to scrap the entire campaign.
But this mode allows for some rediculously fun and interesting suit combinations, from balanced rigs to literally just strapping four machine guns on your arms and going nuts (probably my favorite).
Rogue mode has no budget, and you can't pre-select which mission you want. You go in under the radar and have to get by on salvaging weapon systems that are already on the derelicts, often throwing away weapons you'd rather keep simply because there isn't any ammo left in the magazine.
As for the pioneer suits, there's a wide variety of them with inbuilt special abilities that allow for widely different playstyles - dakka-dakka Gunhead, Rook or Jenner; fast running and gunning with the Weevil which can do short range teleports, even through walls; you can aggro enemies into your destructive flame aftertrail with the Salamander; or play covert with the Ghost using cloaks. And more.
The graphics are good, the music is good, and gameplay is fun. Story is a little sparse - it services the game, rather than the game servicing the story.
Very pleased with this title, kind of came in under the radar for me. I picked it up in a sale, but with the enjoyment I've had with it I could easily recommend it at full price. Get it.

TL;DR: A mix of Metroidvania and Roguelite with a planning/tactical layer and lots of different kinds of content. Fun to play!
CRYPTARK caught my attention during its Early Access days - it looked (at least to me) like it's trying to mix together two seemingly incompatible genres: Roguelite and Metroidvania. That's why I bought it. I'm not entirely sure if that's what the developers were going for - the end result is a pretty unique little gem.
A typical mission in CRYPTARK looks like this: first, you look at the map (which pauses the game - that's very important!), identify the most troublesome systems in the ship, plan your route - and make your approach. You fight your way through the husk of the ancient ships, fighting still-functional drones and turrets. After neutralising your first target, you look at the map again - where to go next? How can I finish the mission as fast as possible while grabbing as much ancient tech as I can? Should I try to go for the challenging objectives for extra cash or artifacts, which unlock new character classes?
The game has a nice layer of planning and strategy to it, as well as fast, lethal shoot-em-up action. The tech you grab while on the job allow you to purchase new weapons - and the selection is huge! There's a number of weapon classes - Machine gun, shotgun, energy weapon, cannon, rocket, melee... you can use up to four during a mission. Finding the combination you like and that works well with your playstyle is essential, because the game is pretty hard.
Or is it? When I first ran the game, I died on my third mission. Difficulty seemed to ramp up impossibly fast. However, the game was fun and enticing enough for me to keep going; and indeed, after a few hours it "clicked" and I managed to beat the game...
...or so I thought! Turns out that there are two extra modes, which are essentially continuation of the story. While the basic shoot-em-up gameplay remains the same, the resource management and general approach to salvaging the ships changes drastically. But it's still very fun!
I managed to beat the final mode after 8 hours of gameplay. I will probably play it more, there's still a lot of weapons and artifacts for me to unlock. Some seem very hard to get, so we'll see if I ever succeed. But damn, the game was a blast and I'm sure glad I played it.

The tutorial doesn't do a great job of familiarizing the player with all of the game's features, which I think takes away from the long term success of this title as a multiplayer game. The multiplayer part of the game can be played somewhat at your leisure by opting to receive e-mail notifications when the enemy has taken their turn, but it's far from an exciting game that will keep you engaged.  I found it to be more fun in short bursts.

Probably one of the best works of Paradox. Contrary to the other titles in the Grand Strategy genre, Crusader Kings II puts emphasis on personal relations, instead of the usual inhuman/transcendental/immortal figure of nations.
This can lead to fun (YMMV) situations such as preparing for an heir to claim a kingdom, by accumulating gold for mercenaries, building up keeps and hiring the best generals... only to have him die of a disease at the last minute. I pesonally like this style for being the best representation of how human politics worked in medieval times; history being full of examples of situations such as the one I described.
Although this difference from other games is very well responsible for a slightly (again, YMMV) steep learning curve, where the meaning of archaic terms such as "demesne" need to become part of your vocabulary, and in the beggining you may have a "how the heck am I supposed to use marriages?" attitude. An honorable mention must go the subrealms mechanic, in which your vassals are sort of their own countries - sometimes growing so powerful they can conquer foreign realms by themselves.
Although the game's mechanics aren't really difficult to learn, this does mean that the game isn't for everyone, in the sense that not everyone has the patience and time to learn the nuances of the game. In my opinion, though it is all worth it, and the game is very fun to play once you know what the heck is going on.
Bonus is the fact that the game has a huge replayability factor, with many different cultures and religions with differing mechanics (most only accessible with DLC, though) and that is without mentioning mods. Owning the game gives you access to the Paradox Forums, where most mods can be downloaded from. I can personally attest to the the Game of Thrones Mod and the After the End mod (which takes place in post-apocalyptic, feudal North America).
In conclusion, the game is good, and definetly worth the money spent. However even for Grand Starategy games it can be weird, so be aware you'll need to get used to unusual mechanics.
*YMMV = Your Mileage May Vary

My first Elder Scrolls game was Skyrim, and I loved it, and efter playing it for a while, I really wanted to explore some more of the lore and stories from the other games in the Elder Scrolls universe.  So I spent a really long time digging around my house for an old CD copy my family had and started playing it in 2013.
Despite not having played Oblivion until after Skyrim seven years after its original release, I really enjoyed it.  Although it is old, the graphics are still fairly decent, and it has this rather pleasant classic feel to it which I truly enjoy.
Although I would say that Skyrim is still a better game overall, primarily because of its simpler leving system, which is less punishing of early mistakes, and isn't difficult to manage.  However, I would say that each game in the series has its own value.  Each one having its own strengths and weaknesses, being better at some things than others.  Oblivion for instance has simpler, more generic dungeons, however, the cities in Oblivion are top-notch.  Despite only having about twelve voice actors, the towns are filled with characters who all have interesting personalities and stories.  And each town has a very special visual style, with load of quests in a more social setting.
Alltogether, Oblivion is a very solid game, highly modable, and I still am having fun with it even ten years after release. I'd highly recommened it to anyone who enjoys a good old fasioned RPG.

100% Orange Juice is a 4-player board game with dice and cards. Most of the time you'll play with your friends, but you can also explore the single player campaign mode with the silly story.
The characters come from various games made by Orange Juice, such as QP and Suguri. These characters have different abilities and stats to adjust the rolls and have a different playstyle to victory (only to be screwed over by luck).

AC: Rogue was an enjoyable title, the gameplay and feel was very much like ACIV, another fantastic title. Rogue felt like an extension of ACIV, and it maintained my interest in the mechanics of the previous game.
Story:
Our story begins with Shay, an assassin who is a pupil of Aquilles, the assassin who teaches us in ACIII. An action by the assassins severs Shay's trust in them and begins his descent toward the Templar side. On our way we begin to understand more about the Templars and really see the other side of the coin. The present day storyline is still present, and we still play as the same Abstergo employee from ACIV. This time we're given even more backstory and introduced to a few new characters that bring us closer to understanding the Templars.
Gameplay:
The gameplay is just like ACIV, with a few new gimmicks and weapons for our character and ship. The part I enjoyed most was the range that the Air Rifle introduced. Taking down an entire compound with it was very easy and fun to do, though it did make fights too easy and took away the challenge of having to hide in haystacks and around corners like in ACII. Also from ACIV we don't have 4 pistols anymore, only 2. We maintain our 2 swords and many other weapons like the rope darts, berserk/sleep darts. and of course our hidden blades. A few new additions are added into the game, such as an enemy type that strikes quickly and quietly like an assassin would, but the game makes it easy to find and kill these enemies if you pay attention. Also there are gang compounds which you can clear out and take over in order to access your fleet and bank. The ship combat is pretty similar to ACIV with some new ship additions and we still have "Legendary Battles."
Bugs/glitches/What I hated
AMD GPU users are at a loss with this game, something caused the game to crash as soon as the story was launched if the environment setting was set beyond normal even if your GPU is more than capable of running the game. This title still suffers from the age old AC problem in which your character will sometimes not respond to commands and plummet to his death instead of jumping to a nearby ledge. One of my favorite glitches was with an assassin we had to kill falling into the ocean and his marker sinking and sinking until I had to restart the mission. Some of the things I hated include the large amounts of animus fragments and the fact that gang HQs really gave no advantage and were just another way for you to see your fleet and visit the bank. There really weren't many new outfits, cool guns, or swords either.
Final verdict:
Get this game if you enjoyed ACIV and would like more of that great ship combat, this is a very solid title and defenitely should be picked up on sale. It adds just enough to feel like it's own story but is pretty plain when compared to ACII or ACIV. I enjoyed playing this game and had fun with it, maybe you will too.

-15 Unique characters with thier own upgrades that you can customize to fit your unique playstyle,

-The "drop-in, drop out" system of the game which many have faults with because Awesomenauts was originally a "casual" MOBA styled game.

Notes:
There is also an expansion which is in development but will be bringing things like:
-Spectator Mode
-Replays (Released)
-5 characters (4 released)
-New map
-Custom games to play different modes such as Team Deathmatch
-Many other features
I would also like to add one more note that even if you don't have the expansion, you can join a friend's custom game to play on the new map as well as play custom game modes through joining your friend.

I rate Gear Up, a free-to-play, online, multiplayer tank game 4/5. Good.
This is a fun, tactically deep and yet simple to use and easy to learn custom tank building (using numerous pre-made tank parts) multiplayer action game. I have yet to notice any kind of hacking or cheating. In a way, this game is sort of like an extremely simplified, cute version of Mechwarrior Online except with small tanks and relatively small levels. This is a good little game to play for an hour at a time before moving on to something else. The biggest drawback to this game is a shortage of maps/environments to play in resulting in a feeling of repetition.
Graphics:
+Bright (except for night time versions of maps), generally happy graphics which are very good nonetheless. Oddly, the tanks all look sort of like baby toys made of plastic but this only increases the game's charm. Textures are smooth and cartoon-like without being comic-book styled. The overall effect reminds me an animated Pixar movie like Up or Cars except with less detail in the scenery. Explosions are nifty but not extremely violent. This game looks like it was intended for children and it succeeds excellently at this.
-The graphics can seem overly bright to the extent that some surfaces can seem difficult to look at if you are playing in a darkened room.
Sound:
-Sounds, while adequate are repetitive and boring though highly functional. Every sound has a useful meaning.
-The music, what little there is, quickly becomes repetitive and boring. Mostly I played this game with both the sound and music turned down pretty far.
Gameplay:
+This game's physics, while seeming realistic enough, makes piloting the tanks challenging and interesting while not being frustrating. Tanks do seem to fall from great heights (if you drive off an elevated area or cliff) in an oddly slow-motion manner but this merely adds to the sense of fun
+Though obviously made for kids, this game features some fairly deep tactical elements. Building and customizing your tank is easy and yet it seems impossible to create a completely perfect tank for all situations. All components have some sort of drawback and there are many potential tank designs and weapon selections which can be effective in different tactical situations. You can literally spend hours trying to design your tank, deciding upon the best tank to fit your play style. Indeed, figuring this out might be the main point of the game as you play match after match to test out your tank's latest modifications.
+The actual tank battles themselves are exciting. Maneuvering, finding cover, locating and guarding useful stationary powerups and aiming are all extremely important. Using tactics which match your tank's current design is critical to success though using the environment of each map to your advantage is also vital.
+Each match only lasts about 10 minutes or so thus staying in a match, even if your side is losing, is almost never very frustrating.
+Very few bugs. The game has booted me out to windows once in a while but such problems are extremely rare.
+This game usually has at least a few players running around in it, even late at night. The game's community is generally friendly too, which is unusual for an action game like this.
+This game has fairly short connection and loading times leading to an extremely smooth and streamlined experience. The game does feature some lag at times but a lot is done to compensate for this. Having a fast internet connection is still very important though.
+/- Contrary to what the game's preview shows, there are not immense crowds of people playing in any given map/area but the lack of crowds merely serves to make the game that much more tactically oriented. Pick your battles well and know when it's better to retreat.
+/-There are several multiplayer modes to choose from but there are some minor problems with how new players arrive as the match continues (they are automatically assigned the red team if the red and blue teams have an even number of people which gives the red team a slight advantage at all times). Ultimately, the standard deathmatch everyone-for-themselves mode is perhaps the most fun.
-This game has very few maps or levels to play on. Roughly 10 or fewer. This causes the game to become more repetitive than it should far too early on. As a result, I have ended up playing this game here and there over the course of several months. I am not certain if the developer ever intends to expand the number of maps this game has (the most recent update was back in 2016). If not, it would be a real shame considering how fun this game is. I suppose it's possible that the developer simply didn't make enough money on this game as playing it is entirely free and buying it only gives you access to a larger inventory or items which do not require any in-game currency to access (which only serves to remove much of the game's challenge/incentive to keep winning).
-Individual tank parts cannot be modified. Parts can merely be added or replaced with other kinds of tank parts.
Controls: I used a mouse and keyboard.
+Controls are slick and simple. Keybindings are easy to map and the game works extremely well with a mouse and keyboard (if you use the mouse to aim and shoot and the keyboard to move).
Story:
+/-There is no story for this game whatsoever. There is no main campaign and no training missions. You learn as you go but if you've ever played a tank game the learning curve is quick and easy. Menus are simple.

It's a sort of economic-RTS Terraria. With maybe a touch of Dwarf Fortress. And good, overall. To begin with, you build a base, run around collecting ingredients, and ship them off (in the form of soup) to hungry aliens. Then, you want to expand the level of automation, because collecting every ingredient by hand is rather slow... but automation is a tricky business. So, you work at balancing the need to keep pouring out soup with the desire to automate just the easiest parts of the process first... and then develop from there.
Some parts of the implementation still feel a little rough around the edges, but I really enjoy the concept, and it's even better if you have a like-minded friend to play couch co-op with. Thumbs up, as they say in the movies.

Probably one of the best works of Paradox. Contrary to the other titles in the Grand Strategy genre, Crusader Kings II puts emphasis on personal relations, instead of the usual inhuman/transcendental/immortal figure of nations.
This can lead to fun (YMMV) situations such as preparing for an heir to claim a kingdom, by accumulating gold for mercenaries, building up keeps and hiring the best generals... only to have him die of a disease at the last minute. I pesonally like this style for being the best representation of how human politics worked in medieval times; history being full of examples of situations such as the one I described.
Although this difference from other games is very well responsible for a slightly (again, YMMV) steep learning curve, where the meaning of archaic terms such as "demesne" need to become part of your vocabulary, and in the beggining you may have a "how the heck am I supposed to use marriages?" attitude. An honorable mention must go the subrealms mechanic, in which your vassals are sort of their own countries - sometimes growing so powerful they can conquer foreign realms by themselves.
Although the game's mechanics aren't really difficult to learn, this does mean that the game isn't for everyone, in the sense that not everyone has the patience and time to learn the nuances of the game. In my opinion, though it is all worth it, and the game is very fun to play once you know what the heck is going on.
Bonus is the fact that the game has a huge replayability factor, with many different cultures and religions with differing mechanics (most only accessible with DLC, though) and that is without mentioning mods. Owning the game gives you access to the Paradox Forums, where most mods can be downloaded from. I can personally attest to the the Game of Thrones Mod and the After the End mod (which takes place in post-apocalyptic, feudal North America).
In conclusion, the game is good, and definetly worth the money spent. However even for Grand Starategy games it can be weird, so be aware you'll need to get used to unusual mechanics.
*YMMV = Your Mileage May Vary
